Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 12, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is entirely Meccan. It was also said that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina at the time of the Hijrah (the migration).

Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration from him, and Qatadah said: "Except for four verses."

Al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surah Yusuf was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated (*wa-sahhahahu*) from Rifaʿah ibn Rafiʿ al-Zuraqi that he set out, together with his maternal cousin Muʿadh ibn ʿAfraʾ, until the two of them reached Mecca. He mentioned a story, and at its end [it states] that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught the two of them Surah Yusuf and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], and then they returned.

Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dalaʾil*, narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) of the Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him reciting Surah Yusuf. He said: 'O Muhammad, who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' The rabbi was amazed at what he heard from him, so he returned to the Jews and said to them: 'By Allah, Muhammad recites the Qur'an just as it was revealed in the Torah.' So he set out with a group of them until they entered upon him. They recognised him by the description, and they looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, and they listened to his recitation of Surah Yusuf, and they were amazed by it, and at that point they embraced Islam."

Al-Thaʿlabi narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Teach your relatives Surah Yusuf, for whichever Muslim recites it or teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will make the agonies of death easy for him, and will give him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

In its chain (*isnad*) there is Sallam ibn Salim, also said to be Ibn Sulaym al-Madaʾini, who is *matruk* (abandoned, i.e. his narrations are discarded by the critics) from Harun ibn Kathir.

Abu Hatim said: he is unknown (*majhul*). The hadith scholar Ibn ʿAsakir mentioned for him a corroborating narration (*mutabaʿah*) through al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam, from Harun ibn Kathir, and through Shababah, from Mijlaz ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid al-Basri, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, and from ʿAta ibn Maymun, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, raised to the Prophet (*marfuʿan*, i.e. traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)), and he related something similar. But it is *munkar* (a rejected narration) in all of its chains.

Al-Qurtubi said: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a period. They said: 'If only you would relate to us (*law haddathtana*),' so the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]." He said: The scholars said: Allah mentioned the stories of the prophets in the Qur'an and repeated them with one meaning in different aspects, with varied wording, at degrees of eloquence. He mentioned the story of Yusuf and did not repeat it, so no opponent is able to oppose what is repeated, nor what is not repeated.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ has already been discussed at the beginning of Surah Yunus. The reference in His words "Those are" (*tilka*) is to the verses of the surah. "The Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*): the surah. That is, "those are the verses of the surah which were revealed to you in this surah," the verses of the surah whose matter is manifest in the inimitability (*iʿjaz*) of the Arabs and in rebuking them. The word "mubin" is from *abana*, meaning *bana* (to be clear): that is, the one whose matter is manifest in that it is from Allah and in its inimitability. Or "mubin" means "clear in meaning," such that it is not ambiguous to its reader or listener. Or "mubin" means "one that makes clear what it contains of rulings."

﴿Indeed We have sent it down﴾, that is, the Clear Book, as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. So, if we assume that "the Book" means the surah, then calling it "Qur'an" is by way of considering that "Qur'an" is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that applies to the whole and to a part. And if we assume that what is meant by "the Book" is the whole Qur'an, then calling it "Qur'an" is clear. "Arabic" is an adjective of "Qur'an": that is, in the language of the Arabs. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, that is, in order that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it.

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. *Qasas* means following the trail of a thing, and from it is His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], that is, follow his track. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the implied construction is: "We relate to you a narrative, the best of narratives," so it has the sense of narrating (*iqtisas*). Or it is in the sense of the passive participle: that is, the narrated (*maqsus*). ﴿By what We have revealed to you﴾, that is, by Our revelation to you, ﴿this Qur'an﴾. The accusative of "the Qur'an" is because it is an attribute of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), or a substitute (*badal*) for it, or an explanatory apposition (*ʿatf bayan*). Al-Zajjaj permitted the nominative, by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive, and the probable reason is that the preposition in "by what We have revealed" is assumed to govern the demonstrative, so the meaning becomes: "We relate to you the best of narratives by this Qur'an." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾. *In* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, as evidenced by the distinguishing *lam* between it and the negative particle. The pronoun in "before it" refers to the revelation implied by "We have revealed," and the meaning is: you, before Our revelation to you, were among those unaware of this story.

It has been disputed in what respect what is in this surah is "the best of stories." It was said: because what is in this surah of stories contains lessons, admonitions and wisdoms that are not found in other [surahs]. It was said: because of its fine dialogue, and what Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) underwent of patience with their harm and his pardoning them. It was said: because it mentions prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the conduct of kings and slaves, merchants, scholars and the ignorant, women and their stratagems and their guile. It was said: because it mentions the beloved and the lover and what passed between them. It was said: that "best" here means "most wondrous." It was said: that everyone mentioned in it ends in happiness.

His saying: ﴿When Yusuf said to his father﴾. *Idh* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed by an implied verb: that is, "remember the time when Yusuf said."

The majority read ﴿Yusuf﴾ with a *damma* on the *sin*. Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with a *kasra* along with a *hamza* in place of the *waw*. Ibn Zayd transmitted the *hamza* with a *fatha* on the *sin*. It is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*) due to foreignness (*ʿujmah*) and proper-name status (*ʿalamiyyah*). It was said that it is Arabic, but the first [view] is better, as evidenced by its not being declined. [Said] to his father, namely Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

﴿O my father﴾: *ya abati* with a *kasra* on the *ta'* in the reading of Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir. According to the Basrans it is the marker of the feminine (*ʿalamat al-taʾnith*), and it attached specifically to the word *ab* in the vocative, as a replacement for the *ya'* (of possession). Its original form is *ya abi*. Its *kasra* indicates that it is a substitute for a letter that suits a *kasra*. Ibn ʿAmir read it with a *fatha*, because the original form for him is *ya abata*, and one may not combine the substitute and what it substitutes, so one does not say *ya abati-ya*. Al-Farra' permitted *ya abatu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*.

﴿Indeed I saw﴾: from the sleeping dream (*al-ruʾya al-nawmiyyah*), not from visual sight, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾.

His saying: ﴿Eleven stars﴾: it is read with a sukun on the *ʿayn* for lightening, to avoid a succession of vowels, and it is read with a *fatha* according to the original form. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾: he placed them after the stars only to show their distinction and nobility, as in the coupling of Jibril and Mikail with the angels. It was said that the *waw* here means "together with." The clause ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ is a new (*mustaʾnafah*) clause explaining the state in which he saw them. It is treated as the rational beings in the pronoun specific to them, because it is described with the description of rational beings, namely prostrating. So said al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The Arabs make plurals of non-rational things in the form of the plural of rational beings when they assign them that rank.

﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers"﴾. *Al-ruʾya* [the dream] is a verbal noun of *raʾa* in sleep, *ruʾya*, on the pattern *fuʿla* like *suqya* and *busra*. Its *alif* is for the feminine, and for this reason it is not declined. Yaʿqub (ʿalayhi al-salam) forbade his son Yusuf from relating his dream to his brothers, because he knew its interpretation and feared that he would relate it to his brothers, and they would understand its interpretation, and envy of him would arise among them. For this reason He said: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾. This is the answer to the prohibition, and it is in the accusative by an implied *an*: that is, "lest they do for you," that is, for your sake, a plot established and firm, from which you cannot be free; or a plot hidden from your understanding. This meaning arising from the addition of the *lam* is more emphatic than saying "lest they plot a plot." It was said that the *lam* was brought only to include the meaning of *ihtiyal* (scheming), which takes *li* [with the object]; so this inclusion yields the meaning of both verbs together, plotting and scheming, as is the rule in inclusion that one of them is taken as the principal and the other as the circumstantial. The clause ﴿Indeed Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾ is a new clause, as if Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) had said: "How could such a thing happen from them?", so [Yaʿqub] alerted him that Satan drives them to that, because he is an enemy of humankind, openly showing enmity and proclaiming it.

His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾: that is, like that choosing (*ijtiba'*), wondrous, which you saw in the dream, of the prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon, your Lord will choose you, and will realise in you the interpretation of that vision, so He will make you a prophet and choose you over the rest of the servants, and will subject them to you, just as those heavenly bodies you saw in your dream were subjected to you, becoming prostrate to you. Al-Nahhas said: The root of *ijtiba'* is from *jabaytu al-shay'* (I gathered the thing), meaning I obtained it, and from it *jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd* (I collected water in the pool). The meaning of *ijtiba'* is *istifa'* (selection). This includes praise of Yusuf and enumeration of the blessings of Allah upon him, and among them ﴿and teach you of the interpretation of events﴾, that is, the interpretation of dreams.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that this refers to the interpretation of dreams, and Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) was indeed the most knowledgeable of people about its interpretation. It was said that what is meant is: "and teach you of the interpretation of the stories of nations and books." It was said that what is meant by it is making his brothers need him. It was said that it is his deliverance from every hardship. It was said that it is his deliverance from killing specifically. ﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾: so He will combine for you prophethood and kingship, as this dream that Allah showed you indicates, or He will combine for you the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And upon the family of Yaʿqub﴾: they are his kin, his brothers, his children and those after them. That is because Allah, glorified is He, gave them prophethood, as a number of exegetes said. And it is not far-fetched that it is an indication of what came to them after entering Egypt of blessings, among which is that kingship was among them while they were prophets. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that is, a completion like its completion upon your two fathers, namely the blessing of prophethood upon them both, together with Ibrahim having been taken by Allah as a friend (*khalil*), and together with Ishaq having been delivered by Allah, glorified is He, from the sacrifice, and they had righteous offspring: they are Yaʿqub, Yusuf, and the rest of the tribes (*asbat*). The meaning of ﴿from your father﴾ is: before this time in which you are, or before you. Ibrahim and Ishaq are an explanatory apposition to "your two fathers." He referred to them both as "the two fathers," although one of them was a grandfather, namely Ibrahim, because a grandfather is also a father. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Knowing﴾ of everything, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. The clause is a new clause confirming what precedes it, giving its reason: that is, He did that because He is Knowing and Wise. This was a statement by Yaʿqub to his son Yusuf interpreting his dream in a general way, or he knew that by way of revelation, or he recognised it through physiognomy (*firasah*) and what the signs in Yusuf indicated.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿Those are the verses of the Clear Book﴾, that he said: Allah made clear its lawful and unlawful.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muʿadh, who said: Allah made clear the letters which fell from the tongues of non-Arabs, and they are six letters.

Al-Hakim narrated from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited an Arabic Qur'an, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ishmael was inspired with this Arabic tongue by inspiration."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of Quraysh, and it is their speech.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us." So the words were revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, concerning His words ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "From the earlier Scriptures and the past affairs of God among the nations." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ means: before this Qur'an.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, that he said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli, Ibn Hibban in al-Du'afa', Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "A Jewish man from Bustan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about the stars which Yusuf saw prostrating to him. What are their names?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent and did not answer him at all. Then Jibril descended to him and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent for the Jewish man from Bustan and said: 'Will you believe if I tell you their names?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Kharthan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Katafan, Qabis, Wathab, 'Amudan, al-Fayliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, Dhu al-Farigh, al-Diya' and al-Nur. He saw them in the horizon of the sky prostrating to him.' When Yusuf related it to Ya'qub, he said: 'This is a scattered matter which God will gather later.' Then the Jew said: 'Yes, by God, these are indeed their names.'" Thus al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur. As for Ibn Kathir, he made the words "When Yusuf related..." etc. a separate narration and said: "It was related solely by al-Hakam ibn Zahirah al-Fazari. They weakened him, and most of them abandoned him."

al-Jawzajani said: "Discarded (saqit)."

Ibn al-Jawzi said: "It is fabricated (mawdu')."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿eleven stars﴾, that he said: "His brothers. And the sun," he said: "his mother. And the moon," he said: "his father." 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Jarir also narrated the like of it from Ibn Zayd.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾, that he said: "He will select you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid (p-684) concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of dreams."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of knowledge and of dreams. And Yusuf was among the most skilled of people in interpreting."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning ﴿as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that he said: "His blessing upon Ibrahim was that He saved him from the fire, and upon Ishaq that He saved him from the sacrifice."

It is treated as the rational beings in the pronoun specific to them, because it is described with the description of rational beings, namely prostrating. So said al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The Arabs make plurals of non-rational things in the form of the plural of rational beings when they assign them that rank.

﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers"﴾. *Al-ruʾya* [the dream] is a verbal noun of *raʾa* in sleep, *ruʾya*, on the pattern *fuʿla* like *suqya* and *busra*. Its *alif* is for the feminine, and for this reason it is not declined. Yaʿqub (ʿalayhi al-salam) forbade his son Yusuf from relating his dream to his brothers, because he knew its interpretation and feared that he would relate it to his brothers, and they would understand its interpretation, and envy of him would arise among them. For this reason He said: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾. This is the answer to the prohibition, and it is in the accusative by an implied *an*: that is, "lest they do for you," that is, for your sake, a plot established and firm, from which you cannot be free; or a plot hidden from your understanding. This meaning arising from the addition of the *lam* is more emphatic than saying "lest they plot a plot." It was said that the *lam* was brought only to include the meaning of *ihtiyal* (scheming), which takes *li* [with the object]; so this inclusion yields the meaning of both verbs together, plotting and scheming, as is the rule in inclusion that one of them is taken as the principal and the other as the circumstantial. The clause ﴿Indeed Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾ is a new clause, as if Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) had said: "How could such a thing happen from them?", so [Yaʿqub] alerted him that Satan drives them to that, because he is an enemy of humankind, openly showing enmity and proclaiming it.

His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾: that is, like that choosing (*ijtiba'*), wondrous, which you saw in the dream, of the prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon, your Lord will choose you, and will realise in you the interpretation of that vision, so He will make you a prophet and choose you over the rest of the servants, and will subject them to you, just as those heavenly bodies you saw in your dream were subjected to you, becoming prostrate to you. Al-Nahhas said: The root of *ijtiba'* is from *jabaytu al-shay'* (I gathered the thing), meaning I obtained it, and from it *jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd* (I collected water in the pool). The meaning of *ijtiba'* is *istifa'* (selection). This includes praise of Yusuf and enumeration of the blessings of Allah upon him, and among them ﴿and teach you of the interpretation of events﴾, that is, the interpretation of dreams.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that this refers to the interpretation of dreams, and Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) was indeed the most knowledgeable of people about its interpretation. It was said that what is meant is: "and teach you of the interpretation of the stories of nations and books." It was said that what is meant by it is making his brothers need him. It was said that it is his deliverance from every hardship. It was said that it is his deliverance from killing specifically. ﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾: so He will combine for you prophethood and kingship, as this dream that Allah showed you indicates, or He will combine for you the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And upon the family of Yaʿqub﴾: they are his kin, his brothers, his children and those after them. That is because Allah, glorified is He, gave them prophethood, as a number of exegetes said. And it is not far-fetched that it is an indication of what came to them after entering Egypt of blessings, among which is that kingship was among them while they were prophets. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that is, a completion like its completion upon your two fathers, namely the blessing of prophethood upon them both, together with Ibrahim having been taken by Allah as a friend (*khalil*), and together with Ishaq having been delivered by Allah, glorified is He, from the sacrifice, and they had righteous offspring: they are Yaʿqub, Yusuf, and the rest of the tribes (*asbat*). The meaning of ﴿from your father﴾ is: before this time in which you are, or before you. Ibrahim and Ishaq are an explanatory apposition to "your two fathers." He referred to them both as "the two fathers," although one of them was a grandfather, namely Ibrahim, because a grandfather is also a father. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Knowing﴾ of everything, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. The clause is a new clause confirming what precedes it, giving its reason: that is, He did that because He is Knowing and Wise. This was a statement by Yaʿqub to his son Yusuf interpreting his dream in a general way, or he knew that by way of revelation, or he recognised it through physiognomy (*firasah*) and what the signs in Yusuf indicated.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 12, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is entirely Meccan. It was also said that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina at the time of the Hijrah (the migration).

Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration from him, and Qatadah said: "Except for four verses."

Al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surah Yusuf was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated (*wa-sahhahahu*) from Rifaʿah ibn Rafiʿ al-Zuraqi that he set out, together with his maternal cousin Muʿadh ibn ʿAfraʾ, until the two of them reached Mecca. He mentioned a story, and at its end [it states] that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught the two of them Surah Yusuf and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], and then they returned.

Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dalaʾil*, narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) of the Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him reciting Surah Yusuf. He said: 'O Muhammad, who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' The rabbi was amazed at what he heard from him, so he returned to the Jews and said to them: 'By Allah, Muhammad recites the Qur'an just as it was revealed in the Torah.' So he set out with a group of them until they entered upon him. They recognised him by the description, and they looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, and they listened to his recitation of Surah Yusuf, and they were amazed by it, and at that point they embraced Islam."

Al-Thaʿlabi narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Teach your relatives Surah Yusuf, for whichever Muslim recites it or teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will make the agonies of death easy for him, and will give him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

In its chain (*isnad*) there is Sallam ibn Salim, also said to be Ibn Sulaym al-Madaʾini, who is *matruk* (abandoned, i.e. his narrations are discarded by the critics) from Harun ibn Kathir.

Abu Hatim said: he is unknown (*majhul*). The hadith scholar Ibn ʿAsakir mentioned for him a corroborating narration (*mutabaʿah*) through al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam, from Harun ibn Kathir, and through Shababah, from Mijlaz ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid al-Basri, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, and from ʿAta ibn Maymun, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, raised to the Prophet (*marfuʿan*, i.e. traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)), and he related something similar. But it is *munkar* (a rejected narration) in all of its chains.

Al-Qurtubi said: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a period. They said: 'If only you would relate to us (*law haddathtana*),' so the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]." He said: The scholars said: Allah mentioned the stories of the prophets in the Qur'an and repeated them with one meaning in different aspects, with varied wording, at degrees of eloquence. He mentioned the story of Yusuf and did not repeat it, so no opponent is able to oppose what is repeated, nor what is not repeated.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ has already been discussed at the beginning of Surah Yunus. The reference in His words "Those are" (*tilka*) is to the verses of the surah. "The Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*): the surah. That is, "those are the verses of the surah which were revealed to you in this surah," the verses of the surah whose matter is manifest in the inimitability (*iʿjaz*) of the Arabs and in rebuking them. The word "mubin" is from *abana*, meaning *bana* (to be clear): that is, the one whose matter is manifest in that it is from Allah and in its inimitability. Or "mubin" means "clear in meaning," such that it is not ambiguous to its reader or listener. Or "mubin" means "one that makes clear what it contains of rulings."

﴿Indeed We have sent it down﴾, that is, the Clear Book, as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. So, if we assume that "the Book" means the surah, then calling it "Qur'an" is by way of considering that "Qur'an" is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that applies to the whole and to a part. And if we assume that what is meant by "the Book" is the whole Qur'an, then calling it "Qur'an" is clear. "Arabic" is an adjective of "Qur'an": that is, in the language of the Arabs. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, that is, in order that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it.

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. *Qasas* means following the trail of a thing, and from it is His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], that is, follow his track. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the implied construction is: "We relate to you a narrative, the best of narratives," so it has the sense of narrating (*iqtisas*). Or it is in the sense of the passive participle: that is, the narrated (*maqsus*). ﴿By what We have revealed to you﴾, that is, by Our revelation to you, ﴿this Qur'an﴾. The accusative of "the Qur'an" is because it is an attribute of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), or a substitute (*badal*) for it, or an explanatory apposition (*ʿatf bayan*). Al-Zajjaj permitted the nominative, by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive, and the probable reason is that the preposition in "by what We have revealed" is assumed to govern the demonstrative, so the meaning becomes: "We relate to you the best of narratives by this Qur'an." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾. *In* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, as evidenced by the distinguishing *lam* between it and the negative particle. The pronoun in "before it" refers to the revelation implied by "We have revealed," and the meaning is: you, before Our revelation to you, were among those unaware of this story.

It has been disputed in what respect what is in this surah is "the best of stories." It was said: because what is in this surah of stories contains lessons, admonitions and wisdoms that are not found in other [surahs]. It was said: because of its fine dialogue, and what Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) underwent of patience with their harm and his pardoning them. It was said: because it mentions prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the conduct of kings and slaves, merchants, scholars and the ignorant, women and their stratagems and their guile. It was said: because it mentions the beloved and the lover and what passed between them. It was said: that "best" here means "most wondrous." It was said: that everyone mentioned in it ends in happiness.

His saying: ﴿When Yusuf said to his father﴾. *Idh* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed by an implied verb: that is, "remember the time when Yusuf said."

The majority read ﴿Yusuf﴾ with a *damma* on the *sin*. Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with a *kasra* along with a *hamza* in place of the *waw*. Ibn Zayd transmitted the *hamza* with a *fatha* on the *sin*. It is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*) due to foreignness (*ʿujmah*) and proper-name status (*ʿalamiyyah*). It was said that it is Arabic, but the first [view] is better, as evidenced by its not being declined. [Said] to his father, namely Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

﴿O my father﴾: *ya abati* with a *kasra* on the *ta'* in the reading of Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir. According to the Basrans it is the marker of the feminine (*ʿalamat al-taʾnith*), and it attached specifically to the word *ab* in the vocative, as a replacement for the *ya'* (of possession). Its original form is *ya abi*. Its *kasra* indicates that it is a substitute for a letter that suits a *kasra*. Ibn ʿAmir read it with a *fatha*, because the original form for him is *ya abata*, and one may not combine the substitute and what it substitutes, so one does not say *ya abati-ya*. Al-Farra' permitted *ya abatu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 12, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is entirely Meccan. It was also said that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina at the time of the Hijrah (the migration).

Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration from him, and Qatadah said: "Except for four verses."

Al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surah Yusuf was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated (*wa-sahhahahu*) from Rifaʿah ibn Rafiʿ al-Zuraqi that he set out, together with his maternal cousin Muʿadh ibn ʿAfraʾ, until the two of them reached Mecca. He mentioned a story, and at its end [it states] that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught the two of them Surah Yusuf and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], and then they returned.

Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dalaʾil*, narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) of the Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him reciting Surah Yusuf. He said: 'O Muhammad, who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' The rabbi was amazed at what he heard from him, so he returned to the Jews and said to them: 'By Allah, Muhammad recites the Qur'an just as it was revealed in the Torah.' So he set out with a group of them until they entered upon him. They recognised him by the description, and they looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, and they listened to his recitation of Surah Yusuf, and they were amazed by it, and at that point they embraced Islam."

Al-Thaʿlabi narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Teach your relatives Surah Yusuf, for whichever Muslim recites it or teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will make the agonies of death easy for him, and will give him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

In its chain (*isnad*) there is Sallam ibn Salim, also said to be Ibn Sulaym al-Madaʾini, who is *matruk* (abandoned, i.e. his narrations are discarded by the critics) from Harun ibn Kathir.

Abu Hatim said: he is unknown (*majhul*). The hadith scholar Ibn ʿAsakir mentioned for him a corroborating narration (*mutabaʿah*) through al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam, from Harun ibn Kathir, and through Shababah, from Mijlaz ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid al-Basri, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, and from ʿAta ibn Maymun, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, raised to the Prophet (*marfuʿan*, i.e. traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)), and he related something similar. But it is *munkar* (a rejected narration) in all of its chains.

Al-Qurtubi said: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a period. They said: 'If only you would relate to us (*law haddathtana*),' so the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]." He said: The scholars said: Allah mentioned the stories of the prophets in the Qur'an and repeated them with one meaning in different aspects, with varied wording, at degrees of eloquence. He mentioned the story of Yusuf and did not repeat it, so no opponent is able to oppose what is repeated, nor what is not repeated.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ has already been discussed at the beginning of Surah Yunus. The reference in His words "Those are" (*tilka*) is to the verses of the surah. "The Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*): the surah. That is, "those are the verses of the surah which were revealed to you in this surah," the verses of the surah whose matter is manifest in the inimitability (*iʿjaz*) of the Arabs and in rebuking them. The word "mubin" is from *abana*, meaning *bana* (to be clear): that is, the one whose matter is manifest in that it is from Allah and in its inimitability. Or "mubin" means "clear in meaning," such that it is not ambiguous to its reader or listener. Or "mubin" means "one that makes clear what it contains of rulings."

﴿Indeed We have sent it down﴾, that is, the Clear Book, as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. So, if we assume that "the Book" means the surah, then calling it "Qur'an" is by way of considering that "Qur'an" is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that applies to the whole and to a part. And if we assume that what is meant by "the Book" is the whole Qur'an, then calling it "Qur'an" is clear. "Arabic" is an adjective of "Qur'an": that is, in the language of the Arabs. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, that is, in order that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it.

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. *Qasas* means following the trail of a thing, and from it is His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], that is, follow his track. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the implied construction is: "We relate to you a narrative, the best of narratives," so it has the sense of narrating (*iqtisas*). Or it is in the sense of the passive participle: that is, the narrated (*maqsus*). ﴿By what We have revealed to you﴾, that is, by Our revelation to you, ﴿this Qur'an﴾. The accusative of "the Qur'an" is because it is an attribute of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), or a substitute (*badal*) for it, or an explanatory apposition (*ʿatf bayan*). Al-Zajjaj permitted the nominative, by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive, and the probable reason is that the preposition in "by what We have revealed" is assumed to govern the demonstrative, so the meaning becomes: "We relate to you the best of narratives by this Qur'an." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾. *In* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, as evidenced by the distinguishing *lam* between it and the negative particle. The pronoun in "before it" refers to the revelation implied by "We have revealed," and the meaning is: you, before Our revelation to you, were among those unaware of this story.

It has been disputed in what respect what is in this surah is "the best of stories." It was said: because what is in this surah of stories contains lessons, admonitions and wisdoms that are not found in other [surahs]. It was said: because of its fine dialogue, and what Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) underwent of patience with their harm and his pardoning them. It was said: because it mentions prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the conduct of kings and slaves, merchants, scholars and the ignorant, women and their stratagems and their guile. It was said: because it mentions the beloved and the lover and what passed between them. It was said: that "best" here means "most wondrous." It was said: that everyone mentioned in it ends in happiness.

His saying: ﴿When Yusuf said to his father﴾. *Idh* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed by an implied verb: that is, "remember the time when Yusuf said."

The majority read ﴿Yusuf﴾ with a *damma* on the *sin*. Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with a *kasra* along with a *hamza* in place of the *waw*. Ibn Zayd transmitted the *hamza* with a *fatha* on the *sin*. It is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*) due to foreignness (*ʿujmah*) and proper-name status (*ʿalamiyyah*). It was said that it is Arabic, but the first [view] is better, as evidenced by its not being declined. [Said] to his father, namely Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

﴿O my father﴾: *ya abati* with a *kasra* on the *ta'* in the reading of Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir. According to the Basrans it is the marker of the feminine (*ʿalamat al-taʾnith*), and it attached specifically to the word *ab* in the vocative, as a replacement for the *ya'* (of possession). Its original form is *ya abi*. Its *kasra* indicates that it is a substitute for a letter that suits a *kasra*. Ibn ʿAmir read it with a *fatha*, because the original form for him is *ya abata*, and one may not combine the substitute and what it substitutes, so one does not say *ya abati-ya*. Al-Farra' permitted *ya abatu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*.

﴿Indeed I saw﴾: from the sleeping dream (*al-ruʾya al-nawmiyyah*), not from visual sight, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾.

His saying: ﴿Eleven stars﴾: it is read with a sukun on the *ʿayn* for lightening, to avoid a succession of vowels, and it is read with a *fatha* according to the original form. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾: he placed them after the stars only to show their distinction and nobility, as in the coupling of Jibril and Mikail with the angels. It was said that the *waw* here means "together with." The clause ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ is a new (*mustaʾnafah*) clause explaining the state in which he saw them. It is treated as the rational beings in the pronoun specific to them, because it is described with the description of rational beings, namely prostrating. So said al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The Arabs make plurals of non-rational things in the form of the plural of rational beings when they assign them that rank.

﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers"﴾. *Al-ruʾya* [the dream] is a verbal noun of *raʾa* in sleep, *ruʾya*, on the pattern *fuʿla* like *suqya* and *busra*. Its *alif* is for the feminine, and for this reason it is not declined. Yaʿqub (ʿalayhi al-salam) forbade his son Yusuf from relating his dream to his brothers, because he knew its interpretation and feared that he would relate it to his brothers, and they would understand its interpretation, and envy of him would arise among them. For this reason He said: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾. This is the answer to the prohibition, and it is in the accusative by an implied *an*: that is, "lest they do for you," that is, for your sake, a plot established and firm, from which you cannot be free; or a plot hidden from your understanding. This meaning arising from the addition of the *lam* is more emphatic than saying "lest they plot a plot." It was said that the *lam* was brought only to include the meaning of *ihtiyal* (scheming), which takes *li* [with the object]; so this inclusion yields the meaning of both verbs together, plotting and scheming, as is the rule in inclusion that one of them is taken as the principal and the other as the circumstantial. The clause ﴿Indeed Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾ is a new clause, as if Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) had said: "How could such a thing happen from them?", so [Yaʿqub] alerted him that Satan drives them to that, because he is an enemy of humankind, openly showing enmity and proclaiming it.

His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾: that is, like that choosing (*ijtiba'*), wondrous, which you saw in the dream, of the prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon, your Lord will choose you, and will realise in you the interpretation of that vision, so He will make you a prophet and choose you over the rest of the servants, and will subject them to you, just as those heavenly bodies you saw in your dream were subjected to you, becoming prostrate to you. Al-Nahhas said: The root of *ijtiba'* is from *jabaytu al-shay'* (I gathered the thing), meaning I obtained it, and from it *jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd* (I collected water in the pool). The meaning of *ijtiba'* is *istifa'* (selection). This includes praise of Yusuf and enumeration of the blessings of Allah upon him, and among them ﴿and teach you of the interpretation of events﴾, that is, the interpretation of dreams.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that this refers to the interpretation of dreams, and Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) was indeed the most knowledgeable of people about its interpretation. It was said that what is meant is: "and teach you of the interpretation of the stories of nations and books." It was said that what is meant by it is making his brothers need him. It was said that it is his deliverance from every hardship. It was said that it is his deliverance from killing specifically. ﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾: so He will combine for you prophethood and kingship, as this dream that Allah showed you indicates, or He will combine for you the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And upon the family of Yaʿqub﴾: they are his kin, his brothers, his children and those after them. That is because Allah, glorified is He, gave them prophethood, as a number of exegetes said. And it is not far-fetched that it is an indication of what came to them after entering Egypt of blessings, among which is that kingship was among them while they were prophets. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that is, a completion like its completion upon your two fathers, namely the blessing of prophethood upon them both, together with Ibrahim having been taken by Allah as a friend (*khalil*), and together with Ishaq having been delivered by Allah, glorified is He, from the sacrifice, and they had righteous offspring: they are Yaʿqub, Yusuf, and the rest of the tribes (*asbat*). The meaning of ﴿from your father﴾ is: before this time in which you are, or before you. Ibrahim and Ishaq are an explanatory apposition to "your two fathers." He referred to them both as "the two fathers," although one of them was a grandfather, namely Ibrahim, because a grandfather is also a father. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Knowing﴾ of everything, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. The clause is a new clause confirming what precedes it, giving its reason: that is, He did that because He is Knowing and Wise. This was a statement by Yaʿqub to his son Yusuf interpreting his dream in a general way, or he knew that by way of revelation, or he recognised it through physiognomy (*firasah*) and what the signs in Yusuf indicated.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿Those are the verses of the Clear Book﴾, that he said: Allah made clear its lawful and unlawful.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muʿadh, who said: Allah made clear the letters which fell from the tongues of non-Arabs, and they are six letters.

Al-Hakim narrated from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited an Arabic Qur'an, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ishmael was inspired with this Arabic tongue by inspiration."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of Quraysh, and it is their speech.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us." So the words were revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, concerning His words ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "From the earlier Scriptures and the past affairs of God among the nations." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ means: before this Qur'an.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, that he said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli, Ibn Hibban in al-Du'afa', Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "A Jewish man from Bustan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about the stars which Yusuf saw prostrating to him. What are their names?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent and did not answer him at all. Then Jibril descended to him and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent for the Jewish man from Bustan and said: 'Will you believe if I tell you their names?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Kharthan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Katafan, Qabis, Wathab, 'Amudan, al-Fayliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, Dhu al-Farigh, al-Diya' and al-Nur. He saw them in the horizon of the sky prostrating to him.' When Yusuf related it to Ya'qub, he said: 'This is a scattered matter which God will gather later.' Then the Jew said: 'Yes, by God, these are indeed their names.'" Thus al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur. As for Ibn Kathir, he made the words "When Yusuf related..." etc. a separate narration and said: "It was related solely by al-Hakam ibn Zahirah al-Fazari. They weakened him, and most of them abandoned him."

al-Jawzajani said: "Discarded (saqit)."

Ibn al-Jawzi said: "It is fabricated (mawdu')."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿eleven stars﴾, that he said: "His brothers. And the sun," he said: "his mother. And the moon," he said: "his father." 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Jarir also narrated the like of it from Ibn Zayd.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾, that he said: "He will select you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid (p-684) concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of dreams."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of knowledge and of dreams. And Yusuf was among the most skilled of people in interpreting."

Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning ﴿as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that he said: "His blessing upon Ibrahim was that He saved him from the fire, and upon Ishaq that He saved him from the sacrifice."

﴿Indeed I saw﴾: from the sleeping dream (*al-ruʾya al-nawmiyyah*), not from visual sight, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Do not relate your dream to your brothers﴾.

His saying: ﴿Eleven stars﴾: it is read with a sukun on the *ʿayn* for lightening, to avoid a succession of vowels, and it is read with a *fatha* according to the original form. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾: he placed them after the stars only to show their distinction and nobility, as in the coupling of Jibril and Mikail with the angels. It was said that the *waw* here means "together with." The clause ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ is a new (*mustaʾnafah*) clause explaining the state in which he saw them. It is treated as the rational beings in the pronoun specific to them, because it is described with the description of rational beings, namely prostrating. So said al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The Arabs make plurals of non-rational things in the form of the plural of rational beings when they assign them that rank.

﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers"﴾. *Al-ruʾya* [the dream] is a verbal noun of *raʾa* in sleep, *ruʾya*, on the pattern *fuʿla* like *suqya* and *busra*. Its *alif* is for the feminine, and for this reason it is not declined. Yaʿqub (ʿalayhi al-salam) forbade his son Yusuf from relating his dream to his brothers, because he knew its interpretation and feared that he would relate it to his brothers, and they would understand its interpretation, and envy of him would arise among them. For this reason He said: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾. This is the answer to the prohibition, and it is in the accusative by an implied *an*: that is, "lest they do for you," that is, for your sake, a plot established and firm, from which you cannot be free; or a plot hidden from your understanding. This meaning arising from the addition of the *lam* is more emphatic than saying "lest they plot a plot." It was said that the *lam* was brought only to include the meaning of *ihtiyal* (scheming), which takes *li* [with the object]; so this inclusion yields the meaning of both verbs together, plotting and scheming, as is the rule in inclusion that one of them is taken as the principal and the other as the circumstantial. The clause ﴿Indeed Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾ is a new clause, as if Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) had said: "How could such a thing happen from them?", so [Yaʿqub] alerted him that Satan drives them to that, because he is an enemy of humankind, openly showing enmity and proclaiming it.

His saying: ﴿And thus will your Lord choose you﴾: that is, like that choosing (*ijtiba'*), wondrous, which you saw in the dream, of the prostration of the stars, the sun and the moon, your Lord will choose you, and will realise in you the interpretation of that vision, so He will make you a prophet and choose you over the rest of the servants, and will subject them to you, just as those heavenly bodies you saw in your dream were subjected to you, becoming prostrate to you. Al-Nahhas said: The root of *ijtiba'* is from *jabaytu al-shay'* (I gathered the thing), meaning I obtained it, and from it *jabaytu al-ma' fi al-hawd* (I collected water in the pool). The meaning of *ijtiba'* is *istifa'* (selection). This includes praise of Yusuf and enumeration of the blessings of Allah upon him, and among them ﴿and teach you of the interpretation of events﴾, that is, the interpretation of dreams.

Al-Qurtubi said: They agreed that this refers to the interpretation of dreams, and Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) was indeed the most knowledgeable of people about its interpretation. It was said that what is meant is: "and teach you of the interpretation of the stories of nations and books." It was said that what is meant by it is making his brothers need him. It was said that it is his deliverance from every hardship. It was said that it is his deliverance from killing specifically. ﴿And complete His favour upon you﴾: so He will combine for you prophethood and kingship, as this dream that Allah showed you indicates, or He will combine for you the good of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And upon the family of Yaʿqub﴾: they are his kin, his brothers, his children and those after them. That is because Allah, glorified is He, gave them prophethood, as a number of exegetes said. And it is not far-fetched that it is an indication of what came to them after entering Egypt of blessings, among which is that kingship was among them while they were prophets. ﴿Just as He completed it upon your two fathers﴾, that is, a completion like its completion upon your two fathers, namely the blessing of prophethood upon them both, together with Ibrahim having been taken by Allah as a friend (*khalil*), and together with Ishaq having been delivered by Allah, glorified is He, from the sacrifice, and they had righteous offspring: they are Yaʿqub, Yusuf, and the rest of the tribes (*asbat*). The meaning of ﴿from your father﴾ is: before this time in which you are, or before you. Ibrahim and Ishaq are an explanatory apposition to "your two fathers." He referred to them both as "the two fathers," although one of them was a grandfather, namely Ibrahim, because a grandfather is also a father. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Knowing﴾ of everything, ﴿Wise﴾ in all His acts. The clause is a new clause confirming what precedes it, giving its reason: that is, He did that because He is Knowing and Wise. This was a statement by Yaʿqub to his son Yusuf interpreting his dream in a general way, or he knew that by way of revelation, or he recognised it through physiognomy (*firasah*) and what the signs in Yusuf indicated.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿Those are the verses of the Clear Book﴾, that he said: Allah made clear its lawful and unlawful.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muʿadh, who said: Allah made clear the letters which fell from the tongues of non-Arabs, and they are six letters.

Al-Hakim narrated from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited an Arabic Qur'an, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ishmael was inspired with this Arabic tongue by inspiration."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of Quraysh, and it is their speech.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us." So the words were revealed: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, concerning His words ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "From the earlier Scriptures and the past affairs of God among the nations." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ means: before this Qur'an.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾, that he said: "The dreams of the prophets are revelation."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-'Uqayli, Ibn Hibban in al-Du'afa', Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "A Jewish man from Bustan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about the stars which Yusuf saw prostrating to him. What are their names?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent and did not answer him at all. Then Jibril descended to him and informed him of their names. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent for the Jewish man from Bustan and said: 'Will you believe if I tell you their names?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Kharthan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Katafan, Qabis, Wathab, 'Amudan, al-Fayliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, Dhu al-Farigh, al-Diya' and al-Nur. He saw them in the horizon of the sky prostrating to him.' When Yusuf related it to Ya'qub, he said: 'This is a scattered matter which God will gather later.' Then the Jew said: 'Yes, by God, these are indeed their names.'" Thus al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur. As for Ibn Kathir, he made the words "When Yusuf related..." etc. a separate narration and said: "It was related solely by al-Hakam ibn Zahirah al-Fazari. They weakened him, and most of them abandoned him."

al-Jawzajani said: "Discarded (saqit)."

Ibn al-Jawzi said: "It is fabricated (mawdu')."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿eleven stars﴾, that he said: "His brothers. And the sun," he said: "his mother. And the moon," he said: "his father." 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Jarir also narrated the like of it from Ibn Zayd.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾, that he said: "He will select you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid (p-684) concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of dreams."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿and teach you the interpretation of events﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of knowledge and of dreams. And Yusuf was among the most skilled of people in interpreting."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 12, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

It is entirely Meccan. It was also said that it was revealed between Mecca and Medina at the time of the Hijrah (the migration).

Ibn ʿAbbas, in one narration from him, and Qatadah said: "Except for four verses."

Al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surah Yusuf was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated (*wa-sahhahahu*) from Rifaʿah ibn Rafiʿ al-Zuraqi that he set out, together with his maternal cousin Muʿadh ibn ʿAfraʾ, until the two of them reached Mecca. He mentioned a story, and at its end [it states] that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught the two of them Surah Yusuf and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], and then they returned.

Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Dalaʾil*, narrated through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "A rabbi (*ḥabr*) of the Jews entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him reciting Surah Yusuf. He said: 'O Muhammad, who taught you this?' He said: 'Allah taught it to me.' The rabbi was amazed at what he heard from him, so he returned to the Jews and said to them: 'By Allah, Muhammad recites the Qur'an just as it was revealed in the Torah.' So he set out with a group of them until they entered upon him. They recognised him by the description, and they looked at the seal of prophethood between his shoulders, and they listened to his recitation of Surah Yusuf, and they were amazed by it, and at that point they embraced Islam."

Al-Thaʿlabi narrated from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Teach your relatives Surah Yusuf, for whichever Muslim recites it or teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will make the agonies of death easy for him, and will give him the strength not to envy a Muslim."

In its chain (*isnad*) there is Sallam ibn Salim, also said to be Ibn Sulaym al-Madaʾini, who is *matruk* (abandoned, i.e. his narrations are discarded by the critics) from Harun ibn Kathir.

Abu Hatim said: he is unknown (*majhul*). The hadith scholar Ibn ʿAsakir mentioned for him a corroborating narration (*mutabaʿah*) through al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam, from Harun ibn Kathir, and through Shababah, from Mijlaz ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid al-Basri, from ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Judʿan, and from ʿAta ibn Maymun, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, raised to the Prophet (*marfuʿan*, i.e. traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)), and he related something similar. But it is *munkar* (a rejected narration) in all of its chains.

Al-Qurtubi said: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "The Qur'an was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited it to them for a period. They said: 'If only you would relate to us (*law haddathtana*),' so the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]." He said: The scholars said: Allah mentioned the stories of the prophets in the Qur'an and repeated them with one meaning in different aspects, with varied wording, at degrees of eloquence. He mentioned the story of Yusuf and did not repeat it, so no opponent is able to oppose what is repeated, nor what is not repeated.

* *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ has already been discussed at the beginning of Surah Yunus. The reference in His words "Those are" (*tilka*) is to the verses of the surah. "The Clear Book" (*al-kitab al-mubin*): the surah. That is, "those are the verses of the surah which were revealed to you in this surah," the verses of the surah whose matter is manifest in the inimitability (*iʿjaz*) of the Arabs and in rebuking them. The word "mubin" is from *abana*, meaning *bana* (to be clear): that is, the one whose matter is manifest in that it is from Allah and in its inimitability. Or "mubin" means "clear in meaning," such that it is not ambiguous to its reader or listener. Or "mubin" means "one that makes clear what it contains of rulings."

﴿Indeed We have sent it down﴾, that is, the Clear Book, as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾. So, if we assume that "the Book" means the surah, then calling it "Qur'an" is by way of considering that "Qur'an" is a generic noun (*ism jins*) that applies to the whole and to a part. And if we assume that what is meant by "the Book" is the whole Qur'an, then calling it "Qur'an" is clear. "Arabic" is an adjective of "Qur'an": that is, in the language of the Arabs. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, that is, in order that you may know its meanings and comprehend what is in it.

﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. *Qasas* means following the trail of a thing, and from it is His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up"﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], that is, follow his track. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and the implied construction is: "We relate to you a narrative, the best of narratives," so it has the sense of narrating (*iqtisas*). Or it is in the sense of the passive participle: that is, the narrated (*maqsus*). ﴿By what We have revealed to you﴾, that is, by Our revelation to you, ﴿this Qur'an﴾. The accusative of "the Qur'an" is because it is an attribute of the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), or a substitute (*badal*) for it, or an explanatory apposition (*ʿatf bayan*). Al-Zajjaj permitted the nominative, by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive, and the probable reason is that the preposition in "by what We have revealed" is assumed to govern the demonstrative, so the meaning becomes: "We relate to you the best of narratives by this Qur'an." ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾. *In* here is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, as evidenced by the distinguishing *lam* between it and the negative particle. The pronoun in "before it" refers to the revelation implied by "We have revealed," and the meaning is: you, before Our revelation to you, were among those unaware of this story.

It has been disputed in what respect what is in this surah is "the best of stories." It was said: because what is in this surah of stories contains lessons, admonitions and wisdoms that are not found in other [surahs]. It was said: because of its fine dialogue, and what Yusuf (ʿalayhi al-salam) underwent of patience with their harm and his pardoning them. It was said: because it mentions prophets, the righteous, angels, devils, jinn, humans, livestock, birds, the conduct of kings and slaves, merchants, scholars and the ignorant, women and their stratagems and their guile. It was said: because it mentions the beloved and the lover and what passed between them. It was said: that "best" here means "most wondrous." It was said: that everyone mentioned in it ends in happiness.

His saying: ﴿When Yusuf said to his father﴾. *Idh* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed by an implied verb: that is, "remember the time when Yusuf said."

The majority read ﴿Yusuf﴾ with a *damma* on the *sin*. Talhah ibn Musarrif read it with a *kasra* along with a *hamza* in place of the *waw*. Ibn Zayd transmitted the *hamza* with a *fatha* on the *sin*. It is not declinable (*ghayr munsarif*) due to foreignness (*ʿujmah*) and proper-name status (*ʿalamiyyah*). It was said that it is Arabic, but the first [view] is better, as evidenced by its not being declined. [Said] to his father, namely Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

﴿O my father﴾: *ya abati* with a *kasra* on the *ta'* in the reading of Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir. According to the Basrans it is the marker of the feminine (*ʿalamat al-taʾnith*), and it attached specifically to the word *ab* in the vocative, as a replacement for the *ya'* (of possession). Its original form is *ya abi*. Its *kasra* indicates that it is a substitute for a letter that suits a *kasra*. That is, ﴿There was certainly﴾ in their story ﴿signs﴾ indicating the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His creation, ﴿for those who ask﴾ among the people about it. The people of Mecca read āyatun (in the singular), in accordance with tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), while the rest read it in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd (a noted early philologist) chose the plural reading.

Al-Nahhas said: Āyatun here is a good reading. It has also been said that the meaning is: there were signs in Yusuf and his brothers indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) for those among the Jews who asked him. It is reported that a group of Jews said to him while he was in Mecca: "Tell us about a man among the prophets who was in al-Sham and sent his son to Egypt, and he wept for him until he went blind." No one in Mecca was among the People of the Book or knew the news of the prophets. They had only sent him people from Medina who would ask him about this, so Allah revealed the Surah of Yusuf all at once, as it is in the Torah.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿signs for those who ask﴾ is: a wonder for them; it has been said: insight; and it has been said: a lesson.

Al-Qurtubi said: Their names, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, were: Ruwbil, who was the eldest of them; Shim'un; Lawi; Yahudha; Rayalun; and Yashjur. Their mother was Liya, daughter of Layan, who was the daughter of Yaqub's maternal uncle. Yaqub had four sons from two concubines: Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Ashir. Then Liya died, and Yaqub married her sister Rahil, who bore him Yusuf and Binyamin. Al-Suhayli said: The mother of Yusuf was named Wiqfa, and Rahil died in childbirth with Binyamin, who was older than Yusuf.

﴿When they said: Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are﴾. That is, at the time they said it, and the adverbial clause is connected to kāna (was). By "his brother" is meant Binyamin. They singled him out as "his brother" although they were all his brothers, because he was his brother through both parents, as mentioned earlier. The predicate is given in the singular, "dearer" (aḥabb), despite the plurality of the subject, because the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is used in the singular, dual, and plural when it is not definite. The lam in la-Yusufu is the lam that introduces an oath. They only said this because news of the dream had reached them, so they united their opinion on plotting against him. The clause ﴿while we are a band﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. ʿUṣba means a group. It has been said it ranges from one to ten, and it has been said up to fifteen, and it has been said from ten up to forty. It has no singular from its own form; rather it is like nafar and rahṭ. They were ten in number. ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾, that is, in clear departure from the right course of management, by favouring the two of them over us and preferring them to us, although we are equal in our connection to him. It is not valid that they meant he was in error regarding his religion.

﴿Kill Yusuf or cast him out to some land﴾. That is, they said: Do one of two things to him: either kill him, or cast him into some land. Or, some of them urged killing and the others urged casting him out, or one of them spoke these words and the rest agreed with him, so they were like the speaker in attributing this statement to them. The accusative of "land" (arḍan) is adverbial of place, and the indefiniteness is for vagueness: that is, an unknown land. The answer to the imperative is ﴿your father's face will be free for you﴾, that is, it will become clear and sincere, and he will turn toward you and love you with complete love. ﴿And you will be﴾ is conjoined to "will be free." It may also be in the accusative, governed by an implied "an" after it, meaning after Yusuf, i.e. after finishing with killing him or casting him out. It has been said: after the sin they had committed against Yusuf. ﴿A righteous people﴾, in the affairs of your religion and in obedience to your father, or righteous in the affairs of your worldly life, since what was preoccupying you from that would be gone, namely envy of Yusuf and the disturbance of your hearts through his influence over you, he and his brother. Or it is meant by "the righteous": those who repent of the sin.

﴿One of them said﴾, that is, one of the brothers. It has been said it was Yahudha; it has been said Ruwbil; it has been said Shim'un. ﴿Do not kill Yusuf, but cast him into the depths of the well﴾. It has been said that the reason for the explicit naming of Yusuf in "do not kill Yusuf" was to elicit their compassion for him.

The people of Mecca, Basra, Kufa and Syria read ﹙fī ghayābati al-jubb﹚ in the singular. The people of Medina read fī ghayābāti in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd chose the singular and rejected the plural, because the place into which they cast him is one. Al-Nahhas said: This is a restriction in the language, and ghayābāt in the plural is permissible. A ghayaba is anything that hides something from you, and it has been said that a grave is called a ghayaba. Here it means the bottom of the well which the eye cannot reach, or a recess in it. The poet said:

Ala fa-l-bathā shahrayni aw niṣfa thālithin ilā dhākumā qad ghayyatnī ghiyābiyā

The jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone; before it is lined it is called rakiyya, and once it is lined it is called bi'r. It is called jubb because it has been cut into the earth by cutting. The plural of jubb is jubab, jibab and ajbab. The combination of ghayaba and jubb is for emphasis, that they should throw him into a place in the well of extreme darkness, so that the gaze of the onlookers cannot reach him. It has been said this well is in Bayt al-Maqdis, and it has been said in al-Urdunn.

The answer to the imperative is ﴿some of the travellers will pick him up﴾. Mujahid, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Qatada read takaltiquhu with the feminine ta' (taltaqitu), and its basis is that "some of the travellers" is a caravan (sayyara). It is reported from Sibawayh that "some of his fingers fell off" (saqaṭat baʿḍu aṣābiʿihi), and from this is the poet's saying:

Arā marra al-sinīna akhadhna minnī kamā akhadha al-sirāru min al-hilāli

The rest read yaltaqithu with the masculine ya'. The sayyara is the group that travels along the road. Iltiqat is taking something that is about to be lost. They seem to have intended that if some of the caravan picked him up, they would carry him to a distant place, so that he would be hidden from his father and from anyone who knew him, and they would not need to travel to the distant place themselves, since their father might not permit them to do so. The meaning of ﴿if you are going to act﴾ is: if you are going to act on what I have suggested to you about him. It is as though he did not insist on the matter but left it to what they agreed upon, as an adviser does with one who has consulted him.

This is evidence that the brothers of Yusuf were not prophets, since prophets are not permitted to conspire to kill a Muslim unjustly and out of aggression. It has been said they were prophets, and that this was a slip of the foot, which the blazing of the fire of envy in their breasts and the kindling of embers of rage in their hearts led them into.

This is rejected: prophets are protected from such a great and extreme sin of this kind, together with the severing of kinship, disobedience to a parent, and the fabrication of lies. It has been said that they were not prophets at that time, but became prophets afterwards.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding ﴿signs for those who ask﴾: he said, a lesson. He also reported from Qatada on the verse: he said, whoever asks about this, it is like this: what Allah has related to you and informed you of. Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Allah only related to Muhammad (ﷺ) the story of Yusuf and the transgression of his brothers against him and their envy of him, when he mentioned his dream, because of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw of his people's transgression against him and their envy of him when Allah honoured him with prophethood, so that he might take consolation in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿when they said: Yusuf and his brother﴾: he means Binyamin, who was his brother through father and mother. Regarding ﴿while we are a band﴾ he said: the ʿuṣba is between ten and forty.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, the ʿuṣba is the group. ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾: he said, in error in his opinion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported regarding ﴿One of them said: do not kill Yusuf﴾: he said, it was said by their eldest, who had remained behind. He said: al-jubb is a well in Syria. ﴿Some of the travellers will pick him up﴾: he said, some Bedouin people picked him up.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding ﴿and cast him into the depths of the well﴾: he meant the well (rakiyya).

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak: he said, al-jubb is the well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported: he said, it is a well in Bayt al-Maqdis, in some of its regions.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, al-jubb is opposite Tiberias, with a few miles between it and it.
