He also reported from Qatada on the verse: he said, whoever asks about this, it is like this: what Allah has related to you and informed you of. Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Allah only related to Muhammad (ﷺ) the story of Yusuf and the transgression of his brothers against him and their envy of him, when he mentioned his dream, because of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw of his people's transgression against him and their envy of him when Allah honoured him with prophethood, so that he might take consolation in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿when they said: Yusuf and his brother﴾: he means Binyamin, who was his brother through father and mother. Regarding ﴿while we are a band﴾ he said: the ʿuṣba is between ten and forty.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, the ʿuṣba is the group. ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾: he said, in error in his opinion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported regarding ﴿One of them said: do not kill Yusuf﴾: he said, it was said by their eldest, who had remained behind. He said: al-jubb is a well in Syria. ﴿Some of the travellers will pick him up﴾: he said, some Bedouin people picked him up.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding ﴿and cast him into the depths of the well﴾: he meant the well (rakiyya).

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak: he said, al-jubb is the well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported: he said, it is a well in Bayt al-Maqdis, in some of its regions.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, al-jubb is opposite Tiberias, with a few miles between it and it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 7–10:

That is, ﴿There was certainly﴾ in their story ﴿signs﴾ indicating the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His creation, ﴿for those who ask﴾ among the people about it. The people of Mecca read āyatun (in the singular), in accordance with tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), while the rest read it in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd (a noted early philologist) chose the plural reading.

Al-Nahhas said: Āyatun here is a good reading. It has also been said that the meaning is: there were signs in Yusuf and his brothers indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) for those among the Jews who asked him. It is reported that a group of Jews said to him while he was in Mecca: "Tell us about a man among the prophets who was in al-Sham and sent his son to Egypt, and he wept for him until he went blind." No one in Mecca was among the People of the Book or knew the news of the prophets. They had only sent him people from Medina who would ask him about this, so Allah revealed the Surah of Yusuf all at once, as it is in the Torah.

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿signs for those who ask﴾ is: a wonder for them; it has been said: insight; and it has been said: a lesson.

Al-Qurtubi said: Their names, meaning the brothers of Yusuf, were: Ruwbil, who was the eldest of them; Shim'un; Lawi; Yahudha; Rayalun; and Yashjur. Their mother was Liya, daughter of Layan, who was the daughter of Yaqub's maternal uncle. Yaqub had four sons from two concubines: Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Ashir. Then Liya died, and Yaqub married her sister Rahil, who bore him Yusuf and Binyamin. Al-Suhayli said: The mother of Yusuf was named Wiqfa, and Rahil died in childbirth with Binyamin, who was older than Yusuf.

﴿When they said: Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we are﴾. That is, at the time they said it, and the adverbial clause is connected to kāna (was). By "his brother" is meant Binyamin. They singled him out as "his brother" although they were all his brothers, because he was his brother through both parents, as mentioned earlier. The predicate is given in the singular, "dearer" (aḥabb), despite the plurality of the subject, because the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is used in the singular, dual, and plural when it is not definite. The lam in la-Yusufu is the lam that introduces an oath. They only said this because news of the dream had reached them, so they united their opinion on plotting against him. The clause ﴿while we are a band﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. ʿUṣba means a group. It has been said it ranges from one to ten, and it has been said up to fifteen, and it has been said from ten up to forty. It has no singular from its own form; rather it is like nafar and rahṭ. They were ten in number. ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾, that is, in clear departure from the right course of management, by favouring the two of them over us and preferring them to us, although we are equal in our connection to him. It is not valid that they meant he was in error regarding his religion.

﴿Kill Yusuf or cast him out to some land﴾. That is, they said: Do one of two things to him: either kill him, or cast him into some land. Or, some of them urged killing and the others urged casting him out, or one of them spoke these words and the rest agreed with him, so they were like the speaker in attributing this statement to them. The accusative of "land" (arḍan) is adverbial of place, and the indefiniteness is for vagueness: that is, an unknown land. The answer to the imperative is ﴿your father's face will be free for you﴾, that is, it will become clear and sincere, and he will turn toward you and love you with complete love. ﴿And you will be﴾ is conjoined to "will be free." It may also be in the accusative, governed by an implied "an" after it, meaning after Yusuf, i.e. after finishing with killing him or casting him out. It has been said: after the sin they had committed against Yusuf. ﴿A righteous people﴾, in the affairs of your religion and in obedience to your father, or righteous in the affairs of your worldly life, since what was preoccupying you from that would be gone, namely envy of Yusuf and the disturbance of your hearts through his influence over you, he and his brother. Or it is meant by "the righteous": those who repent of the sin.

﴿One of them said﴾, that is, one of the brothers. It has been said it was Yahudha; it has been said Ruwbil; it has been said Shim'un. ﴿Do not kill Yusuf, but cast him into the depths of the well﴾. It has been said that the reason for the explicit naming of Yusuf in "do not kill Yusuf" was to elicit their compassion for him.

The people of Mecca, Basra, Kufa and Syria read ﹙fī ghayābati al-jubb﹚ in the singular. The people of Medina read fī ghayābāti in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd chose the singular and rejected the plural, because the place into which they cast him is one. Al-Nahhas said: This is a restriction in the language, and ghayābāt in the plural is permissible. A ghayaba is anything that hides something from you, and it has been said that a grave is called a ghayaba. Here it means the bottom of the well which the eye cannot reach, or a recess in it. The poet said:

Ala fa-l-bathā shahrayni aw niṣfa thālithin ilā dhākumā qad ghayyatnī ghiyābiyā

The jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone; before it is lined it is called rakiyya, and once it is lined it is called bi'r. It is called jubb because it has been cut into the earth by cutting. The plural of jubb is jubab, jibab and ajbab. The combination of ghayaba and jubb is for emphasis, that they should throw him into a place in the well of extreme darkness, so that the gaze of the onlookers cannot reach him. It has been said this well is in Bayt al-Maqdis, and it has been said in al-Urdunn.

The answer to the imperative is ﴿some of the travellers will pick him up﴾. Mujahid, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and Qatada read takaltiquhu with the feminine ta' (taltaqitu), and its basis is that "some of the travellers" is a caravan (sayyara). It is reported from Sibawayh that "some of his fingers fell off" (saqaṭat baʿḍu aṣābiʿihi), and from this is the poet's saying:

Arā marra al-sinīna akhadhna minnī kamā akhadha al-sirāru min al-hilāli

The rest read yaltaqithu with the masculine ya'. The sayyara is the group that travels along the road. Iltiqat is taking something that is about to be lost. They seem to have intended that if some of the caravan picked him up, they would carry him to a distant place, so that he would be hidden from his father and from anyone who knew him, and they would not need to travel to the distant place themselves, since their father might not permit them to do so. The meaning of ﴿if you are going to act﴾ is: if you are going to act on what I have suggested to you about him. It is as though he did not insist on the matter but left it to what they agreed upon, as an adviser does with one who has consulted him.

This is evidence that the brothers of Yusuf were not prophets, since prophets are not permitted to conspire to kill a Muslim unjustly and out of aggression. It has been said they were prophets, and that this was a slip of the foot, which the blazing of the fire of envy in their breasts and the kindling of embers of rage in their hearts led them into.

This is rejected: prophets are protected from such a great and extreme sin of this kind, together with the severing of kinship, disobedience to a parent, and the fabrication of lies. It has been said that they were not prophets at that time, but became prophets afterwards.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan regarding ﴿signs for those who ask﴾: he said, a lesson. He also reported from Qatada on the verse: he said, whoever asks about this, it is like this: what Allah has related to you and informed you of. Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Allah only related to Muhammad (ﷺ) the story of Yusuf and the transgression of his brothers against him and their envy of him, when he mentioned his dream, because of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw of his people's transgression against him and their envy of him when Allah honoured him with prophethood, so that he might take consolation in it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿when they said: Yusuf and his brother﴾: he means Binyamin, who was his brother through father and mother. Regarding ﴿while we are a band﴾ he said: the ʿuṣba is between ten and forty.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, the ʿuṣba is the group. ﴿Indeed our father is in clear error﴾: he said, in error in his opinion.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported regarding ﴿One of them said: do not kill Yusuf﴾: he said, it was said by their eldest, who had remained behind. He said: al-jubb is a well in Syria. ﴿Some of the travellers will pick him up﴾: he said, some Bedouin people picked him up.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding ﴿and cast him into the depths of the well﴾: he meant the well (rakiyya).

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak: he said, al-jubb is the well.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported: he said, it is a well in Bayt al-Maqdis, in some of its regions.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd: he said, al-jubb is opposite Tiberias, with a few miles between it and it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 11–18 (part 1 of 2):

When their opinion became settled on casting him into the dark depths of the well (ghayabat al-jubb), they came to their father and addressed him with the word "father," seeking to win his sympathy and to stir the tenderness with which the natures of fathers are made toward their sons, and as a means of reaching the full accomplishment of the scheme they had devised. They asked him in the manner of one who disapproves of a matter whose reality ought to be the opposite. So ﴿They said: "O our father, why do you not entrust us with Joseph?"﴾ That is: what is the matter with you that you do not make us trustworthy regarding him? It seems they had asked him before this to let Joseph go out with them, and he refused. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and al-Zuhri read "la ta'manna" with idgham (assimilation) without ishmam.

Talha ibn Musarrif read "la ta'mananu" with two clearly pronounced nuns, according to the original form. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Razin and al-A'mash read "la tayamanna," which is the dialect of Tamim, as has previously been mentioned. The rest of the reciters read with idgham and ishmam, to indicate the state of the letter before its assimilation. ﴿And indeed we are to him sincere advisers﴾ in guarding him and looking after him, until we return him to you.

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ that is, to the desert to which they intended to go out. "Ghadan" (tomorrow) is an adverbial of time, and its original form according to Sibawayh is "ghuduwa."

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: what is between the dawn and the rising of the sun is called "ghudwa," and it is likewise called "bukra."

﴿"...that he may enjoy himself and play"﴾ this is the answer to the imperative.

The people of Basra, the people of Makka and the people of Syria read "nartaʿ" with the nun and with sukun on the ʿayn, as some of them transmitted from them. They also read with ikhtilas (rapid vowel reduction). The rest read with the nun and kasra on the ʿayn. The first reading is derived from the Arabs' saying "rataʿa al-insan aw al-baʿir" when someone or a camel eats as it wishes, or the meaning is: we expand in abundance, and every one who is fertile is "rati'" (grazing richly). The poet said:

*Then graze Fazara, for there is no pasture there for you.*

And from it is the saying of the poet:

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until when she remembers, then it is advance and retreat.*

The second reading is derived from the grazing of sheep.

Mujahid and Qatada read "yarta' wa yal'ab" with the yā' (third person) in both, and read "yal'abu" in the nominative as a resumption, the pronoun referring to Joseph.

Al-Qutayabi said: the meaning of "narta'" is "we guard and protect one another, and each of us watches over the others," from their saying "ra'aka Allah," that is, "may God keep you." And "nal'ab" is from play.

It was said to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': how did they say "and we play" when they were prophets? He said: They were not prophets at that time. It was also said that what is meant is permissible play of the prophets, which is mere relaxation. It was said that it is the play through which they learn war and strengthen themselves for it, as in their saying: ﴿Indeed we went racing﴾, not forbidden play which is the opposite of truth. For this reason Ya'qub did not object to them when they said "and we play." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Jabir: "Why not a virgin, you play with her and she plays with you?"

Ya'qub replied to them with his words: ﴿"Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away"﴾ that is, your going off with him. The lam in "la-yahzununi" is the lam of the beginning, for emphasis and to restrict the present tense to the present. He informed them that he grieves at Joseph's absence from him, because of the intensity of his love for him and his fear for him. ﴿"And I fear that the wolf will devour him"﴾ that is, and along with that I fear that the wolf will devour him.

Ya'qub said this as an expression of his apprehension of them concerning him, so he alluded to that by the wolf. It was also said that he feared the wolf would devour him literally, because that place had many wolves; and if he had feared that they would kill him, he would have sent with them someone to guard him.

Tha'lab said: "al-dhi'b" (wolf) is derived from "tadhabbat al-rih," when the wind rages from every direction. He said: "al-dhi'b" is hamzated because it comes from every direction. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' in one narration from him read it with hamza according to the original form, and likewise Abu 'Amr in one narration from him, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza. The rest read it without hamza (with tashdid-free light form). ﴿"And you are heedless of him"﴾ because of your occupation with grazing and play, or because they were not concerned with guarding him.

﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band"﴾ the lam is the one preceding an oath. The meaning: by God, if the wolf devours him while we are a band, that is, a large group of ten. ﴿"Indeed we would then be losers"﴾ that is, in that case, at the time of the wolf devouring him, we would indeed be losers, perishing in weakness and incapacity; or deserving of destruction for not being valued and for lacking power over the least and simplest thing; or deserving that curse be invoked upon us with ruin and destruction. It was also said: "losers" means "ignorant of his right." This sentence is the answer of the implied oath in the sentence before it.

So when they took him away from Ya'qub's presence and agreed upon their plan ﴿to put him into the depths of the well﴾, the explanation of "ghayabah" and "jubb" has been given shortly before, and the answer of "lamma" is omitted for its clarity and because the context indicates it. The estimate is: they did to him what they did. It was also said its answer is ﴿They said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾. It was also said the implied answer is "they put him in it," and it was said the answer is "We revealed," with the waw being superfluous, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted and he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ ﴿and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104], that is, "We called to him." ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, that is, to Joseph, as facilitation for him and as comfort for his loneliness, even though he was a child, when ten men of his brothers had united in inflicting harm upon him, with hard hearts from which mercy had been removed and compassion stripped away. For the human nature, leave aside religion, overlooks the wrongdoing of a child and forgives it because of his weakness in repelling and his incapacity for the least thing that is demanded of him. How much more so a child who has no fault! Rather, how much more so a child who is a brother to them and who has for them and for himself a father like Ya'qub! So far from the truth is whoever says that they were prophets at that time. Such is not the conduct of prophets nor the deed of the righteous.

In this is evidence that it is permissible for God to reveal to one who is a child and to give him prophethood at that time, as occurred with 'Isa and Yahya ibn Zakariyya. It has been said that at that time he had reached the stage of men, but this is very far-fetched, for one who had reached the stage of men is not feared to be devoured by the wolf. ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs"﴾ that is, you will surely tell your brothers of this deed of theirs which they did to you, after you are freed from what they intended for you of scheming and after the harm they inflicted upon you. The clause ﴿"while they do not perceive"﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, they do not perceive that you are their brother Joseph, because of their belief in your destruction by their casting you into the depths of the well, and because of the length of time since they last saw you, and because you had by then come to a state other than what you were in and contrary to what they had known of you. What he said to them when they entered upon him after he had come to the kingship of Egypt will come later.

His saying: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾. "ʿishaʾan" is accusative as an adverb of time, and it is the end of the day; it was also said it is in the night. "Yabkuna" (weeping) is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, weeping or feigning weeping, because they did not really weep, but rather acted the deed of one who weeps, to lend currency to their lie and to make their deceit and treachery pass.

When they reached their father, ﴿they said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾, that is, we raced one another in running or in shooting; it was also said we were shooting arrows, and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "nantadil." Al-Zajjaj said: this is a kind of racing. Al-Zuhri said: "al-nidal" is with arrows, "al-rihan" with horses, and "al-musabaqa" includes both. Al-Qushayri said: "nastabiq," that is, in shooting, or on horseback, or on foot. The purpose of the racing was training in that for war. ﴿"And we left Joseph by our belongings"﴾, that is, by our clothes, to guard them, ﴿"so the wolf devoured him"﴾. The fa' is for sequence: that is, it devoured him immediately after that.

They made excuses for it by what they had feared beforehand. ﴿"But you will not believe us"﴾, that is, you will not give credence to us in this excuse which we have presented, and to the statement which we made — "even if we were truthful" — whether in your presence or in fact, because of the suspicion that has taken hold of your heart concerning us in this matter, together with your intense love for him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: even if we were among the people of trust and truthfulness in your presence, you would not believe us in this matter because of the intensity of your love for Joseph. Ibn Jarir and others mentioned it likewise.

﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood﴾. "ʿala qamisihi" is in a place of accusative as an adverbial of place: that is, they came with blood upon his shirt. The blood was described as "false" (kadhib) as an intensification, as is well known in describing a concrete noun by an abstract one. It was also said the meaning is: with blood that has falsehood in it, or with blood about which lies were told.

Al-Hasan and 'A'isha read "bi-damin kadhibin" with the unpointed dal: that is, with fresh blood; fresh blood is called "kadhib."

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the altered (discoloured) blood. And "kadhib" also means the whiteness that emerges on the nails of young children, so it is permissible that he likened the blood on the shirt to the whiteness that emerges on the nail in terms of the two colours.

Ya'qub argued against their lie by the soundness of the shirt and said to them: when has a wolf been wise, devouring Joseph and not tearing the shirt? Then God the Exalted mentioned what Ya'qub replied to them, and said: ﴿He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you"﴾, that is, adorned it and made it easy.

Al-Naysaburi said: "al-taswil" is an affirmation in the soul's meaning together with hope for its fulfilment. It is a form (taf'il) from "al-sul," which is wishful desire. Al-Azhari said: its origin is hamzated, but the Arabs found the hamza burdensome in it.

﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, my concern, or what I believe, is beautiful patience. Qutrub said: that is, my patience is beautiful patience. It was also said: "so beautiful patience is more fitting for me."

It was said: beautiful patience is that with which there is no complaint.

Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa ibn 'Umar read, according to what Sahl ibn Yusuf claimed, "fa-sabran jamilan" (accusative), and he said: likewise in the codex of Anas.

Al-Mubarrad said: "fa-sabrun jamilun" with the nominative is more fitting than the accusative, because the meaning is: "He said: my Lord, with me is beautiful patience," whereas the accusative is as an infinitive: that is, "I will surely be patient with beautiful patience."

The poet said:
*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey, "beautiful patience," for both of us are afflicted.*

﴿And God is the one sought for help﴾, that is, the one from whom help is to be requested ﴿against what you describe﴾, that is, against the manifestation of the state of what you describe, or against bearing what you describe. This, from him (peace be upon him), is an expression of supplication, not a report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: "Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play," he said: "We will run and be active and amuse ourselves."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Silafi in al-Tuyuriyyat transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not dictate to people, lest they lie. For the sons of Ya'qub did not know that the wolf eats people; then when their father dictated to them, they lied, and said: 'The wolf devoured him.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning God's saying: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, the verse, he said: It was revealed to Joseph while he was in the well: "You will surely inform your brothers of what they did, while they do not perceive that revelation."

These same transmitters related from Qatada, who said: God revealed to him a revelation while he was in the well, that he would inform them of what they did, "while they," that is, his brothers, "do not perceive that revelation." So that revelation made easy for him what had been done to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾: he said: They did not know of God's revelation to him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon Joseph, he recognised them while they were unaware of him. The bowl was brought, and he placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This goblet informs me that you had a brother from your father called Joseph, whom he brought nearer than you; and that you took him away and cast him into the depths of the well, then you came to your father and said: 'The wolf devoured him,' and brought his shirt stained with false blood." Some of them said to others: "This goblet is informing him of your news." Ibn 'Abbas said: So we do not see that this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs, while they do not perceive"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: Joseph remained in the well for three days.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding ﴿And you will not be believing us﴾, that he said: "Not one who confirms us."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "It was the blood of a young goat."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid something similar. Al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "When Yaʿqūb was brought Yūsuf's shirt and he saw no tear in it, he said: 'You have lied. Had it been as you say, that the wolf ate him, it would have torn the shirt.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Your souls commanded you."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Rather, your souls have made attractive to you a matter." ﴿So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾, i.e., against what you lie about.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Kitāb al-Ṣabr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ḥibbān ibn Abī Ḥablah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, and he said: 'There is no complaint in it; whoever spreads out his grief has not been patient.'" This is from the route of Hushaym from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Ḥibbān ibn Abī Ḥablah, and it is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, that he said: "It is free of impatient complaint."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 11–18 (part 1 of 2):

When their opinion became settled on casting him into the dark depths of the well (ghayabat al-jubb), they came to their father and addressed him with the word "father," seeking to win his sympathy and to stir the tenderness with which the natures of fathers are made toward their sons, and as a means of reaching the full accomplishment of the scheme they had devised. They asked him in the manner of one who disapproves of a matter whose reality ought to be the opposite. So ﴿They said: "O our father, why do you not entrust us with Joseph?"﴾ That is: what is the matter with you that you do not make us trustworthy regarding him? It seems they had asked him before this to let Joseph go out with them, and he refused. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and al-Zuhri read "la ta'manna" with idgham (assimilation) without ishmam.

Talha ibn Musarrif read "la ta'mananu" with two clearly pronounced nuns, according to the original form. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Razin and al-A'mash read "la tayamanna," which is the dialect of Tamim, as has previously been mentioned. The rest of the reciters read with idgham and ishmam, to indicate the state of the letter before its assimilation. ﴿And indeed we are to him sincere advisers﴾ in guarding him and looking after him, until we return him to you.

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ that is, to the desert to which they intended to go out. "Ghadan" (tomorrow) is an adverbial of time, and its original form according to Sibawayh is "ghuduwa."

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: what is between the dawn and the rising of the sun is called "ghudwa," and it is likewise called "bukra."

﴿"...that he may enjoy himself and play"﴾ this is the answer to the imperative.

The people of Basra, the people of Makka and the people of Syria read "nartaʿ" with the nun and with sukun on the ʿayn, as some of them transmitted from them. They also read with ikhtilas (rapid vowel reduction). The rest read with the nun and kasra on the ʿayn. The first reading is derived from the Arabs' saying "rataʿa al-insan aw al-baʿir" when someone or a camel eats as it wishes, or the meaning is: we expand in abundance, and every one who is fertile is "rati'" (grazing richly). The poet said:

*Then graze Fazara, for there is no pasture there for you.*

And from it is the saying of the poet:

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until when she remembers, then it is advance and retreat.*

The second reading is derived from the grazing of sheep.

Mujahid and Qatada read "yarta' wa yal'ab" with the yā' (third person) in both, and read "yal'abu" in the nominative as a resumption, the pronoun referring to Joseph.

Al-Qutayabi said: the meaning of "narta'" is "we guard and protect one another, and each of us watches over the others," from their saying "ra'aka Allah," that is, "may God keep you." And "nal'ab" is from play.

It was said to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': how did they say "and we play" when they were prophets? He said: They were not prophets at that time. It was also said that what is meant is permissible play of the prophets, which is mere relaxation. It was said that it is the play through which they learn war and strengthen themselves for it, as in their saying: ﴿Indeed we went racing﴾, not forbidden play which is the opposite of truth. For this reason Ya'qub did not object to them when they said "and we play." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Jabir: "Why not a virgin, you play with her and she plays with you?"

Ya'qub replied to them with his words: ﴿"Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away"﴾ that is, your going off with him. The lam in "la-yahzununi" is the lam of the beginning, for emphasis and to restrict the present tense to the present. He informed them that he grieves at Joseph's absence from him, because of the intensity of his love for him and his fear for him. ﴿"And I fear that the wolf will devour him"﴾ that is, and along with that I fear that the wolf will devour him.

Ya'qub said this as an expression of his apprehension of them concerning him, so he alluded to that by the wolf. It was also said that he feared the wolf would devour him literally, because that place had many wolves; and if he had feared that they would kill him, he would have sent with them someone to guard him.

Tha'lab said: "al-dhi'b" (wolf) is derived from "tadhabbat al-rih," when the wind rages from every direction. He said: "al-dhi'b" is hamzated because it comes from every direction. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' in one narration from him read it with hamza according to the original form, and likewise Abu 'Amr in one narration from him, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza. The rest read it without hamza (with tashdid-free light form). ﴿"And you are heedless of him"﴾ because of your occupation with grazing and play, or because they were not concerned with guarding him.

﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band"﴾ the lam is the one preceding an oath. The meaning: by God, if the wolf devours him while we are a band, that is, a large group of ten. ﴿"Indeed we would then be losers"﴾ that is, in that case, at the time of the wolf devouring him, we would indeed be losers, perishing in weakness and incapacity; or deserving of destruction for not being valued and for lacking power over the least and simplest thing; or deserving that curse be invoked upon us with ruin and destruction. It was also said: "losers" means "ignorant of his right." This sentence is the answer of the implied oath in the sentence before it.

So when they took him away from Ya'qub's presence and agreed upon their plan ﴿to put him into the depths of the well﴾, the explanation of "ghayabah" and "jubb" has been given shortly before, and the answer of "lamma" is omitted for its clarity and because the context indicates it. The estimate is: they did to him what they did. It was also said its answer is ﴿They said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾. It was also said the implied answer is "they put him in it," and it was said the answer is "We revealed," with the waw being superfluous, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted and he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ ﴿and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104], that is, "We called to him." ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, that is, to Joseph, as facilitation for him and as comfort for his loneliness, even though he was a child, when ten men of his brothers had united in inflicting harm upon him, with hard hearts from which mercy had been removed and compassion stripped away. For the human nature, leave aside religion, overlooks the wrongdoing of a child and forgives it because of his weakness in repelling and his incapacity for the least thing that is demanded of him. How much more so a child who has no fault! Rather, how much more so a child who is a brother to them and who has for them and for himself a father like Ya'qub! So far from the truth is whoever says that they were prophets at that time. Such is not the conduct of prophets nor the deed of the righteous.

In this is evidence that it is permissible for God to reveal to one who is a child and to give him prophethood at that time, as occurred with 'Isa and Yahya ibn Zakariyya. It has been said that at that time he had reached the stage of men, but this is very far-fetched, for one who had reached the stage of men is not feared to be devoured by the wolf. ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs"﴾ that is, you will surely tell your brothers of this deed of theirs which they did to you, after you are freed from what they intended for you of scheming and after the harm they inflicted upon you. The clause ﴿"while they do not perceive"﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, they do not perceive that you are their brother Joseph, because of their belief in your destruction by their casting you into the depths of the well, and because of the length of time since they last saw you, and because you had by then come to a state other than what you were in and contrary to what they had known of you. What he said to them when they entered upon him after he had come to the kingship of Egypt will come later.

His saying: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾. "ʿishaʾan" is accusative as an adverb of time, and it is the end of the day; it was also said it is in the night. "Yabkuna" (weeping) is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, weeping or feigning weeping, because they did not really weep, but rather acted the deed of one who weeps, to lend currency to their lie and to make their deceit and treachery pass.

When they reached their father, ﴿they said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾, that is, we raced one another in running or in shooting; it was also said we were shooting arrows, and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "nantadil." Al-Zajjaj said: this is a kind of racing. Al-Zuhri said: "al-nidal" is with arrows, "al-rihan" with horses, and "al-musabaqa" includes both. Al-Qushayri said: "nastabiq," that is, in shooting, or on horseback, or on foot. The purpose of the racing was training in that for war. ﴿"And we left Joseph by our belongings"﴾, that is, by our clothes, to guard them, ﴿"so the wolf devoured him"﴾. The fa' is for sequence: that is, it devoured him immediately after that.

They made excuses for it by what they had feared beforehand. ﴿"But you will not believe us"﴾, that is, you will not give credence to us in this excuse which we have presented, and to the statement which we made — "even if we were truthful" — whether in your presence or in fact, because of the suspicion that has taken hold of your heart concerning us in this matter, together with your intense love for him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: even if we were among the people of trust and truthfulness in your presence, you would not believe us in this matter because of the intensity of your love for Joseph. Ibn Jarir and others mentioned it likewise.

﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood﴾. "ʿala qamisihi" is in a place of accusative as an adverbial of place: that is, they came with blood upon his shirt. The blood was described as "false" (kadhib) as an intensification, as is well known in describing a concrete noun by an abstract one. It was also said the meaning is: with blood that has falsehood in it, or with blood about which lies were told.

Al-Hasan and 'A'isha read "bi-damin kadhibin" with the unpointed dal: that is, with fresh blood; fresh blood is called "kadhib."

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the altered (discoloured) blood. And "kadhib" also means the whiteness that emerges on the nails of young children, so it is permissible that he likened the blood on the shirt to the whiteness that emerges on the nail in terms of the two colours.

Ya'qub argued against their lie by the soundness of the shirt and said to them: when has a wolf been wise, devouring Joseph and not tearing the shirt? Then God the Exalted mentioned what Ya'qub replied to them, and said: ﴿He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you"﴾, that is, adorned it and made it easy.

Al-Naysaburi said: "al-taswil" is an affirmation in the soul's meaning together with hope for its fulfilment. It is a form (taf'il) from "al-sul," which is wishful desire. Al-Azhari said: its origin is hamzated, but the Arabs found the hamza burdensome in it.

﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, my concern, or what I believe, is beautiful patience. Qutrub said: that is, my patience is beautiful patience. It was also said: "so beautiful patience is more fitting for me."

It was said: beautiful patience is that with which there is no complaint.

Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa ibn 'Umar read, according to what Sahl ibn Yusuf claimed, "fa-sabran jamilan" (accusative), and he said: likewise in the codex of Anas.

Al-Mubarrad said: "fa-sabrun jamilun" with the nominative is more fitting than the accusative, because the meaning is: "He said: my Lord, with me is beautiful patience," whereas the accusative is as an infinitive: that is, "I will surely be patient with beautiful patience."

The poet said:
*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey, "beautiful patience," for both of us are afflicted.*

﴿And God is the one sought for help﴾, that is, the one from whom help is to be requested ﴿against what you describe﴾, that is, against the manifestation of the state of what you describe, or against bearing what you describe. This, from him (peace be upon him), is an expression of supplication, not a report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: "Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play," he said: "We will run and be active and amuse ourselves."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Silafi in al-Tuyuriyyat transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not dictate to people, lest they lie. For the sons of Ya'qub did not know that the wolf eats people; then when their father dictated to them, they lied, and said: 'The wolf devoured him.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning God's saying: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, the verse, he said: It was revealed to Joseph while he was in the well: "You will surely inform your brothers of what they did, while they do not perceive that revelation."

These same transmitters related from Qatada, who said: God revealed to him a revelation while he was in the well, that he would inform them of what they did, "while they," that is, his brothers, "do not perceive that revelation." So that revelation made easy for him what had been done to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾: he said: They did not know of God's revelation to him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon Joseph, he recognised them while they were unaware of him. The bowl was brought, and he placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This goblet informs me that you had a brother from your father called Joseph, whom he brought nearer than you; and that you took him away and cast him into the depths of the well, then you came to your father and said: 'The wolf devoured him,' and brought his shirt stained with false blood." Some of them said to others: "This goblet is informing him of your news." Ibn 'Abbas said: So we do not see that this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs, while they do not perceive"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: Joseph remained in the well for three days.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding ﴿And you will not be believing us﴾, that he said: "Not one who confirms us."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "It was the blood of a young goat."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid something similar. Al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "When Yaʿqūb was brought Yūsuf's shirt and he saw no tear in it, he said: 'You have lied. Had it been as you say, that the wolf ate him, it would have torn the shirt.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Your souls commanded you."

﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band"﴾ the lam is the one preceding an oath. The meaning: by God, if the wolf devours him while we are a band, that is, a large group of ten. ﴿"Indeed we would then be losers"﴾ that is, in that case, at the time of the wolf devouring him, we would indeed be losers, perishing in weakness and incapacity; or deserving of destruction for not being valued and for lacking power over the least and simplest thing; or deserving that curse be invoked upon us with ruin and destruction. It was also said: "losers" means "ignorant of his right." This sentence is the answer of the implied oath in the sentence before it.

So when they took him away from Ya'qub's presence and agreed upon their plan ﴿to put him into the depths of the well﴾, the explanation of "ghayabah" and "jubb" has been given shortly before, and the answer of "lamma" is omitted for its clarity and because the context indicates it. The estimate is: they did to him what they did. It was also said its answer is ﴿They said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾. It was also said the implied answer is "they put him in it," and it was said the answer is "We revealed," with the waw being superfluous, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted and he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ ﴿and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104], that is, "We called to him." ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, that is, to Joseph, as facilitation for him and as comfort for his loneliness, even though he was a child, when ten men of his brothers had united in inflicting harm upon him, with hard hearts from which mercy had been removed and compassion stripped away. For the human nature, leave aside religion, overlooks the wrongdoing of a child and forgives it because of his weakness in repelling and his incapacity for the least thing that is demanded of him. How much more so a child who has no fault! Rather, how much more so a child who is a brother to them and who has for them and for himself a father like Ya'qub! The fa' is for sequence: that is, it devoured him immediately after that.

They asked him in the manner of one who disapproves of a matter whose reality ought to be the opposite. Talha ibn Musarrif read "la ta'mananu" with two clearly pronounced nuns, according to the original form. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Razin and al-A'mash read "la tayamanna," which is the dialect of Tamim, as has previously been mentioned. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: what is between the dawn and the rising of the sun is called "ghudwa," and it is likewise called "bukra."

﴿"...that he may enjoy himself and play"﴾ this is the answer to the imperative.

The poet said:

*Then graze Fazara, for there is no pasture there for you.*

And from it is the saying of the poet:

The second reading is derived from the grazing of sheep.

This is from the route of Hushaym from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Ḥibbān ibn Abī Ḥablah, and it is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, that he said: "It is free of impatient complaint."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 11–18 (part 1 of 2):

When their opinion became settled on casting him into the dark depths of the well (ghayabat al-jubb), they came to their father and addressed him with the word "father," seeking to win his sympathy and to stir the tenderness with which the natures of fathers are made toward their sons, and as a means of reaching the full accomplishment of the scheme they had devised. They asked him in the manner of one who disapproves of a matter whose reality ought to be the opposite. So ﴿They said: "O our father, why do you not entrust us with Joseph?"﴾ That is: what is the matter with you that you do not make us trustworthy regarding him? It seems they had asked him before this to let Joseph go out with them, and he refused. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and al-Zuhri read "la ta'manna" with idgham (assimilation) without ishmam.

Talha ibn Musarrif read "la ta'mananu" with two clearly pronounced nuns, according to the original form. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Abu Razin and al-A'mash read "la tayamanna," which is the dialect of Tamim, as has previously been mentioned. The rest of the reciters read with idgham and ishmam, to indicate the state of the letter before its assimilation. ﴿And indeed we are to him sincere advisers﴾ in guarding him and looking after him, until we return him to you.

﴿Send him with us tomorrow﴾ that is, to the desert to which they intended to go out. "Ghadan" (tomorrow) is an adverbial of time, and its original form according to Sibawayh is "ghuduwa."

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: what is between the dawn and the rising of the sun is called "ghudwa," and it is likewise called "bukra."

﴿"...that he may enjoy himself and play"﴾ this is the answer to the imperative.

The people of Basra, the people of Makka and the people of Syria read "nartaʿ" with the nun and with sukun on the ʿayn, as some of them transmitted from them. They also read with ikhtilas (rapid vowel reduction). The rest read with the nun and kasra on the ʿayn. The first reading is derived from the Arabs' saying "rataʿa al-insan aw al-baʿir" when someone or a camel eats as it wishes, or the meaning is: we expand in abundance, and every one who is fertile is "rati'" (grazing richly). The poet said:

*Then graze Fazara, for there is no pasture there for you.*

And from it is the saying of the poet:

*She grazes as long as she grazes, until when she remembers, then it is advance and retreat.*

The second reading is derived from the grazing of sheep.

Mujahid and Qatada read "yarta' wa yal'ab" with the yā' (third person) in both, and read "yal'abu" in the nominative as a resumption, the pronoun referring to Joseph.

Al-Qutayabi said: the meaning of "narta'" is "we guard and protect one another, and each of us watches over the others," from their saying "ra'aka Allah," that is, "may God keep you." And "nal'ab" is from play.

It was said to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': how did they say "and we play" when they were prophets? He said: They were not prophets at that time. It was also said that what is meant is permissible play of the prophets, which is mere relaxation. It was said that it is the play through which they learn war and strengthen themselves for it, as in their saying: ﴿Indeed we went racing﴾, not forbidden play which is the opposite of truth. For this reason Ya'qub did not object to them when they said "and we play." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Jabir: "Why not a virgin, you play with her and she plays with you?"

Ya'qub replied to them with his words: ﴿"Indeed it grieves me that you should take him away"﴾ that is, your going off with him. The lam in "la-yahzununi" is the lam of the beginning, for emphasis and to restrict the present tense to the present. He informed them that he grieves at Joseph's absence from him, because of the intensity of his love for him and his fear for him. ﴿"And I fear that the wolf will devour him"﴾ that is, and along with that I fear that the wolf will devour him.

Ya'qub said this as an expression of his apprehension of them concerning him, so he alluded to that by the wolf. It was also said that he feared the wolf would devour him literally, because that place had many wolves; and if he had feared that they would kill him, he would have sent with them someone to guard him.

Tha'lab said: "al-dhi'b" (wolf) is derived from "tadhabbat al-rih," when the wind rages from every direction. He said: "al-dhi'b" is hamzated because it comes from every direction. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' in one narration from him read it with hamza according to the original form, and likewise Abu 'Amr in one narration from him, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza. The rest read it without hamza (with tashdid-free light form). ﴿"And you are heedless of him"﴾ because of your occupation with grazing and play, or because they were not concerned with guarding him.

﴿They said: "If the wolf devours him while we are a band"﴾ the lam is the one preceding an oath. The meaning: by God, if the wolf devours him while we are a band, that is, a large group of ten. ﴿"Indeed we would then be losers"﴾ that is, in that case, at the time of the wolf devouring him, we would indeed be losers, perishing in weakness and incapacity; or deserving of destruction for not being valued and for lacking power over the least and simplest thing; or deserving that curse be invoked upon us with ruin and destruction. It was also said: "losers" means "ignorant of his right." This sentence is the answer of the implied oath in the sentence before it.

So when they took him away from Ya'qub's presence and agreed upon their plan ﴿to put him into the depths of the well﴾, the explanation of "ghayabah" and "jubb" has been given shortly before, and the answer of "lamma" is omitted for its clarity and because the context indicates it. The estimate is: they did to him what they did. It was also said its answer is ﴿They said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾. It was also said the implied answer is "they put him in it," and it was said the answer is "We revealed," with the waw being superfluous, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they both submitted and he threw him down upon his forehead﴾ ﴿and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104], that is, "We called to him." ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, that is, to Joseph, as facilitation for him and as comfort for his loneliness, even though he was a child, when ten men of his brothers had united in inflicting harm upon him, with hard hearts from which mercy had been removed and compassion stripped away. For the human nature, leave aside religion, overlooks the wrongdoing of a child and forgives it because of his weakness in repelling and his incapacity for the least thing that is demanded of him. How much more so a child who has no fault! Rather, how much more so a child who is a brother to them and who has for them and for himself a father like Ya'qub! So far from the truth is whoever says that they were prophets at that time. Such is not the conduct of prophets nor the deed of the righteous.

In this is evidence that it is permissible for God to reveal to one who is a child and to give him prophethood at that time, as occurred with 'Isa and Yahya ibn Zakariyya. It has been said that at that time he had reached the stage of men, but this is very far-fetched, for one who had reached the stage of men is not feared to be devoured by the wolf. ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs"﴾ that is, you will surely tell your brothers of this deed of theirs which they did to you, after you are freed from what they intended for you of scheming and after the harm they inflicted upon you. The clause ﴿"while they do not perceive"﴾ is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, they do not perceive that you are their brother Joseph, because of their belief in your destruction by their casting you into the depths of the well, and because of the length of time since they last saw you, and because you had by then come to a state other than what you were in and contrary to what they had known of you. What he said to them when they entered upon him after he had come to the kingship of Egypt will come later.

His saying: ﴿And they came to their father in the evening, weeping﴾. "ʿishaʾan" is accusative as an adverb of time, and it is the end of the day; it was also said it is in the night. "Yabkuna" (weeping) is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, weeping or feigning weeping, because they did not really weep, but rather acted the deed of one who weeps, to lend currency to their lie and to make their deceit and treachery pass.

When they reached their father, ﴿they said: "O our father, indeed we went racing"﴾, that is, we raced one another in running or in shooting; it was also said we were shooting arrows, and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "nantadil." Al-Zajjaj said: this is a kind of racing. Al-Zuhri said: "al-nidal" is with arrows, "al-rihan" with horses, and "al-musabaqa" includes both. Al-Qushayri said: "nastabiq," that is, in shooting, or on horseback, or on foot. The purpose of the racing was training in that for war. ﴿"And we left Joseph by our belongings"﴾, that is, by our clothes, to guard them, ﴿"so the wolf devoured him"﴾. The fa' is for sequence: that is, it devoured him immediately after that.

They made excuses for it by what they had feared beforehand. ﴿"But you will not believe us"﴾, that is, you will not give credence to us in this excuse which we have presented, and to the statement which we made — "even if we were truthful" — whether in your presence or in fact, because of the suspicion that has taken hold of your heart concerning us in this matter, together with your intense love for him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: even if we were among the people of trust and truthfulness in your presence, you would not believe us in this matter because of the intensity of your love for Joseph. Ibn Jarir and others mentioned it likewise.

﴿And they brought his shirt stained with false blood﴾. "ʿala qamisihi" is in a place of accusative as an adverbial of place: that is, they came with blood upon his shirt. The blood was described as "false" (kadhib) as an intensification, as is well known in describing a concrete noun by an abstract one. It was also said the meaning is: with blood that has falsehood in it, or with blood about which lies were told.

Al-Hasan and 'A'isha read "bi-damin kadhibin" with the unpointed dal: that is, with fresh blood; fresh blood is called "kadhib."

Al-Sha'bi said: it is the altered (discoloured) blood. And "kadhib" also means the whiteness that emerges on the nails of young children, so it is permissible that he likened the blood on the shirt to the whiteness that emerges on the nail in terms of the two colours.

Ya'qub argued against their lie by the soundness of the shirt and said to them: when has a wolf been wise, devouring Joseph and not tearing the shirt? Then God the Exalted mentioned what Ya'qub replied to them, and said: ﴿He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you"﴾, that is, adorned it and made it easy.

Al-Naysaburi said: "al-taswil" is an affirmation in the soul's meaning together with hope for its fulfilment. It is a form (taf'il) from "al-sul," which is wishful desire. Al-Azhari said: its origin is hamzated, but the Arabs found the hamza burdensome in it.

﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, my concern, or what I believe, is beautiful patience. Qutrub said: that is, my patience is beautiful patience. It was also said: "so beautiful patience is more fitting for me."

It was said: beautiful patience is that with which there is no complaint.

Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa ibn 'Umar read, according to what Sahl ibn Yusuf claimed, "fa-sabran jamilan" (accusative), and he said: likewise in the codex of Anas.

Al-Mubarrad said: "fa-sabrun jamilun" with the nominative is more fitting than the accusative, because the meaning is: "He said: my Lord, with me is beautiful patience," whereas the accusative is as an infinitive: that is, "I will surely be patient with beautiful patience."

The poet said:
*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey, "beautiful patience," for both of us are afflicted.*

﴿And God is the one sought for help﴾, that is, the one from whom help is to be requested ﴿against what you describe﴾, that is, against the manifestation of the state of what you describe, or against bearing what you describe. This, from him (peace be upon him), is an expression of supplication, not a report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: "Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play," he said: "We will run and be active and amuse ourselves."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Silafi in al-Tuyuriyyat transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not dictate to people, lest they lie. For the sons of Ya'qub did not know that the wolf eats people; then when their father dictated to them, they lied, and said: 'The wolf devoured him.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning God's saying: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, the verse, he said: It was revealed to Joseph while he was in the well: "You will surely inform your brothers of what they did, while they do not perceive that revelation."

These same transmitters related from Qatada, who said: God revealed to him a revelation while he was in the well, that he would inform them of what they did, "while they," that is, his brothers, "do not perceive that revelation." So that revelation made easy for him what had been done to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾: he said: They did not know of God's revelation to him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon Joseph, he recognised them while they were unaware of him. The bowl was brought, and he placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This goblet informs me that you had a brother from your father called Joseph, whom he brought nearer than you; and that you took him away and cast him into the depths of the well, then you came to your father and said: 'The wolf devoured him,' and brought his shirt stained with false blood." Some of them said to others: "This goblet is informing him of your news." Ibn 'Abbas said: So we do not see that this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs, while they do not perceive"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: Joseph remained in the well for three days.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding ﴿And you will not be believing us﴾, that he said: "Not one who confirms us."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "It was the blood of a young goat."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid something similar. Al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "When Yaʿqūb was brought Yūsuf's shirt and he saw no tear in it, he said: 'You have lied. Had it been as you say, that the wolf ate him, it would have torn the shirt.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Your souls commanded you."
