Al-Sha'bi said: it is the altered (discoloured) blood. And "kadhib" also means the whiteness that emerges on the nails of young children, so it is permissible that he likened the blood on the shirt to the whiteness that emerges on the nail in terms of the two colours.

Ya'qub argued against their lie by the soundness of the shirt and said to them: when has a wolf been wise, devouring Joseph and not tearing the shirt? Then God the Exalted mentioned what Ya'qub replied to them, and said: ﴿He said: "Rather, your own souls have made a matter attractive to you"﴾, that is, adorned it and made it easy.

Al-Naysaburi said: "al-taswil" is an affirmation in the soul's meaning together with hope for its fulfilment. It is a form (taf'il) from "al-sul," which is wishful desire. Al-Azhari said: its origin is hamzated, but the Arabs found the hamza burdensome in it.

﴿So patience is beautiful﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, my concern, or what I believe, is beautiful patience. Qutrub said: that is, my patience is beautiful patience. It was also said: "so beautiful patience is more fitting for me."

It was said: beautiful patience is that with which there is no complaint.

Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa ibn 'Umar read, according to what Sahl ibn Yusuf claimed, "fa-sabran jamilan" (accusative), and he said: likewise in the codex of Anas.

Al-Mubarrad said: "fa-sabrun jamilun" with the nominative is more fitting than the accusative, because the meaning is: "He said: my Lord, with me is beautiful patience," whereas the accusative is as an infinitive: that is, "I will surely be patient with beautiful patience."

The poet said:
*My camel complained to me of the length of the journey, "beautiful patience," for both of us are afflicted.*

﴿And God is the one sought for help﴾, that is, the one from whom help is to be requested ﴿against what you describe﴾, that is, against the manifestation of the state of what you describe, or against bearing what you describe. This, from him (peace be upon him), is an expression of supplication, not a report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: "Send him with us tomorrow, that he may enjoy himself and play," he said: "We will run and be active and amuse ourselves."

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Silafi in al-Tuyuriyyat transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not dictate to people, lest they lie. For the sons of Ya'qub did not know that the wolf eats people; then when their father dictated to them, they lied, and said: 'The wolf devoured him.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning God's saying: ﴿And We revealed to him﴾, the verse, he said: It was revealed to Joseph while he was in the well: "You will surely inform your brothers of what they did, while they do not perceive that revelation."

These same transmitters related from Qatada, who said: God revealed to him a revelation while he was in the well, that he would inform them of what they did, "while they," that is, his brothers, "do not perceive that revelation." So that revelation made easy for him what had been done to him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾: he said: They did not know of God's revelation to him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon Joseph, he recognised them while they were unaware of him. The bowl was brought, and he placed it on his hand, then struck it so that it rang, and said: "This goblet informs me that you had a brother from your father called Joseph, whom he brought nearer than you; and that you took him away and cast him into the depths of the well, then you came to your father and said: 'The wolf devoured him,' and brought his shirt stained with false blood." Some of them said to others: "This goblet is informing him of your news." Ibn 'Abbas said: So we do not see that this verse was revealed except concerning that: ﴿"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs, while they do not perceive"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, who said: Joseph remained in the well for three days.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding ﴿And you will not be believing us﴾, that he said: "Not one who confirms us."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "It was the blood of a young goat."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Mujāhid something similar. Al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾, that he said: "When Yaʿqūb was brought Yūsuf's shirt and he saw no tear in it, he said: 'You have lied. Had it been as you say, that the wolf ate him, it would have torn the shirt.'"

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Your souls commanded you."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His words ﴿Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter﴾, that he said: "Rather, your souls have made attractive to you a matter." ﴿So patience is beautiful, and Allah is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾, i.e., against what you lie about.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Kitāb al-Ṣabr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ḥibbān ibn Abī Ḥablah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, and he said: 'There is no complaint in it; whoever spreads out his grief has not been patient.'" This is from the route of Hushaym from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Ḥibbān ibn Abī Ḥablah, and it is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾, that he said: "It is free of impatient complaint."

This is the start of the narration of Joseph's rescue and what came after it. The tafsir of "al-sayyara" has already been given earlier. Here it means a passing caravan travelling from Syria to Egypt. They went astray and wandered until they camped near the well. The well was in a desolate spot far from settlements. The "warid" (the one who comes down to the water to draw it for the people) was, according to the exegetes, named Malik ibn Dhu'r, from the Arab al-'Aariba.

﴿Then he let down his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down to fill it. One says "adla dalwahu" when one lets it down to fill it, and "dallaha" when one draws it up. This is what al-Asma'i and others said.

Joseph held on to the rope. When the bucket came up out of the well, the warid saw him and ﴿said: "Good news!"﴾ The people of Madina, Makka and Basra, and the people of Syria, read it with "bushra" in the construct form with the pronoun attached. The people of Kufa read "ya bushra" without the attachment. The meaning of calling out to good news is that he wanted it to be present at that time, as if he said: "This is the time of your coming and the moment of your arrival." It has also been said that he called out to a man named Bushra. The first is more preferred.

Al-Nahhas said: The meaning of calling out to good news is announcing the good news to whoever is present. This is more emphatic than saying "bashshartuhu," just as one says "ya 'ajaban," meaning "O wonder! This is one of your days, so be present." He said: This is the position of Sibawayh.

﴿And they concealed him﴾, meaning the warid and his companions who were with him concealed Joseph and did not reveal him to them. It has been said that they did not hide him, but rather concealed the fact that they had found him in the well. They claimed that the people of the water had handed him over to them so that they could sell him for them in Egypt. It has also been said that the subject of "asarroohu" refers to Joseph's brothers and the object refers to Joseph. That is because his brother Yahudha used to come to him every day with food. On the day he came out of the well, Yahudha came and informed his brothers, and they came to the caravan and said: "This is a slave who ran away from us," and bought him from them. Joseph kept silent for fear that they would take him and kill him.

The first is more preferred.

The accusative of ﴿merchandise﴾ (bid'a) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they concealed him while he was merchandise, that is, goods for trade. "Bid'a" is what is taken out of wealth (yubda'), that is, cut off from it, because it is a portion of the wealth that is traded. It was said that the warid and his companions said to them that he was merchandise they had acquired from Syria, for fear that they would share in him.

In His words ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what they do﴾ there is a severe warning for whoever's action was the cause of what Joseph suffered of trials, and of the humiliation he came to be subjected to through the process of buying and selling. He was "the noble son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble": Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, as our Prophet (ﷺ) said in describing him with that.

His words: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams﴾. It is said "shara" meaning "ishtara" (bought), and "shara" meaning "baa'a" (sold).

The poet said:
"I sold a cloak, would that after one cloak I had been a [ruined] man"
meaning I sold it.

Another said:
"So when he bought her, tears overflowed in tears,"
meaning he bought her.

What is meant here is: they sold him. That is, the warid and his companions sold him for a paltry price, meaning deficient or counterfeit. It has been said that it refers to Joseph's brothers according to the earlier view, and it has been said that it refers to the caravan, and the meaning is: they bought him. It has been said that "bakhs" means injustice, and it has been said that it means unlawful.

It has been said they sold him for twenty dirhams, and it has been said for forty. "Dirhams" is a substitution for "thaman" (price), that is, dinars. "Ma'duda" (counted) is an attribute of "dirhams," and in this there is an indication that they were few, to be counted and not weighed, because they did not weigh anything less than an "uqiyya," which is forty dirhams.

﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to him﴾. One says "zahidtu" and "zahadtu" with fatha and kasra on the ha'. Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i said: The people of the language said: "zahida fihi" means he desired it, and "zahida 'anhu" means he desired it. The meaning is that they were among those who were disinclined toward him, who did not care about him, and for this reason they sold him for that paltry price. That is because they had picked him up, and one who picks up a thing treats it with contempt. The pronoun in "kanu" refers to what precedes it, according to the difference of opinions about it.

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾: he is the 'Aziz, who was over the treasuries of Egypt and was a minister to the king of Egypt. He was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid from the 'Amaliq. It has been said that the king was Pharaoh of Musa. It has been said he bought him for twenty dinars. It has been said they bid up his price until it reached many times his weight in musk, ambergris, silk, silver, gold, pearls and jewels. When the 'Aziz bought him, he said to his wife, and the lam is connected to "ishtarahu": "Make his lodging honourable," meaning his dwelling in which he stays, with good food and fine clothing. One says "thawa bil-makan," meaning he stayed in the place. "Perhaps he will benefit us," meaning he will suffice us in some of the important matters for which we need someone like him. ﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾, meaning we will adopt him and make him a son for us. It was said the 'Aziz was impotent and could not have children. It was also said he did not approach women. He had discerned in him that he would take his place in the affairs of the kingdom entrusted to him.

His words: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾. The "ka" is in the position of the accusative, as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. The reference is to what preceded of his deliverance from his brothers, his removal from the well, and the 'Aziz's heart being inclined toward him. That is, like that wondrous establishment, We established Joseph until he became empowered in commanding and forbidding. One says "makkanahu fihi," meaning he established him in it, and "makkana lahu fihi," meaning he made a place for him in it. Because the two meanings are close, each is used in place of the other.

His words: ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾. This is a reason for an omitted thing being caused, as if it were said: We did that establishment so that We might teach him the interpretation of events, or that rescue was for this reason. Or it is coordinated with something presumed, which is that it is said: We established Joseph so that there would follow from that what followed of what happened between him and the 'Aziz's wife, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. The meaning of "interpretation of events" is the interpretation of dreams, for they were among the causes by which he reached the level of establishment he attained. It has been said the meaning of "interpretation of events" is understanding the secrets of the divine books and the ways of the prophets before him. There is no obstacle to taking it in all these senses.

﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾, meaning over His own affair. Nothing can resist Him, and none of His creatures can overpower Him in it.

﴿His command is only, when He intends a thing, that He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. Among what falls under this general statement, as the attachment of the generic noun to the pronoun indicates, are the matters concerning Joseph (peace be upon him) which Allah, glorified is He, willed in his regard. It has been said the meaning of ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾ is that it was among Ya'qub's commands that he should not relate Joseph's dream to his brothers, but Allah's command prevailed until it was related to them, and until what happened between them happened. This is very far-fetched.

﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾, meaning they do not come to know the unseen of Allah and what is folded within it of great secrets and beneficial wisdoms. It has been said the intended "most" is all, because none knows the unseen except Allah. It has been said that Allah, glorified is He, may inform some of His servants of some of His unseen, as in His words: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27]. It has been said the meaning is: But most of mankind do not know that Allah is dominant over His affair, and they are the polytheists and those who do not believe in predestination.

His words: ﴿And when he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. "Al-ashudd" (full strength).

Sibawayh said: It is a plural whose singular is "shidda."

Al-Kisa'i said: Its singular is "shadd."

Abu 'Ubayd said: It has no singular from its own form among the Arabs. This is refuted by the poet's words:
"My covenant with him was the day's ashudd, as if he had dyed his fingers and head with henna."

"Al-ashudd" is the time of attaining full strength, after which decline follows.

It has been said it is thirty-three years. It has been said it is reaching puberty. It has been said it is eighteen years. It has been said other than that, as we have already explained in al-Nisa' and al-An'am.

"Hukm" (judgment) is what he issued of rulings within the authority of the king of Egypt. "'Ilm" (knowledge) is knowledge of the judgment he was ruling by. It has been said "'aql" (intellect), understanding and prophethood. Al-Sabiyy said: The intended meaning of this judgment and knowledge which Allah gave him is the increase in them.

﴿And thus We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning and like that wondrous reward, We reward the doers of good. So whoever does good in his deed, Allah makes his reward good, and makes the outcome of good among what He rewards him with. This is general, and Joseph's reward for his good patience enters under it first of all. Al-Tabari said: Although its wording appears to apply to every doer of good, what is intended is Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah, the Exalted, says: Just as this Joseph did, then I gave him what I gave him, so likewise I will rescue you from the polytheists of your people who intend enmity against you, and I will establish you in the land.

What we have mentioned is preferred, namely taking the generality in its apparent sense, so that what Ibn Jarir al-Tabari mentioned enters under it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿And a caravan came﴾: he said: A caravan came and stopped at the well. ﴿They sent their water-drawer﴾, and he asked for water and drew Joseph up. They rejoiced that they had found a boy whose knowledge and standing with his Lord they did not know. So they were indifferent to him and sold him, and his sale was unlawful, and they sold him for a few counted dirhams.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding ﴿They sent their water-drawer﴾, that he said: They sent their messenger. ﴿Then he let down his bucket﴾, so the boy got caught in the bucket, and when it came out, ﴿he said: "Good news! This is a boy!"﴾ They rejoiced at him when they drew him out. It is a well at Bayt al-Maqdis, whose location is known.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words "Good news!", that he said: The name of his companion was Bushra, just as you say "ya Zayd." This, despite its remoteness, can only be complete according to the reading of the one who reads "ya bushra" without attachment.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾, meaning Joseph's brothers concealed his matter and hid that he was their brother, and Joseph concealed his matter for fear that his brothers would kill him, and he chose sale, so his brothers sold him for a paltry price.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: The merchants concealed him from one another.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, regarding ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾, that he said: The owner of the bucket and those with him said to their companions: "We have acquired him as merchandise, for fear that they would share in him if they knew about him." His brothers followed them, saying to the one who let down the bucket and his companions: "Secure him so that he does not run away." Until they stopped in Egypt, and he said: "Who will buy me and be glad?" The king bought him, and the king was a Muslim.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And they sold him﴾, that he said: Joseph's brothers sold him when the one who let down his bucket brought him up.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He was sold among them for a paltry price. He said: It was unlawful; it was not lawful for them to sell him, nor to eat his price.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, regarding ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾, that he said: They were the caravan.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he judged regarding a foundling that he is free, and he recited ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Bakhs" means few. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Joseph was only bought for twenty dirhams. His family, when he sent for them to Egypt, were three hundred and ninety persons: their men were prophets, their women were truthful, and by Allah, they did not leave with Musa until they reached six hundred and seventy thousand. Other figures have been reported for the price of Joseph, besides this amount, and there is no need to lengthen the discussion by mentioning them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾, that he said: His name was Qitfir.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i that the name of the wife of al-'Aziz was Zulaykha.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: The one who bought him was Utayfir ibn Rawhab, and the name of his wife was Ra'il, daughter of Ra'ayil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The name of the one who sold him to al-'Aziz was Malik ibn Du'r.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas) concerning His saying ﴿Honor his residence﴾, that he said: "His station (manzilah)." Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from Qatadah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The most perceptive of people are three: al-'Aziz, when he perceived in Yusuf and said to his wife ﴿Honor his residence; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾; the woman who came to Musa and said to her father ﴿O father, hire him﴾; and Abu Bakr when he appointed 'Umar as successor."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of dreams."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Adad, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And when he reached his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾, that he said: "Thirty-three years."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "Forty years."

He narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Twenty-five years."

He narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "Thirty years." He narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Eighteen years."

He narrated from Rabi'ah, who said: "The ahlam (dreams/maturity of intellect)." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Twenty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾, that he said: "It is understanding (fiqh), knowledge and intellect before prophethood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, that he said: "The guided ones (al-muhtadin)."

This is the start of the narration of Joseph's rescue and what came after it. The tafsir of "al-sayyara" has already been given earlier. Here it means a passing caravan travelling from Syria to Egypt. They went astray and wandered until they camped near the well. The well was in a desolate spot far from settlements. The "warid" (the one who comes down to the water to draw it for the people) was, according to the exegetes, named Malik ibn Dhu'r, from the Arab al-'Aariba.

"I sold a cloak, would that after one cloak I had been a [ruined] man"
meaning I sold it.

meaning he bought her.

﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to him﴾. One says "zahidtu" and "zahadtu" with fatha and kasra on the ha'. Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i said: The people of the language said: "zahida fihi" means he desired it, and "zahida 'anhu" means he desired it. The meaning is that they were among those who were disinclined toward him, who did not care about him, and for this reason they sold him for that paltry price. That is because they had picked him up, and one who picks up a thing treats it with contempt. The pronoun in "kanu" refers to what precedes it, according to the difference of opinions about it.

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾: he is the 'Aziz, who was over the treasuries of Egypt and was a minister to the king of Egypt. He was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid from the 'Amaliq. It has been said that the king was Pharaoh of Musa. It has been said he bought him for twenty dinars. It has been said they bid up his price until it reached many times his weight in musk, ambergris, silk, silver, gold, pearls and jewels. When the 'Aziz bought him, he said to his wife, and the lam is connected to "ishtarahu": "Make his lodging honourable," meaning his dwelling in which he stays, with good food and fine clothing. One says "thawa bil-makan," meaning he stayed in the place. "Perhaps he will benefit us," meaning he will suffice us in some of the important matters for which we need someone like him. ﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾, meaning we will adopt him and make him a son for us. It was said the 'Aziz was impotent and could not have children. It was also said he did not approach women. He had discerned in him that he would take his place in the affairs of the kingdom entrusted to him.

His words: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾. The "ka" is in the position of the accusative, as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. The reference is to what preceded of his deliverance from his brothers, his removal from the well, and the 'Aziz's heart being inclined toward him. That is, like that wondrous establishment, We established Joseph until he became empowered in commanding and forbidding. One says "makkanahu fihi," meaning he established him in it, and "makkana lahu fihi," meaning he made a place for him in it. Because the two meanings are close, each is used in place of the other.

His words: ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾. This is a reason for an omitted thing being caused, as if it were said: We did that establishment so that We might teach him the interpretation of events, or that rescue was for this reason. Or it is coordinated with something presumed, which is that it is said: We established Joseph so that there would follow from that what followed of what happened between him and the 'Aziz's wife, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. The meaning of "interpretation of events" is the interpretation of dreams, for they were among the causes by which he reached the level of establishment he attained. It has been said the meaning of "interpretation of events" is understanding the secrets of the divine books and the ways of the prophets before him. There is no obstacle to taking it in all these senses.

﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾, meaning over His own affair. Nothing can resist Him, and none of His creatures can overpower Him in it.

﴿His command is only, when He intends a thing, that He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. Among what falls under this general statement, as the attachment of the generic noun to the pronoun indicates, are the matters concerning Joseph (peace be upon him) which Allah, glorified is He, willed in his regard. It has been said the meaning of ﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾ is that it was among Ya'qub's commands that he should not relate Joseph's dream to his brothers, but Allah's command prevailed until it was related to them, and until what happened between them happened. This is very far-fetched.

﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾, meaning they do not come to know the unseen of Allah and what is folded within it of great secrets and beneficial wisdoms. It has been said the intended "most" is all, because none knows the unseen except Allah. It has been said that Allah, glorified is He, may inform some of His servants of some of His unseen, as in His words: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27]. It has been said the meaning is: But most of mankind do not know that Allah is dominant over His affair, and they are the polytheists and those who do not believe in predestination.

His words: ﴿And when he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. "Al-ashudd" (full strength).

Sibawayh said: It is a plural whose singular is "shidda."

Al-Kisa'i said: Its singular is "shadd."

Abu 'Ubayd said: It has no singular from its own form among the Arabs. This is refuted by the poet's words:
"My covenant with him was the day's ashudd, as if he had dyed his fingers and head with henna."

"Al-ashudd" is the time of attaining full strength, after which decline follows.

It has been said it is thirty-three years. It has been said it is reaching puberty. It has been said it is eighteen years. It has been said other than that, as we have already explained in al-Nisa' and al-An'am.

"Hukm" (judgment) is what he issued of rulings within the authority of the king of Egypt. "'Ilm" (knowledge) is knowledge of the judgment he was ruling by. It has been said "'aql" (intellect), understanding and prophethood. Al-Sabiyy said: The intended meaning of this judgment and knowledge which Allah gave him is the increase in them.

﴿And thus We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning and like that wondrous reward, We reward the doers of good. So whoever does good in his deed, Allah makes his reward good, and makes the outcome of good among what He rewards him with. This is general, and Joseph's reward for his good patience enters under it first of all. Al-Tabari said: Although its wording appears to apply to every doer of good, what is intended is Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah, the Exalted, says: Just as this Joseph did, then I gave him what I gave him, so likewise I will rescue you from the polytheists of your people who intend enmity against you, and I will establish you in the land.

What we have mentioned is preferred, namely taking the generality in its apparent sense, so that what Ibn Jarir al-Tabari mentioned enters under it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿And a caravan came﴾: he said: A caravan came and stopped at the well. ﴿They sent their water-drawer﴾, and he asked for water and drew Joseph up. They rejoiced that they had found a boy whose knowledge and standing with his Lord they did not know. So they were indifferent to him and sold him, and his sale was unlawful, and they sold him for a few counted dirhams.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada, regarding ﴿They sent their water-drawer﴾, that he said: They sent their messenger. ﴿Then he let down his bucket﴾, so the boy got caught in the bucket, and when it came out, ﴿he said: "Good news! This is a boy!"﴾ They rejoiced at him when they drew him out. It is a well at Bayt al-Maqdis, whose location is known.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words "Good news!", that he said: The name of his companion was Bushra, just as you say "ya Zayd." This, despite its remoteness, can only be complete according to the reading of the one who reads "ya bushra" without attachment.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾, meaning Joseph's brothers concealed his matter and hid that he was their brother, and Joseph concealed his matter for fear that his brothers would kill him, and he chose sale, so his brothers sold him for a paltry price.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: The merchants concealed him from one another.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, regarding ﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾, that he said: The owner of the bucket and those with him said to their companions: "We have acquired him as merchandise, for fear that they would share in him if they knew about him." His brothers followed them, saying to the one who let down the bucket and his companions: "Secure him so that he does not run away." Until they stopped in Egypt, and he said: "Who will buy me and be glad?" The king bought him, and the king was a Muslim.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And they sold him﴾, that he said: Joseph's brothers sold him when the one who let down his bucket brought him up.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: He was sold among them for a paltry price. He said: It was unlawful; it was not lawful for them to sell him, nor to eat his price.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada, regarding ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾, that he said: They were the caravan.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib that he judged regarding a foundling that he is free, and he recited ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Bakhs" means few. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Joseph was only bought for twenty dirhams. His family, when he sent for them to Egypt, were three hundred and ninety persons: their men were prophets, their women were truthful, and by Allah, they did not leave with Musa until they reached six hundred and seventy thousand. Other figures have been reported for the price of Joseph, besides this amount, and there is no need to lengthen the discussion by mentioning them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾, that he said: His name was Qitfir.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i that the name of the wife of al-'Aziz was Zulaykha.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: The one who bought him was Utayfir ibn Rawhab, and the name of his wife was Ra'il, daughter of Ra'ayil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The name of the one who sold him to al-'Aziz was Malik ibn Du'r.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas) concerning His saying ﴿Honor his residence﴾, that he said: "His station (manzilah)." Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated the like of it from Qatadah.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The most perceptive of people are three: al-'Aziz, when he perceived in Yusuf and said to his wife ﴿Honor his residence; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son﴾; the woman who came to Musa and said to her father ﴿O father, hire him﴾; and Abu Bakr when he appointed 'Umar as successor."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾, that he said: "The interpretation of dreams."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in Kitab al-Adad, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And when he reached his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾, that he said: "Thirty-three years."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "Forty years."

He narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Twenty-five years."

He narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "Thirty years." He narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Eighteen years."

He narrated from Rabi'ah, who said: "The ahlam (dreams/maturity of intellect)." 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated the like of it from al-Sha'bi.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Twenty years."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾, that he said: "It is understanding (fiqh), knowledge and intellect before prophethood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, that he said: "The guided ones (al-muhtadin)."

This is the start of the narration of Joseph's rescue and what came after it. The tafsir of "al-sayyara" has already been given earlier. Here it means a passing caravan travelling from Syria to Egypt. They went astray and wandered until they camped near the well. The well was in a desolate spot far from settlements. The "warid" (the one who comes down to the water to draw it for the people) was, according to the exegetes, named Malik ibn Dhu'r, from the Arab al-'Aariba.

﴿Then he let down his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down to fill it. One says "adla dalwahu" when one lets it down to fill it, and "dallaha" when one draws it up. This is what al-Asma'i and others said.

Joseph held on to the rope. When the bucket came up out of the well, the warid saw him and ﴿said: "Good news!"﴾ The people of Madina, Makka and Basra, and the people of Syria, read it with "bushra" in the construct form with the pronoun attached. The people of Kufa read "ya bushra" without the attachment. The meaning of calling out to good news is that he wanted it to be present at that time, as if he said: "This is the time of your coming and the moment of your arrival." It has also been said that he called out to a man named Bushra. The first is more preferred.

Al-Nahhas said: The meaning of calling out to good news is announcing the good news to whoever is present. This is more emphatic than saying "bashshartuhu," just as one says "ya 'ajaban," meaning "O wonder! This is one of your days, so be present." He said: This is the position of Sibawayh.

﴿And they concealed him﴾, meaning the warid and his companions who were with him concealed Joseph and did not reveal him to them. It has been said that they did not hide him, but rather concealed the fact that they had found him in the well. They claimed that the people of the water had handed him over to them so that they could sell him for them in Egypt. It has also been said that the subject of "asarroohu" refers to Joseph's brothers and the object refers to Joseph. That is because his brother Yahudha used to come to him every day with food. On the day he came out of the well, Yahudha came and informed his brothers, and they came to the caravan and said: "This is a slave who ran away from us," and bought him from them. Joseph kept silent for fear that they would take him and kill him.

The first is more preferred.

The accusative of ﴿merchandise﴾ (bid'a) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they concealed him while he was merchandise, that is, goods for trade. "Bid'a" is what is taken out of wealth (yubda'), that is, cut off from it, because it is a portion of the wealth that is traded. It was said that the warid and his companions said to them that he was merchandise they had acquired from Syria, for fear that they would share in him.

In His words ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what they do﴾ there is a severe warning for whoever's action was the cause of what Joseph suffered of trials, and of the humiliation he came to be subjected to through the process of buying and selling. He was "the noble son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble": Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, as our Prophet (ﷺ) said in describing him with that.

His words: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams﴾. It is said "shara" meaning "ishtara" (bought), and "shara" meaning "baa'a" (sold).

The poet said:
"I sold a cloak, would that after one cloak I had been a [ruined] man"
meaning I sold it.

Another said:
"So when he bought her, tears overflowed in tears,"
meaning he bought her.

What is meant here is: they sold him. That is, the warid and his companions sold him for a paltry price, meaning deficient or counterfeit. It has been said that it refers to Joseph's brothers according to the earlier view, and it has been said that it refers to the caravan, and the meaning is: they bought him. It has been said that "bakhs" means injustice, and it has been said that it means unlawful.

It has been said they sold him for twenty dirhams, and it has been said for forty. "Dirhams" is a substitution for "thaman" (price), that is, dinars. "Ma'duda" (counted) is an attribute of "dirhams," and in this there is an indication that they were few, to be counted and not weighed, because they did not weigh anything less than an "uqiyya," which is forty dirhams.

﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to him﴾. One says "zahidtu" and "zahadtu" with fatha and kasra on the ha'. Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i said: The people of the language said: "zahida fihi" means he desired it, and "zahida 'anhu" means he desired it. The meaning is that they were among those who were disinclined toward him, who did not care about him, and for this reason they sold him for that paltry price. That is because they had picked him up, and one who picks up a thing treats it with contempt. The pronoun in "kanu" refers to what precedes it, according to the difference of opinions about it.

﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾: he is the 'Aziz, who was over the treasuries of Egypt and was a minister to the king of Egypt. He was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid from the 'Amaliq. It has been said that the king was Pharaoh of Musa. It has been said he bought him for twenty dinars. The reference is to what preceded of his deliverance from his brothers, his removal from the well, and the 'Aziz's heart being inclined toward him. That is, like that wondrous establishment, We established Joseph until he became empowered in commanding and forbidding. One says "makkanahu fihi," meaning he established him in it, and "makkana lahu fihi," meaning he made a place for him in it. Because the two meanings are close, each is used in place of the other.

His words: ﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾. This is a reason for an omitted thing being caused, as if it were said: We did that establishment so that We might teach him the interpretation of events, or that rescue was for this reason. Or it is coordinated with something presumed, which is that it is said: We established Joseph so that there would follow from that what followed of what happened between him and the 'Aziz's wife, and that We might teach him the interpretation of events. The meaning of "interpretation of events" is the interpretation of dreams, for they were among the causes by which he reached the level of establishment he attained. It has been said the meaning of "interpretation of events" is understanding the secrets of the divine books and the ways of the prophets before him. There is no obstacle to taking it in all these senses.

﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾, meaning over His own affair. Nothing can resist Him, and none of His creatures can overpower Him in it.

﴿His command is only, when He intends a thing, that He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. ﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾, meaning they do not come to know the unseen of Allah and what is folded within it of great secrets and beneficial wisdoms. It has been said that Allah, glorified is He, may inform some of His servants of some of His unseen, as in His words: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27]. It has been said the meaning is: But most of mankind do not know that Allah is dominant over His affair, and they are the polytheists and those who do not believe in predestination.

His words: ﴿And when he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. "Al-ashudd" (full strength).

Sibawayh said: It is a plural whose singular is "shidda."

Al-Kisa'i said: Its singular is "shadd."

Abu 'Ubayd said: It has no singular from its own form among the Arabs. This is refuted by the poet's words:
"My covenant with him was the day's ashudd, as if he had dyed his fingers and head with henna."

"Al-ashudd" is the time of attaining full strength, after which decline follows.

It has been said it is thirty-three years. It has been said it is reaching puberty. It has been said it is eighteen years. It has been said other than that, as we have already explained in al-Nisa' and al-An'am.

"Hukm" (judgment) is what he issued of rulings within the authority of the king of Egypt. "'Ilm" (knowledge) is knowledge of the judgment he was ruling by. It has been said "'aql" (intellect), understanding and prophethood. Al-Sabiyy said: The intended meaning of this judgment and knowledge which Allah gave him is the increase in them.

﴿And thus We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning and like that wondrous reward, We reward the doers of good. So whoever does good in his deed, Allah makes his reward good, and makes the outcome of good among what He rewards him with. This is general, and Joseph's reward for his good patience enters under it first of all. Al-Tabari said: Although its wording appears to apply to every doer of good, what is intended is Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah, the Exalted, says: Just as this Joseph did, then I gave him what I gave him, so likewise I will rescue you from the polytheists of your people who intend enmity against you, and I will establish you in the land.

What we have mentioned is preferred, namely taking the generality in its apparent sense, so that what Ibn Jarir al-Tabari mentioned enters under it.
