You are written among the prophets, and yet you act like the foolish?" It is also said that he saw the image of Ya'qub on the wall, biting his finger and threatening him. And other things have been said which would take long to mention.

The conclusion is that he saw something that came between him and what he desired.

His saying: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾. The kaf (ك) is an adjective for a deleted verbal noun. The reference of "dhalika" (that) is either to the showing (ira'ah) implied by ﴿had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, or to the strengthening (tathbit) understood from that. That is: "We showed him the like of that showing," or "We strengthened him with the like of that strengthening." ﴿That We might turn away from him evil﴾, meaning everything that would harm him, ﴿and immorality﴾, meaning every matter of extreme ugliness. It has been said that "evil" means betrayal of the Aziz regarding his household, and "immorality" means fornication. It has also been said that "evil" means desire, and "immorality" means physical contact. It has also been said that "evil" means a bad reputation.

Taking it in its general sense is preferable, so that it includes first and foremost whatever the context indicates. The clause ﴿Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾ is a reason for what precedes it.

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited al-mukhlisin (المُخْلِصِينَ) with a kasra on the lam. The others recited it with a fatha.

According to the first reading, the meaning is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was one who sincerely devoted his obedience to Allah. According to the second, it means he was one whom Allah chose (istakhlasahu) for prophethood.

He, peace be upon him, was both sincere and chosen.

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾, meaning they raced to it. The preposition is deleted and the verb is connected directly to its object, or the verb is given the meaning of another verb that is transitive by itself, like ibtadara al-bab (they hastened to the door). This statement is connected to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interruption. The manner of their racing was that Yusuf wanted to flee and exit through the door, while the wife of the Aziz wanted to get there first to prevent him. The word "door" is singular here but plural in what preceded, because their racing was to the door through which one exits the house.

﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾, meaning she pulled his shirt from behind him so that it tore down to the bottom. Al-qadd (القَدّ) means cutting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. Al-qatt (القَطّ) with a ta is used for what is crosswise. That happened when Yusuf fled upon seeing the proof of his Lord, and she wanted to prevent him from leaving by pulling his shirt.

﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾, meaning they found the Aziz there. By "master" (sayyid) is meant the husband, because the Copts call the husband "sayyid." He did not say "their master" (sayyidahuma), because his ownership of Yusuf was not valid, so he was not a master to him.

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the penalty for one who intended evil to your household, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ is a new sentence, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: "What happened between them when they found her husband at the door?" The word "ma" is interrogative. By "evil" is meant here fornication. She said this statement seeking a stratagem and to conceal herself, so she attributed what she had done to Yusuf: what penalty does he deserve who does such a deed? Then she answered her own question with her words: ﴿except that he be imprisoned﴾, meaning the penalty for him is only that he be imprisoned. It is possible that "ma" is negative, meaning: his penalty is none but imprisonment or a painful punishment. It is said that the painful punishment is flogging with whips. The apparent meaning is that it includes whatever counts as a painful punishment, whether beating or otherwise. The vagueness regarding the punishment adds to its frightfulness.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself"﴾ is a new sentence, like the first.

The meaning of solicitation has already been explained. That is: she is the one who asked me for that, and I did not intend her any harm.

﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾, meaning from her relatives. The judgment between them was called testimony because it requires examination and scrutiny. It is said that when the matter was confused for the Aziz, he needed a judge to decide between them so that the truthful might be distinguished from the liar.

It is said that he was her cousin standing with the Aziz at the door. It is also said he was her maternal cousin. It is also said he was an infant in the cradle who spoke.

[p. 691]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 23–30 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Suhayli said: "This is the sound view, because of the hadith reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning those who spoke in the cradle." He mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. It was also said that he was a wise man whom the Aziz (the governor) consulted on his affairs, and that he was one of the woman's relatives. ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾, meaning: the witness said this statement, deducing from it the evidence for distinguishing the truthful one of the two from the liar, namely that if Yusuf's shirt is torn from the front, that is, from the direction of the front, ﴿then she has told the truth﴾, meaning she has told the truth that he intended her harm, ﴿and he is among the liars﴾ in his claim that she solicited him.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿min qubul﴾ with a *damma* on the *lam* (*min qubulu*). Likewise they read ﴿min duburu﴾ (with a *damma* on the *ra*). Al-Zajjaj said: "They made both of them (qubul and dubur) into ends (*ghayat*, adverbial limits of direction), like *qabla* and *ba'da*. It is as if it were said: *min qablih* and *min dubur-h*. When the genitive complement (*mudaf ilayh*) is omitted while still intended, the *mudaf* becomes an end after the complement, which had itself been the end."

﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind﴾, meaning from his back, ﴿then she has lied in her claim against him, and he is among the truthful in his claim against her.﴾ It is not hidden that these two conditional sentences have no necessary connection between their protasis and apodosis, neither rationally nor customarily. There is only a mere indicator that is not consistent, for it is possible that she pulled him toward herself while he was facing her, so that the shirt is torn from behind, and that she pulled him while he was turning away from her, so that the shirt is torn from the front.

﴿So when he saw his shirt﴾, that is, the Aziz saw the shirt of Yusuf ﴿torn from behind﴾, ﴿he said: "Indeed, it is a plot of your women."﴾ That is, this matter over which they disagreed, or that your statement ﴿"What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your family"﴾ ﴿is a plot of your (kind)﴾, meaning it is of the kind of your plotting, O women. ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great.﴾ *Al-kayd* means cunning and stratagem.

Then the Aziz addressed Yusuf with his words: ﴿"Yusuf, turn away from this"﴾, meaning from this matter that has occurred, and keep it secret and do not speak of it. Then he turned to her with address and said: ﴿"And ask forgiveness for your sin, for you have indeed been among the sinners,"﴾ that is, among their kind because of that. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, the command to seek forgiveness. He did not say *al-khati'at* (feminine) but *al-khati'in* (masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine, as in His words ﴿and she was among the devout﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. The meaning of ﴿among the sinners﴾ is among the deliberate ones; it is said *khati'a* when one sins intentionally. It was also said that the one who spoke this statement to Yusuf and to the wife of the Aziz was the witness who judged between them.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿And she in whose house he was solicited him for himself﴾: "She is the wife of the Aziz."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd who said: "She solicited him when he reached the stage of men."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Hayta laka﴾, that he said: "*Halumma laka* (come, for you): she was calling him to herself."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him: "*Halumma laka* in Coptic." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan who said: "It is a word in Syriac, meaning: *'alayka* (upon you)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "Its meaning is *ta'ala* (come)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that it is an Arabic dialect by which she was calling him to herself.

Abu Ubayda, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he recited *hi'tu laka* with a *kasra* on the *ha'* and a *damma* on the *ta'*, hamzated, and said: "*Tahayya'tu laka* (I have prepared myself for you)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾ that he said: "*Sayyidi* (my master)." He meant: the husband of the woman.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Abbas who said: "When she desired him she adorned herself, then lay down on her bed. When he desired her he sat between her legs, untying his garments. Then he was called from the sky: 'O son of Ya'qub, do not be like a bird whose feathers have been plucked, so that it remains featherless.' He did not heed the call at all until he saw the proof of his Lord, Jibril, in the form of Ya'qub, biting on his finger. He was startled, and his desire came out from his fingertips. He leapt toward the door and found it locked. Yusuf raised his leg and struck the lower door with it, and it opened for him. She followed him and overtook him, placed her hands on his shirt and tore it until it reached the muscle of his calf. They found her master at the door."

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿She desired him and he desired her﴾ that he said: "She was greedy for him and he was greedy for her." Part of his greed was that he resolved to undo the belt. Then she went to an idol of hers, adorned with pearls and rubies, in a corner of the house, and covered it with a white cloth between herself and him. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before my god that he should see me in this state of shame." Yusuf said: "Are you ashamed before an idol that does not eat or drink, and I am not ashamed before my God, who watches over every soul for what it has earned?" Then he said: "Do not let her touch me ever." That is the proof he saw.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub was depicted for him, and he struck his chest with his hand, and his desire came out from his fingertips."

The exegetes have gone to great lengths in specifying the proof that he saw, and their statements differ greatly on this.

Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Thabit: "*Al-sayyid* is the husband," meaning in His words ﴿and they found her master at the door﴾. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment﴾ that he said: "The shackle."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾ that he said: "A child whom God made to speak, who was in the house."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Four spoke while they were infants: the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Isa son of Maryam."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾ that he said: "He was a man with a beard."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him who said: "He was among the king's intimates."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan who said: "He was a man who had understanding and knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: "He was a paternal cousin of hers, who was wise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid who said: "He was neither a human nor a jinn; he is a creature among the creatures of God."

I say: Perhaps he did not recall His words, Exalted is He: ﴿from her family﴾.

Al-murawada (المُراوَدَةُ) means seeking or desiring something gently and softly. Some say it derives from al-rawd (الرَّوْد), meaning gentleness and patience. It is said: arwidni, meaning "give me time." Others say it derives from rada yarudu, meaning to come and go. The sense is that she acted toward him in her solicitation like one who deceives, and from this comes al-ra'id (الرّائِد), the one who seeks water and pasture. It may be specifically restricted to attempting sexual intercourse. It is said: "Fulan solicited his slave-girl for herself" (raawada fulanun jariyatahu 'an nafsiha), and "she solicited him for himself" (raawadat-hu hiya 'an nafsihi), when each of the two tries to have intercourse. It has the form of mufa'ala, and originally it should be from both sides. Here the cause is placed on one side in place of the effect. So since Yusuf, peace be upon him, had been given perfection of form and an increase in beauty, which was the cause of the wife of the Aziz soliciting him, he is called murawid (مُراوِد, one who is solicited).

As for His saying ﴿the woman in whose house he was﴾, He said this rather than "the wife of the Aziz" or "Zulaykha," intending to emphasize the situation while disliking the explicit naming of the woman and maintaining her concealment. ﴿And she bolted the doors﴾. It is said that this form (ghallaqa) indicates multiplicity, so one says ghallaqa al-abwab (bolted the doors), and one does not say ghalaqa al-bab (locked the door). Rather one says aghlaqa al-bab, and it may be said aghlaqa al-abwab. From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq about Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala':

"I kept locking doors and opening them, until you came to Abu 'Amr ibn 'Ammar."

It is said the doors were seven.

His saying ﴿Hayta laka﴾ (هَيْتَ لَكَ).

Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Hamzah and al-A'mash recited it with a fatha on the ha, a sukun on the ya, and a fatha on the ta. This reading was also recited by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. Ibn Mas'ud said: "Do not be excessive in recitation; it is merely like one of you saying halumma (come) and ta'al (come)."

Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Nahwi recited it with a fatha on the ha and a kasra on the ta.

'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Ibn Kathir recited hayta with a fatha on the ha and a damma on the ta. From this is the verse of Tarafah:

"My people are not the most distant when a caller from the clan says: Hayta!"

Abu Ja'far and Nafi' recited it with a kasra on the ha, a sukun on the ya, and a fatha on the ta.

'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, in one narration from him, and Hisham recited it with a kasra on the ha, followed by a silent hamzah, and a damma on the ta.

Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria recited it with a kasra on the ha, the hamzah, and a fatha on the ta.

The meaning of hayta in all the readings is the meaning of halumma and ta'al, because it is one of the ism al-fi'l (verb-nouns), except in the reading of the one who recited with a kasra on the ha, followed by a hamzah and a damma on the ta. That reading means: "I have prepared myself for you" (tahayya'tu laka).

Abu 'Amr denied this reading. Abu 'Ubaydah said: Abu 'Amr was asked about the reading of the one who recited with a kasra on the ha and the hamzah and a damma on the ta, and he said: "It is false to take it to mean 'I have prepared myself.' Go and survey the Arabs until you reach Yemen; do you know anyone who says it this way?" al-Kisa'i also denied it.

Al-Nahhas said: "It is good according to the Basrans, because it is said: haa al-rajulu yahaa'u and yahi'u haay'atan (the man prepared himself)." Al-Zajjaj preferred the first reading and recited the verse of Tarafah with hayta with a fatha. From this is the verse of a poet about 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him:

"Convey to the Commander of the Faithful, the brother of Iraq, when you come:
Indeed Iraq and its people are at peace with you, so hayta, hayta."

In the first readings in which the lam is found in "laka," it is a clarifying lam with the meaning of ism al-fi'l, meaning: "for you" (laka). I say: this is as in halumma laka.

The grammarians said: hayta comes with all three vowels. The fatha is for lightness, the kasra for the meeting of two sukuns, and the damma is by analogy with haythu. When it is clarified with the lam, as in hayta laka, it is a sound standing in place of the verbal noun, like uff lahu (an expression of disgust), meaning: "to you I say this." If it is not clarified with the lam, it is a sound standing in place of the verbal noun of the verb, and so it is an ism al-fi'l, either as a statement, meaning "I have prepared myself," or as a command, meaning "come forward."

Al-Sihah (الصِّحاح) says: it is said huwita bihi and hiyta bihi when one calls out to him and summons him. From this is the verse of the poet:

"Every youth drives them on with cries of hayyat."

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan that it is a Syriac word whose meaning is that she was calling him to herself.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Kisa'i used to say: "It is a dialect of the people of Hawran, which reached the people of the Hijaz, and its meaning is 'come.'" Abu 'Ubaydah said: "So I asked a learned elder from Hawran, and he mentioned that it is their dialect."

﴿He said: "Allah forbid!"﴾ meaning: I seek refuge in Allah with a refuge from what you call me to. It is a verbal noun in the accusative, governed by a deleted verb and attached to the name of Allah, glorified is He. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my stay good﴾ is a reason for his refusal, based on some of the causes that are closer to the understanding of the wife of the Aziz. The pronoun is for the matter, meaning: the matter is that my Lord, meaning the Aziz, that is, my master who raised me and made my stay good, when he commanded you with his words: ﴿Honour his residence﴾. So how could I betray him in his household and respond to you in what you desire from that?

Al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: Allah is my Lord; He took care of me with His kindness, so I do not commit what He has forbidden. The clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ is another reason for his refusal to respond to her. Al-falah (الفَلاح) means success. The meaning is: the wrongdoers will not attain their aims. Among the wrongdoers are those who fall into such a sin as the wife of the Aziz seeks from Yusuf.

His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾. It is said: hamma bi-al-amr means he intended it and resolved upon it.

The meaning is that he desired to be intimate with her, just as she desired to be intimate with him, and each of them inclined toward the other according to the requirement of human nature and innate disposition. Yet Yusuf, peace be upon him, did not intend that by choice, as is shown by what preceded of his seeking refuge in Allah. And that is a kind of wrong.

Since the prophets are protected from desiring sin and intending it, the scholars have gone to extremes in interpreting this verse with something that involves some artificiality. Among that is what Abu Hatim said: "I was reading the rare words of the Qur'an to Abu 'Ubaydah, and when I reached ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her﴾, he said: 'This is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir): as if he said: "She desired him, and had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her."'"

Tha'lab, Ahmad ibn Yahya, said: meaning Zulaykha desired the sin and was persistent, while Yusuf desired but did not carry out what he desired. So there is a difference between the two desires. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I desired them from the Pass of Lu'lu', and I cured the burning passions of love from my heart."

This is merely a whisper of the soul without resolve. It is also said: hamma bi-ha means he intended to strike her. It is also said: hamma bi-ha in the sense of wishing to marry her. The majority of the commentators, from the early and later generations, have gone to what we have mentioned, interpreting the wording in its linguistic meaning. What points to this is what will come later in His saying: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret﴾ [Yusuf: 52], and His saying: ﴿Nor do I absolve myself; indeed, the soul is ever inciting to evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53]. Mere desire does not contradict infallibility, for infallibility means protection from falling into sin, and that is what is required.

The answer to "lawla" in ﴿Had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾ is omitted, meaning: had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord, he would have done what he desired.

They differed about what this proof he saw was. It is said that when she desired him and he desired her, Zulaykha went to an idol she had in a corner of the house and covered it with a cloth. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before my God that he should see me in this state." Yusuf said: "I have more right to be ashamed before Allah, exalted is He."

It is also said that he saw written on the ceiling of the house: ﴿And do not approach adultery; indeed, it is ever an immorality﴾ [al-Isra': 32], and so on. It is said he saw a hand on which was written: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10]. It is also said that the proof is his remembrance of the covenant of Allah and His pledge, and what He took from His servants. It is also said that a voice called: "O Yusuf! You are written among the prophets, and yet you act like the foolish?" It is also said that he saw the image of Ya'qub on the wall, biting his finger and threatening him. And other things have been said which would take long to mention.

The conclusion is that he saw something that came between him and what he desired.

His saying: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality﴾. The kaf (ك) is an adjective for a deleted verbal noun. The reference of "dhalika" (that) is either to the showing (ira'ah) implied by ﴿had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, or to the strengthening (tathbit) understood from that. That is: "We showed him the like of that showing," or "We strengthened him with the like of that strengthening." ﴿That We might turn away from him evil﴾, meaning everything that would harm him, ﴿and immorality﴾, meaning every matter of extreme ugliness. It has been said that "evil" means betrayal of the Aziz regarding his household, and "immorality" means fornication. It has also been said that "evil" means desire, and "immorality" means physical contact. It has also been said that "evil" means a bad reputation.

Taking it in its general sense is preferable, so that it includes first and foremost whatever the context indicates. The clause ﴿Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾ is a reason for what precedes it.

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited al-mukhlisin (المُخْلِصِينَ) with a kasra on the lam. The others recited it with a fatha.

According to the first reading, the meaning is that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was one who sincerely devoted his obedience to Allah. According to the second, it means he was one whom Allah chose (istakhlasahu) for prophethood.

He, peace be upon him, was both sincere and chosen.

﴿And they both raced to the door﴾, meaning they raced to it. The preposition is deleted and the verb is connected directly to its object, or the verb is given the meaning of another verb that is transitive by itself, like ibtadara al-bab (they hastened to the door). This statement is connected to His saying: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had it not been that he saw the proof of his Lord﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interruption. The manner of their racing was that Yusuf wanted to flee and exit through the door, while the wife of the Aziz wanted to get there first to prevent him. The word "door" is singular here but plural in what preceded, because their racing was to the door through which one exits the house.

﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾, meaning she pulled his shirt from behind him so that it tore down to the bottom. Al-qadd (القَدّ) means cutting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. Al-qatt (القَطّ) with a ta is used for what is crosswise. That happened when Yusuf fled upon seeing the proof of his Lord, and she wanted to prevent him from leaving by pulling his shirt.

﴿And they found her husband at the door﴾, meaning they found the Aziz there. By "master" (sayyid) is meant the husband, because the Copts call the husband "sayyid." He did not say "their master" (sayyidahuma), because his ownership of Yusuf was not valid, so he was not a master to him.

The clause ﴿She said: "What is the penalty for one who intended evil to your household, except that he be imprisoned or [suffer] a painful punishment?"﴾ is a new sentence, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: "What happened between them when they found her husband at the door?" The word "ma" is interrogative. By "evil" is meant here fornication. She said this statement seeking a stratagem and to conceal herself, so she attributed what she had done to Yusuf: what penalty does he deserve who does such a deed? Then she answered her own question with her words: ﴿except that he be imprisoned﴾, meaning the penalty for him is only that he be imprisoned. It is possible that "ma" is negative, meaning: his penalty is none but imprisonment or a painful punishment. It is said that the painful punishment is flogging with whips. The apparent meaning is that it includes whatever counts as a painful punishment, whether beating or otherwise. The vagueness regarding the punishment adds to its frightfulness.

The clause ﴿He said: "It was she who sought to seduce me from myself"﴾ is a new sentence, like the first.

The meaning of solicitation has already been explained. That is: she is the one who asked me for that, and I did not intend her any harm.

It is said that when the matter was confused for the Aziz, he needed a judge to decide between them so that the truthful might be distinguished from the liar.

It is said that he was her cousin standing with the Aziz at the door. It is also said he was her maternal cousin. It is also said he was an infant in the cradle who spoke.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 23–30 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Suhayli said: "This is the sound view, because of the hadith reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning those who spoke in the cradle." He mentioned among them the witness of Yusuf. It was also said that he was a wise man whom the Aziz (the governor) consulted on his affairs, and that he was one of the woman's relatives. ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front﴾, meaning: the witness said this statement, deducing from it the evidence for distinguishing the truthful one of the two from the liar, namely that if Yusuf's shirt is torn from the front, that is, from the direction of the front, ﴿then she has told the truth﴾, meaning she has told the truth that he intended her harm, ﴿and he is among the liars﴾ in his claim that she solicited him.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿min qubul﴾ with a *damma* on the *lam* (*min qubulu*). Likewise they read ﴿min duburu﴾ (with a *damma* on the *ra*). Al-Zajjaj said: "They made both of them (qubul and dubur) into ends (*ghayat*, adverbial limits of direction), like *qabla* and *ba'da*. It is as if it were said: *min qablih* and *min dubur-h*. When the genitive complement (*mudaf ilayh*) is omitted while still intended, the *mudaf* becomes an end after the complement, which had itself been the end."

﴿And if his shirt is torn from behind﴾, meaning from his back, ﴿then she has lied in her claim against him, and he is among the truthful in his claim against her.﴾ It is not hidden that these two conditional sentences have no necessary connection between their protasis and apodosis, neither rationally nor customarily. There is only a mere indicator that is not consistent, for it is possible that she pulled him toward herself while he was facing her, so that the shirt is torn from behind, and that she pulled him while he was turning away from her, so that the shirt is torn from the front.

﴿So when he saw his shirt﴾, that is, the Aziz saw the shirt of Yusuf ﴿torn from behind﴾, ﴿he said: "Indeed, it is a plot of your women."﴾ That is, this matter over which they disagreed, or that your statement ﴿"What is the recompense for one who intended harm to your family"﴾ ﴿is a plot of your (kind)﴾, meaning it is of the kind of your plotting, O women. ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great.﴾ *Al-kayd* means cunning and stratagem.

Then the Aziz addressed Yusuf with his words: ﴿"Yusuf, turn away from this"﴾, meaning from this matter that has occurred, and keep it secret and do not speak of it. Then he turned to her with address and said: ﴿"And ask forgiveness for your sin, for you have indeed been among the sinners,"﴾ that is, among their kind because of that. The clause is a justification for what precedes it, the command to seek forgiveness. He did not say *al-khati'at* (feminine) but *al-khati'in* (masculine plural), giving precedence to the masculine over the feminine, as in His words ﴿and she was among the devout﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. The meaning of ﴿among the sinners﴾ is among the deliberate ones; it is said *khati'a* when one sins intentionally. It was also said that the one who spoke this statement to Yusuf and to the wife of the Aziz was the witness who judged between them.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿And she in whose house he was solicited him for himself﴾: "She is the wife of the Aziz."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd who said: "She solicited him when he reached the stage of men."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Hayta laka﴾, that he said: "*Halumma laka* (come, for you): she was calling him to herself."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him: "*Halumma laka* in Coptic." Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan who said: "It is a word in Syriac, meaning: *'alayka* (upon you)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "Its meaning is *ta'ala* (come)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that it is an Arabic dialect by which she was calling him to herself.

Abu Ubayda, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he recited *hi'tu laka* with a *kasra* on the *ha'* and a *damma* on the *ta'*, hamzated, and said: "*Tahayya'tu laka* (I have prepared myself for you)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Indeed, he is my lord﴾ that he said: "*Sayyidi* (my master)." He meant: the husband of the woman.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Abbas who said: "When she desired him she adorned herself, then lay down on her bed. When he desired her he sat between her legs, untying his garments. Then he was called from the sky: 'O son of Ya'qub, do not be like a bird whose feathers have been plucked, so that it remains featherless.' He did not heed the call at all until he saw the proof of his Lord, Jibril, in the form of Ya'qub, biting on his finger. He was startled, and his desire came out from his fingertips. He leapt toward the door and found it locked. Yusuf raised his leg and struck the lower door with it, and it opened for him. She followed him and overtook him, placed her hands on his shirt and tore it until it reached the muscle of his calf. They found her master at the door."

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His words ﴿She desired him and he desired her﴾ that he said: "She was greedy for him and he was greedy for her." Part of his greed was that he resolved to undo the belt. Then she went to an idol of hers, adorned with pearls and rubies, in a corner of the house, and covered it with a white cloth between herself and him. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "I am ashamed before my god that he should see me in this state of shame." Yusuf said: "Are you ashamed before an idol that does not eat or drink, and I am not ashamed before my God, who watches over every soul for what it has earned?" Then he said: "Do not let her touch me ever." That is the proof he saw.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub was depicted for him, and he struck his chest with his hand, and his desire came out from his fingertips."

The exegetes have gone to great lengths in specifying the proof that he saw, and their statements differ greatly on this.

Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Thabit: "*Al-sayyid* is the husband," meaning in His words ﴿and they found her master at the door﴾. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿except that he be imprisoned or a painful punishment﴾ that he said: "The shackle."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾ that he said: "A child whom God made to speak, who was in the house."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Four spoke while they were infants: the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Isa son of Maryam."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾ that he said: "He was a man with a beard."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him who said: "He was among the king's intimates."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan who said: "He was a man who had understanding and knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zayd ibn Aslam who said: "He was a paternal cousin of hers, who was wise."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid who said: "He was neither a human nor a jinn; he is a creature among the creatures of God."

I say: Perhaps he did not recall His words, Exalted is He: ﴿from her family﴾.

[p. 692]

The Arabic word *nuswah* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* (*nuswatun*), which is the reading of al-A'mash, al-Fadl and Sulayman. It is also said as *niswatun* with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, which is the reading of the rest. The meaning is a group of women, and the verb attached to them may be masculine or feminine.

It is said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-'Azīz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, the wife of his jailer, and the wife of his chamberlain.

In the speech of the Arabs, *al-fatā* means the young man and *al-fatāh* means the young woman. Here it means his servant. One says *fatāy* and *fatātī*, meaning "my servant" and "my maidservant."

The clause ﴿قَدْ شَغَفَهَا حُبًّا﴾ (indeed, love has gripped her) is in a position of *raf'* (nominative) as a second predicate of the subject, or in a position of *naṣb* (accusative) as a circumstantial clause. The meaning of *shaghafahā ḥubban* is: his love overwhelmed her. It is also said that his love entered into her *shighāf*.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the *shighāf* of the heart is its covering, which is a membrane over it. It is also said that it is the middle of the heart.

On this view, the meaning is: his love entered into her *shighāf* and so overcame her. Al-Asma'i cited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*"He follows her, and she is for him a shighāf."*

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Ibn Muhayṣin and al-Hasan read *shaʿafahā* with the unpointed *ʿayn* (*ʿ*). Ibn al-A'rabi said: its meaning is that he made his love run over her.

Others read it with the pointed *ghayn* (*gh*). Al-Jawhari said: *shaʿafahu al-ḥubbu* means that love burned his heart. Abu Zayd said: it means that it made him ill.

Al-Nahhas said: according to most lexicographers the meaning is that it has taken her in every direction, because *shiʿāf al-jibāl* are the peaks of the mountains. One says *shaghifa bi-dhālika shaghafan* (with a sukūn on the *ghayn*) when one is passionately attached to it. Abu 'Ubayda cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will you kill me, when I have gripped her heart,*
*as a man who has climbed high grips a mahnūwa (a sick or emaciated she-camel)?"*

He said: the agony of love is compared to this.

Al-Hasan read *qad shaghufahā* with a *ḍamma* on the *ghayn*. Al-Nahhas said: it is also reported as *qad shaghifahā* with a *kasra* on the *ghayn*, but this is not known in the speech of the Arabs; only *shaghafahā* with a *fatḥa* on the *ghayn* is known. It is said that the *shighāf* is the thin membrane that clings to the liver and is not seen, which is the white membrane. So his love clung to her heart as the membrane clings to the liver.

The clause ﴿إِنَّا لَنَرَاهَا فِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ (indeed, we see her in clear error) confirms the content of what came before it. The meaning: "Indeed we see her," that is, we know her, "in this act of hers, which is seeking to seduce her servant, in error far from the path of right guidance and correctness, clear, not confused for one who looks at it."

[p. 693]

When the wife of al-'Azīz heard of their *makr* (scheming), that is, of their backbiting about her, the backbiting was called *makr* because both involve concealment. It is also said that they intended by this to reach a means of seeing Yusuf, and so their talk was called *makr*. It is also said that she had confided a secret to them and they spread her secret, and so it was called *makr*. She sent for them, that is, invited them to her, so that they might look at Yusuf and fall into what she had fallen into.

﴿وَأَعْتَدَتْ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَأً﴾ (and she prepared for them a reclining place) means she prepared for them seats on which they might recline. *A'taddat* is from *al-i'tidād*, which is everything you make ready for something.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mutkan* with a light *ṭā'* and without hamza. *Al-mutk* is the citron in the language of the Copts. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We drink sin openly from the cup,*
*and we see the citron passed among us."*

It is also said that this is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, and it is said this was reported from al-Akhfash.

Al-Farra' said that it is rose water.

The majority read *muttaka'an* with hamza and *tashdīd* (doubling of the *tā'*). The most correct of what has been said about it is that it is a sitting place. It is also said that it is food. It is also said that *al-muttaka'* is everything one reclines upon at food, drink or conversation.

Al-Qutaybi reported that one says *ittaka'nā 'inda fulān*, meaning "we ate at so-and-so's." From this is the verse of the poet:

*"So we were shaded in favor, and we reclined,*
*and we drank lawful drink from its jars."*

This is supported by His words ﴿وَآتَتْ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِّنْهُنَّ سِكِّينًا﴾ (and she gave each one of them a knife), for that is only for something they would eat after cutting it. *Al-sikkīn* (the knife) may be masculine or feminine, as al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said.

Al-Jawhari said: the more common usage of it is masculine. The purpose of giving each one of them a knife is that they would cut what needed cutting from the food. It is possible that she intended by this what would happen from them, that is, the cutting of their own hands. And she said to Yusuf: "Go out to them," that is, in the state in which they are, of reclining, eating and cutting what needs cutting of the food.

His words ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَيْنَهُ أَكْبَرْنَهُ﴾ (so when they saw him, they greatly admired him) mean they glorified him. It is also said that it means they menstruated. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When they see the stallion from atop a hill,*
*they neigh and ejaculate the spurting semen."*

It is also said that it means they menstruated.

Al-Azhari said: *akbarna* in the sense of *ḥain* (menstruated) and the *hā'* is for pausing. One says *akbarati al-mar'a*, meaning the woman entered into the state of menstruation. It happened to them out of amazement and fright at what they witnessed of his surpassing beauty and his delightful loveliness. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We come to women in their purity,*
*and we do not come to women when they have menstruated the menstruation."*

Abu 'Ubayda and others denied this and said that this is not in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Zajjaj said: one says *akbarnahu* and one does not say *ḥiḍnahu*, so *al-ikbār* does not mean menstruation.

Al-Azhari answered and said: it is possible that the *hā'* is the *hā' al-waqf* (pausal *hā'*) and not the *hā' al-kināya* (pronominal *hā'*).

This was rejected on the ground that the *hā' al-waqf* drops in continuous speech.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the *hā'* is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of the verb: that is, they "greatly admired" (*akbarna ikbāran*) in the sense of "menstruated a menstruation" (*ḥiḍna ḥayḍan*).

﴿وَقَطَّعْنَ أَيْدِيَهُنَّ﴾ (and they cut their hands) means they wounded them. The intended meaning is not the cutting that separates the hand, but scratching and gashing. This is known in the language, as al-Nahhas said. One says *qaṭaʿa yada ṣāḥibihi* when he scratched it. It is also said that the intended meaning of *aydīhinna* here is their fingertips, and it is also said their sleeves.

The meaning: when Yusuf went out to them, they greatly admired him and were dumbfounded, and his beauty overwhelmed them so that their hands trembled and the cutting fell upon them, while they were preoccupied with what had come upon them, by which dreams are scattered, bodies tremble and minds depart.

﴿وَقُلْنَ حَاشَ لِلَّهِ﴾ (and they said, "Far be it from Allah!"). Thus Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read it with the *alif* in *ḥāshā*. The rest read it without it.

Al-Hasan read *ḥāsh lillāh* with a *sukūn* on the *shīn*. It is reported from him that he read *ḥāsh lillāh*. Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read *ḥāshā lillāh*.

Al-Zajjaj said: the root of the word is from *al-ḥāshiya*, meaning the side, as one says "I was on the side of so-and-so," that is, on his side. So your saying *ḥāshā li-Zayd* means: he kept away from him.

Abu 'Ali said: it is from *al-muḥāshāh* (keeping away). It is said that *ḥāsh* is a particle and *ḥāshā* is a verb. The discussion of the grammarians about this word is well known. Its meaning here is declaring Allah free of imperfection (*tanzīh*), as you say: "The people excepted Zayd," so the meaning of *ḥāshā lillāh* is: a clearing of Allah and a declaring Him free from imperfection.

His words ﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾ (this is not a human) — the use of *mā* to work like *laysa* (*iʿmāl mā ʿamalat laysa*) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the Qur'an was revealed in it, as in this verse and His words, glorified is He, ﴿مَا هُنَّ أُمَّهَاتِهِمْ﴾ (they are not their mothers) [al-Mujadila: 2]. As for the Banu Tamim, they do not make it work like *laysa*.

The Kufans said: its original form is *mā hādhā bi-basharin*, and when the *bā'* was dropped, it took the accusative (*naṣb*).

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: when I say *mā Zaydun bi-muntaliq*, the place of the *bā'* is a place of accusative, and so is the case with all the prepositions.

As for al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the majority of grammarians, they made it work like *laysa*, and the Basrans said likewise. The discussion is established in the books of grammar with its evidence and arguments.

They denied humanness of him only because he appeared in a form dressed in a wondrous beauty such as had not been seen in any human, and the beholders had not seen anything close to him in all human forms. Then, when they denied humanness of him for this reason, they affirmed for him angelhood, although they did not know the angels. But it is established in natural disposition that they (the angels) are in a form above the form of humans in essence and attributes, and that they surpass in everything, just as it is established that the devils are the opposite of that. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"I am not of humankind, but of an angel*
*who descended from the air of the sky, calling out."*

Al-Hasan read *mā hādhā bi-shirā'in*, taking the *bā'* as a preposition, with the *shīn* in the *kasra*: that is, "this is not a slave to be bought." This reading is weak and does not fit what follows it, His words ﴿إِنْ هَذَا إِلَّا مَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾ (this is none but a noble angel).

Know that it does not follow from the women's saying this that the angels' forms are better than the forms of the children of Adam, for they did not say it on evidence, but judged about the unseen merely by the belief settled in their natures, and that is not allowed, for Allah, glorified is He, says ﴿لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنسَانَ فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ﴾ (We certainly created man in the best stature) [al-Tin: 4].

The apparent meaning of this is that there was nothing like him among the kinds of created beings in the excellence of his form and the perfection of his shape. So what the author of al-Kashshaf said in this place is among his partisanship toward what was firmly fixed in his mind from the sayings of the Mu'tazilites (a rationalist school). Moreover, this question, I mean the question of the superiority of the angels over humans, is not among the matters of religion, neither in its source nor its branches. So how little it benefits the servants of Allah, and how much they need other matters of obligation instead of it.

﴿قَالَتْ فَذَلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ﴾ (She said, "That is the one you blamed me for") — the reference is to Yusuf, and the address is to the women: that is, "you reproached me about him."

She said this to them when she saw their infatuation with Yusuf, as a display of excuse for herself. The meaning of *fīhi* is: about his love. It is also said that the reference is to the love, and the pronoun also refers to it, and the meaning: "that love about which you blamed me is that very love." The first is preferable, and Ibn Jarir preferred it.

The root of *al-lawm* is describing with what is ugly. Then, when she displayed her excuse to the women by what they had witnessed of what they had fallen into upon his appearance to them, her chest could no longer contain what she felt in her heart of his love, so she confessed to that and stated plainly what had happened from her of seeking to seduce him. She said ﴿وَلَقَدْ رَاوَدْتُّهُ عَن نَّفْسِهِ فَاسْتَعْصَمَ﴾ (I did seek to seduce him, but he refused), that is, he kept himself chaste and refused what I wanted, seeking to preserve his soul from that. Then she threatened him if he did not do what she wanted, uncovering the cloak of modesty and tearing the veil of chastity, and she said ﴿وَلَئِن لَّمْ يَفْعَلْ مَا آمُرُهُ لَيُسْجَنَنَّ وَلَيَكُونًا مِّنَ الصَّاغِرِينَ﴾ (If he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and be among the humiliated). That is: if he does not do what she had commanded him in what was mentioned earlier, when she locked the doors and said "Come, you" (*hayta laka*), "he will certainly be imprisoned," that is, detained in prison, "and he will certainly be among the humiliated," the abject, because of the humiliation he would suffer, and be stripped of the blessing and honor, in her claim.

It was read *layakūnanna* with the *tashdīd* (doubled *nūn*) and with the lightened *nūn*. It is said that the lightened reading is preferable, because the *nūn* was written in the Muṣḥaf as an *alif* according to the rule of pausing, and that occurs only with the light *nūn*. As for *layusjanannа* (he will certainly be imprisoned), it is only with the doubled *nūn*.

When Yusuf heard her words and knew that this was her firm resolve, along with what he knew of the effectiveness of her word with her husband, al-'Azīz, he said, speaking privately to his Lord, glorified is He:

﴿رَبِّ السِّجْنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدْعُونَنِي إِلَيْهِ﴾ (My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to) — that is: O my Lord, the prison with which this woman threatened me is dearer to me than what they invite me to of compliance with them and falling into the great disobedience which takes away the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, entering the prison, and he omitted the annexed noun.

Abu Hatim reported that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, read *al-saḥn* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Abd al-Rahman, al-A'raj and Ya'qub read it likewise, and it is the verbal noun of *sajanahu sajnan* (he imprisoned him).

The attribution of the invitation to all of them is because the women encouraged him to comply with her and frightened him from opposing her. Then the same manner was followed in attributing the scheming to all of them, so He said: ﴿وَإِلَّا تَصْرِفْ عَنِّي كَيْدَهُنَّ﴾ (And unless You turn away their scheming from me). As for the scheming of the wife of al-'Azīz, that is what Allah, glorified is He, has related in this sūrah. As for the scheming of the rest of the women, it is what came before of the encouragement to him to comply and the frightening of him from opposing.

It is also said that each one of them would be alone with him and say to him: "O Yusuf, fulfill my need, for I am better for you than the wife of al-'Azīz." It is also said that he addressed the wife of al-'Azīz with what is suitable for addressing a group of women, out of honoring her, or as a shift from explicit speech to indirect reference.

*Al-kayd* is scheming. The *jazm* (apocope) of *aṣbu* is on the basis that it is the answer to the condition: that is, "I will incline (*amal*) to them," from *ṣabā yaṣbū* when one inclines and longs. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"To Hind my heart has inclined,*
*and Hind's love makes it incline."*

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 31–35 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And [that] I may be among the ignorant﴾ is conjoined to "I will incline" (aṣbu): that is, that I may be among those who are ignorant of what is forbidden to commit and who go ahead with it; or among those who act in the manner of the ignorant.

As for His saying ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾: when he said, "And if You do not turn away from me their plotting, I might incline toward them," this was, on his part, a veiled supplication (taʿarruḍ li-l-duʿāʾ), as though he had said, "O Allah, turn away from me their plotting." So Allah's responding to him is in this sense, because no sincere supplication had preceded it from him, peace be upon him. The meaning is that He showed kindness to him and protected him from falling into disobedience, for when He turned away from him their plotting, nothing of what they desired from him came to pass. The manner of attributing the plotting (kayd) to them has already been mentioned. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ gives the reason for what precedes it, namely the turning away of the women's plotting from him: that is, He is the All-Hearing of the supplications of those who call upon Him, the All-Knowing of the states of those who take refuge in Him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾ (shaghafahā), that he said: "It overcame her."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, regarding ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾, that he said: "The love of Yusuf killed her. Shaghaf is the deadly love, and shaghaf is a love short of that, while shighaf is the covering of the heart."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾, that he said: "She had fallen in love with him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿when she heard of their plotting﴾, that he said: "Of their talk."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan, ﴿when she heard of their plotting﴾, that he said: "Of their deed. Every 'makr' in the Qur'an is a deed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related, regarding His saying ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining-couch (muttaka')﴾, that he said: "She prepared for them a gathering place. Their custom was that when they set out the food-table they gave each person a knife to eat with. When they saw him, he said: ﴿when he came out to them, the women glorified him﴾" — he said: "they magnified him and looked at him, and began to slice their hands with the knives, while they thought they were cutting the food."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining-couch﴾, that he said: "She gave them citrons (utrunj), and gave each of them a knife. When they saw Yusuf they glorified him, and began to cut their hands while they thought they were cutting the citron."

Musaddad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from him: "al-muttaka' is the citron," and he used to recite it lightly (khafīfatan).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding muttaka'an, that he said: "food."

Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "It is the citron."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah that he said: "It is everything that is cut with a knife."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak the like of it.

Abu al-Shaykh related through ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn al-Wazir ibn al-Kumayt ibn Zayd, who said: my father told me, from my grandfather, who said, regarding His saying ﴿when they saw him, they glorified him (akbarnahu)﴾: "They became aroused (amnayna)," and he recited:

"When the horses saw him from a lofty height, / they neighed and ejaculated the spurting semen."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿAbd al-Samad ibn ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, from his father, from his grandfather Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿when they saw him, they glorified him﴾, that he said: "When Yusuf came out to them, they menstruated from joy," and he mentioned the line of the poet we mentioned earlier:

"We come to women during their purity..."

—the verse [continues].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying akbarnahu, that he said: "They magnified him." ﴿and cut their hands﴾: he said: "slicing with the knife until they threw them down," and ﴿and they said: "Hashā lillāh"﴾: he said: "God forbid."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada (p-695) regarding His saying ﴿this is not but a noble angel﴾, that he said: "They said: he is an angel among the angels, because of his beauty."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Munabbih, from his father, who said: "Nineteen of the women who cut their hands died of grief."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim related from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yusuf and his mother were given half of beauty." Reports have come from a number of the early generations describing Yusuf's beauty and exaggerating it: in some of them he was given half of beauty, in some a third, and in some two-thirds. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿but he preserved himself (fa-staʿṣama)﴾, that he said: "He refrained."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding fa-staʿṣama, that he said: "He disobeyed (fa-staʿṣā)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿And if You do not turn away from me their plotting﴾, that he said: "If there is not from You the strength and protection, there will not be from me nor with me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related regarding aṣbu ilayhinna ("I incline toward them"), that he said: "I follow them." Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "I obey them."

The Arabic word *nuswah* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* (*nuswatun*), which is the reading of al-A'mash, al-Fadl and Sulayman. It is also said as *niswatun* with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, which is the reading of the rest. The meaning is a group of women, and the verb attached to them may be masculine or feminine.

It is said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-'Azīz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, the wife of his jailer, and the wife of his chamberlain.

In the speech of the Arabs, *al-fatā* means the young man and *al-fatāh* means the young woman. Here it means his servant. One says *fatāy* and *fatātī*, meaning "my servant" and "my maidservant."

The clause ﴿قَدْ شَغَفَهَا حُبًّا﴾ (indeed, love has gripped her) is in a position of *raf'* (nominative) as a second predicate of the subject, or in a position of *naṣb* (accusative) as a circumstantial clause. The meaning of *shaghafahā ḥubban* is: his love overwhelmed her. It is also said that his love entered into her *shighāf*.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the *shighāf* of the heart is its covering, which is a membrane over it. It is also said that it is the middle of the heart.

On this view, the meaning is: his love entered into her *shighāf* and so overcame her. Al-Asma'i cited the verse of the rajaz poet:

*"He follows her, and she is for him a shighāf."*

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Ibn Muhayṣin and al-Hasan read *shaʿafahā* with the unpointed *ʿayn* (*ʿ*). Ibn al-A'rabi said: its meaning is that he made his love run over her.

Others read it with the pointed *ghayn* (*gh*). Al-Jawhari said: *shaʿafahu al-ḥubbu* means that love burned his heart. Abu Zayd said: it means that it made him ill.

Al-Nahhas said: according to most lexicographers the meaning is that it has taken her in every direction, because *shiʿāf al-jibāl* are the peaks of the mountains. One says *shaghifa bi-dhālika shaghafan* (with a sukūn on the *ghayn*) when one is passionately attached to it. Abu 'Ubayda cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will you kill me, when I have gripped her heart,*
*as a man who has climbed high grips a mahnūwa (a sick or emaciated she-camel)?"*

He said: the agony of love is compared to this.

Al-Hasan read *qad shaghufahā* with a *ḍamma* on the *ghayn*. Al-Nahhas said: it is also reported as *qad shaghifahā* with a *kasra* on the *ghayn*, but this is not known in the speech of the Arabs; only *shaghafahā* with a *fatḥa* on the *ghayn* is known. It is said that the *shighāf* is the thin membrane that clings to the liver and is not seen, which is the white membrane. So his love clung to her heart as the membrane clings to the liver.

The clause ﴿إِنَّا لَنَرَاهَا فِي ضَلَالٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾ (indeed, we see her in clear error) confirms the content of what came before it. The meaning: "Indeed we see her," that is, we know her, "in this act of hers, which is seeking to seduce her servant, in error far from the path of right guidance and correctness, clear, not confused for one who looks at it."

[p. 693]

When the wife of al-'Azīz heard of their *makr* (scheming), that is, of their backbiting about her, the backbiting was called *makr* because both involve concealment. It is also said that they intended by this to reach a means of seeing Yusuf, and so their talk was called *makr*. It is also said that she had confided a secret to them and they spread her secret, and so it was called *makr*. She sent for them, that is, invited them to her, so that they might look at Yusuf and fall into what she had fallen into.

﴿وَأَعْتَدَتْ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَأً﴾ (and she prepared for them a reclining place) means she prepared for them seats on which they might recline. *A'taddat* is from *al-i'tidād*, which is everything you make ready for something.

Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read *mutkan* with a light *ṭā'* and without hamza. *Al-mutk* is the citron in the language of the Copts. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We drink sin openly from the cup,*
*and we see the citron passed among us."*

It is also said that this is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, and it is said this was reported from al-Akhfash.

Al-Farra' said that it is rose water.

The majority read *muttaka'an* with hamza and *tashdīd* (doubling of the *tā'*). The most correct of what has been said about it is that it is a sitting place. It is also said that it is food. It is also said that *al-muttaka'* is everything one reclines upon at food, drink or conversation.

Al-Qutaybi reported that one says *ittaka'nā 'inda fulān*, meaning "we ate at so-and-so's." From this is the verse of the poet:

*"So we were shaded in favor, and we reclined,*
*and we drank lawful drink from its jars."*

This is supported by His words ﴿وَآتَتْ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِّنْهُنَّ سِكِّينًا﴾ (and she gave each one of them a knife), for that is only for something they would eat after cutting it. *Al-sikkīn* (the knife) may be masculine or feminine, as al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said.

Al-Jawhari said: the more common usage of it is masculine. The purpose of giving each one of them a knife is that they would cut what needed cutting from the food. It is possible that she intended by this what would happen from them, that is, the cutting of their own hands. And she said to Yusuf: "Go out to them," that is, in the state in which they are, of reclining, eating and cutting what needs cutting of the food.

His words ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَيْنَهُ أَكْبَرْنَهُ﴾ (so when they saw him, they greatly admired him) mean they glorified him. It is also said that it means they menstruated. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"When they see the stallion from atop a hill,*
*they neigh and ejaculate the spurting semen."*

It is also said that it means they menstruated.

Al-Azhari said: *akbarna* in the sense of *ḥain* (menstruated) and the *hā'* is for pausing. One says *akbarati al-mar'a*, meaning the woman entered into the state of menstruation. It happened to them out of amazement and fright at what they witnessed of his surpassing beauty and his delightful loveliness. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We come to women in their purity,*
*and we do not come to women when they have menstruated the menstruation."*

Abu 'Ubayda and others denied this and said that this is not in the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Zajjaj said: one says *akbarnahu* and one does not say *ḥiḍnahu*, so *al-ikbār* does not mean menstruation.

Al-Azhari answered and said: it is possible that the *hā'* is the *hā' al-waqf* (pausal *hā'*) and not the *hā' al-kināya* (pronominal *hā'*).

This was rejected on the ground that the *hā' al-waqf* drops in continuous speech.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the *hā'* is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun of the verb: that is, they "greatly admired" (*akbarna ikbāran*) in the sense of "menstruated a menstruation" (*ḥiḍna ḥayḍan*).

﴿وَقَطَّعْنَ أَيْدِيَهُنَّ﴾ (and they cut their hands) means they wounded them. The intended meaning is not the cutting that separates the hand, but scratching and gashing. This is known in the language, as al-Nahhas said. One says *qaṭaʿa yada ṣāḥibihi* when he scratched it. It is also said that the intended meaning of *aydīhinna* here is their fingertips, and it is also said their sleeves.

The meaning: when Yusuf went out to them, they greatly admired him and were dumbfounded, and his beauty overwhelmed them so that their hands trembled and the cutting fell upon them, while they were preoccupied with what had come upon them, by which dreams are scattered, bodies tremble and minds depart.

﴿وَقُلْنَ حَاشَ لِلَّهِ﴾ (and they said, "Far be it from Allah!"). Thus Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read it with the *alif* in *ḥāshā*. The rest read it without it.

Al-Hasan read *ḥāsh lillāh* with a *sukūn* on the *shīn*. It is reported from him that he read *ḥāsh lillāh*. Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read *ḥāshā lillāh*.

Al-Zajjaj said: the root of the word is from *al-ḥāshiya*, meaning the side, as one says "I was on the side of so-and-so," that is, on his side. So your saying *ḥāshā li-Zayd* means: he kept away from him.

Abu 'Ali said: it is from *al-muḥāshāh* (keeping away). It is said that *ḥāsh* is a particle and *ḥāshā* is a verb. The discussion of the grammarians about this word is well known. Its meaning here is declaring Allah free of imperfection (*tanzīh*), as you say: "The people excepted Zayd," so the meaning of *ḥāshā lillāh* is: a clearing of Allah and a declaring Him free from imperfection.

His words ﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾ (this is not a human) — the use of *mā* to work like *laysa* (*iʿmāl mā ʿamalat laysa*) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the Qur'an was revealed in it, as in this verse and His words, glorified is He, ﴿مَا هُنَّ أُمَّهَاتِهِمْ﴾ (they are not their mothers) [al-Mujadila: 2]. As for the Banu Tamim, they do not make it work like *laysa*.

The Kufans said: its original form is *mā hādhā bi-basharin*, and when the *bā'* was dropped, it took the accusative (*naṣb*).

Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said: when I say *mā Zaydun bi-muntaliq*, the place of the *bā'* is a place of accusative, and so is the case with all the prepositions.

As for al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the majority of grammarians, they made it work like *laysa*, and the Basrans said likewise. The discussion is established in the books of grammar with its evidence and arguments.

They denied humanness of him only because he appeared in a form dressed in a wondrous beauty such as had not been seen in any human, and the beholders had not seen anything close to him in all human forms. Then, when they denied humanness of him for this reason, they affirmed for him angelhood, although they did not know the angels. But it is established in natural disposition that they (the angels) are in a form above the form of humans in essence and attributes, and that they surpass in everything, just as it is established that the devils are the opposite of that. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"I am not of humankind, but of an angel*
*who descended from the air of the sky, calling out."*

Al-Hasan read *mā hādhā bi-shirā'in*, taking the *bā'* as a preposition, with the *shīn* in the *kasra*: that is, "this is not a slave to be bought." This reading is weak and does not fit what follows it, His words ﴿إِنْ هَذَا إِلَّا مَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾ (this is none but a noble angel).

Know that it does not follow from the women's saying this that the angels' forms are better than the forms of the children of Adam, for they did not say it on evidence, but judged about the unseen merely by the belief settled in their natures, and that is not allowed, for Allah, glorified is He, says ﴿لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنسَانَ فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ﴾ (We certainly created man in the best stature) [al-Tin: 4].

The apparent meaning of this is that there was nothing like him among the kinds of created beings in the excellence of his form and the perfection of his shape. So what the author of al-Kashshaf said in this place is among his partisanship toward what was firmly fixed in his mind from the sayings of the Mu'tazilites (a rationalist school). Moreover, this question, I mean the question of the superiority of the angels over humans, is not among the matters of religion, neither in its source nor its branches. So how little it benefits the servants of Allah, and how much they need other matters of obligation instead of it.

﴿قَالَتْ فَذَلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ﴾ (She said, "That is the one you blamed me for") — the reference is to Yusuf, and the address is to the women: that is, "you reproached me about him."

She said this to them when she saw their infatuation with Yusuf, as a display of excuse for herself. The meaning of *fīhi* is: about his love. It is also said that the reference is to the love, and the pronoun also refers to it, and the meaning: "that love about which you blamed me is that very love." The first is preferable, and Ibn Jarir preferred it.

The root of *al-lawm* is describing with what is ugly. Then, when she displayed her excuse to the women by what they had witnessed of what they had fallen into upon his appearance to them, her chest could no longer contain what she felt in her heart of his love, so she confessed to that and stated plainly what had happened from her of seeking to seduce him. She said ﴿وَلَقَدْ رَاوَدْتُّهُ عَن نَّفْسِهِ فَاسْتَعْصَمَ﴾ (I did seek to seduce him, but he refused), that is, he kept himself chaste and refused what I wanted, seeking to preserve his soul from that. Then she threatened him if he did not do what she wanted, uncovering the cloak of modesty and tearing the veil of chastity, and she said ﴿وَلَئِن لَّمْ يَفْعَلْ مَا آمُرُهُ لَيُسْجَنَنَّ وَلَيَكُونًا مِّنَ الصَّاغِرِينَ﴾ (If he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and be among the humiliated). That is: if he does not do what she had commanded him in what was mentioned earlier, when she locked the doors and said "Come, you" (*hayta laka*), "he will certainly be imprisoned," that is, detained in prison, "and he will certainly be among the humiliated," the abject, because of the humiliation he would suffer, and be stripped of the blessing and honor, in her claim.

It was read *layakūnanna* with the *tashdīd* (doubled *nūn*) and with the lightened *nūn*. It is said that the lightened reading is preferable, because the *nūn* was written in the Muṣḥaf as an *alif* according to the rule of pausing, and that occurs only with the light *nūn*. As for *layusjanannа* (he will certainly be imprisoned), it is only with the doubled *nūn*.

When Yusuf heard her words and knew that this was her firm resolve, along with what he knew of the effectiveness of her word with her husband, al-'Azīz, he said, speaking privately to his Lord, glorified is He:

﴿رَبِّ السِّجْنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدْعُونَنِي إِلَيْهِ﴾ (My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to) — that is: O my Lord, the prison with which this woman threatened me is dearer to me than what they invite me to of compliance with them and falling into the great disobedience which takes away the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, entering the prison, and he omitted the annexed noun.

Abu Hatim reported that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, read *al-saḥn* with a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*. Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Abd al-Rahman, al-A'raj and Ya'qub read it likewise, and it is the verbal noun of *sajanahu sajnan* (he imprisoned him).

The attribution of the invitation to all of them is because the women encouraged him to comply with her and frightened him from opposing her. Then the same manner was followed in attributing the scheming to all of them, so He said: ﴿وَإِلَّا تَصْرِفْ عَنِّي كَيْدَهُنَّ﴾ (And unless You turn away their scheming from me). As for the scheming of the wife of al-'Azīz, that is what Allah, glorified is He, has related in this sūrah. As for the scheming of the rest of the women, it is what came before of the encouragement to him to comply and the frightening of him from opposing.

It is also said that each one of them would be alone with him and say to him: "O Yusuf, fulfill my need, for I am better for you than the wife of al-'Azīz." It is also said that he addressed the wife of al-'Azīz with what is suitable for addressing a group of women, out of honoring her, or as a shift from explicit speech to indirect reference.

*Al-kayd* is scheming. The *jazm* (apocope) of *aṣbu* is on the basis that it is the answer to the condition: that is, "I will incline (*amal*) to them," from *ṣabā yaṣbū* when one inclines and longs. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"To Hind my heart has inclined,*
*and Hind's love makes it incline."*

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 31–35 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And [that] I may be among the ignorant﴾ is conjoined to "I will incline" (aṣbu): that is, that I may be among those who are ignorant of what is forbidden to commit and who go ahead with it; or among those who act in the manner of the ignorant.

As for His saying ﴿So his Lord responded to him﴾: when he said, "And if You do not turn away from me their plotting, I might incline toward them," this was, on his part, a veiled supplication (taʿarruḍ li-l-duʿāʾ), as though he had said, "O Allah, turn away from me their plotting." So Allah's responding to him is in this sense, because no sincere supplication had preceded it from him, peace be upon him. The meaning is that He showed kindness to him and protected him from falling into disobedience, for when He turned away from him their plotting, nothing of what they desired from him came to pass. The manner of attributing the plotting (kayd) to them has already been mentioned. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ gives the reason for what precedes it, namely the turning away of the women's plotting from him: that is, He is the All-Hearing of the supplications of those who call upon Him, the All-Knowing of the states of those who take refuge in Him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾ (shaghafahā), that he said: "It overcame her."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him, regarding ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾, that he said: "The love of Yusuf killed her. Shaghaf is the deadly love, and shaghaf is a love short of that, while shighaf is the covering of the heart."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, ﴿she was smitten with love for him﴾, that he said: "She had fallen in love with him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿when she heard of their plotting﴾, that he said: "Of their talk."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan, ﴿when she heard of their plotting﴾, that he said: "Of their deed. Every 'makr' in the Qur'an is a deed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related, regarding His saying ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining-couch (muttaka')﴾, that he said: "She prepared for them a gathering place. Their custom was that when they set out the food-table they gave each person a knife to eat with. When they saw him, he said: ﴿when he came out to them, the women glorified him﴾" — he said: "they magnified him and looked at him, and began to slice their hands with the knives, while they thought they were cutting the food."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining-couch﴾, that he said: "She gave them citrons (utrunj), and gave each of them a knife. When they saw Yusuf they glorified him, and began to cut their hands while they thought they were cutting the citron."

Musaddad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from him: "al-muttaka' is the citron," and he used to recite it lightly (khafīfatan).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid, regarding muttaka'an, that he said: "food."

Abu ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him that he said: "It is the citron."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah that he said: "It is everything that is cut with a knife."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak the like of it.

Abu al-Shaykh related through ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn al-Wazir ibn al-Kumayt ibn Zayd, who said: my father told me, from my grandfather, who said, regarding His saying ﴿when they saw him, they glorified him (akbarnahu)﴾: "They became aroused (amnayna)," and he recited:

"When the horses saw him from a lofty height, / they neighed and ejaculated the spurting semen."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through ʿAbd al-Samad ibn ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, from his father, from his grandfather Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿when they saw him, they glorified him﴾, that he said: "When Yusuf came out to them, they menstruated from joy," and he mentioned the line of the poet we mentioned earlier:

"We come to women during their purity..."

—the verse [continues].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding His saying akbarnahu, that he said: "They magnified him." ﴿and cut their hands﴾: he said: "slicing with the knife until they threw them down," and ﴿and they said: "Hashā lillāh"﴾: he said: "God forbid."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada (p-695) regarding His saying ﴿this is not but a noble angel﴾, that he said: "They said: he is an angel among the angels, because of his beauty."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Munabbih, from his father, who said: "Nineteen of the women who cut their hands died of grief."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim related from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yusuf and his mother were given half of beauty." Reports have come from a number of the early generations describing Yusuf's beauty and exaggerating it: in some of them he was given half of beauty, in some a third, and in some two-thirds. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿but he preserved himself (fa-staʿṣama)﴾, that he said: "He refrained."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding fa-staʿṣama, that he said: "He disobeyed (fa-staʿṣā)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿And if You do not turn away from me their plotting﴾, that he said: "If there is not from You the strength and protection, there will not be from me nor with me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related regarding aṣbu ilayhinna ("I incline toward them"), that he said: "I follow them." Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "I obey them."

The Arabic word *nuswah* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* (*nuswatun*), which is the reading of al-A'mash, al-Fadl and Sulayman. It is also said as *niswatun* with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, which is the reading of the rest. The meaning is a group of women, and the verb attached to them may be masculine or feminine.

It is said that they were the wife of the cupbearer of al-'Azīz, the wife of his baker, the wife of the keeper of his animals, the wife of his jailer, and the wife of his chamberlain.
