This statement from him (peace be upon him) came from heedlessness and forgetfulness of the remembrance of God, caused by Satan. So the object pronoun in *ansahu* refers to Yusuf, as some exegetes said. The meaning of "his lord" in His words "the remembrance of his lord" is God, glorified be He. That is: Satan caused Yusuf to forget the remembrance of God, the Exalted, in that state. ﴿He said to the one he thought would be saved from the two﴾: he mentions him to his master, so that this would be the cause of the man's attentiveness to the clear injustice inflicted upon him by his imprisonment, after he had seen the signs that indicate his innocence.

A number of exegetes went to the view that the one whom Satan caused to forget the remembrance of his lord was the one of the two youths who was saved, namely the cupbearer. The meaning is: Satan caused the cupbearer to forget the remembrance of his master, that is, to forget his mentioning to his master, so he did not convey to him what Yusuf had enjoined upon him, although he had mentioned him to his master. The meaning would be: Satan caused him to forget to report what Yusuf had commanded him, upon his release from prison and his return to what he had been doing, namely serving the king his drink. This view has been preferred on the ground that Satan has no power over the prophets.

It was also preferred on the ground that forgetting is not a sin, so if the one whom Satan caused to forget the remembrance of his lord had been Yusuf, he would not have deserved punishment for it by remaining in prison several years.

It was answered that forgetting here means abandoning (*at-tark*), and that he was punished because of his seeking help from other than God, glorified be He. What supports the reference of the pronoun to Yusuf is what follows it, His words: ﴿So he remained in the prison several years﴾. What supports its reference to the one of the two youths who was saved is His words later: ﴿And the one of the two who was saved said, after a long time (*ummah*), and remembered﴾, that is, after a span of years (*sanah*). ﴿So he remained﴾, that is, Yusuf remained in prison because of that statement he had said to the one of the two youths who was saved, or because of that forgetting, ﴿several years﴾. *Al-bid'* (several) is what lies between three and nine, as al-Harawi related it from the Arabs.

It is related from Abu 'Ubaydah that *al-bid'* is less than half a decade (*al-'iqd*), meaning between one and four. It was also said it is between three and seven, as Qutrub related. Al-Zajjaj related that it is between three and five.

People have differed about determining the length of time that Yusuf remained in prison. It was said seven years, it was said twelve years, it was said fourteen years, and it was said five years.

Ibn Jarir related from 'Ikrimah, regarding His words "As for one of you", that he said: [the cupbearer] came to him and said: "I saw in a dream that I had planted a vine-stock of grapes, and it grew, and clusters came out on it. I pressed them and then gave the king to drink." He said: "You will remain in prison three days, then you will come out and give him wine to drink."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The two companions of Yusuf had seen nothing; they had only dreamed together to test his knowledge. When he interpreted their dreams they said: 'We were only playing and had seen nothing.' So he said: ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire﴾," meaning: the interpretation came to pass, and the matter became as Yusuf had interpreted.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Mijlaz, who said: "One of the two who recounted the dream to Yusuf was lying."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Sabat regarding ﴿And he said to the one he thought would be saved from the two: Mention me to your lord﴾, that he said: "To the king of the land."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Kitab al-'Uqubat*, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Had Yusuf not uttered that word which he uttered, he would not have remained in prison as long as he did, since he sought relief from other than God."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from 'Ikrimah, traced to the Prophet (*marfu'an*) something similar to it, and it is a *mursal* (a report whose chain omits the companion).

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet, something similar to it.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan, traced to the Prophet, something similar to it, and it is a *mursal*.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, who mentioned something similar to it, and it is also a *mursal*.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Anas, who said: "It was revealed to Yusuf: 'Who rescued you from being killed when your brothers resolved to kill you?' He said: 'You, my Lord.' He said: 'Who rescued you from the well when they threw you into it?' He said: 'You, my Lord.' He said: 'Who rescued you from the woman when she desired you?' He said: 'You, my Lord.' He said: 'Why, then, did you forget Me and remember a human being?' He said: 'Out of anxiety, and a word my tongue uttered.' He said: 'By My might, I will keep you in prison for several years.' So he remained in it seven years."

The early scholars (*salaf*) differed in estimating the length of his stay in prison, according to what we have already mentioned, so we will not occupy ourselves here with mentioning who said that and who related it.

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 12, verses 49–51:

The king here is the greatest king, who is al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, whose vizier was al-Aziz. When Yusuf's (peace be upon him) release drew near, he saw in his sleep that he had come out of a dry river seven fat cows (plural of samin and samina), followed by seven lean ones, i.e., emaciated ones, and the lean ones came upon the fat ones and devoured them.

The meaning is "I saw," but he used the present tense (al-mudari') to make the scene present to the mind (li-istihdar al-sura). Likewise, his words "yaʾkuluhunna" (they devour them) use the present tense for the same reason. The word al-ʿijaf is the plural of ʿajfaʾ. Its regular plural would be ʿujuf, because faʿlaʾ and afʿal are not pluralized on the pattern fiʿal. However, he departed from the regular form by analogy with samin. "Seven other ears of grain" (sabʿa sunbulatin) is coordinated with "seven cows" (sabʿa baqarat). By "green" (khudr) he means that their grain had formed, and by "dry" (yabisat) he means those that had reached harvest. The meaning is: "And I see seven others that are dry." He had seen that the seven dry ears had reached the green ones and had wrapped around them until they overcame them. Perhaps the Qur'anic text does not mention this because the description of the cows is sufficient.

﴿O chiefs﴾ is an address to the nobles of his people. ﴿Explain to me my vision﴾ means: tell me the judgment of this dream. ﴿If you are able to interpret dreams﴾ means: if you know the interpretation (ʿibara) of dreams. The root of ʿibara derives from the crossing of a river (ʿubur al-nahr). So ʿabartu al-nahr means "I reached its far bank," and thus the interpreter of a dream (ʿabir al-ruʾya) tells what its matter will come to.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam in "li-l-ruʾya" is for specification (lil-tabyin), meaning "if you are interpreters," and then he specified, saying "for the vision." It was also said that it is for emphasis (lil-taqwiya), and that the verb governing it is placed later for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil).

The clause ﴿They said: "Confused dreams"﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa), an answer to an implied question. "Adghath" is the plural of "dighth," which is any mixture of herbs, grass, or other things. The meaning: "A jumble of dreams." "Ahlam" is the plural of "hulm," which is a false vision with no reality, such as that which arises from the soul's talk and the whispering of Satan. The construction is in the sense of "min" (of). They used the plural "ahlam" although the king had only one vision, as hyperbole in describing it as baseless. It is also possible that he had, along with this vision, others that Allah did not relate to us. ﴿We are not learned in the interpretation of dreams﴾: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is the interpretation of confused dreams. They denied knowledge of what has no interpretation, not knowledge of interpretation in general. It was also said that they denied knowledge of interpretation absolutely, and did not claim that this vision has no interpretation. It was also said that they intended to erase it from the king's breast so that he would not be occupied with it, and what they mentioned of denying knowledge was not true in reality.

﴿And the one who was saved from the two said﴾, that is, of the two youths, and he is the cupbearer to whom Yusuf had said: "Mention me to your lord" (Yusuf 42). He "remembered after a time" (wa-iddakara baʿda ummah). With the unpointed dal, as read by the majority, which is the eloquent reading, meaning: the cupbearer remembered Yusuf and what he had witnessed of his knowledge of interpreting dreams.

It is also read with the dotted letter (dhal), and the meaning of "baʿda ummah" is "after a period," as in ﴿until a specified period﴾ (Hud 8), meaning until a time.

Ibn Darastawayh said: "Ummah" is not used for a period except with the omission of a modifier and the substitution of the modified term in its place, as if he said: "and Allah knows best, and he remembered after a period of ummah" or "after the time of an ummah."

"Ummah" means a large group of people. Al-Akhfash said: it is singular in form and plural in meaning. Every species of animal is also an ummah.

Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrima read "baʿda amah" with an open hamza and a light mim, meaning "after forgetfulness." From this is the poet's saying:

"I forgot, though I was not one who forgets a story; so does time bring ruin upon minds."

It is said "amaha yaʾmahu amhan" when one forgets.

Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli read "baʿda immah" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning "after a blessing," which is the blessing of deliverance.

﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ means: I will tell you of it by asking about it the one who has knowledge of its interpretation, and that is Yusuf. ﴿So send me forth﴾: he addressed the king with a respectful expression, or he addressed him and those present among the nobles, asking them to send him to Yusuf so that he could relate the king's vision to him, until he informs him of its interpretation, and returns with it to the king.

﴿Yusuf, O truthful one﴾ means: O Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they sent him to Yusuf, and he went to him, and said to him, ﴿Yusuf, O truthful one﴾ to the end of the speech. The meaning is: "Inform us regarding the vision of one who saw seven fat cows..." etc. He left that out, relying on what he was confident Yusuf would understand, that it was a vision and that what was required of him was its interpretation. ﴿So that I may return to the people﴾ means: to the king and those with him among the nobles, ﴿that perhaps they may know﴾ what you bring of the interpretation of this vision, or they may know your merit and your knowledge of the science of interpretation.

The clause "He said: You will sow..." etc. is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, like other clauses that occur in this position. ﴿Seven years, consecutively﴾ (daʾban): that is, successive and continuous. It is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "persistently." It was also said it is an attribute of "seven," meaning "a persistent [period]." Abu Hatim related from Yaʿqub that he read "daʾban" with a vowelled hamza, and likewise Hafs related from ʿAsim; both are dialectal forms (lughatan).

Al-Farra' said: it is vowelled because it contains one of the throat letters (huruf al-halq), and every word whose first letter is open and second letter is sukun may be pronounced heavily in known words.

So Yusuf (peace be upon him) interpreted the seven fat cows as seven years in which there is abundance, and the lean ones as seven years in which there is drought. Thus he interpreted the seven green ears and the seven dry ears. He based his interpretation of the seven green ears on what he mentioned in the interpretation: ﴿So what you harvest, leave it in its ear﴾, that is, what you harvest in each of the years of abundance, leave that harvest in its ear and do not separate it from it, lest the weevil eat it, except a little of what you eat in these years of abundance, for you must separate it from its ear and remove it from there. He limited the exception to what is eaten, and not what they need of seed that they sow on their lands, because that is known from His saying "you sow."

﴿Then there will come after that﴾ means: after the seven years of abundance, seven hard years, that is, seven years of drought whose affair will be difficult for people, ﴿they will consume what you have stored for them of those grains left in their ears.﴾

Attributing the eating to the years is figurative (majaz). The meaning is: people will eat in them, or their inhabitants will eat what you have stored for them, that is, what you saved for their sake. This is of the type "his day is fasting" (nahāruhu ṣāʾimun), and from it is the poet's saying:

"Your day, O deceived one, is heedlessness and negligence; your night is sleep, and ruin is clinging to you."

﴿Except a little of what you store﴾ means: of the grain you keep back in order to sow with it, because in preserving the seed lies the storing of provisions.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning of "tuhsinun" is "you guard," and it was said "you save," and the meaning is one.

His words: ﴿Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain, and in which they will press﴾ mean: after the years of drought. So the reference is to them, and "year" means a year. ﴿In it the people will be given rain﴾ comes from "ighatha" or "ghawth." "Ghayth" is rain, and "ghat al-ghayth al-ard" means it reached the land, and Allah "ghawwatha" the lands with His rain, meaning He sent rain on them. So "yughathu al-nas" means "the people will receive rain." ﴿And in it they will press﴾ means they will press things that are pressed, such as grapes, sesame, and olives. It was also said it means milking milk. It was also said the meaning of "yaʿsirun" is "they will be delivered," derived from "al-ʿusra," which is refuge and deliverance. Abu ʿUbayda said: "al-ʿasar," with vowelling, means refuge and deliverance, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Thirsty, he seeks help without being helped, and he had been a refuge for the one being saved."

"Iʿtasartu bi-Fulan" means I took refuge in him.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "taʿsirun" with the second person.

It is also read "yuʿsarun" with a dammah on the imperfect letter and an open ṣad, meaning "they will be given rain," and from it is the Most High's saying: ﴿And We send down from the clouds water pouring forth﴾ (al-Naba 14).

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, who said: Yusuf said to the cupbearer, "Mention me to your lord," meaning the greatest king, and my wrongful treatment and my imprisonment for no reason. He said, "I will do it." When the cupbearer went out, he was restored to his position, and his companion was pleased with him. Satan made him forget the mention of the king to whom Yusuf had told him to speak. So Yusuf remained in the prison for several years after that. Then the king al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid saw his vision in which he was shown what he was shown. It alarmed him, and he knew that it was a true vision, but he did not know its interpretation. So he said to the nobles around him from the people of his kingdom: ﴿I see seven fat cows, devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears, and others dry.﴾ When the cupbearer heard from the king what he heard, and the king's question about its interpretation, he remembered Yusuf and what he had interpreted for him and his companion, and what came to pass according to what he had said. So he said: "I will inform you of its interpretation."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying "confused dreams" that he said: "mixed up (mushtabiha)."

Abu Yaʿla and Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "of the false dreams." Ibn Jarir also related from al-Dahhak the same.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying "wa-iddakara baʿda ummah" that he said: "after a time (hin)."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, and al-Suddi the same.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "after years."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: "after a nation of people (ummah min al-nas)."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Explain to us regarding seven fat cows﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "As for the fat ones, they are years of abundance in which there is plenty. As for the lean ones, they are years of drought. And seven green ears are the years of abundance, in which the earth brings forth its plants, its crops and its fruits. And other dry ones are the barren years of drought, which produce nothing."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrima, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am amazed at Yusuf, his generosity, and his patience, and Allah forgives him when he was asked about the lean and fat cows. If I had been in his place, I would not have informed them until I had stipulated that they bring me out. And I am amazed at Yusuf, his patience and his generosity, and Allah forgives him when the messenger came to him. If I had been in his place, I would have rushed to the door toward them, but he wanted to have the excuse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿except a little of what you store﴾, he said: "You hoard." And regarding His saying "and in it they will press," he said: "The grapes and the oil."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿In it the people will be given rain﴾, he said: "They will be given rain in it, and in it they will press": "they will press in it grapes, and they will press in it raisins, and they will press from all fruits."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from him also, regarding "and in it they will press," that he said: "They will milk."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from him also regarding ﴿Then there will come after that a year﴾ that he said: "He informed them of something they had not asked him about, as if Allah had taught him it. 'In it the people will be given rain,' and 'in it they will press sesame for oil, grapes for wine, and olives for oil.'"

He said, "I will do it." When the cupbearer went out, he was restored to his position, and his companion was pleased with him. Satan made him forget the mention of the king to whom Yusuf had told him to speak. So Yusuf remained in the prison for several years after that. Then the king al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid saw his vision in which he was shown what he was shown. It alarmed him, and he knew that it was a true vision, but he did not know its interpretation. So he said to the nobles around him from the people of his kingdom: ﴿I see seven fat cows, devoured by seven lean ones, and seven green ears, and others dry.﴾ When the cupbearer heard from the king what he heard, and the king's question about its interpretation, he remembered Yusuf and what he had interpreted for him and his companion, and what came to pass according to what he had said. So he said: "I will inform you of its interpretation."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying "confused dreams" that he said: "mixed up (mushtabiha)."

Abu Yaʿla and Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "of the false dreams." Ibn Jarir also related from al-Dahhak the same.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related through various chains from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying "wa-iddakara baʿda ummah" that he said: "after a time (hin)."

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, and al-Suddi the same.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "after years."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: "after a nation of people (ummah min al-nas)."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿Explain to us regarding seven fat cows﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "As for the fat ones, they are years of abundance in which there is plenty. As for the lean ones, they are years of drought. And seven green ears are the years of abundance, in which the earth brings forth its plants, its crops and its fruits. And other dry ones are the barren years of drought, which produce nothing."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrima, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am amazed at Yusuf, his generosity, and his patience, and Allah forgives him when he was asked about the lean and fat cows. If I had been in his place, I would not have informed them until I had stipulated that they bring me out. And I am amazed at Yusuf, his patience and his generosity, and Allah forgives him when the messenger came to him. If I had been in his place, I would have rushed to the door toward them, but he wanted to have the excuse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿except a little of what you store﴾, he said: "You hoard." And regarding His saying "and in it they will press," he said: "The grapes and the oil."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding His saying: ﴿In it the people will be given rain﴾, he said: "They will be given rain in it, and in it they will press": "they will press in it grapes, and they will press in it raisins, and they will press from all fruits."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from him also, regarding "and in it they will press," that he said: "They will milk."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from him also regarding ﴿Then there will come after that a year﴾ that he said: "He informed them of something they had not asked him about, as if Allah had taught him it. 'In it the people will be given rain,' and 'in it they will press sesame for oil, grapes for wine, and olives for oil.'"

The Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 12, verses 49–51:

The king here is the greatest king, who is al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, whose vizier was al-Aziz. When Yusuf's (peace be upon him) release drew near, he saw in his sleep that he had come out of a dry river seven fat cows (plural of samin and samina), followed by seven lean ones, i.e., emaciated ones, and the lean ones came upon the fat ones and devoured them.

The meaning is "I saw," but he used the present tense (al-mudari') to make the scene present to the mind (li-istihdar al-sura). Likewise, his words "yaʾkuluhunna" (they devour them) use the present tense for the same reason. The word al-ʿijaf is the plural of ʿajfaʾ. Its regular plural would be ʿujuf, because faʿlaʾ and afʿal are not pluralized on the pattern fiʿal. However, he departed from the regular form by analogy with samin. "Seven other ears of grain" (sabʿa sunbulatin) is coordinated with "seven cows" (sabʿa baqarat). By "green" (khudr) he means that their grain had formed, and by "dry" (yabisat) he means those that had reached harvest. The meaning is: "And I see seven others that are dry." He had seen that the seven dry ears had reached the green ones and had wrapped around them until they overcame them. Perhaps the Qur'anic text does not mention this because the description of the cows is sufficient.

﴿O chiefs﴾ is an address to the nobles of his people. ﴿Explain to me my vision﴾ means: tell me the judgment of this dream. ﴿If you are able to interpret dreams﴾ means: if you know the interpretation (ʿibara) of dreams. The root of ʿibara derives from the crossing of a river (ʿubur al-nahr). So ʿabartu al-nahr means "I reached its far bank," and thus the interpreter of a dream (ʿabir al-ruʾya) tells what its matter will come to.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam in "li-l-ruʾya" is for specification (lil-tabyin), meaning "if you are interpreters," and then he specified, saying "for the vision." It was also said that it is for emphasis (lil-taqwiya), and that the verb governing it is placed later for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil).

The clause ﴿They said: "Confused dreams"﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa), an answer to an implied question. "Adghath" is the plural of "dighth," which is any mixture of herbs, grass, or other things. The meaning: "A jumble of dreams." "Ahlam" is the plural of "hulm," which is a false vision with no reality, such as that which arises from the soul's talk and the whispering of Satan. The construction is in the sense of "min" (of). They used the plural "ahlam" although the king had only one vision, as hyperbole in describing it as baseless. It is also possible that he had, along with this vision, others that Allah did not relate to us. ﴿We are not learned in the interpretation of dreams﴾: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is the interpretation of confused dreams. They denied knowledge of what has no interpretation, not knowledge of interpretation in general. It was also said that they denied knowledge of interpretation absolutely, and did not claim that this vision has no interpretation. It was also said that they intended to erase it from the king's breast so that he would not be occupied with it, and what they mentioned of denying knowledge was not true in reality.

﴿And the one who was saved from the two said﴾, that is, of the two youths, and he is the cupbearer to whom Yusuf had said: "Mention me to your lord" (Yusuf 42). He "remembered after a time" (wa-iddakara baʿda ummah). With the unpointed dal, as read by the majority, which is the eloquent reading, meaning: the cupbearer remembered Yusuf and what he had witnessed of his knowledge of interpreting dreams.

It is also read with the dotted letter (dhal), and the meaning of "baʿda ummah" is "after a period," as in ﴿until a specified period﴾ (Hud 8), meaning until a time.

Ibn Darastawayh said: "Ummah" is not used for a period except with the omission of a modifier and the substitution of the modified term in its place, as if he said: "and Allah knows best, and he remembered after a period of ummah" or "after the time of an ummah."

"Ummah" means a large group of people. Al-Akhfash said: it is singular in form and plural in meaning. Every species of animal is also an ummah.

Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrima read "baʿda amah" with an open hamza and a light mim, meaning "after forgetfulness." From this is the poet's saying:

"I forgot, though I was not one who forgets a story; so does time bring ruin upon minds."

It is said "amaha yaʾmahu amhan" when one forgets.

Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli read "baʿda immah" with a kasra on the hamza, meaning "after a blessing," which is the blessing of deliverance.

﴿I will inform you of its interpretation﴾ means: I will tell you of it by asking about it the one who has knowledge of its interpretation, and that is Yusuf. ﴿So send me forth﴾: he addressed the king with a respectful expression, or he addressed him and those present among the nobles, asking them to send him to Yusuf so that he could relate the king's vision to him, until he informs him of its interpretation, and returns with it to the king.

﴿Yusuf, O truthful one﴾ means: O Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they sent him to Yusuf, and he went to him, and said to him, ﴿Yusuf, O truthful one﴾ to the end of the speech. The meaning is: "Inform us regarding the vision of one who saw seven fat cows..." etc. He left that out, relying on what he was confident Yusuf would understand, that it was a vision and that what was required of him was its interpretation. ﴿So that I may return to the people﴾ means: to the king and those with him among the nobles, ﴿that perhaps they may know﴾ what you bring of the interpretation of this vision, or they may know your merit and your knowledge of the science of interpretation.

The clause "He said: You will sow..." etc. is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, like other clauses that occur in this position. ﴿Seven years, consecutively﴾ (daʾban): that is, successive and continuous. It is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "persistently." It was also said it is an attribute of "seven," meaning "a persistent [period]." Abu Hatim related from Yaʿqub that he read "daʾban" with a vowelled hamza, and likewise Hafs related from ʿAsim; both are dialectal forms (lughatan).

Al-Farra' said: it is vowelled because it contains one of the throat letters (huruf al-halq), and every word whose first letter is open and second letter is sukun may be pronounced heavily in known words.

So Yusuf (peace be upon him) interpreted the seven fat cows as seven years in which there is abundance, and the lean ones as seven years in which there is drought. Thus he interpreted the seven green ears and the seven dry ears. He based his interpretation of the seven green ears on what he mentioned in the interpretation: ﴿So what you harvest, leave it in its ear﴾, that is, what you harvest in each of the years of abundance, leave that harvest in its ear and do not separate it from it, lest the weevil eat it, except a little of what you eat in these years of abundance, for you must separate it from its ear and remove it from there. He limited the exception to what is eaten, and not what they need of seed that they sow on their lands, because that is known from His saying "you sow."

﴿Then there will come after that﴾ means: after the seven years of abundance, seven hard years, that is, seven years of drought whose affair will be difficult for people, ﴿they will consume what you have stored for them of those grains left in their ears.﴾

Attributing the eating to the years is figurative (majaz). The meaning is: people will eat in them, or their inhabitants will eat what you have stored for them, that is, what you saved for their sake. This is of the type "his day is fasting" (nahāruhu ṣāʾimun), and from it is the poet's saying:

"Your day, O deceived one, is heedlessness and negligence; your night is sleep, and ruin is clinging to you."

﴿Except a little of what you store﴾ means: of the grain you keep back in order to sow with it, because in preserving the seed lies the storing of provisions.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the meaning of "tuhsinun" is "you guard," and it was said "you save," and the meaning is one.

His words: ﴿Then there will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain, and in which they will press﴾ mean: after the years of drought. So the reference is to them, and "year" means a year. ﴿In it the people will be given rain﴾ comes from "ighatha" or "ghawth." "Ghayth" is rain, and "ghat al-ghayth al-ard" means it reached the land, and Allah "ghawwatha" the lands with His rain, meaning He sent rain on them. So "yughathu al-nas" means "the people will receive rain." ﴿And in it they will press﴾ means they will press things that are pressed, such as grapes, sesame, and olives. It was also said it means milking milk. It was also said the meaning of "yaʿsirun" is "they will be delivered," derived from "al-ʿusra," which is refuge and deliverance. Abu ʿUbayda said: "al-ʿasar," with vowelling, means refuge and deliverance, and from it is the poet's saying:

"Thirsty, he seeks help without being helped, and he had been a refuge for the one being saved."

"Iʿtasartu bi-Fulan" means I took refuge in him.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "taʿsirun" with the second person.

It is also read "yuʿsarun" with a dammah on the imperfect letter and an open ṣad, meaning "they will be given rain," and from it is the Most High's saying: ﴿And We send down from the clouds water pouring forth﴾ (al-Naba 14).

He said, "I will do it." When the cupbearer went out, he was restored to his position, and his companion was pleased with him. **Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 52–57 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him, and he is indeed of the truthful.﴾ ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous.﴾ ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today in our presence established and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾ ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful [of Allah].﴾

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me"﴾: there is an omission in the speech before this, and the implied meaning is: So the messenger went to the king and informed him of what Joseph had told him regarding the interpretation of that dream. The king then said to those in his presence, "Bring him to me," meaning Joseph. He desired to see him and to know his condition, after he had learned of his excellence from the description the messenger had given him and from his interpretation of his dream. ﴿So when he came to him﴾, meaning when the messenger came to Joseph and summoned him to the king's presence and ordered him to leave the prison, Joseph said to the messenger, "Return to your lord," meaning your master, ﴿Ask him what was the case of the women who cut their hands﴾. He ordered him to ask the king about that matter, and he held back from leaving the prison and did not hasten to respond to the king, so that he might show the people the innocence of his person and the purity of his conduct, and that he had been wronged by the plot of the wife of the Aziz, a manifest wrong. Peace be upon him was given such forbearance, patience and deliberateness that minds fall short of conceiving it. For this reason it is established in the Sahih, from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph remained, I would have answered the caller." He meant the messenger who came calling him to the king.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This act of Joseph's was deliberateness and patience, and a seeking of the clearing of his name. He feared that if he came out and attained a station with the king, while remaining silent about the matter of his offence, people would see him with that eye and say, "This is the one who sought to seduce the wife of the Aziz." He only said, ﴿Ask him about the women﴾, and was silent about the wife of the Aziz, out of regard for the protection of the honourable king, or out of fear of her plotting and her great evil. He mentioned the question about the cutting of the hands and did not mention their seeking to seduce him, out of his disdain for attributing that to them. For this reason he did not attribute the seduction in what preceded to the wife of the Aziz, except after she had accused him of her own fault and slipped away.

Here he was content with a general allusion in his saying ﴿Indeed my Lord is aware of their plot﴾, making Allah's knowledge of what befell him from their plotting sufficient in place of explicit statement.

The clause ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did the king say after the messenger conveyed to him what Joseph had said? The word *khatb* (خَطْب) means a great matter that entitles one to address his companion specifically about it.

The meaning is: What is your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?

The meaning of seduction (*muraawadah*, مُرَاوَدَة) has already been explained. He attributed the seduction to them (plural) because each one of them had done it, as previously mentioned. Among those included in the king's address was the wife of the Aziz. Alternatively, by attributing it to them he meant that it occurred from them in general, just as it occurred from the wife of the Aziz, avoiding explicit attribution of it to her because she was the wife of his minister, who was the Aziz. Thus they replied to him with their words: ﴿They said, "Far be Allah [from imperfection]"﴾, meaning God forbid, ﴿We know of him no evil﴾, meaning no bad matter attributed to him.

At that point ﴿the wife of the Aziz said﴾, clearing his side and acknowledging against herself her seduction of him: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, meaning it became clear and evident.

Its root is *ḥaṣṣ* (حَصّ), so it was said *ḥaṣḥaṣa* (حَصْحَصَ), as it was said *kubbū* → *kubkibū* (كُبُّوا كُبْكِبُوا), as al-Zajjaj said. The basic sense of *ḥaṣṣ* is the uprooting of a thing. One says *ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu* when he shaved it off completely. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*The helmet has shaved my head, so I taste no sleep except a brief doze.*

The meaning is that the truth was cut off from falsehood by its manifestation and clarification. From this is also:

*So who will convey from me to Khidash, for he is a liar, when the truth becomes manifest, a wrongdoer?*

It was also said that it is derived from *ḥiṣṣah* (حِصَّة), a share, and the meaning is: the share of falsehood has become distinct.

Al-Khalil said: its meaning is that the truth became apparent after being hidden. Then she clarified that by her saying ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾, and the seduction never occurred from him toward me at all, ﴿and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ in what he said about clearing his own self and attributing the seduction to her. By "now" she meant the time of her speaking these words.

His saying ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾: most of the exegetes held that this is from Joseph's speech, peace be upon him.

Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to join one person's speech to another person's speech when the context indicates to each of them what is fitting for him.

The reference is to the incident that occurred from him, which was his steadfastness and deliberateness, meaning: I did that so that the Aziz may know that I did not betray him in his household in his absence. The meaning is "in the absence" (*bi-zahr al-ghayb*).

The prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa'l-majrūr*) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him.

It was said that he said this while he was in prison after the messenger had informed him of what the women had said and what the wife of the Aziz had said. It was also said that he said this when he had come to the king, and the first is preferable.

Most exegetes, however, held that this is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, and the meaning is: that statement which I made in clearing him, and in confessing against myself to the seduction, so that Joseph may know that I did not betray him, so that I would not attribute to him what did not come from him while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning He does not establish or direct it, or He does not guide them in their plotting, so that their scheme would have an effect by which it is established and endures.

If it is from the speech of Joseph, then it contains an allusion to the wife of the Aziz, since the plotting and treachery against her husband came from her, and an allusion to the Aziz, since he helped to imprison him after he had known his innocence and purity.

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾: if it is from Joseph's speech, then it is from the category of humbling oneself and not praising oneself, although he and other people knew that he was innocent, and that was manifest like the sun, and the woman who had falsely accused him acknowledged it, and the women who cut their hands declared him pure. If it is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, then it is in actual fact, because she had acknowledged the sin and confessed the seduction and the fabrication against Joseph.

It has been said that this is from the speech of the Aziz, but this is very far-fetched. Its meaning is: I do not absolve myself of an evil opinion of Joseph, and of assisting in his imprisonment after I had known of his innocence. ﴿Indeed the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾, meaning this category of human souls is characterized by commanding evil, because of its inclination toward desires, the natural influence of those desires, and the difficulty of subduing them and restraining them from that. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, meaning except those souls upon whom He has mercy, so He preserves them from being commanding to evil; or except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His preserving of it. It was said the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but the mercy of my Lord is what restrains it from being commanding to evil. The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, meaning that it is part of His nature to forgive His servants much and to show them mercy.

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾: the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, not the Aziz, as previously mentioned. The meaning of ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is: I will make him exclusively mine, apart from others, though before that he had been exclusively the Aziz's. *Istikhlāṣ* (اسْتِخْلاص) means seeking that a thing be purified from the impurities of partnership. He said this because Joseph was precious, and it is the custom of kings to make precious things exclusively theirs and not for others.

﴿So when he spoke with him﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: So they brought him to him, and so when he spoke with him, meaning when the king spoke with Joseph. It is possible that the meaning is: when Joseph spoke with the king. It was said the first is preferable, because the gatherings of kings are not addressed first except by them, not by those who enter upon them. It was said the second is preferable, because of the king's saying ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾, for this indicates that when Joseph spoke in the station of the king, he brought what made him beloved to the king and brought him close to his heart, so he said this statement to him. The meaning of *makīn* (مَكِين) is one of standing and trustworthiness, such that he is able to attain what he wants from the king, and the king trusts him with what he is informed of concerning his affairs, or with what he entrusts to him of those matters.

So he interpreted it for him with the most complete clarity and the most perfect expression. When the king heard that from him, he said to him, ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾. When Joseph heard that from him,

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 52–57 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him, and he is indeed of the truthful.﴾ ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous.﴾ ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today in our presence established and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾ ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful [of Allah].﴾

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me"﴾: there is an omission in the speech before this, and the implied meaning is: So the messenger went to the king and informed him of what Joseph had told him regarding the interpretation of that dream. The king then said to those in his presence, "Bring him to me," meaning Joseph. He desired to see him and to know his condition, after he had learned of his excellence from the description the messenger had given him and from his interpretation of his dream. ﴿So when he came to him﴾, meaning when the messenger came to Joseph and summoned him to the king's presence and ordered him to leave the prison, Joseph said to the messenger, "Return to your lord," meaning your master, ﴿Ask him what was the case of the women who cut their hands﴾. He ordered him to ask the king about that matter, and he held back from leaving the prison and did not hasten to respond to the king, so that he might show the people the innocence of his person and the purity of his conduct, and that he had been wronged by the plot of the wife of the Aziz, a manifest wrong. Peace be upon him was given such forbearance, patience and deliberateness that minds fall short of conceiving it. For this reason it is established in the Sahih, from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph remained, I would have answered the caller." He meant the messenger who came calling him to the king.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This act of Joseph's was deliberateness and patience, and a seeking of the clearing of his name. He feared that if he came out and attained a station with the king, while remaining silent about the matter of his offence, people would see him with that eye and say, "This is the one who sought to seduce the wife of the Aziz." He only said, ﴿Ask him about the women﴾, and was silent about the wife of the Aziz, out of regard for the protection of the honourable king, or out of fear of her plotting and her great evil. He mentioned the question about the cutting of the hands and did not mention their seeking to seduce him, out of his disdain for attributing that to them. For this reason he did not attribute the seduction in what preceded to the wife of the Aziz, except after she had accused him of her own fault and slipped away.

Here he was content with a general allusion in his saying ﴿Indeed my Lord is aware of their plot﴾, making Allah's knowledge of what befell him from their plotting sufficient in place of explicit statement.

The clause ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did the king say after the messenger conveyed to him what Joseph had said? The word *khatb* (خَطْب) means a great matter that entitles one to address his companion specifically about it.

The meaning is: What is your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?

The meaning of seduction (*muraawadah*, مُرَاوَدَة) has already been explained. He attributed the seduction to them (plural) because each one of them had done it, as previously mentioned. Among those included in the king's address was the wife of the Aziz. Alternatively, by attributing it to them he meant that it occurred from them in general, just as it occurred from the wife of the Aziz, avoiding explicit attribution of it to her because she was the wife of his minister, who was the Aziz. Thus they replied to him with their words: ﴿They said, "Far be Allah [from imperfection]"﴾, meaning God forbid, ﴿We know of him no evil﴾, meaning no bad matter attributed to him.

At that point ﴿the wife of the Aziz said﴾, clearing his side and acknowledging against herself her seduction of him: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, meaning it became clear and evident.

Its root is *ḥaṣṣ* (حَصّ), so it was said *ḥaṣḥaṣa* (حَصْحَصَ), as it was said *kubbū* → *kubkibū* (كُبُّوا كُبْكِبُوا), as al-Zajjaj said. The basic sense of *ḥaṣṣ* is the uprooting of a thing. One says *ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu* when he shaved it off completely. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*The helmet has shaved my head, so I taste no sleep except a brief doze.*

The meaning is that the truth was cut off from falsehood by its manifestation and clarification. From this is also:

*So who will convey from me to Khidash, for he is a liar, when the truth becomes manifest, a wrongdoer?*

It was also said that it is derived from *ḥiṣṣah* (حِصَّة), a share, and the meaning is: the share of falsehood has become distinct.

Al-Khalil said: its meaning is that the truth became apparent after being hidden. Then she clarified that by her saying ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾, and the seduction never occurred from him toward me at all, ﴿and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ in what he said about clearing his own self and attributing the seduction to her. By "now" she meant the time of her speaking these words.

His saying ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾: most of the exegetes held that this is from Joseph's speech, peace be upon him.

Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to join one person's speech to another person's speech when the context indicates to each of them what is fitting for him.

The reference is to the incident that occurred from him, which was his steadfastness and deliberateness, meaning: I did that so that the Aziz may know that I did not betray him in his household in his absence. The meaning is "in the absence" (*bi-zahr al-ghayb*).

The prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa'l-majrūr*) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him.

It was said that he said this while he was in prison after the messenger had informed him of what the women had said and what the wife of the Aziz had said. It was also said that he said this when he had come to the king, and the first is preferable.

Most exegetes, however, held that this is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, and the meaning is: that statement which I made in clearing him, and in confessing against myself to the seduction, so that Joseph may know that I did not betray him, so that I would not attribute to him what did not come from him while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning He does not establish or direct it, or He does not guide them in their plotting, so that their scheme would have an effect by which it is established and endures.

If it is from the speech of Joseph, then it contains an allusion to the wife of the Aziz, since the plotting and treachery against her husband came from her, and an allusion to the Aziz, since he helped to imprison him after he had known his innocence and purity.

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾: if it is from Joseph's speech, then it is from the category of humbling oneself and not praising oneself, although he and other people knew that he was innocent, and that was manifest like the sun, and the woman who had falsely accused him acknowledged it, and the women who cut their hands declared him pure. If it is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, then it is in actual fact, because she had acknowledged the sin and confessed the seduction and the fabrication against Joseph.

It has been said that this is from the speech of the Aziz, but this is very far-fetched. Its meaning is: I do not absolve myself of an evil opinion of Joseph, and of assisting in his imprisonment after I had known of his innocence. ﴿Indeed the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾, meaning this category of human souls is characterized by commanding evil, because of its inclination toward desires, the natural influence of those desires, and the difficulty of subduing them and restraining them from that. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, meaning except those souls upon whom He has mercy, so He preserves them from being commanding to evil; or except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His preserving of it. It was said the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but the mercy of my Lord is what restrains it from being commanding to evil. The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, meaning that it is part of His nature to forgive His servants much and to show them mercy.

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾: the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, not the Aziz, as previously mentioned. The meaning of ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is: I will make him exclusively mine, apart from others, though before that he had been exclusively the Aziz's. *Istikhlāṣ* (اسْتِخْلاص) means seeking that a thing be purified from the impurities of partnership. He said this because Joseph was precious, and it is the custom of kings to make precious things exclusively theirs and not for others.

﴿So when he spoke with him﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: So they brought him to him, and so when he spoke with him, meaning when the king spoke with Joseph. It is possible that the meaning is: when Joseph spoke with the king. It was said the first is preferable, because the gatherings of kings are not addressed first except by them, not by those who enter upon them. It was said the second is preferable, because of the king's saying ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾, for this indicates that when Joseph spoke in the station of the king, he brought what made him beloved to the king and brought him close to his heart, so he said this statement to him. The meaning of *makīn* (مَكِين) is one of standing and trustworthiness, such that he is able to attain what he wants from the king, and the king trusts him with what he is informed of concerning his affairs, or with what he entrusts to him of those matters.

It was said that when he reached the king, he seated him on his throne and said to him, "I love to hear from you the interpretation of my dream." So he interpreted it for him with the most complete clarity and the most perfect expression. When the king heard that from him, he said to him, ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾. When Joseph heard that from him,

﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land."﴾ That is, put me in charge of the land whose affairs are in your hand, which is the land of Egypt. Or it means: appoint me over the keeping of the treasuries of the land, which are the places where wealth is stored.

Joseph, peace be upon him, requested this from him so that he might thereby achieve the establishment of justice and the removal of oppression, and through it call the people of Egypt to faith in Allah and to abandoning the worship of idols. In this is evidence that it is permissible for one who is confident in himself, when he enters into one of the affairs of the authorities, to raise the beacon of truth and demolish as much falsehood as he can, to request that position for himself. It is also permissible for him to describe himself with qualities that encourage what he seeks and incite those kings he addresses to hand over the reins of affairs to him and to make them dependent upon him. However, this permissibility is opposed by what has been transmitted from our Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting the seeking of authority and forbidding the appointing of one who requests it or is eager for it.

﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, meaning and in the same wondrous manner of establishment, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾: meaning We gave him a place, which is an expression for the perfection of his power and the execution of his command and prohibition, until the king acted upon his opinion, and the people acted upon his command and prohibition (p-702) ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, meaning he would dwell in it wherever he wished and take it as a dwelling place. ﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ from among the servants, so We show him mercy in this world by being kind to him and bestowing favour upon him, and in the Hereafter by admitting him into Paradise and saving him from the Fire. ﴿And We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾ in their good deeds which are what Allah demands of them, meaning We do not waste their reward for them in them, nor their recompense for them.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾, meaning their reward in the Hereafter, and the reward is attributed to the Hereafter for suitability. The meaning of seduction (*muraawadah*, مُرَاوَدَة) has already been explained. He attributed the seduction to them (plural) because each one of them had done it, as previously mentioned. Among those included in the king's address was the wife of the Aziz. Alternatively, by attributing it to them he meant that it occurred from them in general, just as it occurred from the wife of the Aziz, avoiding explicit attribution of it to her because she was the wife of his minister, who was the Aziz. Thus they replied to him with their words: ﴿They said, "Far be Allah [from imperfection]"﴾, meaning God forbid, ﴿We know of him no evil﴾, meaning no bad matter attributed to him.

At that point ﴿the wife of the Aziz said﴾, clearing his side and acknowledging against herself her seduction of him: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, meaning it became clear and evident.

Its root is *ḥaṣṣ* (حَصّ), so it was said *ḥaṣḥaṣa* (حَصْحَصَ), as it was said *kubbū* → *kubkibū* (كُبُّوا كُبْكِبُوا), as al-Zajjaj said. The basic sense of *ḥaṣṣ* is the uprooting of a thing. One says *ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu* when he shaved it off completely. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*The helmet has shaved my head, so I taste no sleep except a brief doze.*

The meaning is that the truth was cut off from falsehood by its manifestation and clarification. From this is also:

*So who will convey from me to Khidash, for he is a liar, when the truth becomes manifest, a wrongdoer?*

It was also said that it is derived from *ḥiṣṣah* (حِصَّة), a share, and the meaning is: the share of falsehood has become distinct.

Al-Khalil said: its meaning is that the truth became apparent after being hidden. Then she clarified that by her saying ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾, and the seduction never occurred from him toward me at all, ﴿and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ in what he said about clearing his own self and attributing the seduction to her. By "now" she meant the time of her speaking these words.

His saying ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾: most of the exegetes held that this is from Joseph's speech, peace be upon him.

Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to join one person's speech to another person's speech when the context indicates to each of them what is fitting for him.

The reference is to the incident that occurred from him, which was his steadfastness and deliberateness, meaning: I did that so that the Aziz may know that I did not betray him in his household in his absence. The meaning is "in the absence" (*bi-zahr al-ghayb*).

The prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa'l-majrūr*) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him.

It was said that he said this while he was in prison after the messenger had informed him of what the women had said and what the wife of the Aziz had said. It was also said that he said this when he had come to the king, and the first is preferable.

Most exegetes, however, held that this is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, and the meaning is: that statement which I made in clearing him, and in confessing against myself to the seduction, so that Joseph may know that I did not betray him, so that I would not attribute to him what did not come from him while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning He does not establish or direct it, or He does not guide them in their plotting, so that their scheme would have an effect by which it is established and endures.

If it is from the speech of Joseph, then it contains an allusion to the wife of the Aziz, since the plotting and treachery against her husband came from her, and an allusion to the Aziz, since he helped to imprison him after he had known his innocence and purity.

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾: if it is from Joseph's speech, then it is from the category of humbling oneself and not praising oneself, although he and other people knew that he was innocent, and that was manifest like the sun, and the woman who had falsely accused him acknowledged it, and the women who cut their hands declared him pure. If it is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, then it is in actual fact, because she had acknowledged the sin and confessed the seduction and the fabrication against Joseph.

It has been said that this is from the speech of the Aziz, but this is very far-fetched. Its meaning is: I do not absolve myself of an evil opinion of Joseph, and of assisting in his imprisonment after I had known of his innocence. ﴿Indeed the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾, meaning this category of human souls is characterized by commanding evil, because of its inclination toward desires, the natural influence of those desires, and the difficulty of subduing them and restraining them from that. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, meaning except those souls upon whom He has mercy, so He preserves them from being commanding to evil; or except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His preserving of it. It was said the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but the mercy of my Lord is what restrains it from being commanding to evil. The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, meaning that it is part of His nature to forgive His servants much and to show them mercy.

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾: the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, not the Aziz, as previously mentioned. The meaning of ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is: I will make him exclusively mine, apart from others, though before that he had been exclusively the Aziz's. *Istikhlāṣ* (اسْتِخْلاص) means seeking that a thing be purified from the impurities of partnership. He said this because Joseph was precious, and it is the custom of kings to make precious things exclusively theirs and not for others.

﴿So when he spoke with him﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: So they brought him to him, and so when he spoke with him, meaning when the king spoke with Joseph. It is possible that the meaning is: when Joseph spoke with the king. It was said the first is preferable, because the gatherings of kings are not addressed first except by them, not by those who enter upon them. It was said the second is preferable, because of the king's saying ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾, for this indicates that when Joseph spoke in the station of the king, he brought what made him beloved to the king and brought him close to his heart, so he said this statement to him. The meaning of *makīn* (مَكِين) is one of standing and trustworthiness, such that he is able to attain what he wants from the king, and the king trusts him with what he is informed of concerning his affairs, or with what he entrusts to him of those matters.

It was said that when he reached the king, he seated him on his throne and said to him, "I love to hear from you the interpretation of my dream." So he interpreted it for him with the most complete clarity and the most perfect expression. When the king heard that from him, he said to him, ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾. When Joseph heard that from him,

﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land."﴾ That is, put me in charge of the land whose affairs are in your hand, which is the land of Egypt. Or it means: appoint me over the keeping of the treasuries of the land, which are the places where wealth is stored.

Joseph, peace be upon him, requested this from him so that he might thereby achieve the establishment of justice and the removal of oppression, and through it call the people of Egypt to faith in Allah and to abandoning the worship of idols. In this is evidence that it is permissible for one who is confident in himself, when he enters into one of the affairs of the authorities, to raise the beacon of truth and demolish as much falsehood as he can, to request that position for himself. It is also permissible for him to describe himself with qualities that encourage what he seeks and incite those kings he addresses to hand over the reins of affairs to him and to make them dependent upon him. However, this permissibility is opposed by what has been transmitted from our Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting the seeking of authority and forbidding the appointing of one who requests it or is eager for it.

*Khazāʾin* (خَزَائِن) is the plural of *khizānah* (خِزَانَة), which is the name of the place where a thing is stored. *Ḥafīẓ* (حَفِيظ) is one who guards a thing, meaning: ﴿I am a guardian﴾ of what you have entrusted to me of guarding the wealth, not letting it out in other than its proper exits, nor spending it in other than its proper channels, ﴿knowing﴾ of the manner of its gathering and dispersal, its entry and its exit.

﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, meaning and in the same wondrous manner of establishment, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾: meaning We gave him a place, which is an expression for the perfection of his power and the execution of his command and prohibition, until the king acted upon his opinion, and the people acted upon his command and prohibition (p-702) ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, meaning he would dwell in it wherever he wished and take it as a dwelling place. This is an expression for the perfection of his power as previously mentioned, and it is as if he disposed of the land whose affairs were under the authority of Egypt as a man disposes of his own home.

Ibn Kathir recited it with the *nūn* (نُصِيبُ).

This verse has been used as evidence that it is permissible to take up government offices from an unjust authority, or even a disbelieving one, for one who is confident in himself of standing by the truth. We have already presented the discussion on this in full in His saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾ (Hud 11:113).

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ from among the servants, so We show him mercy in this world by being kind to him and bestowing favour upon him, and in the Hereafter by admitting him into Paradise and saving him from the Fire. ﴿And We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾ in their good deeds which are what Allah demands of them, meaning We do not waste their reward for them in them, nor their recompense for them.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾, meaning their reward in the Hereafter, and the reward is attributed to the Hereafter for suitability. Their reward is the recompense which Allah repays them with there, which is Paradise, whose bliss never ends and whose duration never terminates. ﴿Is better for those who believed﴾ in Allah ﴿and used to be mindful﴾ of falling into what He has forbidden them. The intended ones are the doers of good mentioned previously, and in this is an indication that the good deed that is credited is faith and piety.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 52–57 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿What was the matter with the women?﴾ He said: Yusuf intended to present his excuse before he left the prison.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated from him, who said: When the wife of the ʿAziz said, "It was I who sought to seduce him," Yusuf said, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, and Jibril nudged him and said: "Nor when you desired her?" So he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿The truth has become manifest﴾ — he said: it became clear.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi the like of this.

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hakim ibn Hizam regarding His words: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, that Jibril said to him: "Nor when you untied the trousers?" Thereupon he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself...﴾.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, via the chain of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself"﴾, said: The messenger came to him and said: "Take off your prison garments, put on new clothes, and go to the king." The people of the prison prayed for him, and he was then thirty years old. When he came to him, the king saw a young man, and said: "Does this one know my dream when the magicians and the soothsayers do not know it?" And he seated him before him and said, "Do not fear."

He clothed him with a collar of gold and garments of silk, and gave him a mount saddled and adorned like the king's mount, and the drum was beaten in Egypt: "Indeed Yusuf is the king's deputy."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The king said to Yusuf: "I love that you mix with me in everything except my family, and I am too proud that you should eat with me." Yusuf became angry and said: "I have more right to be proud. I am the son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah, I am the son of Ishaq, the sacrifice of Allah, and I am the son of Yaʿqub, the prophet of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shaybah ibn Nuʿamah al-Dabbi regarding His words: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, he said: over all the food; ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ of what You entrust to me, ﴿knowing of the years of famine﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Thus did We establish Yusuf in the land﴾, he said: We made him king over it, so that he could be wherever he wished in that world, doing in it whatever he wished.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that Yusuf married the wife of the ʿAziz, and found her a virgin, and her husband had been impotent.
