Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿The truth has become manifest﴾ — he said: it became clear.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi the like of this.

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hakim ibn Hizam regarding His words: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, that Jibril said to him: "Nor when you untied the trousers?" Thereupon he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself...﴾.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, via the chain of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself"﴾, said: The messenger came to him and said: "Take off your prison garments, put on new clothes, and go to the king." The people of the prison prayed for him, and he was then thirty years old. When he came to him, the king saw a young man, and said: "Does this one know my dream when the magicians and the soothsayers do not know it?" And he seated him before him and said, "Do not fear."

He clothed him with a collar of gold and garments of silk, and gave him a mount saddled and adorned like the king's mount, and the drum was beaten in Egypt: "Indeed Yusuf is the king's deputy."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The king said to Yusuf: "I love that you mix with me in everything except my family, and I am too proud that you should eat with me." Yusuf became angry and said: "I have more right to be proud. I am the son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah, I am the son of Ishaq, the sacrifice of Allah, and I am the son of Yaʿqub, the prophet of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shaybah ibn Nuʿamah al-Dabbi regarding His words: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, he said: over all the food; ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ of what You entrust to me, ﴿knowing of the years of famine﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Thus did We establish Yusuf in the land﴾, he said: We made him king over it, so that he could be wherever he wished in that world, doing in it whatever he wished.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that Yusuf married the wife of the ʿAziz, and found her a virgin, and her husband had been impotent.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 52–57 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Now the truth has become manifest. It was I who sought to seduce him, and he is indeed of the truthful.﴾ ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous.﴾ ﴿And I do not absolve myself. Indeed, the soul is ever commanding to evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself." So when he spoke with him, he said, "Indeed, you are today in our presence established and trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land. Indeed, I am a knowing guardian."﴾ ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle therein wherever he willed. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost.﴾ ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and used to be mindful [of Allah].﴾

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me"﴾: there is an omission in the speech before this, and the implied meaning is: So the messenger went to the king and informed him of what Joseph had told him regarding the interpretation of that dream. The king then said to those in his presence, "Bring him to me," meaning Joseph. He desired to see him and to know his condition, after he had learned of his excellence from the description the messenger had given him and from his interpretation of his dream. ﴿So when he came to him﴾, meaning when the messenger came to Joseph and summoned him to the king's presence and ordered him to leave the prison, Joseph said to the messenger, "Return to your lord," meaning your master, ﴿Ask him what was the case of the women who cut their hands﴾. He ordered him to ask the king about that matter, and he held back from leaving the prison and did not hasten to respond to the king, so that he might show the people the innocence of his person and the purity of his conduct, and that he had been wronged by the plot of the wife of the Aziz, a manifest wrong. Peace be upon him was given such forbearance, patience and deliberateness that minds fall short of conceiving it. For this reason it is established in the Sahih, from the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph remained, I would have answered the caller." He meant the messenger who came calling him to the king.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This act of Joseph's was deliberateness and patience, and a seeking of the clearing of his name. He feared that if he came out and attained a station with the king, while remaining silent about the matter of his offence, people would see him with that eye and say, "This is the one who sought to seduce the wife of the Aziz." He only said, ﴿Ask him about the women﴾, and was silent about the wife of the Aziz, out of regard for the protection of the honourable king, or out of fear of her plotting and her great evil. He mentioned the question about the cutting of the hands and did not mention their seeking to seduce him, out of his disdain for attributing that to them. For this reason he did not attribute the seduction in what preceded to the wife of the Aziz, except after she had accused him of her own fault and slipped away.

Here he was content with a general allusion in his saying ﴿Indeed my Lord is aware of their plot﴾, making Allah's knowledge of what befell him from their plotting sufficient in place of explicit statement.

The clause ﴿He said, "What was your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?"﴾ is a resumptive clause, an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: What did the king say after the messenger conveyed to him what Joseph had said? The word *khatb* (خَطْب) means a great matter that entitles one to address his companion specifically about it.

The meaning is: What is your affair when you sought to seduce Joseph from himself?

The meaning of seduction (*muraawadah*, مُرَاوَدَة) has already been explained. He attributed the seduction to them (plural) because each one of them had done it, as previously mentioned. Among those included in the king's address was the wife of the Aziz. Alternatively, by attributing it to them he meant that it occurred from them in general, just as it occurred from the wife of the Aziz, avoiding explicit attribution of it to her because she was the wife of his minister, who was the Aziz. Thus they replied to him with their words: ﴿They said, "Far be Allah [from imperfection]"﴾, meaning God forbid, ﴿We know of him no evil﴾, meaning no bad matter attributed to him.

At that point ﴿the wife of the Aziz said﴾, clearing his side and acknowledging against herself her seduction of him: ﴿Now the truth has become manifest﴾, meaning it became clear and evident.

Its root is *ḥaṣṣ* (حَصّ), so it was said *ḥaṣḥaṣa* (حَصْحَصَ), as it was said *kubbū* → *kubkibū* (كُبُّوا كُبْكِبُوا), as al-Zajjaj said. The basic sense of *ḥaṣṣ* is the uprooting of a thing. One says *ḥaṣṣa sha'rahu* when he shaved it off completely. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*The helmet has shaved my head, so I taste no sleep except a brief doze.*

The meaning is that the truth was cut off from falsehood by its manifestation and clarification. From this is also:

*So who will convey from me to Khidash, for he is a liar, when the truth becomes manifest, a wrongdoer?*

It was also said that it is derived from *ḥiṣṣah* (حِصَّة), a share, and the meaning is: the share of falsehood has become distinct.

Al-Khalil said: its meaning is that the truth became apparent after being hidden. Then she clarified that by her saying ﴿It was I who sought to seduce him﴾, and the seduction never occurred from him toward me at all, ﴿and indeed he is of the truthful﴾ in what he said about clearing his own self and attributing the seduction to her. By "now" she meant the time of her speaking these words.

His saying ﴿That [he did so] so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾: most of the exegetes held that this is from Joseph's speech, peace be upon him.

Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to join one person's speech to another person's speech when the context indicates to each of them what is fitting for him.

The reference is to the incident that occurred from him, which was his steadfastness and deliberateness, meaning: I did that so that the Aziz may know that I did not betray him in his household in his absence. The meaning is "in the absence" (*bi-zahr al-ghayb*).

The prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa'l-majrūr*) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him.

It was said that he said this while he was in prison after the messenger had informed him of what the women had said and what the wife of the Aziz had said. It was also said that he said this when he had come to the king, and the first is preferable.

Most exegetes, however, held that this is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, and the meaning is: that statement which I made in clearing him, and in confessing against myself to the seduction, so that Joseph may know that I did not betray him, so that I would not attribute to him what did not come from him while he was absent from me, or while I was absent from him. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the plot of the treacherous﴾, meaning He does not establish or direct it, or He does not guide them in their plotting, so that their scheme would have an effect by which it is established and endures.

If it is from the speech of Joseph, then it contains an allusion to the wife of the Aziz, since the plotting and treachery against her husband came from her, and an allusion to the Aziz, since he helped to imprison him after he had known his innocence and purity.

﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾: if it is from Joseph's speech, then it is from the category of humbling oneself and not praising oneself, although he and other people knew that he was innocent, and that was manifest like the sun, and the woman who had falsely accused him acknowledged it, and the women who cut their hands declared him pure. If it is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, then it is in actual fact, because she had acknowledged the sin and confessed the seduction and the fabrication against Joseph.

It has been said that this is from the speech of the Aziz, but this is very far-fetched. Its meaning is: I do not absolve myself of an evil opinion of Joseph, and of assisting in his imprisonment after I had known of his innocence. ﴿Indeed the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾, meaning this category of human souls is characterized by commanding evil, because of its inclination toward desires, the natural influence of those desires, and the difficulty of subduing them and restraining them from that. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, meaning except those souls upon whom He has mercy, so He preserves them from being commanding to evil; or except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His preserving of it. It was said the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but the mercy of my Lord is what restrains it from being commanding to evil. The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, meaning that it is part of His nature to forgive His servants much and to show them mercy.

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾: the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, not the Aziz, as previously mentioned. The meaning of ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is: I will make him exclusively mine, apart from others, though before that he had been exclusively the Aziz's. *Istikhlāṣ* (اسْتِخْلاص) means seeking that a thing be purified from the impurities of partnership. He said this because Joseph was precious, and it is the custom of kings to make precious things exclusively theirs and not for others.

﴿So when he spoke with him﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: So they brought him to him, and so when he spoke with him, meaning when the king spoke with Joseph. It is possible that the meaning is: when Joseph spoke with the king. It was said the first is preferable, because the gatherings of kings are not addressed first except by them, not by those who enter upon them. It was said the second is preferable, because of the king's saying ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾, for this indicates that when Joseph spoke in the station of the king, he brought what made him beloved to the king and brought him close to his heart, so he said this statement to him. The meaning of *makīn* (مَكِين) is one of standing and trustworthiness, such that he is able to attain what he wants from the king, and the king trusts him with what he is informed of concerning his affairs, or with what he entrusts to him of those matters.

It was said that when he reached the king, he seated him on his throne and said to him, "I love to hear from you the interpretation of my dream." So he interpreted it for him with the most complete clarity and the most perfect expression. When the king heard that from him, he said to him, ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾. When Joseph heard that from him,

﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land."﴾ That is, put me in charge of the land whose affairs are in your hand, which is the land of Egypt. Or it means: appoint me over the keeping of the treasuries of the land, which are the places where wealth is stored.

Joseph, peace be upon him, requested this from him so that he might thereby achieve the establishment of justice and the removal of oppression, and through it call the people of Egypt to faith in Allah and to abandoning the worship of idols. In this is evidence that it is permissible for one who is confident in himself, when he enters into one of the affairs of the authorities, to raise the beacon of truth and demolish as much falsehood as he can, to request that position for himself. It is also permissible for him to describe himself with qualities that encourage what he seeks and incite those kings he addresses to hand over the reins of affairs to him and to make them dependent upon him. However, this permissibility is opposed by what has been transmitted from our Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting the seeking of authority and forbidding the appointing of one who requests it or is eager for it.

*Khazāʾin* (خَزَائِن) is the plural of *khizānah* (خِزَانَة), which is the name of the place where a thing is stored. *Ḥafīẓ* (حَفِيظ) is one who guards a thing, meaning: ﴿I am a guardian﴾ of what you have entrusted to me of guarding the wealth, not letting it out in other than its proper exits, nor spending it in other than its proper channels, ﴿knowing﴾ of the manner of its gathering and dispersal, its entry and its exit.

﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, meaning and in the same wondrous manner of establishment, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾: meaning We gave him a place, which is an expression for the perfection of his power and the execution of his command and prohibition, until the king acted upon his opinion, and the people acted upon his command and prohibition (p-702) ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, meaning he would dwell in it wherever he wished and take it as a dwelling place. This is an expression for the perfection of his power as previously mentioned, and it is as if he disposed of the land whose affairs were under the authority of Egypt as a man disposes of his own home.

Ibn Kathir recited it with the *nūn* (نُصِيبُ).

This verse has been used as evidence that it is permissible to take up government offices from an unjust authority, or even a disbelieving one, for one who is confident in himself of standing by the truth. We have already presented the discussion on this in full in His saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾ (Hud 11:113).

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ from among the servants, so We show him mercy in this world by being kind to him and bestowing favour upon him, and in the Hereafter by admitting him into Paradise and saving him from the Fire. ﴿And We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾ in their good deeds which are what Allah demands of them, meaning We do not waste their reward for them in them, nor their recompense for them.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾, meaning their reward in the Hereafter, and the reward is attributed to the Hereafter for suitability. Their reward is the recompense which Allah repays them with there, which is Paradise, whose bliss never ends and whose duration never terminates. ﴿Is better for those who believed﴾ in Allah ﴿and used to be mindful﴾ of falling into what He has forbidden them. The intended ones are the doers of good mentioned previously, and in this is an indication that the good deed that is credited is faith and piety.

If it is from the speech of the wife of the Aziz, then it is in actual fact, because she had acknowledged the sin and confessed the seduction and the fabrication against Joseph.

It has been said that this is from the speech of the Aziz, but this is very far-fetched. Its meaning is: I do not absolve myself of an evil opinion of Joseph, and of assisting in his imprisonment after I had known of his innocence. ﴿Indeed the soul is ever commanding to evil﴾, meaning this category of human souls is characterized by commanding evil, because of its inclination toward desires, the natural influence of those desires, and the difficulty of subduing them and restraining them from that. ﴿Except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾, meaning except those souls upon whom He has mercy, so He preserves them from being commanding to evil; or except at the time of my Lord's mercy and His preserving of it. It was said the exception is disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but the mercy of my Lord is what restrains it from being commanding to evil. The clause ﴿Indeed my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, meaning that it is part of His nature to forgive His servants much and to show them mercy.

His saying ﴿And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself."﴾: the king was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, not the Aziz, as previously mentioned. The meaning of ﴿I will take him for myself﴾ is: I will make him exclusively mine, apart from others, though before that he had been exclusively the Aziz's. *Istikhlāṣ* (اسْتِخْلاص) means seeking that a thing be purified from the impurities of partnership. He said this because Joseph was precious, and it is the custom of kings to make precious things exclusively theirs and not for others.

﴿So when he spoke with him﴾: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: So they brought him to him, and so when he spoke with him, meaning when the king spoke with Joseph. It is possible that the meaning is: when Joseph spoke with the king. It was said the first is preferable, because the gatherings of kings are not addressed first except by them, not by those who enter upon them. It was said the second is preferable, because of the king's saying ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾, for this indicates that when Joseph spoke in the station of the king, he brought what made him beloved to the king and brought him close to his heart, so he said this statement to him. The meaning of *makīn* (مَكِين) is one of standing and trustworthiness, such that he is able to attain what he wants from the king, and the king trusts him with what he is informed of concerning his affairs, or with what he entrusts to him of those matters.

It was said that when he reached the king, he seated him on his throne and said to him, "I love to hear from you the interpretation of my dream." So he interpreted it for him with the most complete clarity and the most perfect expression. When the king heard that from him, he said to him, ﴿Indeed you are today in our presence established and trustworthy﴾. When Joseph heard that from him,

﴿He said, "Appoint me over the treasuries of the land."﴾ That is, put me in charge of the land whose affairs are in your hand, which is the land of Egypt. Or it means: appoint me over the keeping of the treasuries of the land, which are the places where wealth is stored.

Joseph, peace be upon him, requested this from him so that he might thereby achieve the establishment of justice and the removal of oppression, and through it call the people of Egypt to faith in Allah and to abandoning the worship of idols. In this is evidence that it is permissible for one who is confident in himself, when he enters into one of the affairs of the authorities, to raise the beacon of truth and demolish as much falsehood as he can, to request that position for himself. It is also permissible for him to describe himself with qualities that encourage what he seeks and incite those kings he addresses to hand over the reins of affairs to him and to make them dependent upon him. However, this permissibility is opposed by what has been transmitted from our Prophet (ﷺ) prohibiting the seeking of authority and forbidding the appointing of one who requests it or is eager for it.

*Khazāʾin* (خَزَائِن) is the plural of *khizānah* (خِزَانَة), which is the name of the place where a thing is stored. *Ḥafīẓ* (حَفِيظ) is one who guards a thing, meaning: ﴿I am a guardian﴾ of what you have entrusted to me of guarding the wealth, not letting it out in other than its proper exits, nor spending it in other than its proper channels, ﴿knowing﴾ of the manner of its gathering and dispersal, its entry and its exit.

﴿And thus We established Joseph﴾, meaning and in the same wondrous manner of establishment, ﴿We established Joseph in the land﴾: meaning We gave him a place, which is an expression for the perfection of his power and the execution of his command and prohibition, until the king acted upon his opinion, and the people acted upon his command and prohibition (p-702) ﴿to settle therein wherever he willed﴾, meaning he would dwell in it wherever he wished and take it as a dwelling place. This is an expression for the perfection of his power as previously mentioned, and it is as if he disposed of the land whose affairs were under the authority of Egypt as a man disposes of his own home.

Ibn Kathir recited it with the *nūn* (نُصِيبُ).

This verse has been used as evidence that it is permissible to take up government offices from an unjust authority, or even a disbelieving one, for one who is confident in himself of standing by the truth. We have already presented the discussion on this in full in His saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾ (Hud 11:113).

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾ from among the servants, so We show him mercy in this world by being kind to him and bestowing favour upon him, and in the Hereafter by admitting him into Paradise and saving him from the Fire. ﴿And We do not allow the reward of the doers of good to be lost﴾ in their good deeds which are what Allah demands of them, meaning We do not waste their reward for them in them, nor their recompense for them.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾, meaning their reward in the Hereafter, and the reward is attributed to the Hereafter for suitability. Their reward is the recompense which Allah repays them with there, which is Paradise, whose bliss never ends and whose duration never terminates. ﴿Is better for those who believed﴾ in Allah ﴿and used to be mindful﴾ of falling into what He has forbidden them. The intended ones are the doers of good mentioned previously, and in this is an indication that the good deed that is credited is faith and piety.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 52–57 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿What was the matter with the women?﴾ He said: Yusuf intended to present his excuse before he left the prison.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated from him, who said: When the wife of the ʿAziz said, "It was I who sought to seduce him," Yusuf said, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, and Jibril nudged him and said: "Nor when you desired her?" So he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself...﴾ the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿The truth has become manifest﴾ — he said: it became clear.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi the like of this.

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hakim ibn Hizam regarding His words: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, that Jibril said to him: "Nor when you untied the trousers?" Thereupon he said, ﴿Nor do I absolve myself...﴾.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam in Futuh Misr, via the chain of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿The king said, "Bring him to me; I will take him for myself"﴾, said: The messenger came to him and said: "Take off your prison garments, put on new clothes, and go to the king." The people of the prison prayed for him, and he was then thirty years old. When he came to him, the king saw a young man, and said: "Does this one know my dream when the magicians and the soothsayers do not know it?" And he seated him before him and said, "Do not fear."

He clothed him with a collar of gold and garments of silk, and gave him a mount saddled and adorned like the king's mount, and the drum was beaten in Egypt: "Indeed Yusuf is the king's deputy."

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: The king said to Yusuf: "I love that you mix with me in everything except my family, and I am too proud that you should eat with me." Yusuf became angry and said: "I have more right to be proud. I am the son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah, I am the son of Ishaq, the sacrifice of Allah, and I am the son of Yaʿqub, the prophet of Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shaybah ibn Nuʿamah al-Dabbi regarding His words: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, he said: over all the food; ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ of what You entrust to me, ﴿knowing of the years of famine﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿Thus did We establish Yusuf in the land﴾, he said: We made him king over it, so that he could be wherever he wished in that world, doing in it whatever he wished.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that Yusuf married the wife of the ʿAziz, and found her a virgin, and her husband had been impotent.

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him.
