Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future. As for the present, he had already given them their full measure. The meaning of "nor shall you come near me" is: do not enter my lands, let alone that I should do good to you. It was also said its meaning is: I will not lodge you with me as I lodged you this time. He did not intend that they could not approach his lands. "Taqrabun" is in the jussive mood, either because "la" is a prohibitive particle or because it is a negative particle; it is conjoined to the position of the conditional clause and falls under its ruling, as if he had said: "If you do not bring me, you will be deprived and will not be brought near." When they heard this from him, they promised him what he had asked of them.

So they ﴿said: We will seek to get him from his father﴾, that is, we will request him from him and strive in that with what we are able to do. It was said that the meaning of "seeking to get" (murawada) here is deception on their part toward their father and a stratagem against him until they take him away from him. ﴿And indeed we will surely do it﴾, that is, we will carry out this seeking without falling short in it. It was also said its meaning is: we are indeed capable of that, and we will not be negligent about it or treat it as a great matter.

﴿And he said to his servants (lifityanihi): Put their merchandise into their saddlebags⌋﴾. The people of Madina, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Shu'ba, and Ibn 'Amir read "li-fityatihi" (to his young man). Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas and others chose this reading.

The rest of the Kufans read "li-fityanihi" (to his servants), and Abu 'Ubayda chose this reading. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it is like the latter reading.

Al-Nahhas said: "li-fityanihi" differs from the majority, and the consensus of the majority is not to be abandoned for this disconnected chain of transmission (isnad). Also, fityah resembles more closely the plural "fityan," because in Arabic fitya is used for the smallest number. The command to a few persons to put the merchandise into the saddlebags is more fitting. The sentence is a new independent clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say after their promise to him in that?" So it was answered: he said to his young men.

Al-Zajjaj said: "fityah" and "fityan" in this place mean slaves (mamalik). Al-Tha'labi said: both are good dialects, like "sibyan" and "sibyah."

What is meant here by the merchandise is what they had brought with them from their lands to buy food with. It was leather and skins. Yusuf, peace be upon him, did this as a favour to them. It was said he did it so that they would return to him a second time, since he knew they would not accept food except for a price. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said he did it so that they would be helped by it to return to him to buy food. It was also said that he found it repugnant to take the price of food from his father and brothers.

Then Yusuf, peace be upon him, gave the reason for what he had commanded regarding placing the merchandise in their saddlebags, with his words: ﴿so that they may recognise it when they return to their family﴾. So the reason for placing the merchandise in the saddlebags was that they would recognise it when they returned to their family. This is because they would not know of the return of the merchandise to them except when they emptied the containers in which they had put the food, and they would not empty them except upon arriving at their family. Then he gave the reason for their recognising the returned merchandise placed in their saddlebags with his words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. For when they recognised that and knew that they had taken the food without price, and that what they had given as its exchange had come back to them, and that the one to whom they had come had done them a favour, they would be eager to return to him. This is especially so with the severe drought they were in, their need for food, and its absence from them, for that is among the greatest of things that prompt them to return. By this it becomes clear that Yusuf, peace be upon him, returned the merchandise to them only for this purpose, namely their return to him. So the explanation for returning it cannot be completed by anything else. "Rihal" is the plural of "rahl," and what is meant here is the baggage a man takes with him of household goods.

Al-Wahidi said: "al-rahl" is everything prepared for travel, such as a container for goods, a saddle for a camel, a seat, or a rope. End of quotation.

What is meant here is the containers in which they put the grain they buy.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "rahl" is said of a container, and "rahl" is also said of a house.

﴿So when they returned to their father, they said: O our father, measure has been withheld from us.﴾ By this they meant what Yusuf had said to them earlier: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾, that is: measure has been withheld from us in the future. This indicates that buying grain again and again was a known practice between them and him. Perhaps they said this statement to him before they opened their goods and learned of the return of their merchandise, as his words later indicate: ﴿And when they opened their goods﴾ to the end. Then they mentioned to him what Yusuf had commanded them, and they said: ﴿So send our brother with us﴾, meaning Binyamin, ﴿and we shall get measure﴾. The verb "nakthal" is the answer to the command: that is, we shall get measure by the sending of him with us of the food we want.

The people of the two sanctuaries (Makka and Madina), Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim read "naktal" with the nun.

The rest of the Kufans read it with the yā' (yaktal, third person). Abu 'Ubayd chose the first reading. He said: "all of them will be included among those who measure," and he claimed that if it were with the yā', it would be only for the brother alone, that is, "our brother Binyamin will measure." Al-Nahhas objected to this with what amounts to: attributing the measuring to the brother does not contradict its being for all, and the meaning is: Binyamin will measure for all of us.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if you send him, we will get measure; otherwise we will be denied measure. ﴿And indeed we are to him﴾, that is, to their brother Binyamin, ﴿surely guardians﴾ against any harm or misfortune befalling him.

The sentence ﴿He said: Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother before?﴾ is a new independent sentence answering an implied question, as has been stated in similar places in many passages. The meaning is: he does not trust them with Binyamin except as he trusted them with his brother Yusuf, and they had said to him about Yusuf: "And indeed we are to him guardians," as they say here: "And indeed we are to him guardians." Then they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. So if he trusts them with Binyamin, he fears they will betray him concerning him as they betrayed him concerning Yusuf. ﴿But God is the best guardian, and He is the most merciful of the merciful.﴾ The particle "la" here has an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Ya'qub relied upon God, handed him over to them, and said: "God is the best guardian" (hifdhan).

The people of Madina read ﴿hifdhan﴾ (guardian/guarding), which is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). This is also the reading of Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir.

The rest of the Kufans read ﴿hafidhan﴾, which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Al-Zajjaj said: (p-704) "it is by way of explanation (bayan)," meaning specification (tamyiz). The meaning of the verse: God's guarding of him is better than their guarding of him. When Ya'qub committed his guarding to God, may He be glorified, God guarded him and returned him to him. But when he had said about Yusuf: ﴿And I fear that the wolf may devour him﴾ [Yusuf: 13], there befell him from the trial what befell him.

﴿And when they opened their goods﴾, that is, the containers of the food, or what is more general than that, of what the word "goods" (mata') applies to, whether what was in it was food or not, ﴿they found their merchandise returned to them﴾, that is, the merchandise they had brought to Misr to buy grain with, and its description has already been given. The sentence ﴿They said: O our father﴾ is a new independent sentence, as has been mentioned. "Ma nabghi" may be interrogative, and the meaning is: what do we seek from this king after he has done with us what he has done of kindness by returning the merchandise and honouring us upon our arrival to him, and giving us in full what we wanted of grain? The interrogative would then be for denial. The sentence ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾ confirms what the interrogative indicates of denial of seeking anything when it has already been returned to them. It was also said that "ma" in "ma nabghi" is a negation, meaning: we do not exaggerate in what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour toward us. Then they proved what they had experienced of exaggeration in describing the king by their words: ﴿This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾, for whoever favoured them by returning that deserves praise from them and is worthy of what they have described him with.

The meaning of "and we will provision our family" (wa-namir ahlana) is that we will bring to them provisions, which is food. The one who brings the food is "the mir."

Al-Sulami read "wa-numiru" with a damma on the nun, and it is conjoined to something implied that the context indicates, and the implied meaning is: "This is our merchandise, returned to us, so we will be helped by it to return, and we will provision our family." ﴿And we will guard our brother﴾, Binyamin, from what you fear for him, and we will gain, by sending him with us, a camel's load in addition to what we have brought this time, because a load for each man was measured as a camel's burden (wiqr). The meaning of that: it is a small measure, meaning that adding a camel's load for our brother will be easy for the king and it will not be forbidden for us from him, since it is small and will not weigh heavily on him or burden us. It was also said that the meaning is: that measure, for our sake, is small, and we want a camel's load to be added to it for our brother.

Al-Zajjaj chose the first interpretation.

It was also said that this is from the words of Ya'qub in response to what his sons had said: ﴿And we will gain a camel's load﴾, meaning that a camel's load is a small thing, and one does not risk the child for its sake. This is weak.

Because Jacob's answer was, ﴿He said, "I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name"﴾, meaning: until you give me something I can trust and rely on, from God, glory be to Him, namely, swearing by Him. The lam in ﴿لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ﴾ (*la-ta'tunnanni bihi*, "you will surely bring him back to me") is the response of the oath (*jawab al-qasam*, the clause that answers an oath). The meaning of ﴿until you give me a solemn pledge in God's name﴾ is: until you swear by God that you will surely bring him back to me, that is, that you will surely return Benjamin to me. The exception in His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾ is an exception from the most general category (*istithna' min a'amm al-'amm*, an exception from the broadest general term). Although ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is affirmative in form, it carries the sense of a negation, as if he had said: "You will not be prevented from bringing him back to me in any circumstance, for any reason, except the reason of being surrounded by you." *Al-ihatah* (being surrounded) is taken from the surrounding of an enemy, and whoever is surrounded by an enemy has either been overcome or destroyed. Jacob therefore took from them a covenant to bring him Benjamin, except if they were overpowered regarding him or perished before him, in which case that would be an excuse for them before him. So when ﴿they gave him their solemn pledge﴾, that is, they gave him what he asked of them of oaths, ﴿he said, "God is Witness over what we say."﴾ That is, Jacob said: God is witness to what we have said, to my request for a pledge from you and to your giving me what I asked of you. He is the One who observes and watches, nothing is hidden from Him. He is the One who punishes whoever breaks his covenant and swears falsely by Him. Or it means: the matter is entrusted to Him, to carry out what He has witnessed of us.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Joseph's brothers entered upon him, he recognised them while they did not recognise him. He brought the king's *suwa'* (drinking cup) from which he used to drink, placed it on his hand, and began to tap it and let it ring (*yanqur* and *yatinn*). He said: "This cup informs me about you, a report: Was there a brother of yours from your father called Joseph?" Their father loved him more than you. You took him away, threw him into the well, and told your father that a wolf had eaten him, and you brought his shirt stained with false blood." He said: Some of them began looking at others and wondering.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wuhayb, who said: When Joseph began tapping the cup and telling them about themselves, one of his brothers stood up and said: "I beseech you by God not to expose a shameful secret of ours to us."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾: he said: He means Benjamin, who is Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿and I am the best of hosts﴾: he said: the best of those who host guests in Egypt.

Ibn Jarir reported from Qatadah concerning His words, to his *fityan* (servants), that is, his *ghilman* (attendants), ﴿put their merchandise back﴾, that is, their *awraq* (money/goods they had paid).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿What more could we desire? This is our merchandise, returned to us﴾: they say, "We desire nothing beyond this," ﴿and we will gain a camel's load (*kayl ba'ir*)﴾, that is, the load of one camel.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid, concerning ﴿and gain a camel's load﴾, that he said: "the load of a donkey." He said: "It is a dialect (*lughah*) usage." Abu 'Ubayd said: Mujahid means that in some dialects the donkey is called *ba'ir* (camel).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (*yuhatha bikum*)﴾: he said: "that you all perish." And concerning His words ﴿when they gave him their pledge (*mawthiqahum*)﴾: he said: "their covenant."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿unless you are surrounded﴾: he said: "that you are overcome to the point that you are unable to do that."

The brothers of Yusuf came, and they went to Misr from the land of Kan'an to buy grain when the famine struck them. They entered upon Yusuf, and he recognised them, because he had parted from them as boys. ﴿And they did not recognise him.﴾ This is because they had left him as a child being sold for silver coins among the caravan travellers after they had taken him out of the well. Now they entered upon him as a man bearing the majesty of kingship and the splendour of rule, with attendants and retinue around him. It was also said that they did not recognise him because he was in the form of the king of Misr at that time, wearing his crown and adorned with his necklace. It was said that they were far from him and so did not recognise him. Other opinions were also given.

﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾: what is meant here is that he gave them what they had asked for of grain and whatever would equip them for their journey of the supplies a traveller needs. It is said: "I equipped the people (jahhaztu al-qawm) with equipment (tajhiz)" when I arranged for them the gear for the journey.

Al-Azhari said: All the readers read the jim with a fatha (jahhazahum), and kasr is a good dialect. ﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father.﴾ It was said: There must be a speech from which his request for them arises, namely that they should bring him a brother of theirs from their father. It was related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "What are you and what is your business? For I do not recognise you." They said: "We are a people from the people of al-Sham; we have come to buy grain, and we have an aged father, a truthful prophet among the prophets, whose name is Ya'qub."

He said: "How many are you?" They said: "Ten, and we had been twelve. A brother of ours went out into the desert and perished, and he was the most beloved of us to our father. After him he has leaned upon another brother of his, younger than him, who remains with him, and he is consoled by him." Then he said to them: ﴿Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾, meaning his brother Binyamin, who was mentioned earlier, and who was the full brother of Yusuf, from the same father and mother.

They promised him this, and he asked them to leave one of them as a pledge with him until they brought him the brother he had requested. They drew lots, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, so they left him with him. Then he said to them: ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾, that is, I complete it. The verb came in the present form, although he said this to them after equipping them, to indicate that this was his continual custom. Then he informed them of what would increase their confidence in him and their belief in his words, and he said: ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾, that is, while the case is that I am the best of hosts for whoever comes to me, as I have done with you in excellent hospitality and good lodging.

Al-Zajjaj said: Yusuf said ﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ because when he lodged them he treated them with the finest hospitality.

Then he threatened them if they did not bring him, and he said: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me.﴾ That is, I will not sell you anything in the future.
