More astonishing than the denial of these people of what the texts of this Shari'ah have stated is what some of them do in disparaging those who act upon a contrary evidence, merely because of rational improbability, and in their affectation in expression, like al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir. For he, in many places, does not stop at rejecting the evidence of the Law by the rational improbability he claims, until he adds to that the audacity of expression, in a manner that leads the negligent into false sayings and deceitful doctrines.

In sum, the view of these people is refuted by the abundant evidences and by the consensus (ijma') of those whose consensus is considered from this Ummah, both among the earlier and later generations, and by what is observed in existence: how many a person of this human kind, and other kinds of animals, has perished by this cause.

The scholars differed concerning one who is known to cause harm by the evil eye. Some said: he is to be prevented from mixing with people, by imprisonment or other means, or by being obliged to remain in his house, to ward off his harm. It was said: he is to be exiled. And those who went furthest said: he is to be killed, unless he deliberately does this, and his affliction depends upon his choice and intention, and he does not refrain from it. In that case, if he kills, he has the ruling of a killer.

Then Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God﴾, meaning: I cannot ward off harm from you, nor bring you any benefit, by this plan of mine. Rather, what God has decreed for you will certainly come to pass.

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: If it was decreed in the knowledge of God that the evil eye would destroy them when they gathered, then their dispersal would be the same as their gathering.

Others said: Ya'qub never availed them anything at all, since what befell them, despite their dispersal, was the accusation of theft against them. Then Ya'qub declared that there is no judge except God the Exalted, saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, not to anyone else, and no one shares with Him in that. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in every coming and going, and not upon anyone else; that is, I have depended, trusted, and relied upon Him alone, and not upon other than Him. ﴿Let those who rely, rely upon Him﴾ in general.

His sons are included in this, as a primary entry. ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, that is, from the separate gates, and they did not enter together through one gate. The answer to "lamma" (when) is ﴿it did not avail them anything from God﴾, meaning: that entering, from His side, was of no benefit to them in anything of what God had decreed for them, because caution does not avert the decree. The exception in His saying ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: "but rather, there was a need in the soul of Ya'qub." It was his compassion for them and his love for their safety, which he fulfilled, that is, he displayed it to them and enjoined it upon them, without believing that the plan he devised for them had any effect in averting what God had decreed for them. It was also said: it occurred to Ya'qub that the king, if he saw them gathered, together with the perfection of their physique and the signs of courage that appeared in them, would fall into envy and malice toward them, or fear of them, so he ordered them to disperse for this reason.

Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "There is no meaning for the evil eye here."

But it can be objected: if this were the cause, he would have ordered them to disperse in any case, and would not have specified the prohibition to gathering at the time of entering through a single gate, because this envy or fear arises from their gathering inside the city just as it arises from their gathering at the entrance through one gate.

It was also said that the subject of ﴿fulfilled﴾ is a pronoun referring to the entering, not to Ya'qub. The meaning: the entering did not avail them anything from God, but that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub, because it occurred according to his will.

﴿And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾, that is: Ya'qub was truly a man of knowledge, owing to God's teaching him what He had revealed, namely that caution does not avert the decree, and that what God the Exalted has decreed will certainly come to pass. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this as they should. It was also said: they do not know that caution is recommended, even though it cannot avert anything from the decree; but the context rejects this.

It was also said that by "most people" is meant the polytheists.

﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾, that is, he took his brother Binyamin to himself. It is said that he ordered that every two should be lodged in one dwelling, so his brother remained alone, and he took him to himself and ﴿said: "Indeed, I am your brother"﴾, that is, Yusuf said this to him in secret, without his other brothers being made aware of it. ﴿So do not grieve﴾, that is, do not be sad ﴿over what they used to do﴾, that is, over the past deeds which your brothers did.

It was also said: he did not inform him that he was Yusuf, but said to him: "I am your brother in place of your brother Yusuf, so do not grieve over what you encountered from them of harshness, through envy and wrongdoing."

It was also said: he informed him of what he would devise with them, namely placing the drinking-vessel in his baggage, and he said: "I do not mind."

It was also said: when Yusuf informed his brother Binyamin that he was his brother, he said: "Do not send me back to them." Yusuf said: "You know the distress of our father Ya'qub; if I detain you with me, his grief will increase." Then he came to Binyamin and Yusuf said to him: "It is not possible to detain you with me except by ascribing to you what is not becoming for you." He said: "I do not mind." So he put the cup (al-siqayah) in his baggage. This is what is meant by al-siqayah; its origin is the vessel from which one drinks, and it was made into a measure (sa') by which grain is measured. It was also said that animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It was also said it was of silver, and it was also said it was of gold, and other things were said.

The explanation of al-jihaz (provision) and al-rahl (baggage) has already been given.

The meaning: he placed the cup, which is the drinking-vessel (al-suwa'), in the baggage of his brother, which is the container in which one places what one buys of food from Egypt.

Then after that, ﴿a crier cried out﴾, that is, a herald called out, saying: ﴿O caravan!﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "O companions of the caravan." Everything on which grain is carried, of camels, donkeys, and mules, is called "'ir" (caravan), and it was said it is a caravan of donkeys. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-'ir means the camels that are led and ridden. ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. The attribution of theft to them is in its literal sense, because the herald did not know what Yusuf had arranged. It was also said that the meaning is: your situation is the situation of thieves, in that the drinking-vessel has come into your possession without the king's consent.

They said, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, and they turned toward them, that is, while facing those among them whom the herald had addressed, from the king's men: ﴿What is it that you have lost?﴾, that is, what is it that you have missed? One says "faqadta al-shay'" when one has lost something through disappearance or the like, so it is as if they said: "What has gone missing from you?" The use of the present form is to call the scene to mind.

They replied: ﴿We have lost the drinking-vessel of the king.﴾ Yahya ibn Ya'mur read ṣuwāgh with the dotted ghayn. Abu Raja' read ṣawʿ with a non-dotted ṣād, a sukun on the waw, and a non-dotted 'ayn after it. Ubayy read ṣiyā'. Abu Ja'far read ṣā', and Abu Hurayrah also read it so. The majority (al-jumhur) read ṣuwā' with the non-dotted ṣād and 'ayn.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣuwā' is the same as al-ṣā', and it may be masculine or feminine; it is the siqayah. From it is the poet's saying:

"We drink wine openly from the ṣuwā'"

﴿And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load.﴾ That is, they said: "And for whoever brings the drinking-vessel from himself, there is a camel's load."

Al-ba'ir is the male camel, and in the dialect of some Arabs it means the donkey. The "load" here means what the camel carries of food. Then the herald said: ﴿And I am its guarantor.﴾ That is, for the camel's load promised to whoever brings the drinking-vessel, before the search of the containers. Al-za'im is the surety (kafil). Perhaps the one who said "We have lost the king's drinking-vessel" was the herald, and the saying was attributed to the group because he was one of them; then the speech returned to attributing the saying to the herald alone, because he was truly the speaker.

﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ The "t" (in tallahi) is a substitute for the waw of oath according to the majority; it was said it is from the ba', and it was said it is an original particle in itself. It is not used except with this noble Name, to the exclusion of His other names; it has rarely been used with "al-Rabb" (the Lord) and "al-Rahman," and the discussion on this is complete in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). They took the sworn statement to be their knowledge, that Yusuf and his men knew of the purity of their conduct and the cleanliness of their garments from the defilement of corruption in the land, of which theft is among the greatest kinds. For during their first visit and this visit, they had witnessed from them such abstinence and asceticism, far beyond theft, that it yields certain knowledge that they are not people who would venture into this great kind of corruption. Even if there were nothing of this except their returning their merchandise, which they had found in their baggage, it would suffice.

By "the land" here is meant the land of Egypt. Then they emphasized this statement which they had sworn by God with their saying: ﴿And we have never been thieves﴾, to increase their disavowal of what they had been accused of, and their distancing from this base defect and vile, hideous vice.

﴿They said: "What then shall be its recompense, if you are liars?"﴾ This sentence is a new beginning (mustanaffah), as has been mentioned more than once in similar cases. The speakers are the men of Yusuf, or the herald among them alone, as has passed. The pronoun in "its recompense" refers to the drinking-vessel, with an elided modifier, meaning: "What is the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel according to you?" Or the pronoun refers to the thief, meaning: "What is the recompense of the one who steals the drinking-vessel according to you?" ﴿If you are liars﴾ in what you claim for yourselves of innocence from theft, which would be shown by the drinking-vessel being found with you. The brothers of Yusuf then answered.

They said: ﴿Its recompense is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense.﴾ That is, the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel, or the recompense for the thief of the drinking-vessel. "Its recompense" is the subject, and the conditional clause, namely ﴿whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense﴾, is the predicate of the subject, with the explicit noun placed in the position of the pronoun. The original would be: "Its recompense: whoever is found in his baggage, he is [its recompense]," so the second pronoun refers to the subject, and the first to "whoever." It is also permissible that the predicate of the subject be ﴿whoever is found in his baggage﴾, and the estimated meaning is: the recompense of theft of the drinking-vessel is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, and the clause ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ serves to confirm and establish the first clause.

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ is an addition for clarification, meaning: its recompense is the taking of the thief, he himself is its recompense and nothing else.

The exegetes said: The ruling for a thief among the family of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for one year. That is why they gave this as the judgment concerning his recompense. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the like of that complete recompense We give to wrongdoers against others among people, by stealing their goods. This sentence confirms what precedes it if it is from the words of the brothers of Yusuf. It is also permissible that it is from the words of the men of Yusuf, meaning: thus do we recompense wrongdoers with theft.

Then, when they had mentioned the penalty for the thief, they wanted to search their belongings so that the matter would become clear.

Yusuf turned to this and began by searching their containers, that is, the containers of the ten brothers, ﴿before the container of his brother﴾, meaning before searching the container of his brother Benjamin, in order to dispel suspicion and to remove what he had devised as a stratagem. Then he brought it out, that is, the *siqayah* or the *suwa'*, since it may be masculine or feminine in grammatical gender. ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, that is, in this wondrous scheme We devised for Yusuf. Meaning: We taught him it and inspired him with it. *Kayd* (scheming, a stratagem) begins with striving in trickery and deception, and its end is bringing the one who is deceived, without his realizing it, into a disliked matter from which there is no way to repel it. When it is attributed to God, the Exalted, it is understood in terms of its outcome, not its beginning.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of *kidna* is *dabbarna* (We arranged).
Ibn al-Anbari said: *aradna* (We willed).

In the verse there is evidence for the permissibility of reaching legitimate aims by means that take the form of a stratagem or a ruse, provided that this does not contradict an established law. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, meaning Yusuf could not have taken his brother Benjamin under the king's religion, that is, the king of Egypt, and his law which he followed. Rather, his religion and judgment was that the thief be beaten and made to pay twice what he stole, without enslavement for a year, as was the religion and law of Ya'qub. (p. 707)

The sum of this is that Yusuf would not have been able to carry out Ya'qub's ruling against his brother, though it contradicted the king's religion and law, had it not been for what God plotted for him, arranged for him and willed for him, until he found the way to it. That was what God caused to occur on the tongues of his brothers when they said: the penalty for the thief is enslavement. So their statement was by the will of God and His arrangement. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿except that God wills﴾, meaning except in the state of His willing, His permission for that, and His desire for it. This sentence, namely ﴿he could not have taken his brother﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what God did of the scheme for Yusuf, or an interpretation of it.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ with various kinds of knowledge, cognizance, gifts and honors, as We raised Yusuf's rank by these. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge﴾ among those whom God has raised through knowledge, ﴿there is one who is more knowing﴾, of higher rank and loftier degree than they; they cannot reach his extent nor attain his level.

It has been said: the meaning of this is that above all the people of knowledge is the All-Knowing, who is God, the Exalted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter by one gate"﴾, that he said: Ya'qub feared the evil eye for them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: He feared the evil eye for them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿and enter by separate gates﴾, that he said: Ya'qub wished that Yusuf would meet his brother in seclusion.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾, that he said: it was fear of the evil eye for his sons.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge for what We had taught him﴾, that he said: indeed he acted upon what he was taught, and one who does not act is not a person of knowledge.

These same narrators related from him regarding His words: ﴿he took his brother to himself﴾, that he said: he embraced him.

And regarding His words: ﴿so do not be distressed﴾, he said: do not grieve and do not despair. And regarding His words: ﴿when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, he said: he fulfilled their need and measured out their food for them. And regarding His words: ﴿he placed the cup﴾, he said: it was the king's vessel from which he drank. ﴿in his brother's bag﴾, he said: in his brother's belongings.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿he placed the cup﴾, that he said: it was the *suwa'* (the royal drinking vessel), and everything from which one drinks is a *suwa'*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd also something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿O caravan﴾, that he said: the caravan was of donkeys.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿and for him who brings it, a camel's load﴾, that he said: a donkey's load of food; and this is a dialect usage.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾, that he said: it means "its surety."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak the same.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His words: ﴿We did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, that he said: we did not come to disobey in the land.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿then what is its penalty﴾, that he said: they made the ruling known in their judgment, saying: ﴿he in whose bag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾. The ruling among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that the thief be taken for his theft as a slave who is to be enslaved.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿So he began with their containers﴾, that he said: it was mentioned to us that whenever he opened a man's belongings he sought forgiveness, out of sinfulness for what he was doing, until only the boy's belongings remained. He said: "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said: "Yes, he has; so search him."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words: ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, that he said: thus did We act for Yusuf. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, he says: under the king's authority. He said: in the religion of their king it was that whoever stole, the theft was taken from him along with its equivalent from his property, and it was given to the one who had been robbed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, that he says: under the king's authority.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿except that God wills﴾, that he said: except by a pretext which God devised for Yusuf, and by which he made an excuse.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, that he said: Yusuf and his brothers were given knowledge, and We raised Yusuf above them by a degree in knowledge.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: We were with Ibn Abbas when he related a narration. A man present said: ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Evil is what you said. God is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, and He is above every scholar."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: A man asked Ali about a question, and he answered it. The man said: "It is not so, rather it is such and such." Ali said: "You are right and I am wrong. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾, that he said: the knowledge of God is above the knowledge of every knower.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 12, verses 67–76 (part 1 of 2):

.
When the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob) made ready to depart for Egypt, their father feared that the evil eye (al-'ayn) might afflict them, because they were people of conspicuous beauty and fine clothing, and because they were all sons of one man.

He forbade them to enter together through one gate, because that would be a cause for the evil eye to strike them. He ordered them to enter through separate gates. He did not suffice with his saying ﴿Do not enter through one gate﴾ instead of his saying ﴿but enter through different gates﴾, because if they had entered through two gates, for example, they would have complied with the prohibition against entering through a single gate. However, since entering through two gates still involved a degree of gathering, which made them vulnerable to the evil eye, he ordered them to enter through different gates. It is said that Egypt had four gates.

Some of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), such as Abu Hashim and al-Balkhi, denied that the evil eye has any effect. They said: "It is not impossible that the person with the evil eye, when he sees a thing and is impressed by it, is in his interest that God should alter that thing, so that the heart of that responsible person is no longer attached to it."

This is not surprising from these two and their followers, for they have made the rejection of the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah, merely through rational conjectures, their habit and their way. And what prevents the evil eye from striking, by the decree of God the Exalted? Authentic hadiths have come that the evil eye is real, and a group of people in the age of prophethood were afflicted by it, including the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

More astonishing than the denial of these people of what the texts of this Shari'ah have stated is what some of them do in disparaging those who act upon a contrary evidence, merely because of rational improbability, and in their affectation in expression, like al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir. For he, in many places, does not stop at rejecting the evidence of the Law by the rational improbability he claims, until he adds to that the audacity of expression, in a manner that leads the negligent into false sayings and deceitful doctrines.

In sum, the view of these people is refuted by the abundant evidences and by the consensus (ijma') of those whose consensus is considered from this Ummah, both among the earlier and later generations, and by what is observed in existence: how many a person of this human kind, and other kinds of animals, has perished by this cause.

The scholars differed concerning one who is known to cause harm by the evil eye. Some said: he is to be prevented from mixing with people, by imprisonment or other means, or by being obliged to remain in his house, to ward off his harm. It was said: he is to be exiled. And those who went furthest said: he is to be killed, unless he deliberately does this, and his affliction depends upon his choice and intention, and he does not refrain from it. In that case, if he kills, he has the ruling of a killer.

Then Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God﴾, meaning: I cannot ward off harm from you, nor bring you any benefit, by this plan of mine. Rather, what God has decreed for you will certainly come to pass.

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: If it was decreed in the knowledge of God that the evil eye would destroy them when they gathered, then their dispersal would be the same as their gathering.

Others said: Ya'qub never availed them anything at all, since what befell them, despite their dispersal, was the accusation of theft against them. Then Ya'qub declared that there is no judge except God the Exalted, saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, not to anyone else, and no one shares with Him in that. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in every coming and going, and not upon anyone else; that is, I have depended, trusted, and relied upon Him alone, and not upon other than Him. ﴿Let those who rely, rely upon Him﴾ in general.

His sons are included in this, as a primary entry. ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, that is, from the separate gates, and they did not enter together through one gate. The answer to "lamma" (when) is ﴿it did not avail them anything from God﴾, meaning: that entering, from His side, was of no benefit to them in anything of what God had decreed for them, because caution does not avert the decree. The exception in His saying ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: "but rather, there was a need in the soul of Ya'qub." It was his compassion for them and his love for their safety, which he fulfilled, that is, he displayed it to them and enjoined it upon them, without believing that the plan he devised for them had any effect in averting what God had decreed for them. It was also said: it occurred to Ya'qub that the king, if he saw them gathered, together with the perfection of their physique and the signs of courage that appeared in them, would fall into envy and malice toward them, or fear of them, so he ordered them to disperse for this reason.

Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "There is no meaning for the evil eye here."

But it can be objected: if this were the cause, he would have ordered them to disperse in any case, and would not have specified the prohibition to gathering at the time of entering through a single gate, because this envy or fear arises from their gathering inside the city just as it arises from their gathering at the entrance through one gate.

It was also said that the subject of ﴿fulfilled﴾ is a pronoun referring to the entering, not to Ya'qub. The meaning: the entering did not avail them anything from God, but that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub, because it occurred according to his will.

﴿And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾, that is: Ya'qub was truly a man of knowledge, owing to God's teaching him what He had revealed, namely that caution does not avert the decree, and that what God the Exalted has decreed will certainly come to pass. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this as they should. It was also said: they do not know that caution is recommended, even though it cannot avert anything from the decree; but the context rejects this.

It was also said that by "most people" is meant the polytheists.

﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾, that is, he took his brother Binyamin to himself. It is said that he ordered that every two should be lodged in one dwelling, so his brother remained alone, and he took him to himself and ﴿said: "Indeed, I am your brother"﴾, that is, Yusuf said this to him in secret, without his other brothers being made aware of it. ﴿So do not grieve﴾, that is, do not be sad ﴿over what they used to do﴾, that is, over the past deeds which your brothers did.

It was also said: he did not inform him that he was Yusuf, but said to him: "I am your brother in place of your brother Yusuf, so do not grieve over what you encountered from them of harshness, through envy and wrongdoing."

It was also said: he informed him of what he would devise with them, namely placing the drinking-vessel in his baggage, and he said: "I do not mind."

It was also said: when Yusuf informed his brother Binyamin that he was his brother, he said: "Do not send me back to them." Yusuf said: "You know the distress of our father Ya'qub; if I detain you with me, his grief will increase." Then he came to Binyamin and Yusuf said to him: "It is not possible to detain you with me except by ascribing to you what is not becoming for you." He said: "I do not mind." So he put the cup (al-siqayah) in his baggage. This is what is meant by al-siqayah; its origin is the vessel from which one drinks, and it was made into a measure (sa') by which grain is measured. It was also said that animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It was also said it was of silver, and it was also said it was of gold, and other things were said.

The explanation of al-jihaz (provision) and al-rahl (baggage) has already been given.

The meaning: he placed the cup, which is the drinking-vessel (al-suwa'), in the baggage of his brother, which is the container in which one places what one buys of food from Egypt.

Then after that, ﴿a crier cried out﴾, that is, a herald called out, saying: ﴿O caravan!﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "O companions of the caravan." Everything on which grain is carried, of camels, donkeys, and mules, is called "'ir" (caravan), and it was said it is a caravan of donkeys. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-'ir means the camels that are led and ridden. ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. The attribution of theft to them is in its literal sense, because the herald did not know what Yusuf had arranged. It was also said that the meaning is: your situation is the situation of thieves, in that the drinking-vessel has come into your possession without the king's consent.

They said, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, and they turned toward them, that is, while facing those among them whom the herald had addressed, from the king's men: ﴿What is it that you have lost?﴾, that is, what is it that you have missed? One says "faqadta al-shay'" when one has lost something through disappearance or the like, so it is as if they said: "What has gone missing from you?" The use of the present form is to call the scene to mind.

They replied: ﴿We have lost the drinking-vessel of the king.﴾ Yahya ibn Ya'mur read ṣuwāgh with the dotted ghayn. Abu Raja' read ṣawʿ with a non-dotted ṣād, a sukun on the waw, and a non-dotted 'ayn after it. Ubayy read ṣiyā'. Abu Ja'far read ṣā', and Abu Hurayrah also read it so. The majority (al-jumhur) read ṣuwā' with the non-dotted ṣād and 'ayn.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣuwā' is the same as al-ṣā', and it may be masculine or feminine; it is the siqayah. From it is the poet's saying:

"We drink wine openly from the ṣuwā'"

﴿And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load.﴾ That is, they said: "And for whoever brings the drinking-vessel from himself, there is a camel's load."

Al-ba'ir is the male camel, and in the dialect of some Arabs it means the donkey. The "load" here means what the camel carries of food. Then the herald said: ﴿And I am its guarantor.﴾ That is, for the camel's load promised to whoever brings the drinking-vessel, before the search of the containers. Al-za'im is the surety (kafil). Perhaps the one who said "We have lost the king's drinking-vessel" was the herald, and the saying was attributed to the group because he was one of them; then the speech returned to attributing the saying to the herald alone, because he was truly the speaker.

﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ The "t" (in tallahi) is a substitute for the waw of oath according to the majority; it was said it is from the ba', and it was said it is an original particle in itself. It is not used except with this noble Name, to the exclusion of His other names; it has rarely been used with "al-Rabb" (the Lord) and "al-Rahman," and the discussion on this is complete in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). They took the sworn statement to be their knowledge, that Yusuf and his men knew of the purity of their conduct and the cleanliness of their garments from the defilement of corruption in the land, of which theft is among the greatest kinds. For during their first visit and this visit, they had witnessed from them such abstinence and asceticism, far beyond theft, that it yields certain knowledge that they are not people who would venture into this great kind of corruption. Even if there were nothing of this except their returning their merchandise, which they had found in their baggage, it would suffice.

By "the land" here is meant the land of Egypt. Then they emphasized this statement which they had sworn by God with their saying: ﴿And we have never been thieves﴾, to increase their disavowal of what they had been accused of, and their distancing from this base defect and vile, hideous vice.

﴿They said: "What then shall be its recompense, if you are liars?"﴾ This sentence is a new beginning (mustanaffah), as has been mentioned more than once in similar cases. The speakers are the men of Yusuf, or the herald among them alone, as has passed. The pronoun in "its recompense" refers to the drinking-vessel, with an elided modifier, meaning: "What is the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel according to you?" Or the pronoun refers to the thief, meaning: "What is the recompense of the one who steals the drinking-vessel according to you?" ﴿If you are liars﴾ in what you claim for yourselves of innocence from theft, which would be shown by the drinking-vessel being found with you. The brothers of Yusuf then answered.

They said: ﴿Its recompense is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense.﴾ That is, the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel, or the recompense for the thief of the drinking-vessel. "Its recompense" is the subject, and the conditional clause, namely ﴿whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense﴾, is the predicate of the subject, with the explicit noun placed in the position of the pronoun. The original would be: "Its recompense: whoever is found in his baggage, he is [its recompense]," so the second pronoun refers to the subject, and the first to "whoever." It is also permissible that the predicate of the subject be ﴿whoever is found in his baggage﴾, and the estimated meaning is: the recompense of theft of the drinking-vessel is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, and the clause ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ serves to confirm and establish the first clause.

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ is an addition for clarification, meaning: its recompense is the taking of the thief, he himself is its recompense and nothing else.

The exegetes said: The ruling for a thief among the family of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for one year. That is why they gave this as the judgment concerning his recompense. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the like of that complete recompense We give to wrongdoers against others among people, by stealing their goods. This sentence confirms what precedes it if it is from the words of the brothers of Yusuf. It is also permissible that it is from the words of the men of Yusuf, meaning: thus do we recompense wrongdoers with theft.

Then, when they had mentioned the penalty for the thief, they wanted to search their belongings so that the matter would become clear.

Yusuf turned to this and began by searching their containers, that is, the containers of the ten brothers, ﴿before the container of his brother﴾, meaning before searching the container of his brother Benjamin, in order to dispel suspicion and to remove what he had devised as a stratagem. Then he brought it out, that is, the *siqayah* or the *suwa'*, since it may be masculine or feminine in grammatical gender. ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, that is, in this wondrous scheme We devised for Yusuf. Meaning: We taught him it and inspired him with it. *Kayd* (scheming, a stratagem) begins with striving in trickery and deception, and its end is bringing the one who is deceived, without his realizing it, into a disliked matter from which there is no way to repel it. When it is attributed to God, the Exalted, it is understood in terms of its outcome, not its beginning.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of *kidna* is *dabbarna* (We arranged).
Ibn al-Anbari said: *aradna* (We willed).

In the verse there is evidence for the permissibility of reaching legitimate aims by means that take the form of a stratagem or a ruse, provided that this does not contradict an established law. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, meaning Yusuf could not have taken his brother Benjamin under the king's religion, that is, the king of Egypt, and his law which he followed. Rather, his religion and judgment was that the thief be beaten and made to pay twice what he stole, without enslavement for a year, as was the religion and law of Ya'qub. (p. 707)

The sum of this is that Yusuf would not have been able to carry out Ya'qub's ruling against his brother, though it contradicted the king's religion and law, had it not been for what God plotted for him, arranged for him and willed for him, until he found the way to it. That was what God caused to occur on the tongues of his brothers when they said: the penalty for the thief is enslavement. So their statement was by the will of God and His arrangement. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿except that God wills﴾, meaning except in the state of His willing, His permission for that, and His desire for it. This sentence, namely ﴿he could not have taken his brother﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what God did of the scheme for Yusuf, or an interpretation of it.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ with various kinds of knowledge, cognizance, gifts and honors, as We raised Yusuf's rank by these. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge﴾ among those whom God has raised through knowledge, ﴿there is one who is more knowing﴾, of higher rank and loftier degree than they; they cannot reach his extent nor attain his level.

It has been said: the meaning of this is that above all the people of knowledge is the All-Knowing, who is God, the Exalted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter by one gate"﴾, that he said: Ya'qub feared the evil eye for them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: He feared the evil eye for them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿and enter by separate gates﴾, that he said: Ya'qub wished that Yusuf would meet his brother in seclusion.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾, that he said: it was fear of the evil eye for his sons.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And indeed he was a possessor of knowledge for what We had taught him﴾, that he said: indeed he acted upon what he was taught, and one who does not act is not a person of knowledge.

These same narrators related from him regarding His words: ﴿he took his brother to himself﴾, that he said: he embraced him.

And regarding His words: ﴿so do not be distressed﴾, he said: do not grieve and do not despair. And regarding His words: ﴿when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, he said: he fulfilled their need and measured out their food for them. And regarding His words: ﴿he placed the cup﴾, he said: it was the king's vessel from which he drank. ﴿in his brother's bag﴾, he said: in his brother's belongings.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿he placed the cup﴾, that he said: it was the *suwa'* (the royal drinking vessel), and everything from which one drinks is a *suwa'*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd also something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿O caravan﴾, that he said: the caravan was of donkeys.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿and for him who brings it, a camel's load﴾, that he said: a donkey's load of food; and this is a dialect usage.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾, that he said: it means "its surety."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak the same.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding His words: ﴿We did not come to cause corruption in the land﴾, that he said: we did not come to disobey in the land.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His words: ﴿then what is its penalty﴾, that he said: they made the ruling known in their judgment, saying: ﴿he in whose bag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾. The ruling among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that the thief be taken for his theft as a slave who is to be enslaved.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿So he began with their containers﴾, that he said: it was mentioned to us that whenever he opened a man's belongings he sought forgiveness, out of sinfulness for what he was doing, until only the boy's belongings remained. He said: "I do not think this one has taken anything." They said: "Yes, he has; so search him."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words: ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, that he said: thus did We act for Yusuf. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, he says: under the king's authority. He said: in the religion of their king it was that whoever stole, the theft was taken from him along with its equivalent from his property, and it was given to the one who had been robbed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, that he says: under the king's authority.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿except that God wills﴾, that he said: except by a pretext which God devised for Yusuf, and by which he made an excuse.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him regarding His words: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, that he said: Yusuf and his brothers were given knowledge, and We raised Yusuf above them by a degree in knowledge.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: We were with Ibn Abbas when he related a narration. A man present said: ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Evil is what you said. God is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, and He is above every scholar."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: A man asked Ali about a question, and he answered it. The man said: "It is not so, rather it is such and such." Ali said: "You are right and I am wrong. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿and over every possessor of knowledge is one who is All-Knowing﴾, that he said: the knowledge of God is above the knowledge of every knower.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 12, verses 67–76 (part 1 of 2):

.
When the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob) made ready to depart for Egypt, their father feared that the evil eye (al-'ayn) might afflict them, because they were people of conspicuous beauty and fine clothing, and because they were all sons of one man.

He forbade them to enter together through one gate, because that would be a cause for the evil eye to strike them. He ordered them to enter through separate gates. He did not suffice with his saying ﴿Do not enter through one gate﴾ instead of his saying ﴿but enter through different gates﴾, because if they had entered through two gates, for example, they would have complied with the prohibition against entering through a single gate. However, since entering through two gates still involved a degree of gathering, which made them vulnerable to the evil eye, he ordered them to enter through different gates. It is said that Egypt had four gates.

Some of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), such as Abu Hashim and al-Balkhi, denied that the evil eye has any effect. They said: "It is not impossible that the person with the evil eye, when he sees a thing and is impressed by it, is in his interest that God should alter that thing, so that the heart of that responsible person is no longer attached to it."

This is not surprising from these two and their followers, for they have made the rejection of the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah, merely through rational conjectures, their habit and their way. And what prevents the evil eye from striking, by the decree of God the Exalted? Authentic hadiths have come that the evil eye is real, and a group of people in the age of prophethood were afflicted by it, including the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

More astonishing than the denial of these people of what the texts of this Shari'ah have stated is what some of them do in disparaging those who act upon a contrary evidence, merely because of rational improbability, and in their affectation in expression, like al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir. For he, in many places, does not stop at rejecting the evidence of the Law by the rational improbability he claims, until he adds to that the audacity of expression, in a manner that leads the negligent into false sayings and deceitful doctrines.

In sum, the view of these people is refuted by the abundant evidences and by the consensus (ijma') of those whose consensus is considered from this Ummah, both among the earlier and later generations, and by what is observed in existence: how many a person of this human kind, and other kinds of animals, has perished by this cause.

The scholars differed concerning one who is known to cause harm by the evil eye. Some said: he is to be prevented from mixing with people, by imprisonment or other means, or by being obliged to remain in his house, to ward off his harm. It was said: he is to be exiled. And those who went furthest said: he is to be killed, unless he deliberately does this, and his affliction depends upon his choice and intention, and he does not refrain from it. In that case, if he kills, he has the ruling of a killer.

Then Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God﴾, meaning: I cannot ward off harm from you, nor bring you any benefit, by this plan of mine. Rather, what God has decreed for you will certainly come to pass.

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: If it was decreed in the knowledge of God that the evil eye would destroy them when they gathered, then their dispersal would be the same as their gathering.

Others said: Ya'qub never availed them anything at all, since what befell them, despite their dispersal, was the accusation of theft against them. Then Ya'qub declared that there is no judge except God the Exalted, saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, not to anyone else, and no one shares with Him in that. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in every coming and going, and not upon anyone else; that is, I have depended, trusted, and relied upon Him alone, and not upon other than Him. ﴿Let those who rely, rely upon Him﴾ in general.

His sons are included in this, as a primary entry. ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, that is, from the separate gates, and they did not enter together through one gate. The answer to "lamma" (when) is ﴿it did not avail them anything from God﴾, meaning: that entering, from His side, was of no benefit to them in anything of what God had decreed for them, because caution does not avert the decree. The exception in His saying ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: "but rather, there was a need in the soul of Ya'qub." It was his compassion for them and his love for their safety, which he fulfilled, that is, he displayed it to them and enjoined it upon them, without believing that the plan he devised for them had any effect in averting what God had decreed for them. It was also said: it occurred to Ya'qub that the king, if he saw them gathered, together with the perfection of their physique and the signs of courage that appeared in them, would fall into envy and malice toward them, or fear of them, so he ordered them to disperse for this reason.

Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "There is no meaning for the evil eye here."

But it can be objected: if this were the cause, he would have ordered them to disperse in any case, and would not have specified the prohibition to gathering at the time of entering through a single gate, because this envy or fear arises from their gathering inside the city just as it arises from their gathering at the entrance through one gate.

It was also said that the subject of ﴿fulfilled﴾ is a pronoun referring to the entering, not to Ya'qub. The meaning: the entering did not avail them anything from God, but that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub, because it occurred according to his will.

﴿And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾, that is: Ya'qub was truly a man of knowledge, owing to God's teaching him what He had revealed, namely that caution does not avert the decree, and that what God the Exalted has decreed will certainly come to pass. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this as they should. It was also said: they do not know that caution is recommended, even though it cannot avert anything from the decree; but the context rejects this.

It was also said that by "most people" is meant the polytheists.

﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾, that is, he took his brother Binyamin to himself. It is said that he ordered that every two should be lodged in one dwelling, so his brother remained alone, and he took him to himself and ﴿said: "Indeed, I am your brother"﴾, that is, Yusuf said this to him in secret, without his other brothers being made aware of it. ﴿So do not grieve﴾, that is, do not be sad ﴿over what they used to do﴾, that is, over the past deeds which your brothers did.

It was also said: he did not inform him that he was Yusuf, but said to him: "I am your brother in place of your brother Yusuf, so do not grieve over what you encountered from them of harshness, through envy and wrongdoing."

It was also said: he informed him of what he would devise with them, namely placing the drinking-vessel in his baggage, and he said: "I do not mind."

It was also said: when Yusuf informed his brother Binyamin that he was his brother, he said: "Do not send me back to them." Yusuf said: "You know the distress of our father Ya'qub; if I detain you with me, his grief will increase." Then he came to Binyamin and Yusuf said to him: "It is not possible to detain you with me except by ascribing to you what is not becoming for you." He said: "I do not mind." So he put the cup (al-siqayah) in his baggage. This is what is meant by al-siqayah; its origin is the vessel from which one drinks, and it was made into a measure (sa') by which grain is measured. It was also said that animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It was also said it was of silver, and it was also said it was of gold, and other things were said.

The explanation of al-jihaz (provision) and al-rahl (baggage) has already been given.

The meaning: he placed the cup, which is the drinking-vessel (al-suwa'), in the baggage of his brother, which is the container in which one places what one buys of food from Egypt.

Then after that, ﴿a crier cried out﴾, that is, a herald called out, saying: ﴿O caravan!﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "O companions of the caravan." Everything on which grain is carried, of camels, donkeys, and mules, is called "'ir" (caravan), and it was said it is a caravan of donkeys. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-'ir means the camels that are led and ridden. ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. The attribution of theft to them is in its literal sense, because the herald did not know what Yusuf had arranged. It was also said that the meaning is: your situation is the situation of thieves, in that the drinking-vessel has come into your possession without the king's consent.

They said, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, and they turned toward them, that is, while facing those among them whom the herald had addressed, from the king's men: ﴿What is it that you have lost?﴾, that is, what is it that you have missed? One says "faqadta al-shay'" when one has lost something through disappearance or the like, so it is as if they said: "What has gone missing from you?" The use of the present form is to call the scene to mind.

They replied: ﴿We have lost the drinking-vessel of the king.﴾ Yahya ibn Ya'mur read ṣuwāgh with the dotted ghayn. Abu Raja' read ṣawʿ with a non-dotted ṣād, a sukun on the waw, and a non-dotted 'ayn after it. Ubayy read ṣiyā'. Abu Ja'far read ṣā', and Abu Hurayrah also read it so. The majority (al-jumhur) read ṣuwā' with the non-dotted ṣād and 'ayn.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣuwā' is the same as al-ṣā', and it may be masculine or feminine; it is the siqayah. From it is the poet's saying:

"We drink wine openly from the ṣuwā'"

﴿And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load.﴾ That is, they said: "And for whoever brings the drinking-vessel from himself, there is a camel's load."

Al-ba'ir is the male camel, and in the dialect of some Arabs it means the donkey. The "load" here means what the camel carries of food. Then the herald said: ﴿And I am its guarantor.﴾ That is, for the camel's load promised to whoever brings the drinking-vessel, before the search of the containers. Al-za'im is the surety (kafil). Perhaps the one who said "We have lost the king's drinking-vessel" was the herald, and the saying was attributed to the group because he was one of them; then the speech returned to attributing the saying to the herald alone, because he was truly the speaker.

﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ The "t" (in tallahi) is a substitute for the waw of oath according to the majority; it was said it is from the ba', and it was said it is an original particle in itself. It is not used except with this noble Name, to the exclusion of His other names; it has rarely been used with "al-Rabb" (the Lord) and "al-Rahman," and the discussion on this is complete in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). They took the sworn statement to be their knowledge, that Yusuf and his men knew of the purity of their conduct and the cleanliness of their garments from the defilement of corruption in the land, of which theft is among the greatest kinds. For during their first visit and this visit, they had witnessed from them such abstinence and asceticism, far beyond theft, that it yields certain knowledge that they are not people who would venture into this great kind of corruption. Even if there were nothing of this except their returning their merchandise, which they had found in their baggage, it would suffice.

By "the land" here is meant the land of Egypt. Then they emphasized this statement which they had sworn by God with their saying: ﴿And we have never been thieves﴾, to increase their disavowal of what they had been accused of, and their distancing from this base defect and vile, hideous vice.

﴿They said: "What then shall be its recompense, if you are liars?"﴾ This sentence is a new beginning (mustanaffah), as has been mentioned more than once in similar cases. The speakers are the men of Yusuf, or the herald among them alone, as has passed. The pronoun in "its recompense" refers to the drinking-vessel, with an elided modifier, meaning: "What is the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel according to you?" Or the pronoun refers to the thief, meaning: "What is the recompense of the one who steals the drinking-vessel according to you?" ﴿If you are liars﴾ in what you claim for yourselves of innocence from theft, which would be shown by the drinking-vessel being found with you. The brothers of Yusuf then answered.

They said: ﴿Its recompense is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense.﴾ That is, the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel, or the recompense for the thief of the drinking-vessel. "Its recompense" is the subject, and the conditional clause, namely ﴿whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense﴾, is the predicate of the subject, with the explicit noun placed in the position of the pronoun. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ is an addition for clarification, meaning: its recompense is the taking of the thief, he himself is its recompense and nothing else.

The exegetes said: The ruling for a thief among the family of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for one year. This sentence confirms what precedes it if it is from the words of the brothers of Yusuf. It is also permissible that it is from the words of the men of Yusuf, meaning: thus do we recompense wrongdoers with theft.

Then, when they had mentioned the penalty for the thief, they wanted to search their belongings so that the matter would become clear.

Yusuf turned to this and began by searching their containers, that is, the containers of the ten brothers, ﴿before the container of his brother﴾, meaning before searching the container of his brother Benjamin, in order to dispel suspicion and to remove what he had devised as a stratagem. And regarding His words: ﴿so do not be distressed﴾, he said: do not grieve and do not despair. And regarding His words: ﴿when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, he said: he fulfilled their need and measured out their food for them. And regarding His words: ﴿he placed the cup﴾, he said: it was the king's vessel from which he drank. ﴿in his brother's bag﴾, he said: in his brother's belongings.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd also something similar.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 12, verses 67–76 (part 1 of 2):

.
When the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob) made ready to depart for Egypt, their father feared that the evil eye (al-'ayn) might afflict them, because they were people of conspicuous beauty and fine clothing, and because they were all sons of one man.

He forbade them to enter together through one gate, because that would be a cause for the evil eye to strike them. He ordered them to enter through separate gates. He did not suffice with his saying ﴿Do not enter through one gate﴾ instead of his saying ﴿but enter through different gates﴾, because if they had entered through two gates, for example, they would have complied with the prohibition against entering through a single gate. However, since entering through two gates still involved a degree of gathering, which made them vulnerable to the evil eye, he ordered them to enter through different gates. It is said that Egypt had four gates.

Some of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), such as Abu Hashim and al-Balkhi, denied that the evil eye has any effect. They said: "It is not impossible that the person with the evil eye, when he sees a thing and is impressed by it, is in his interest that God should alter that thing, so that the heart of that responsible person is no longer attached to it."

This is not surprising from these two and their followers, for they have made the rejection of the evidences of the Book and the Sunnah, merely through rational conjectures, their habit and their way. And what prevents the evil eye from striking, by the decree of God the Exalted? Authentic hadiths have come that the evil eye is real, and a group of people in the age of prophethood were afflicted by it, including the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

More astonishing than the denial of these people of what the texts of this Shari'ah have stated is what some of them do in disparaging those who act upon a contrary evidence, merely because of rational improbability, and in their affectation in expression, like al-Zamakhshari in his tafsir. For he, in many places, does not stop at rejecting the evidence of the Law by the rational improbability he claims, until he adds to that the audacity of expression, in a manner that leads the negligent into false sayings and deceitful doctrines.

In sum, the view of these people is refuted by the abundant evidences and by the consensus (ijma') of those whose consensus is considered from this Ummah, both among the earlier and later generations, and by what is observed in existence: how many a person of this human kind, and other kinds of animals, has perished by this cause.

The scholars differed concerning one who is known to cause harm by the evil eye. Some said: he is to be prevented from mixing with people, by imprisonment or other means, or by being obliged to remain in his house, to ward off his harm. It was said: he is to be exiled. And those who went furthest said: he is to be killed, unless he deliberately does this, and his affliction depends upon his choice and intention, and he does not refrain from it. In that case, if he kills, he has the ruling of a killer.

Then Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God﴾, meaning: I cannot ward off harm from you, nor bring you any benefit, by this plan of mine. Rather, what God has decreed for you will certainly come to pass.

Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: If it was decreed in the knowledge of God that the evil eye would destroy them when they gathered, then their dispersal would be the same as their gathering.

Others said: Ya'qub never availed them anything at all, since what befell them, despite their dispersal, was the accusation of theft against them. Then Ya'qub declared that there is no judge except God the Exalted, saying: ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, not to anyone else, and no one shares with Him in that. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in every coming and going, and not upon anyone else; that is, I have depended, trusted, and relied upon Him alone, and not upon other than Him. ﴿Let those who rely, rely upon Him﴾ in general.

His sons are included in this, as a primary entry. ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them﴾, that is, from the separate gates, and they did not enter together through one gate. The answer to "lamma" (when) is ﴿it did not avail them anything from God﴾, meaning: that entering, from His side, was of no benefit to them in anything of what God had decreed for them, because caution does not avert the decree. The exception in His saying ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: "but rather, there was a need in the soul of Ya'qub." It was his compassion for them and his love for their safety, which he fulfilled, that is, he displayed it to them and enjoined it upon them, without believing that the plan he devised for them had any effect in averting what God had decreed for them. It was also said: it occurred to Ya'qub that the king, if he saw them gathered, together with the perfection of their physique and the signs of courage that appeared in them, would fall into envy and malice toward them, or fear of them, so he ordered them to disperse for this reason.

Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: "There is no meaning for the evil eye here."

But it can be objected: if this were the cause, he would have ordered them to disperse in any case, and would not have specified the prohibition to gathering at the time of entering through a single gate, because this envy or fear arises from their gathering inside the city just as it arises from their gathering at the entrance through one gate.

It was also said that the subject of ﴿fulfilled﴾ is a pronoun referring to the entering, not to Ya'qub. The meaning: the entering did not avail them anything from God, but that entering fulfilled a need in the soul of Ya'qub, because it occurred according to his will.

﴿And indeed, he was possessed of knowledge because of what We had taught him﴾, that is: Ya'qub was truly a man of knowledge, owing to God's teaching him what He had revealed, namely that caution does not avert the decree, and that what God the Exalted has decreed will certainly come to pass. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ this as they should. It was also said: they do not know that caution is recommended, even though it cannot avert anything from the decree; but the context rejects this.

It was also said that by "most people" is meant the polytheists.

﴿And when they entered upon Yusuf, he drew his brother to himself﴾, that is, he took his brother Binyamin to himself. It is said that he ordered that every two should be lodged in one dwelling, so his brother remained alone, and he took him to himself and ﴿said: "Indeed, I am your brother"﴾, that is, Yusuf said this to him in secret, without his other brothers being made aware of it. ﴿So do not grieve﴾, that is, do not be sad ﴿over what they used to do﴾, that is, over the past deeds which your brothers did.

It was also said: he did not inform him that he was Yusuf, but said to him: "I am your brother in place of your brother Yusuf, so do not grieve over what you encountered from them of harshness, through envy and wrongdoing."

It was also said: he informed him of what he would devise with them, namely placing the drinking-vessel in his baggage, and he said: "I do not mind."

It was also said: when Yusuf informed his brother Binyamin that he was his brother, he said: "Do not send me back to them." Yusuf said: "You know the distress of our father Ya'qub; if I detain you with me, his grief will increase." Then he came to Binyamin and Yusuf said to him: "It is not possible to detain you with me except by ascribing to you what is not becoming for you." He said: "I do not mind." So he put the cup (al-siqayah) in his baggage. This is what is meant by al-siqayah; its origin is the vessel from which one drinks, and it was made into a measure (sa') by which grain is measured. It was also said that animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It was also said it was of silver, and it was also said it was of gold, and other things were said.

The explanation of al-jihaz (provision) and al-rahl (baggage) has already been given.

The meaning: he placed the cup, which is the drinking-vessel (al-suwa'), in the baggage of his brother, which is the container in which one places what one buys of food from Egypt.

Then after that, ﴿a crier cried out﴾, that is, a herald called out, saying: ﴿O caravan!﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "O companions of the caravan." Everything on which grain is carried, of camels, donkeys, and mules, is called "'ir" (caravan), and it was said it is a caravan of donkeys. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-'ir means the camels that are led and ridden. ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾. The attribution of theft to them is in its literal sense, because the herald did not know what Yusuf had arranged. It was also said that the meaning is: your situation is the situation of thieves, in that the drinking-vessel has come into your possession without the king's consent.

They said, that is, the brothers of Yusuf, and they turned toward them, that is, while facing those among them whom the herald had addressed, from the king's men: ﴿What is it that you have lost?﴾, that is, what is it that you have missed? One says "faqadta al-shay'" when one has lost something through disappearance or the like, so it is as if they said: "What has gone missing from you?" The use of the present form is to call the scene to mind.

They replied: ﴿We have lost the drinking-vessel of the king.﴾ Yahya ibn Ya'mur read ṣuwāgh with the dotted ghayn. Abu Raja' read ṣawʿ with a non-dotted ṣād, a sukun on the waw, and a non-dotted 'ayn after it. Ubayy read ṣiyā'. Abu Ja'far read ṣā', and Abu Hurayrah also read it so. The majority (al-jumhur) read ṣuwā' with the non-dotted ṣād and 'ayn.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣuwā' is the same as al-ṣā', and it may be masculine or feminine; it is the siqayah. From it is the poet's saying:

"We drink wine openly from the ṣuwā'"

﴿And for whoever brings it, there is a camel's load.﴾ That is, they said: "And for whoever brings the drinking-vessel from himself, there is a camel's load."

Al-ba'ir is the male camel, and in the dialect of some Arabs it means the donkey. The "load" here means what the camel carries of food. Then the herald said: ﴿And I am its guarantor.﴾ That is, for the camel's load promised to whoever brings the drinking-vessel, before the search of the containers. Al-za'im is the surety (kafil). Perhaps the one who said "We have lost the king's drinking-vessel" was the herald, and the saying was attributed to the group because he was one of them; then the speech returned to attributing the saying to the herald alone, because he was truly the speaker.

﴿They said: "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ The "t" (in tallahi) is a substitute for the waw of oath according to the majority; it was said it is from the ba', and it was said it is an original particle in itself. It is not used except with this noble Name, to the exclusion of His other names; it has rarely been used with "al-Rabb" (the Lord) and "al-Rahman," and the discussion on this is complete in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). They took the sworn statement to be their knowledge, that Yusuf and his men knew of the purity of their conduct and the cleanliness of their garments from the defilement of corruption in the land, of which theft is among the greatest kinds. For during their first visit and this visit, they had witnessed from them such abstinence and asceticism, far beyond theft, that it yields certain knowledge that they are not people who would venture into this great kind of corruption. Even if there were nothing of this except their returning their merchandise, which they had found in their baggage, it would suffice.

By "the land" here is meant the land of Egypt. Then they emphasized this statement which they had sworn by God with their saying: ﴿And we have never been thieves﴾, to increase their disavowal of what they had been accused of, and their distancing from this base defect and vile, hideous vice.

﴿They said: "What then shall be its recompense, if you are liars?"﴾ This sentence is a new beginning (mustanaffah), as has been mentioned more than once in similar cases. The speakers are the men of Yusuf, or the herald among them alone, as has passed. The pronoun in "its recompense" refers to the drinking-vessel, with an elided modifier, meaning: "What is the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel according to you?" Or the pronoun refers to the thief, meaning: "What is the recompense of the one who steals the drinking-vessel according to you?" ﴿If you are liars﴾ in what you claim for yourselves of innocence from theft, which would be shown by the drinking-vessel being found with you. The brothers of Yusuf then answered.

They said: ﴿Its recompense is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense.﴾ That is, the recompense for the theft of the drinking-vessel, or the recompense for the thief of the drinking-vessel. "Its recompense" is the subject, and the conditional clause, namely ﴿whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense﴾, is the predicate of the subject, with the explicit noun placed in the position of the pronoun. The original would be: "Its recompense: whoever is found in his baggage, he is [its recompense]," so the second pronoun refers to the subject, and the first to "whoever." It is also permissible that the predicate of the subject be ﴿whoever is found in his baggage﴾, and the estimated meaning is: the recompense of theft of the drinking-vessel is the taking of whoever is found in his baggage, and the clause ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ serves to confirm and establish the first clause.

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ is an addition for clarification, meaning: its recompense is the taking of the thief, he himself is its recompense and nothing else.

The exegetes said: The ruling for a thief among the family of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for one year. That is why they gave this as the judgment concerning his recompense. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the like of that complete recompense We give to wrongdoers against others among people, by stealing their goods. This sentence confirms what precedes it if it is from the words of the brothers of Yusuf. It is also permissible that it is from the words of the men of Yusuf, meaning: thus do we recompense wrongdoers with theft.

Then, when they had mentioned the penalty for the thief, they wanted to search their belongings so that the matter would become clear.

Yusuf turned to this and began by searching their containers, that is, the containers of the ten brothers, ﴿before the container of his brother﴾, meaning before searching the container of his brother Benjamin, in order to dispel suspicion and to remove what he had devised as a stratagem. Then he brought it out, that is, the *siqayah* or the *suwa'*, since it may be masculine or feminine in grammatical gender. ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf﴾, that is, in this wondrous scheme We devised for Yusuf. Meaning: We taught him it and inspired him with it. *Kayd* (scheming, a stratagem) begins with striving in trickery and deception, and its end is bringing the one who is deceived, without his realizing it, into a disliked matter from which there is no way to repel it. When it is attributed to God, the Exalted, it is understood in terms of its outcome, not its beginning.

Al-Qutaybi said: the meaning of *kidna* is *dabbarna* (We arranged).
Ibn al-Anbari said: *aradna* (We willed).

In the verse there is evidence for the permissibility of reaching legitimate aims by means that take the form of a stratagem or a ruse, provided that this does not contradict an established law. ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion﴾, meaning Yusuf could not have taken his brother Benjamin under the king's religion, that is, the king of Egypt, and his law which he followed. Rather, his religion and judgment was that the thief be beaten and made to pay twice what he stole, without enslavement for a year, as was the religion and law of Ya'qub. (p. 707)

The sum of this is that Yusuf would not have been able to carry out Ya'qub's ruling against his brother, though it contradicted the king's religion and law, had it not been for what God plotted for him, arranged for him and willed for him, until he found the way to it. That was what God caused to occur on the tongues of his brothers when they said: the penalty for the thief is enslavement. So their statement was by the will of God and His arrangement. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿except that God wills﴾, meaning except in the state of His willing, His permission for that, and His desire for it. This sentence, namely ﴿he could not have taken his brother﴾ and so on, is an explanation of what God did of the scheme for Yusuf, or an interpretation of it.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ with various kinds of knowledge, cognizance, gifts and honors, as We raised Yusuf's rank by these. ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge﴾ among those whom God has raised through knowledge, ﴿there is one who is more knowing﴾, of higher rank and loftier degree than they; they cannot reach his extent nor attain his level.

It has been said: the meaning of this is that above all the people of knowledge is the All-Knowing, who is God, the Exalted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter by one gate"﴾, that he said: Ya'qub feared the evil eye for them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: He feared the evil eye for them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Nakha'i regarding His words: ﴿and enter by separate gates﴾, that he said: Ya'qub wished that Yusuf would meet his brother in seclusion.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿except a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾, that he said: it was fear of the evil eye for his sons.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 77–82:

His words: ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his stole before"﴾, meaning Yusuf.

The commentators have differed about this theft attributed to Yusuf: what was it? It was said that Yusuf had an aunt, older than Ya'qub, who had Ishaq's *mintaqah* (belt). Because she was the eldest of his children, they used to inherit it, so whoever was oldest, male or female, would take it. She had nursed Yusuf and loved him very much. and toward us in particular. So complete your kindness to us by agreeing to this request of ours.

﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, meaning: if we took anyone other than the one with whom we found our property, we would be wrongdoers in your religion and in what your judgment requires.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they withdrew, and their brother was not with them, conferring about what they would do when they went back to their father without their brother.

﴿Their eldest said﴾. It was said: he is Ruben, because he was the oldest. It was said: Yahuda, because he had the most intellect. It was said: Shim'un, because he was their leader.

This is coordinated with what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: "Did you not know that your father...? And do you not know your failure regarding Yusuf?" and corresponds to what is right.
