He only said this because he was ashamed before his father to come to him without the son whom they had pledged to bring back to him, unless they were encompassed, as has been explained. ﴿Or God decides for me﴾ regarding parting from it and going out from it. It was also said that the meaning is: or God decides for me by granting me victory over the one who took my brother, so that I fight him and take my brother from him, or I am unable, and then I turn back after that. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, for His judgments only proceed according to what agrees with the truth

and corresponds to what is right.

Then their eldest said, addressing them: ﴿Return to your father and say: "O our father, indeed your son has stolen"﴾. The majority of readers read *saraqa* (has stolen) in the active voice, because they had witnessed the extraction of the drinking cup from its container. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Abu Razin read it in the passive voice, and al-Nahhas related this from al-Kisa'i.

Al-Zajjaj said: *saraqa* may carry two meanings: one, that theft was known from him; the other, that he was accused of theft. ﴿And we testify only to what we know﴾ of the extraction of the drinking cup from its container. It was said: the meaning is: we did not testify before Yusuf that a thief is enslaved except by what we know of your law and the law of your fathers. ﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾, until it becomes clear to us whether the matter is as we witnessed or otherwise. It was said: the meaning is: at the time we took him from you to go out with us to Egypt, we were not guardians of the unseen, that he would commit the theft by which we have been exposed. It was said: *al-ghayb* (the unseen) is the night, and their meaning is that he stole while they were asleep. It was said: their meaning is that he did this while he was absent from them.

So his deed remained hidden from them.

﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾. This is part of the speech of their eldest to them: say to your father, "Ask the town in which we were," that is, Egypt, and the intended meaning is its people: ask the people of the town. It was said: it is a town among the towns of Egypt where they stayed and bought provisions. It was said: the meaning is: ask the town itself, even though it is inanimate, for you are a prophet of God, and God will make it speak and it will answer you. Something that supports this is that Sibawayh said: it is not permissible to say "Speak to Hind" while you mean "the servant of Hind."

﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, that is: say to your father, "Ask the caravan in which we came," that is, its companions, who were known people, neighbours of Ya'qub.

﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾ in what we have said. They brought this sentence with this emphasis because what had previously passed between them and their father Ya'qub necessitates complete doubt about their report in the listener's mind.

Abu al-Shaykh related from 'Atiyyah, who said: he stole two gold dirhams in his youth.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Yusuf stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, made of gold and silver, and broke it and threw it on the road, so his brothers reproached him for that."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 77–82:

His words: ﴿They said: "If he steals, a brother of his stole before"﴾, meaning Yusuf.

The commentators have differed about this theft attributed to Yusuf: what was it? It was said that Yusuf had an aunt, older than Ya'qub, who had Ishaq's *mintaqah* (belt). Because she was the eldest of his children, they used to inherit it, so whoever was oldest, male or female, would take it. She had nursed Yusuf and loved him very much. When he grew up, Ya'qub said to her: "Hand Yusuf over to me." She feared parting from him, so she devised a plan to keep him with her. She placed the belt under his clothes and tied it around him. Then she said: "The belt of Ishaq has been stolen; look for whoever took it." They searched and found it with Yusuf, so she kept him with her, as was the law of the prophets of that time from the family of Ibrahim.

The law of their community regarding theft has already been explained. It was also said that Yusuf took an idol that belonged to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it on the road, as a way of changing the wrong.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that it was an idol of gold.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Zajjaj that he said: "God knows best whether his brother stole or not." Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir, related from al-Zajjaj that he said: "They lied about him in what they attributed to him."

I say: this is the better view, for this lie is not their first lie. We have already presented what refutes the view of those who say that they were prophets at the time these matters occurred from them.

His words: ﴿So Yusuf kept it within himself﴾. Al-Zajjaj and others said: the pronoun in *asarraha* (he kept it hidden) refers to the statement or the sentence, as if it were said: he kept the sentence hidden within himself and did not reveal it to them, then explained it with his words: ﴿He said: "You are worse in position"﴾. Abu Ali al-Farisi rejected this, saying that this kind of pronoun reference, under the condition of explanation, is not in use. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the reply, meaning that Yusuf kept his reply hidden at that time until another time. It was also said: he kept hidden within himself their saying: "If he steals, a brother of his stole before." This last is the better view. The meaning of ﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾ is that he did not disclose to them this statement that he kept hidden within himself, by mentioning to them whether it was true or false. The clause ﴿He said: "You are worse in position"﴾ is explanatory according to the first view, and a new sentence according to the other two views, as if it were said: "What did Yusuf say when he made this statement?" He said: "You are worse in position," meaning in place and station, compared with those you have accused of theft while he is innocent. For you have committed the casting of Yusuf into the well, the lying to your father, and other of your deeds.

Then He said: ﴿And God knows best what you describe﴾, that is, the falsehood of attributing theft to Yusuf, and that there is no truth to it. Then they wanted to move him to compassion so that he would release their brother Benjamin to them, so that they could return with him to their father, because of the covenant he had taken from them to bring him back to him.

﴿They said: "O 'Azīz, indeed he has an aged father, a very old man"﴾, meaning that Benjamin has a father who has this attribute: he is a very old man who cannot bear to be separated from him, cannot endure without him, and cannot reach him. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾ to remain with you. For he has a station in his father's heart that none of us has, so his father will not be harmed by parting from one of us as he would be harmed by parting from Benjamin. Then they gave a reason for this with their words: ﴿Indeed, we see you are of the good-doers﴾ toward all people,

and toward us in particular. So complete your kindness to us by agreeing to this request of ours.

Yusuf answered them with his words: ﴿God forbid that we should take except him with whom we found our property﴾. That is, we seek refuge in God with a seeking of refuge. *Ma'adh* is a verbal noun in the accusative, governed by a deleted verb, and the one who seeks refuge in God is the one who holds fast to Him. *An nakhudha* (that we take) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the original is: "from taking except him with whom we found our property," and that is Benjamin, because he is the one in whose bag the drinking cup was found. Thus it has become lawful for us to enslave him, by your judgment which you gave us when you said: ﴿Its penalty is that he in whose bag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾.

﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, meaning: if we took anyone other than the one with whom we found our property, we would be wrongdoers in your religion and in what your judgment requires.

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of Yusuf and of his granting them their request which they had asked. The *sin* and *ta* (in *istay'asu*) are for emphasis. ﴿they withdrew apart, conferring privately (*najiyyan*)﴾, that is, they went off alone while conferring among themselves. *Najiyy* is a verbal noun that can apply to one or to many, as in His words ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant (*najiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 25].

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they withdrew, and their brother was not with them, conferring about what they would do when they went back to their father without their brother.

﴿Their eldest said﴾. It was said: he is Ruben, because he was the oldest. It was said: Yahuda, because he had the most intellect. It was said: Shim'un, because he was their leader.

﴿Did you not know that your father had taken from you a solemn pledge before God?﴾, that is, a covenant from God to protect his son and return him to him. The fact that it was from God means that it was by His permission. ﴿And before this, you had failed in regard to Yusuf﴾. This is coordinated with what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: "Did you not know that your father...? And do you not know your failure regarding Yusuf?" This was mentioned by al-Nahhas and others. ﴿And before this﴾ is connected to *ta'lamu* (you know), meaning: and you know your failure regarding Yusuf before this, with *ma* being verbal (*masdariyyah*); it may also be a superfluous particle. It was said: *ma farratum* is in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is "before this." It was also said that *ma* is a relative or a qualifying particle, and both are in the accusative or nominative position. What we have mentioned is the better view. The meaning of *farratum* (you failed) is: you fell short regarding his matter and did not observe your father's covenant concerning him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Nay, but your souls have made a thing seem fair to you﴾: that is, adorned it for you. "The matter" here is their saying, ﴿Indeed, your son has stolen﴾ [Yusuf 12:81], and he did not steal in reality. It was also said: the intended "matter" is their taking Binyamin out and going with him to Egypt in pursuit of benefit, but that turned into harm. It was also said: *taswil* (taswil, "making seem fair") means *takhyil* (imagining), that is: your souls imagined for you a matter that has no basis. It was also said: the matter is the verdict their souls made appear fair to them, that the thief is taken for his theft. The *idrab* (idrab, the turning away or switch) here is with regard to what they had affirmed of their own innocence, not with regard to the basic statement, for that is sound. The sentence is a fresh (*mustaʾnafah*) sentence, built on an implied question, like the others.

The sentence ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: so my affair is beautiful patience, more fitting for me and more appropriate for me. Beautiful patience is that in which its possessor does not disclose his complaint, but entrusts his affair to Allah and says "to Him we return." It has been reported that patience is at the first shock of calamity. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, that is, Yusuf and his brother Binyamin, and the third brother who remained in Egypt, who is the eldest of them, as has been mentioned before. He said this only because he held that Yusuf had not died, and that he was still alive, even though news of him had cut off. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what He decrees.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, that is, he withdrew from them and cut off speech with them. ﴿And said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: the original is *ya asafi*, and the yaʾ was changed to an alif because of the lightness of the fatha. *Al-asaf* is intense distress, and it was said: intense sorrow. From it is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"Oh, grief for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

Jacob said this saying when grief reached its utmost limit, in exaggeration, because of his separation from Yusuf, the joining of his separation from his brother Binyamin, and his reaching what he had reached of being a captive before the king of Egypt. So his sorrows multiplied, and the old longing was stirred in him by the latest news it had brought.

It has been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that Jacob did not have what is established in our law (*shariʿah*) of *istirjaʿ* (saying "to Him we return") and patience over calamities. Had he had that, he would not have said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"

The meaning of calling out to grief is requesting its presence, as if he said: "Come, O my grief, and approach me." ﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, that is, the blackness of his eyes changed to whiteness from excessive weeping.

It was said that his perception by the sense of sight completely ceased. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception.

As for the explanation of what befell Jacob, peace be upon him, of this great grief leading to the loss of his sight, wholly or partly, it has been said that this happened to him only because he knew that Yusuf was alive, and he feared for his religion, since he was in the land of Egypt, whose people at that time were unbelievers. It was also said: mere grief is not forbidden; what is forbidden is what leads from it to distraction, tearing of garments, and speaking what is not fitting.

The Prophet ﷺ said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say nothing that displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved for you."

This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, that is, *makzum* (suppressed), for its meaning is that he was filled with grief, holding it in and not letting it out. From it comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger), which is concealing it. So *al-makzum* is the one whose way of expressing grief is closed off, from *kazama al-siqa* (he sealed the waterskin) when he sealed it over what is in it. *Al-kazam* with a fatha on the *zaʾ* is the outlet of breath; it is said: he took him by his *akzam* (throat). It was also said: *al-kazim* has the meaning of *al-kazim* (the one who restrains), that is, the one who contains his grief and holds it in. From it is the verse:

"If I am restraining my tongue for the calamity of people,
then today my tongue is free to speak."

From it also is ﴿those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:134].

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *kazim* is grieved.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: its meaning is distressed and afflicted.

Some lexicographers said: *al-huzn* with a damma and sukun is weeping, and with two fathas is the opposite of joy.

Most lexicographers said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease to remember Yusuf"﴾, that is, you will not cease; the negative particle was omitted because there is no ambiguity.

Al-Kisa'i said: *fati'a* and *fati'tu* with a verb, *af'alu kadhaa*, means "I continued to," that is, "I have not ceased." Al-Farra' said: the *la* (negation) is implied, that is, "you will not cease." Al-Nahhas said: what al-Farra' said is correct.

It has been related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh the same as the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for what he said:

"I said, 'By Allah's oath, I will remain seated
even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs.'"

It is said *fati'a* and *fata'a* are two dialects, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I did not cease until it was as though its dust
was a tent of a day with winds raised up."

﴿Until you become *haradan*﴾. *Al-haras* is a verbal noun in which the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are alike. The attributive adjective is *haris* with a kasra on the *ra*, like *danaf* and *danif*. The root meaning of *haras* is corruption in the body or the mind, from grief, or from passionate love, or from old age. This is related from Abu ʿUbayda and others. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Worry travelled and made me ill,
and it increased me in sickness."

"Thus is love before today
of what brings about *haras*."

It was said: *haras* is what is short of death. It was said: it is old age. It was said: *al-harid* is the worn-out and decaying.

Al-Farra' said: *al-harid* is the one corrupt in body and mind, and so is *haras*.

Mu'arrij said: it is the one melting from worry, and the verse of the poet supports this:

"I am a man whom love has seized and made *ahradani*,
until I became worn out and until sickness wasted me."

It is said *rajul muhraḍ* (a man who is made to be *haradan*), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"The horses pursued him a full day,
and had they overtaken him, he would have become *muhradan*."

Al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers have related *ahradahu al-hamm* (worry made him ill) when it made him sick, and *rajul haris*, that is, a fool.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-haris* is the one who has gone.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the one who is destroyed.

The better explanation of *haras* here is not death or destruction from these meanings mentioned, so that His saying ﴿or you become of those who perish﴾ has a meaning other than the meaning of *haras*. Thus, the establishing of a new meaning (*al-taʾsis*) is better than emphasis (*al-taʾkid*). The meaning of ﴿of those who perish﴾ is: of the dead. Their aim was to prevent Jacob from weeping and grieving, out of compassion for him, even though they themselves were the cause of his sorrows and the source of his worries and griefs.

﴿He said, "I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah"﴾. This sentence is a fresh one, as if it were said: what did Jacob say when they said to him what they said? *Al-bathth* (distress) is what comes upon a person of things by which the grief of its possessor is so great that he cannot conceal it. This is what the lexicographers said, and it is derived from *battha-hu*, that is, he scattered it. So calamity was called *bathth* metaphorically.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stood at the abode of Mayya, O young man,
and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I pour out for it until, from what I pour out,
its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

The commentators mentioned that when a person is able to conceal the calamities that befall him, that is grief; and if he is not able to conceal it, that is *bathth*. So *bathth*, on this view, is the greatest and hardest grief. It was also said: *bathth* is anxiety. It was also said: it is need. On this view, the conjunction of grief with *bathth* has a clear meaning.

As for interpreting *bathth* as great grief, then it is as if he said: I only complain of my great grief and what is less than it of grief, to Allah and not to any other people.

It has been read *huznī* with a damma on the *ḥāʾ* and a sukun on the *zāy*, and *ḥazanī* with a fatha on both.

﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that is: I know from His kindness, His benevolence, and His reward for calamity what you do not know. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that Yusuf is alive. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that his dream is true. It was also said: I know from the answering of the distressed who turn to Allah what you do not know.

﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Yusuf and his brother﴾. *Al-tahassus* with unpointed letters (*ḥ-s-s*) is seeking a thing by the senses, derived from *al-hiss* or *al-ihsas* (sensation). That is: go and learn the news of Yusuf and his brother and seek it out. It is also read with a *jīm* (*tajassus*), which also means seeking. ﴿And do not despair of Allah's mercy﴾, that is, do not lose hope of His relief and His easing.

Al-Asma'i said: *al-rawh* is what a person finds of the breeze of the air, so that he is calmed by it. The root indicates movement and stirring, so everything by whose existence a person is stirred and in which he takes pleasure is *rawh*.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Asma'i also that he said: *al-rawh* is rest from distress of the heart.

Abu ʿUmar said: *al-rawh* is relief. It was also said: mercy.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people﴾, because they do not know Allah's power, His great workmanship, and His hidden kindnesses.

His saying: ﴿So when they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they went, as their father commanded them, to Egypt to seek out news of Yusuf and his brother. So when they entered upon Yusuf, ﴿they said, "O Ruler (*ayyuha al-ʿAziz*)"﴾, that is, the king, the mighty [p. 711] who is able. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that is, hunger and need.

It is said: *abḍaʿtu al-shayʾ* and *istabḍaʿtu-hu*, when you make it merchandise. In the proverb: "like one who sends dates to Hajar (to sell)." *Al-izjaʾ* is driving with a push.

Thaʿlab said: *al-bidaʿah al-muzjah* is the deficient, incomplete merchandise.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the poor dirhams are called *muzjah* only because they are rejected, pushed away, and not accepted.

It is disputed what this merchandise was. It was said: it was dried meat and fermented dates. It was said: wool and ghee. It was said: the green seed and pine nuts. It was said: poor dirhams. It was said: sandals and leather.

Then, after they informed him about the merchandise they had with them, they asked him to fill the measure for them completely, that is, to make it full with no shortfall. They asked him to give them charity, either by adding an increase over what corresponds to their merchandise, or by overlooking the poor quality of the merchandise they had brought, and by treating it as if it were good merchandise when filling the measure for them. Most of the commentators said this. It has been asked: how could they ask for charity when they were prophets, and charity is forbidden to prophets?

It has been answered: this is specific to our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿Indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾, with what He gives them of reward in the Hereafter, or with the expansion upon them in this world.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and their eldest who stayed behind.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph﴾, that he said: "You will not cease remembering Joseph ﴿until you become wasted away﴾," he said: "Emaciated from illness," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾," he said: "among the dead."

These same narrators also transmitted similar wording from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿You will not cease remembering Joseph﴾, that he said: "You will not cease remembering Joseph ﴿until you become wasted away﴾," he said: "Aged," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾," he said: "or you die."

Ibn Jarir and Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, raising it (*marfu'*, i.e., attributing it directly) to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever is overwhelmed by distress (*bathth*, بَثّ) does not endure," then he recited ﴿I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah﴾. Ibn Mandah in *al-Ma'rifah* also narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a *mursal* form (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿I only complain of my distress﴾, that he said: "My concern (*hammi*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that he said: "I know that Joseph's dream is true and that I will indeed prostrate to him."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "From the relief of Allah, ﴿He will relieve you of the distress you are in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that he said: "That is, the adversity (*ad-durr*, الضُّرّ) in livelihood."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: "﴿Meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ) means worn-out goods, a frayed rope, and a torn sack and such things."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Nay, but your souls have made a thing seem fair to you﴾: that is, adorned it for you. "The matter" here is their saying, ﴿Indeed, your son has stolen﴾ [Yusuf 12:81], and he did not steal in reality. It was also said: the intended "matter" is their taking Binyamin out and going with him to Egypt in pursuit of benefit, but that turned into harm. It was also said: *taswil* (taswil, "making seem fair") means *takhyil* (imagining), that is: your souls imagined for you a matter that has no basis. It was also said: the matter is the verdict their souls made appear fair to them, that the thief is taken for his theft. The *idrab* (idrab, the turning away or switch) here is with regard to what they had affirmed of their own innocence, not with regard to the basic statement, for that is sound. The sentence is a fresh (*mustaʾnafah*) sentence, built on an implied question, like the others.

The sentence ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: so my affair is beautiful patience, more fitting for me and more appropriate for me. Beautiful patience is that in which its possessor does not disclose his complaint, but entrusts his affair to Allah and says "to Him we return." It has been reported that patience is at the first shock of calamity. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, that is, Yusuf and his brother Binyamin, and the third brother who remained in Egypt, who is the eldest of them, as has been mentioned before. He said this only because he held that Yusuf had not died, and that he was still alive, even though news of him had cut off. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what He decrees.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, that is, he withdrew from them and cut off speech with them. ﴿And said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: the original is *ya asafi*, and the yaʾ was changed to an alif because of the lightness of the fatha. *Al-asaf* is intense distress, and it was said: intense sorrow. From it is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"Oh, grief for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

Jacob said this saying when grief reached its utmost limit, in exaggeration, because of his separation from Yusuf, the joining of his separation from his brother Binyamin, and his reaching what he had reached of being a captive before the king of Egypt. So his sorrows multiplied, and the old longing was stirred in him by the latest news it had brought.

It has been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that Jacob did not have what is established in our law (*shariʿah*) of *istirjaʿ* (saying "to Him we return") and patience over calamities. Had he had that, he would not have said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"

The meaning of calling out to grief is requesting its presence, as if he said: "Come, O my grief, and approach me." ﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, that is, the blackness of his eyes changed to whiteness from excessive weeping.

It was said that his perception by the sense of sight completely ceased. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception.

As for the explanation of what befell Jacob, peace be upon him, of this great grief leading to the loss of his sight, wholly or partly, it has been said that this happened to him only because he knew that Yusuf was alive, and he feared for his religion, since he was in the land of Egypt, whose people at that time were unbelievers. It was also said: mere grief is not forbidden; what is forbidden is what leads from it to distraction, tearing of garments, and speaking what is not fitting.

The Prophet ﷺ said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say nothing that displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved for you."

This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, that is, *makzum* (suppressed), for its meaning is that he was filled with grief, holding it in and not letting it out. From it comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger), which is concealing it. So *al-makzum* is the one whose way of expressing grief is closed off, from *kazama al-siqa* (he sealed the waterskin) when he sealed it over what is in it. *Al-kazam* with a fatha on the *zaʾ* is the outlet of breath; it is said: he took him by his *akzam* (throat). It was also said: *al-kazim* has the meaning of *al-kazim* (the one who restrains), that is, the one who contains his grief and holds it in. From it is the verse:

"If I am restraining my tongue for the calamity of people,
then today my tongue is free to speak."

From it also is ﴿those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:134].

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *kazim* is grieved.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: its meaning is distressed and afflicted.

Some lexicographers said: *al-huzn* with a damma and sukun is weeping, and with two fathas is the opposite of joy.

Most lexicographers said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease to remember Yusuf"﴾, that is, you will not cease; the negative particle was omitted because there is no ambiguity.

Al-Kisa'i said: *fati'a* and *fati'tu* with a verb, *af'alu kadhaa*, means "I continued to," that is, "I have not ceased." Al-Farra' said: the *la* (negation) is implied, that is, "you will not cease." Al-Nahhas said: what al-Farra' said is correct.

It has been related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh the same as the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for what he said:

"I said, 'By Allah's oath, I will remain seated
even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs.'"

It is said *fati'a* and *fata'a* are two dialects, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I did not cease until it was as though its dust
was a tent of a day with winds raised up."

﴿Until you become *haradan*﴾. *Al-haras* is a verbal noun in which the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are alike. The attributive adjective is *haris* with a kasra on the *ra*, like *danaf* and *danif*. The root meaning of *haras* is corruption in the body or the mind, from grief, or from passionate love, or from old age. This is related from Abu ʿUbayda and others. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Worry travelled and made me ill,
and it increased me in sickness."

"Thus is love before today
of what brings about *haras*."

It was said: *haras* is what is short of death. It was said: it is old age. It was said: *al-harid* is the worn-out and decaying.

Al-Farra' said: *al-harid* is the one corrupt in body and mind, and so is *haras*.

Mu'arrij said: it is the one melting from worry, and the verse of the poet supports this:

"I am a man whom love has seized and made *ahradani*,
until I became worn out and until sickness wasted me."

It is said *rajul muhraḍ* (a man who is made to be *haradan*), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"The horses pursued him a full day,
and had they overtaken him, he would have become *muhradan*."

Al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers have related *ahradahu al-hamm* (worry made him ill) when it made him sick, and *rajul haris*, that is, a fool.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-haris* is the one who has gone.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the one who is destroyed.

The better explanation of *haras* here is not death or destruction from these meanings mentioned, so that His saying ﴿or you become of those who perish﴾ has a meaning other than the meaning of *haras*. Thus, the establishing of a new meaning (*al-taʾsis*) is better than emphasis (*al-taʾkid*). The meaning of ﴿of those who perish﴾ is: of the dead. Their aim was to prevent Jacob from weeping and grieving, out of compassion for him, even though they themselves were the cause of his sorrows and the source of his worries and griefs.

﴿He said, "I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah"﴾. This is what the lexicographers said, and it is derived from *battha-hu*, that is, he scattered it. So calamity was called *bathth* metaphorically.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I pour out for it until, from what I pour out,
its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

The commentators mentioned that when a person is able to conceal the calamities that befall him, that is grief; and if he is not able to conceal it, that is *bathth*. So *bathth*, on this view, is the greatest and hardest grief. It was also said: *bathth* is anxiety. It was also said: it is need. On this view, the conjunction of grief with *bathth* has a clear meaning.

As for interpreting *bathth* as great grief, then it is as if he said: I only complain of my great grief and what is less than it of grief, to Allah and not to any other people.

It has been read *huznī* with a damma on the *ḥāʾ* and a sukun on the *zāy*, and *ḥazanī* with a fatha on both.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿with goods of little value﴾ (بِبِضاعَةٍ), that he said: "dirhams," and ﴿meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ), he said: "unsaleable (*kasidah*)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: "﴿Meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ) means worn-out goods, a frayed rope, and a torn sack and such things."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, regarding ﴿meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ), that he said: "Silver coins (*al-warq*, الوَرِق) that are defective (*al-zuyuf*, الزُّيُوف), which are not accepted in exchange unless something is deducted from them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Jarir, regarding His words ﴿and give us charity﴾, that he said: "Return our brother to us."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Nay, but your souls have made a thing seem fair to you﴾: that is, adorned it for you. "The matter" here is their saying, ﴿Indeed, your son has stolen﴾ [Yusuf 12:81], and he did not steal in reality. It was also said: the intended "matter" is their taking Binyamin out and going with him to Egypt in pursuit of benefit, but that turned into harm. It was also said: *taswil* (taswil, "making seem fair") means *takhyil* (imagining), that is: your souls imagined for you a matter that has no basis. It was also said: the matter is the verdict their souls made appear fair to them, that the thief is taken for his theft. The *idrab* (idrab, the turning away or switch) here is with regard to what they had affirmed of their own innocence, not with regard to the basic statement, for that is sound. The sentence is a fresh (*mustaʾnafah*) sentence, built on an implied question, like the others.

The sentence ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: so my affair is beautiful patience, more fitting for me and more appropriate for me. Beautiful patience is that in which its possessor does not disclose his complaint, but entrusts his affair to Allah and says "to Him we return." It has been reported that patience is at the first shock of calamity. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, that is, Yusuf and his brother Binyamin, and the third brother who remained in Egypt, who is the eldest of them, as has been mentioned before. He said this only because he held that Yusuf had not died, and that he was still alive, even though news of him had cut off. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what He decrees.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, that is, he withdrew from them and cut off speech with them. ﴿And said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: the original is *ya asafi*, and the yaʾ was changed to an alif because of the lightness of the fatha. *Al-asaf* is intense distress, and it was said: intense sorrow. From it is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"Oh, grief for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

Jacob said this saying when grief reached its utmost limit, in exaggeration, because of his separation from Yusuf, the joining of his separation from his brother Binyamin, and his reaching what he had reached of being a captive before the king of Egypt. So his sorrows multiplied, and the old longing was stirred in him by the latest news it had brought.

It has been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that Jacob did not have what is established in our law (*shariʿah*) of *istirjaʿ* (saying "to Him we return") and patience over calamities. Had he had that, he would not have said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"

The meaning of calling out to grief is requesting its presence, as if he said: "Come, O my grief, and approach me." ﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, that is, the blackness of his eyes changed to whiteness from excessive weeping.

It was said that his perception by the sense of sight completely ceased. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception.

As for the explanation of what befell Jacob, peace be upon him, of this great grief leading to the loss of his sight, wholly or partly, it has been said that this happened to him only because he knew that Yusuf was alive, and he feared for his religion, since he was in the land of Egypt, whose people at that time were unbelievers. It was also said: mere grief is not forbidden; what is forbidden is what leads from it to distraction, tearing of garments, and speaking what is not fitting.

The Prophet ﷺ said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say nothing that displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved for you."

This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, that is, *makzum* (suppressed), for its meaning is that he was filled with grief, holding it in and not letting it out. From it comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger), which is concealing it. So *al-makzum* is the one whose way of expressing grief is closed off, from *kazama al-siqa* (he sealed the waterskin) when he sealed it over what is in it. *Al-kazam* with a fatha on the *zaʾ* is the outlet of breath; it is said: he took him by his *akzam* (throat). It was also said: *al-kazim* has the meaning of *al-kazim* (the one who restrains), that is, the one who contains his grief and holds it in. From it is the verse:

"If I am restraining my tongue for the calamity of people,
then today my tongue is free to speak."

From it also is ﴿those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:134].

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *kazim* is grieved.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: its meaning is distressed and afflicted.

Some lexicographers said: *al-huzn* with a damma and sukun is weeping, and with two fathas is the opposite of joy.

Most lexicographers said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease to remember Yusuf"﴾, that is, you will not cease; the negative particle was omitted because there is no ambiguity.

Al-Kisa'i said: *fati'a* and *fati'tu* with a verb, *af'alu kadhaa*, means "I continued to," that is, "I have not ceased." Al-Farra' said: the *la* (negation) is implied, that is, "you will not cease." Al-Nahhas said: what al-Farra' said is correct.

It has been related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh the same as the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for what he said:

"I said, 'By Allah's oath, I will remain seated
even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs.'"

It is said *fati'a* and *fata'a* are two dialects, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I did not cease until it was as though its dust
was a tent of a day with winds raised up."

﴿Until you become *haradan*﴾. *Al-haras* is a verbal noun in which the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are alike. The attributive adjective is *haris* with a kasra on the *ra*, like *danaf* and *danif*. The root meaning of *haras* is corruption in the body or the mind, from grief, or from passionate love, or from old age. This is related from Abu ʿUbayda and others. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Worry travelled and made me ill,
and it increased me in sickness."

"Thus is love before today
of what brings about *haras*."

It was said: *haras* is what is short of death. It was said: it is old age. It was said: *al-harid* is the worn-out and decaying.

Al-Farra' said: *al-harid* is the one corrupt in body and mind, and so is *haras*.

Mu'arrij said: it is the one melting from worry, and the verse of the poet supports this:

"I am a man whom love has seized and made *ahradani*,
until I became worn out and until sickness wasted me."

It is said *rajul muhraḍ* (a man who is made to be *haradan*), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"The horses pursued him a full day,
and had they overtaken him, he would have become *muhradan*."

Al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers have related *ahradahu al-hamm* (worry made him ill) when it made him sick, and *rajul haris*, that is, a fool.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-haris* is the one who has gone.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the one who is destroyed.

The better explanation of *haras* here is not death or destruction from these meanings mentioned, so that His saying ﴿or you become of those who perish﴾ has a meaning other than the meaning of *haras*. Thus, the establishing of a new meaning (*al-taʾsis*) is better than emphasis (*al-taʾkid*). The meaning of ﴿of those who perish﴾ is: of the dead. Their aim was to prevent Jacob from weeping and grieving, out of compassion for him, even though they themselves were the cause of his sorrows and the source of his worries and griefs.

﴿He said, "I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah"﴾. This sentence is a fresh one, as if it were said: what did Jacob say when they said to him what they said? *Al-bathth* (distress) is what comes upon a person of things by which the grief of its possessor is so great that he cannot conceal it. This is what the lexicographers said, and it is derived from *battha-hu*, that is, he scattered it. So calamity was called *bathth* metaphorically.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stood at the abode of Mayya, O young man,
and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I pour out for it until, from what I pour out,
its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

The commentators mentioned that when a person is able to conceal the calamities that befall him, that is grief; and if he is not able to conceal it, that is *bathth*. So *bathth*, on this view, is the greatest and hardest grief. It was also said: *bathth* is anxiety. It was also said: it is need. On this view, the conjunction of grief with *bathth* has a clear meaning.

As for interpreting *bathth* as great grief, then it is as if he said: I only complain of my great grief and what is less than it of grief, to Allah and not to any other people.

It has been read *huznī* with a damma on the *ḥāʾ* and a sukun on the *zāy*, and *ḥazanī* with a fatha on both.

﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that is: I know from His kindness, His benevolence, and His reward for calamity what you do not know. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that Yusuf is alive. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that his dream is true. It was also said: I know from the answering of the distressed who turn to Allah what you do not know.

﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Yusuf and his brother﴾. *Al-tahassus* with unpointed letters (*ḥ-s-s*) is seeking a thing by the senses, derived from *al-hiss* or *al-ihsas* (sensation). That is: go and learn the news of Yusuf and his brother and seek it out. It is also read with a *jīm* (*tajassus*), which also means seeking. ﴿And do not despair of Allah's mercy﴾, that is, do not lose hope of His relief and His easing.

Al-Asma'i said: *al-rawh* is what a person finds of the breeze of the air, so that he is calmed by it. The root indicates movement and stirring, so everything by whose existence a person is stirred and in which he takes pleasure is *rawh*.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Asma'i also that he said: *al-rawh* is rest from distress of the heart.

Abu ʿUmar said: *al-rawh* is relief. It was also said: mercy.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people﴾, because they do not know Allah's power, His great workmanship, and His hidden kindnesses.

His saying: ﴿So when they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they went, as their father commanded them, to Egypt to seek out news of Yusuf and his brother. So when they entered upon Yusuf, ﴿they said, "O Ruler (*ayyuha al-ʿAziz*)"﴾, that is, the king, the mighty [p. 711] who is able. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that is, hunger and need.

In this is evidence that complaint is permitted in cases of necessity, when one fears for himself from harm, just as a sick person may complain to a doctor of the illness he feels. This time, when they entered Egypt, was the third time, as the context of the Noble Book before this indicates. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾. *Bidaʿah* (merchandise) is a portion of wealth intended for buying something. It is said: *abḍaʿtu al-shayʾ* and *istabḍaʿtu-hu*, when you make it merchandise. In the proverb: "like one who sends dates to Hajar (to sell)." *Al-izjaʾ* is driving with a push.

Al-Wahidi said: *al-izjaʾ* in the language is driving and pushing little by little. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds?﴾ [al-Nur 24:43]. The meaning is: it is merchandise that is pushed and that merchants do not accept.

Thaʿlab said: *al-bidaʿah al-muzjah* is the deficient, incomplete merchandise.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the poor dirhams are called *muzjah* only because they are rejected, pushed away, and not accepted.

It is disputed what this merchandise was. It was said: it was dried meat and fermented dates. It was said: wool and ghee. It was said: the green seed and pine nuts. It was said: poor dirhams. It was said: sandals and leather.

Then, after they informed him about the merchandise they had with them, they asked him to fill the measure for them completely, that is, to make it full with no shortfall. They asked him to give them charity, either by adding an increase over what corresponds to their merchandise, or by overlooking the poor quality of the merchandise they had brought, and by treating it as if it were good merchandise when filling the measure for them. Most of the commentators said this. It has been asked: how could they ask for charity when they were prophets, and charity is forbidden to prophets?

It has been answered: this is specific to our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿Indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾, with what He gives them of reward in the Hereafter, or with the expansion upon them in this world.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and Ruwabil.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and their eldest who stayed behind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!", he said: "Oh, sorrow!" Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah the same.

They related from Mujahid, he said: "Oh, distress!"

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, he said: grieved.

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, he said: he suppressed his grief and said nothing but good.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani, he said: *kazim* is distressed and afflicted.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah the same.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak, he said: *al-kazim* is *al-kamad* (the one burning inwardly with grief).

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph﴾, that he said: "You will not cease remembering Joseph ﴿until you become wasted away﴾," he said: "Emaciated from illness," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾," he said: "among the dead."

These same narrators also transmitted similar wording from Mujahid.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a *mursal* form (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿I only complain of my distress﴾, that he said: "My concern (*hammi*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that he said: "I know that Joseph's dream is true and that I will indeed prostrate to him."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated regarding His words ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾, that he said: "of the mercy of Allah." Ibn Jarir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "From the relief of Allah, ﴿He will relieve you of the distress you are in﴾."

"The horses pursued him a full day,
and had they overtaken him, he would have become *muhradan*."

Al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers have related *ahradahu al-hamm* (worry made him ill) when it made him sick, and *rajul haris*, that is, a fool.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-haris* is the one who has gone.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the one who is destroyed.

The better explanation of *haras* here is not death or destruction from these meanings mentioned, so that His saying ﴿or you become of those who perish﴾ has a meaning other than the meaning of *haras*. Thus, the establishing of a new meaning (*al-taʾsis*) is better than emphasis (*al-taʾkid*). The meaning of ﴿of those who perish﴾ is: of the dead. Their aim was to prevent Jacob from weeping and grieving, out of compassion for him, even though they themselves were the cause of his sorrows and the source of his worries and griefs.

﴿He said, "I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah"﴾. This sentence is a fresh one, as if it were said: what did Jacob say when they said to him what they said? *Al-bathth* (distress) is what comes upon a person of things by which the grief of its possessor is so great that he cannot conceal it. This is what the lexicographers said, and it is derived from *battha-hu*, that is, he scattered it. So calamity was called *bathth* metaphorically.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stood at the abode of Mayya, O young man,
and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I pour out for it until, from what I pour out,
its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

The commentators mentioned that when a person is able to conceal the calamities that befall him, that is grief; and if he is not able to conceal it, that is *bathth*. So *bathth*, on this view, is the greatest and hardest grief. It was also said: *bathth* is anxiety. It was also said: it is need. On this view, the conjunction of grief with *bathth* has a clear meaning.

As for interpreting *bathth* as great grief, then it is as if he said: I only complain of my great grief and what is less than it of grief, to Allah and not to any other people.

It has been read *huznī* with a damma on the *ḥāʾ* and a sukun on the *zāy*, and *ḥazanī* with a fatha on both.

﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that is: I know from His kindness, His benevolence, and His reward for calamity what you do not know. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that Yusuf is alive. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that his dream is true. It was also said: I know from the answering of the distressed who turn to Allah what you do not know.

﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Yusuf and his brother﴾. *Al-tahassus* with unpointed letters (*ḥ-s-s*) is seeking a thing by the senses, derived from *al-hiss* or *al-ihsas* (sensation). It is also read with a *jīm* (*tajassus*), which also means seeking. ﴿And do not despair of Allah's mercy﴾, that is, do not lose hope of His relief and His easing.

Al-Asma'i said: *al-rawh* is what a person finds of the breeze of the air, so that he is calmed by it. The root indicates movement and stirring, so everything by whose existence a person is stirred and in which he takes pleasure is *rawh*.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Asma'i also that he said: *al-rawh* is rest from distress of the heart.

Abu ʿUmar said: *al-rawh* is relief. It was also said: mercy.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people﴾, because they do not know Allah's power, His great workmanship, and His hidden kindnesses.

His saying: ﴿So when they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they went, as their father commanded them, to Egypt to seek out news of Yusuf and his brother. So when they entered upon Yusuf, ﴿they said, "O Ruler (*ayyuha al-ʿAziz*)"﴾, that is, the king, the mighty [p. 711] who is able. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that is, hunger and need.

This time, when they entered Egypt, was the third time, as the context of the Noble Book before this indicates. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾. *Bidaʿah* (merchandise) is a portion of wealth intended for buying something. It is said: *abḍaʿtu al-shayʾ* and *istabḍaʿtu-hu*, when you make it merchandise. In the proverb: "like one who sends dates to Hajar (to sell)." *Al-izjaʾ* is driving with a push.

Al-Wahidi said: *al-izjaʾ* in the language is driving and pushing little by little. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds?﴾ [al-Nur 24:43]. The meaning is: it is merchandise that is pushed and that merchants do not accept.

Thaʿlab said: *al-bidaʿah al-muzjah* is the deficient, incomplete merchandise.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the poor dirhams are called *muzjah* only because they are rejected, pushed away, and not accepted.

It is disputed what this merchandise was. It was said: it was dried meat and fermented dates. It was said: wool and ghee. It was said: the green seed and pine nuts. It was said: poor dirhams. It was said: sandals and leather.

Then, after they informed him about the merchandise they had with them, they asked him to fill the measure for them completely, that is, to make it full with no shortfall. They asked him to give them charity, either by adding an increase over what corresponds to their merchandise, or by overlooking the poor quality of the merchandise they had brought, and by treating it as if it were good merchandise when filling the measure for them. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and Ruwabil.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and their eldest who stayed behind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!", he said: "Oh, sorrow!" Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah the same.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah the same.

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 83–88 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph﴾, that he said: "You will not cease remembering Joseph ﴿until you become wasted away﴾," he said: "Emaciated from illness," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾," he said: "among the dead."

These same narrators also transmitted similar wording from Mujahid.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿You will not cease remembering Joseph﴾, that he said: "You will not cease remembering Joseph ﴿until you become wasted away﴾," he said: "Aged," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾," he said: "or you die."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak: ﴿until you become wasted away﴾, he said: "The *haras* (حَرَض) is the worn-out one," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾, he said: "among the dead."

Ibn Jarir and Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, raising it (*marfu'*, i.e., attributing it directly) to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever is overwhelmed by distress (*bathth*, بَثّ) does not endure," then he recited ﴿I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah﴾. Ibn Mandah in *al-Ma'rifah* also narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a *mursal* form (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿I only complain of my distress﴾, that he said: "My concern (*hammi*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that he said: "I know that Joseph's dream is true and that I will indeed prostrate to him."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated regarding His words ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾, that he said: "of the mercy of Allah." Ibn Jarir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "From the relief of Allah, ﴿He will relieve you of the distress you are in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that he said: "That is, the adversity (*ad-durr*, الضُّرّ) in livelihood."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿with goods of little value﴾ (بِبِضاعَةٍ), that he said: "dirhams," and ﴿meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ), he said: "unsaleable (*kasidah*)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: "﴿Meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ) means worn-out goods, a frayed rope, and a torn sack and such things."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Jarir, regarding His words ﴿and give us charity﴾, that he said: "Return our brother to us."

"Oh, grief for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

Jacob said this saying when grief reached its utmost limit, in exaggeration, because of his separation from Yusuf, the joining of his separation from his brother Binyamin, and his reaching what he had reached of being a captive before the king of Egypt. So his sorrows multiplied, and the old longing was stirred in him by the latest news it had brought.

It has been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that Jacob did not have what is established in our law (*shariʿah*) of *istirjaʿ* (saying "to Him we return") and patience over calamities. Had he had that, he would not have said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"

The meaning of calling out to grief is requesting its presence, as if he said: "Come, O my grief, and approach me." ﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, that is, the blackness of his eyes changed to whiteness from excessive weeping.

It was said that his perception by the sense of sight completely ceased. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception.

It was also said: mere grief is not forbidden; what is forbidden is what leads from it to distraction, tearing of garments, and speaking what is not fitting.

The Prophet ﷺ said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say nothing that displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved for you."

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: its meaning is distressed and afflicted.

It has been related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh the same as the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for what he said:

It is said *fati'a* and *fata'a* are two dialects, and from it is the saying of the poet:

These same narrators also transmitted similar wording from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak: ﴿until you become wasted away﴾, he said: "The *haras* (حَرَض) is the worn-out one," ﴿or you become among those who perish﴾, he said: "among the dead."

Ibn Jarir and Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, raising it (*marfu'*, i.e., attributing it directly) to the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever is overwhelmed by distress (*bathth*, بَثّ) does not endure," then he recited ﴿I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah﴾. Ibn Mandah in *al-Ma'rifah* also narrated from Muslim ibn Yasar, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said," and he mentioned it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, raised (*marfu'*) to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'mur, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a *mursal* form (a report whose chain omits the Companion).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿I only complain of my distress﴾, that he said: "My concern (*hammi*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that he said: "I know that Joseph's dream is true and that I will indeed prostrate to him."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated regarding His words ﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾, that he said: "of the mercy of Allah." Ibn Jarir also narrated a similar report from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "From the relief of Allah, ﴿He will relieve you of the distress you are in﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that he said: "That is, the adversity (*ad-durr*, الضُّرّ) in livelihood."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿with goods of little value﴾ (بِبِضاعَةٍ), that he said: "dirhams," and ﴿meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ), he said: "unsaleable (*kasidah*)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: "﴿Meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ) means worn-out goods, a frayed rope, and a torn sack and such things."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, regarding ﴿meager﴾ (مُزْجاةٍ), that he said: "Silver coins (*al-warq*, الوَرِق) that are defective (*al-zuyuf*, الزُّيُوف), which are not accepted in exchange unless something is deducted from them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Jarir, regarding His words ﴿and give us charity﴾, that he said: "Return our brother to us."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 83–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Nay, but your souls have made a thing seem fair to you﴾: that is, adorned it for you. "The matter" here is their saying, ﴿Indeed, your son has stolen﴾ [Yusuf 12:81], and he did not steal in reality. It was also said: the intended "matter" is their taking Binyamin out and going with him to Egypt in pursuit of benefit, but that turned into harm. It was also said: *taswil* (taswil, "making seem fair") means *takhyil* (imagining), that is: your souls imagined for you a matter that has no basis. It was also said: the matter is the verdict their souls made appear fair to them, that the thief is taken for his theft. The *idrab* (idrab, the turning away or switch) here is with regard to what they had affirmed of their own innocence, not with regard to the basic statement, for that is sound. The sentence is a fresh (*mustaʾnafah*) sentence, built on an implied question, like the others.

The sentence ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, that is: so my affair is beautiful patience, more fitting for me and more appropriate for me. Beautiful patience is that in which its possessor does not disclose his complaint, but entrusts his affair to Allah and says "to Him we return." It has been reported that patience is at the first shock of calamity. ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, that is, Yusuf and his brother Binyamin, and the third brother who remained in Egypt, who is the eldest of them, as has been mentioned before. He said this only because he held that Yusuf had not died, and that he was still alive, even though news of him had cut off. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what He decrees.

﴿And he turned away from them﴾, that is, he withdrew from them and cut off speech with them. ﴿And said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"﴾

Al-Zajjaj said: the original is *ya asafi*, and the yaʾ was changed to an alif because of the lightness of the fatha. *Al-asaf* is intense distress, and it was said: intense sorrow. From it is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"Oh, grief for the heart, how it turned away,
and for the soul, when it was consoled, it consoled itself."

Jacob said this saying when grief reached its utmost limit, in exaggeration, because of his separation from Yusuf, the joining of his separation from his brother Binyamin, and his reaching what he had reached of being a captive before the king of Egypt. So his sorrows multiplied, and the old longing was stirred in him by the latest news it had brought.

It has been related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that Jacob did not have what is established in our law (*shariʿah*) of *istirjaʿ* (saying "to Him we return") and patience over calamities. Had he had that, he would not have said, "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!"

The meaning of calling out to grief is requesting its presence, as if he said: "Come, O my grief, and approach me." ﴿And his eyes turned white from the grief﴾, that is, the blackness of his eyes changed to whiteness from excessive weeping.

It was said that his perception by the sense of sight completely ceased. It was also said that he perceived with weak perception.

As for the explanation of what befell Jacob, peace be upon him, of this great grief leading to the loss of his sight, wholly or partly, it has been said that this happened to him only because he knew that Yusuf was alive, and he feared for his religion, since he was in the land of Egypt, whose people at that time were unbelievers. It was also said: mere grief is not forbidden; what is forbidden is what leads from it to distraction, tearing of garments, and speaking what is not fitting.

The Prophet ﷺ said at the death of his son Ibrahim: "The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say nothing that displeases the Lord. Indeed, O Ibrahim, we are grieved for you."

This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, that is, *makzum* (suppressed), for its meaning is that he was filled with grief, holding it in and not letting it out. From it comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger), which is concealing it. So *al-makzum* is the one whose way of expressing grief is closed off, from *kazama al-siqa* (he sealed the waterskin) when he sealed it over what is in it. *Al-kazam* with a fatha on the *zaʾ* is the outlet of breath; it is said: he took him by his *akzam* (throat). It was also said: *al-kazim* has the meaning of *al-kazim* (the one who restrains), that is, the one who contains his grief and holds it in. From it is the verse:

"If I am restraining my tongue for the calamity of people,
then today my tongue is free to speak."

From it also is ﴿those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:134].

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *kazim* is grieved.

It was related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: its meaning is distressed and afflicted.

Some lexicographers said: *al-huzn* with a damma and sukun is weeping, and with two fathas is the opposite of joy.

Most lexicographers said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. ﴿They said, "By Allah, you will not cease to remember Yusuf"﴾, that is, you will not cease; the negative particle was omitted because there is no ambiguity.

Al-Kisa'i said: *fati'a* and *fati'tu* with a verb, *af'alu kadhaa*, means "I continued to," that is, "I have not ceased." Al-Farra' said: the *la* (negation) is implied, that is, "you will not cease." Al-Nahhas said: what al-Farra' said is correct.

It has been related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh the same as the view of al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for what he said:

"I said, 'By Allah's oath, I will remain seated
even if they cut off my head before you and my limbs.'"

It is said *fati'a* and *fata'a* are two dialects, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I did not cease until it was as though its dust
was a tent of a day with winds raised up."

﴿Until you become *haradan*﴾. *Al-haras* is a verbal noun in which the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are alike. The attributive adjective is *haris* with a kasra on the *ra*, like *danaf* and *danif*. The root meaning of *haras* is corruption in the body or the mind, from grief, or from passionate love, or from old age. This is related from Abu ʿUbayda and others. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Worry travelled and made me ill,
and it increased me in sickness."

"Thus is love before today
of what brings about *haras*."

It was said: *haras* is what is short of death. It was said: it is old age. It was said: *al-harid* is the worn-out and decaying.

Al-Farra' said: *al-harid* is the one corrupt in body and mind, and so is *haras*.

Mu'arrij said: it is the one melting from worry, and the verse of the poet supports this:

"I am a man whom love has seized and made *ahradani*,
until I became worn out and until sickness wasted me."

It is said *rajul muhraḍ* (a man who is made to be *haradan*), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"The horses pursued him a full day,
and had they overtaken him, he would have become *muhradan*."

Al-Nahhas said: the lexicographers have related *ahradahu al-hamm* (worry made him ill) when it made him sick, and *rajul haris*, that is, a fool.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-haris* is the one who has gone.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the one who is destroyed.

The better explanation of *haras* here is not death or destruction from these meanings mentioned, so that His saying ﴿or you become of those who perish﴾ has a meaning other than the meaning of *haras*. Thus, the establishing of a new meaning (*al-taʾsis*) is better than emphasis (*al-taʾkid*). The meaning of ﴿of those who perish﴾ is: of the dead. Their aim was to prevent Jacob from weeping and grieving, out of compassion for him, even though they themselves were the cause of his sorrows and the source of his worries and griefs.

﴿He said, "I only complain of my distress and my grief to Allah"﴾. This sentence is a fresh one, as if it were said: what did Jacob say when they said to him what they said? *Al-bathth* (distress) is what comes upon a person of things by which the grief of its possessor is so great that he cannot conceal it. This is what the lexicographers said, and it is derived from *battha-hu*, that is, he scattered it. So calamity was called *bathth* metaphorically.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stood at the abode of Mayya, O young man,
and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it,
and I pour out for it until, from what I pour out,
its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

The commentators mentioned that when a person is able to conceal the calamities that befall him, that is grief; and if he is not able to conceal it, that is *bathth*. So *bathth*, on this view, is the greatest and hardest grief. It was also said: *bathth* is anxiety. It was also said: it is need. On this view, the conjunction of grief with *bathth* has a clear meaning.

As for interpreting *bathth* as great grief, then it is as if he said: I only complain of my great grief and what is less than it of grief, to Allah and not to any other people.

It has been read *huznī* with a damma on the *ḥāʾ* and a sukun on the *zāy*, and *ḥazanī* with a fatha on both.

﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾, that is: I know from His kindness, His benevolence, and His reward for calamity what you do not know. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that Yusuf is alive. It was also said: he meant his knowledge that his dream is true. It was also said: I know from the answering of the distressed who turn to Allah what you do not know.

﴿O my sons, go and seek out news of Yusuf and his brother﴾. *Al-tahassus* with unpointed letters (*ḥ-s-s*) is seeking a thing by the senses, derived from *al-hiss* or *al-ihsas* (sensation). That is: go and learn the news of Yusuf and his brother and seek it out. It is also read with a *jīm* (*tajassus*), which also means seeking. ﴿And do not despair of Allah's mercy﴾, that is, do not lose hope of His relief and His easing.

Al-Asma'i said: *al-rawh* is what a person finds of the breeze of the air, so that he is calmed by it. The root indicates movement and stirring, so everything by whose existence a person is stirred and in which he takes pleasure is *rawh*.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Asma'i also that he said: *al-rawh* is rest from distress of the heart.

Abu ʿUmar said: *al-rawh* is relief. It was also said: mercy.

﴿Indeed, none despairs of Allah's mercy except the disbelieving people﴾, because they do not know Allah's power, His great workmanship, and His hidden kindnesses.

His saying: ﴿So when they entered upon him﴾, that is, upon Yusuf. There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: so they went, as their father commanded them, to Egypt to seek out news of Yusuf and his brother. So when they entered upon Yusuf, ﴿they said, "O Ruler (*ayyuha al-ʿAziz*)"﴾, that is, the king, the mighty [p. 711] who is able. ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, that is, hunger and need.

In this is evidence that complaint is permitted in cases of necessity, when one fears for himself from harm, just as a sick person may complain to a doctor of the illness he feels. This time, when they entered Egypt, was the third time, as the context of the Noble Book before this indicates. ﴿And we have come with meager merchandise﴾. *Bidaʿah* (merchandise) is a portion of wealth intended for buying something. It is said: *abḍaʿtu al-shayʾ* and *istabḍaʿtu-hu*, when you make it merchandise. In the proverb: "like one who sends dates to Hajar (to sell)." *Al-izjaʾ* is driving with a push.

Al-Wahidi said: *al-izjaʾ* in the language is driving and pushing little by little. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds?﴾ [al-Nur 24:43]. The meaning is: it is merchandise that is pushed and that merchants do not accept.

Thaʿlab said: *al-bidaʿah al-muzjah* is the deficient, incomplete merchandise.

Abu ʿUbayda said: the poor dirhams are called *muzjah* only because they are rejected, pushed away, and not accepted.

It is disputed what this merchandise was. It was said: it was dried meat and fermented dates. It was said: wool and ghee. It was said: the green seed and pine nuts. It was said: poor dirhams. It was said: sandals and leather.

Then, after they informed him about the merchandise they had with them, they asked him to fill the measure for them completely, that is, to make it full with no shortfall. They asked him to give them charity, either by adding an increase over what corresponds to their merchandise, or by overlooking the poor quality of the merchandise they had brought, and by treating it as if it were good merchandise when filling the measure for them. Most of the commentators said this. It has been asked: how could they ask for charity when they were prophets, and charity is forbidden to prophets?

It has been answered: this is specific to our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿Indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾, with what He gives them of reward in the Hereafter, or with the expansion upon them in this world.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring them all to me﴾, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and Ruwabil.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning the verse, he said: Yusuf, his brother, and their eldest who stayed behind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: "Oh, my grief over Yusuf!", he said: "Oh, sorrow!" Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah the same.

They related from Mujahid, he said: "Oh, distress!"

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying: ﴿So he was *kazim*﴾, he said: grieved.

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, he said: he suppressed his grief and said nothing but good.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani, he said: *kazim* is distressed and afflicted.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah the same.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak, he said: *al-kazim* is *al-kamad* (the one burning inwardly with grief).

Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid something similar.
