Jacob had placed this shirt in a case and hung it on Joseph's neck, since he feared the evil eye for him. Gabriel informed Joseph to send it to Jacob so that his sight would return to him, for in it was the scent of Paradise, and the scent of Paradise does not fall upon a sick person without his being healed, nor upon one afflicted without his being relieved. ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, i.e. he will become seeing, on the reading that "ya'ti" is one of the sister verbs of "kāna". al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. as-Suddi said: he will return seeing. It was said: its meaning is: "he will come to me in Egypt, and he will be seeing, the blindness having gone from him," and this is supported by His words ﴿and bring me all your family together﴾, i.e. all who are included in the word "family", of women and descendants. It was said they were about seventy, and it was said ninety-three.

(p-713) ﴿When the caravan departed﴾, i.e. it set out, departing from Egypt towards Syria. One says *fasala fusulan*, and *fasaltuhu faslan*, intransitive and transitive; and one says *fasala min al-balad fusulan* when he has separated from it and passed its walls. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e. Jacob, to those with him among his family in the land of Canaan: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾. It was said: a wind arose and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob across the great distance, and so he informed them of what he found. Then he said ﴿"Unless you think me senile"﴾, i.e. unless you attribute me to *fand*, which is the loss of reason from old age; one says *afnada al-rajul* when he becomes senile and his mind changes.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lawla an tusaffihuni* — unless you call me foolish — so he made *fand* into *safah*. az-Zajjaj said: *lawla an tujahhiluni* — unless you call me ignorant — so he made *fand* into ignorance. What supports the view of those who said it means foolishness is the words of an-Nabigha:

*Except Solomon, when the Sovereign said to him: "Stand in the wilderness and restrain it from fand."*

That is, restrain it from foolishness.

Abu ʿUmar ash-Shaybani said: *at-tafnid* is disparagement, and from it is the poet's words:

*O my two companions, leave off reproach and disparagement; what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

It was said: it is lying, and from it is the poet's words:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the saying of the true-speaking one any falsehood?*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ﴿unless you think me senile﴾ — unless you weaken my opinion.

The like of this is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda.

al-Akhfash said: *at-tafnid* is blame and weakness of opinion.

All these meanings return to incapacitating and weakening opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, and *afnada* when he spoke with error, and *al-fanad* is error in speech. Among what indicates its use for blame is the poet's words:

*O my two blamers, leave off blaming and reproach; love has lasted long, and you two have prolonged the disparagement.*

Jacob informed them that the breeze had carried to him the scent of his beloved, and that were it not for what he feared of their disparagement, he would not have doubted it:

*For the breeze, when it breathes upon the soul of one grieving, its griefs are dispelled.*

*When I say this, as I try to forget, the breeze of the morning stirs me, from wherever the dawn rises.*

*And indeed the breeze blows to me from its land, so the touch of your breeze delights and sweetens.*

﴿They said: "By Allah, you are certainly in your old error"﴾, i.e. those present with him from his family said: "Indeed you, O Jacob, are in your going astray from the path of rectitude that you were upon of old, through excess of your love for Joseph, not forgetting him nor slackening from him." The tongue of Jacob's state says to them:

*None knows longing except one who suffers it, nor passion except one who endures it.*

*Do not blame the yearning one in his longings until your inner parts are in his inner parts.*

It was said: the meaning is: "you are in your ancient madness"; and it was said: "in your ancient love."

They said this to him because the arrival of the bearer of good news had not yet reached them. ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾. The commentators said: the bearer was Judah son of Jacob. He said to his brothers: "I brought him the shirt stained with blood; so give me your shirt today, that I may inform him you are alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." ﴿He threw it over his face﴾, i.e. the bearer threw Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, or Jacob threw it over his own face. ﴿He regained his sight﴾. *Irtidad* is the reverting of a thing to a condition it was previously in; the meaning: he returned and came back to his former state of sound sight. ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you?"﴾, i.e. Jacob said to those with him among his family, to whom he had said: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾: "Did I not tell you this statement, and you said what you said?" His words ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be a fresh independent statement not connected with the saying, or the clause ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be the content of the saying, and he intends by it to inform them of what he had said earlier: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ They asked him to seek forgiveness for them and acknowledged their sin. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the sense being: when they returned from Egypt and reached their father, they said this statement, and he promised them what they had asked of him.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. It was also said that he postponed it until he had obtained their pardon from Yusuf, and he did not know that Yusuf had already forgiven them. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ gives the reason for what came before it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His words ﴿no reproach﴾ that he said: "No reproach" means no rebuke.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he turned to the people and said, 'What do you say, and what do you think?' They said, 'A noble cousin.' So he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today; may Allah forgive you.﴾" Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Asking needs of the young is easier than asking them of the elders. Have you not seen the words of Yusuf, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾? And Ya'qub said, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾"

I say: In this statement there is room for examination. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

(p-712) The interrogative in His words, ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ (hal ʿalimtum), is for rebuke and reproach. They were certainly aware of it, but he intended what we have mentioned. It is also understood from it the magnification of the event, since it carries the force of: "How great is the matter you committed against Joseph and his brother, and how ugly is what you undertook!" It is like saying to a wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" As for what they did to Joseph, it is what preceded, which Allah, glorified is He, related to us in this surah. As for what they did to his brother, a group of exegetes said: it is what they inflicted upon him of grief at being separated from his brother Joseph, and the humiliation and abuse he suffered from them. He did not ask them about what they did to their father Jacob, although he had suffered from them what Allah related earlier of various kinds of harm.

al-Wahidi said: He did not mention his father Jacob, despite the great grief that befell him through separation from him, out of honour for him, elevating his rank, and knowledge that this was a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, to increase his degree with Him. ﴿while you were ignorant﴾ — he negated knowledge from them and affirmed the attribute of ignorance, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires. It was said: he attributed ignorance to them with the intent of excusing them and lightening the matter for them, as if he said: you undertook that evil and reprehensible act at a time when you did not know its sin and your understanding fell short of its consequence and what follows from it; or he meant that they were then in the time of youth and the age of childhood, as an excuse for them and a repelling of the shame and bewilderment that overtook them, while he and they knew that at that time they were grown men.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a statement without interrogation. The rest read it as a confirmatory interrogative, and this was from them in the manner of amazement and astonishment. It was said: the reason they recognised him merely by his words to them, ﴿what you did to Joseph and his brother﴾, is that when he said that to them they became alert and understood that none would address them with such a thing except him. It was said: when he said this to them he removed the crown from his head, and so they recognised him. It was said: he smiled, and they recognised his front teeth. ﴿He said: "I am Joseph, and this is my brother."﴾ He answered them by acknowledging what they had asked him about.

Ibn al-Anbari said: he stated the name, saying "I am Joseph", and did not say "I am he", to magnify what had befallen him from the injustice of his brothers, as if he said: "I am the one wronged, whose sanctity was violated, the one they intended to kill." He was content with stating the name instead of these meanings. He said "and this is my brother", although they knew him and did not deny it, because his purpose was: "and this is my brother, the wronged one, like my own wronging." ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾ by delivering us from what we were tried with. It was said: Allah has been gracious to us with every good in this world and the next. It was said: by bringing us together after separation. There is no barrier to intending all of that. ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ — the majority read "yattaqi" with a jussive, taking "man" as a conditional. Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' retained in "yattaqī", as in the words of the poet:

*Did it not reach you, while the news spreads, of what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?*

It was said that he made "man" a relative pronoun, not a conditional, but this is far-fetched. The meaning: whoever performs righteousness, or does what protects him from sins and is patient through calamities, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ in general terms, so that what the context indicates enters it first and foremost. He used the apparent noun where the place called for a pronoun, i.e. "their reward", to show that those described with piety are described with the quality of excellence.

﴿They said: "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, i.e. He has chosen and favoured you over us by what He has singled you out with of the attributes of perfection. This is an acknowledgment from them of his virtue and great station.

That does not necessarily mean they were not prophets, since the ranks of the prophets differ. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾, i.e. indeed the matter was so.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *khati'a* and *akhta'a* have one meaning. al-Azhari said: the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is one who intends what is right but arrives at something else; from it is their saying: "The mujtahid errs and is right." The sinner (*khati'*) is one who deliberately does what is not fitting.

They spoke this statement, which includes acknowledgment of error and sin, seeking to win his pardon and to draw out his forgiveness.

﴿He said: "No reproach upon you today"﴾. *Tathrib* means censure and rebuke, i.e. no censure, no rebuke, and no blame upon you.

al-Asmaʿi said: *tharrabtu ʿalayhi* — I made his deed ugly to him.

az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: no corruption of what is between me and you of sacred kinship and the right of brotherhood; and for you with me there is reconciliation and pardon. The original sense of *tathrib* is corruption, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: my reproach of you has ceased upon your acknowledgment of the sin.

Thaʿlab said: "Tharraba fulan ʿala fulan" means he enumerated his sins against him. The original sense of *tathrib* derives from *ath-thurb*, the fat that covers the paunch, and its meaning is removing the *tathrib*, just as *tajlid* and *taqri'* are removing the skin and the scraping. The accusative of "today" is governed by *tathrib*, i.e. "I do not reproach you," or it is governed by an implied verb in "upon you," which is stable or fixed or the like, i.e. "no reproach is stable or fixed upon you."

Al-Akhfash permitted pausing at "upon you," so that "today" is connected with the verb that follows it. Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned something like this.

Then he prayed for them with his words ﴿May Allah forgive you﴾, on the reading of pausing at "today", or he informed them that Allah had forgiven them that day, on the reading of pausing at "upon you". ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ — He shows mercy to His servants with a mercy by which they do not show mercy to one another, so He rewards their good-doers and forgives their wrong-doers.

His words, ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It was said this shirt is the one Allah clothed Abraham with when he was cast into the fire; Abraham clothed Isaac with it, and Isaac clothed Jacob with it.

Jacob had placed this shirt in a case and hung it on Joseph's neck, since he feared the evil eye for him. Gabriel informed Joseph to send it to Jacob so that his sight would return to him, for in it was the scent of Paradise, and the scent of Paradise does not fall upon a sick person without his being healed, nor upon one afflicted without his being relieved. ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, i.e. he will become seeing, on the reading that "ya'ti" is one of the sister verbs of "kāna". al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. as-Suddi said: he will return seeing. It was said: its meaning is: "he will come to me in Egypt, and he will be seeing, the blindness having gone from him," and this is supported by His words ﴿and bring me all your family together﴾, i.e. all who are included in the word "family", of women and descendants. It was said they were about seventy, and it was said ninety-three.

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

(p-712) The interrogative in His words, ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ (hal ʿalimtum), is for rebuke and reproach. They were certainly aware of it, but he intended what we have mentioned. It is also understood from it the magnification of the event, since it carries the force of: "How great is the matter you committed against Joseph and his brother, and how ugly is what you undertook!" It is like saying to a wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" As for what they did to Joseph, it is what preceded, which Allah, glorified is He, related to us in this surah. As for what they did to his brother, a group of exegetes said: it is what they inflicted upon him of grief at being separated from his brother Joseph, and the humiliation and abuse he suffered from them. He did not ask them about what they did to their father Jacob, although he had suffered from them what Allah related earlier of various kinds of harm.

al-Wahidi said: He did not mention his father Jacob, despite the great grief that befell him through separation from him, out of honour for him, elevating his rank, and knowledge that this was a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, to increase his degree with Him. ﴿while you were ignorant﴾ — he negated knowledge from them and affirmed the attribute of ignorance, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires. It was said: he attributed ignorance to them with the intent of excusing them and lightening the matter for them, as if he said: you undertook that evil and reprehensible act at a time when you did not know its sin and your understanding fell short of its consequence and what follows from it; or he meant that they were then in the time of youth and the age of childhood, as an excuse for them and a repelling of the shame and bewilderment that overtook them, while he and they knew that at that time they were grown men.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a statement without interrogation. The rest read it as a confirmatory interrogative, and this was from them in the manner of amazement and astonishment. It was said: the reason they recognised him merely by his words to them, ﴿what you did to Joseph and his brother﴾, is that when he said that to them they became alert and understood that none would address them with such a thing except him. It was said: when he said this to them he removed the crown from his head, and so they recognised him. It was said: he smiled, and they recognised his front teeth. ﴿He said: "I am Joseph, and this is my brother."﴾ He answered them by acknowledging what they had asked him about.

Ibn al-Anbari said: he stated the name, saying "I am Joseph", and did not say "I am he", to magnify what had befallen him from the injustice of his brothers, as if he said: "I am the one wronged, whose sanctity was violated, the one they intended to kill." He was content with stating the name instead of these meanings. He said "and this is my brother", although they knew him and did not deny it, because his purpose was: "and this is my brother, the wronged one, like my own wronging." ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾ by delivering us from what we were tried with. It was said: Allah has been gracious to us with every good in this world and the next. It was said: by bringing us together after separation. There is no barrier to intending all of that. ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ — the majority read "yattaqi" with a jussive, taking "man" as a conditional. Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' retained in "yattaqī", as in the words of the poet:

*Did it not reach you, while the news spreads, of what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?*

It was said that he made "man" a relative pronoun, not a conditional, but this is far-fetched. The meaning: whoever performs righteousness, or does what protects him from sins and is patient through calamities, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ in general terms, so that what the context indicates enters it first and foremost. He used the apparent noun where the place called for a pronoun, i.e. "their reward", to show that those described with piety are described with the quality of excellence.

﴿They said: "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, i.e. He has chosen and favoured you over us by what He has singled you out with of the attributes of perfection. This is an acknowledgment from them of his virtue and great station.

That does not necessarily mean they were not prophets, since the ranks of the prophets differ. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾, i.e. indeed the matter was so.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *khati'a* and *akhta'a* have one meaning. al-Azhari said: the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is one who intends what is right but arrives at something else; from it is their saying: "The mujtahid errs and is right." The sinner (*khati'*) is one who deliberately does what is not fitting.

They spoke this statement, which includes acknowledgment of error and sin, seeking to win his pardon and to draw out his forgiveness.

﴿He said: "No reproach upon you today"﴾. *Tathrib* means censure and rebuke, i.e. no censure, no rebuke, and no blame upon you.

al-Asmaʿi said: *tharrabtu ʿalayhi* — I made his deed ugly to him.

az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: no corruption of what is between me and you of sacred kinship and the right of brotherhood; and for you with me there is reconciliation and pardon. The original sense of *tathrib* is corruption, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: my reproach of you has ceased upon your acknowledgment of the sin.

Thaʿlab said: "Tharraba fulan ʿala fulan" means he enumerated his sins against him. The original sense of *tathrib* derives from *ath-thurb*, the fat that covers the paunch, and its meaning is removing the *tathrib*, just as *tajlid* and *taqri'* are removing the skin and the scraping. The accusative of "today" is governed by *tathrib*, i.e. "I do not reproach you," or it is governed by an implied verb in "upon you," which is stable or fixed or the like, i.e. "no reproach is stable or fixed upon you."

Al-Akhfash permitted pausing at "upon you," so that "today" is connected with the verb that follows it. Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned something like this.

Then he prayed for them with his words ﴿May Allah forgive you﴾, on the reading of pausing at "today", or he informed them that Allah had forgiven them that day, on the reading of pausing at "upon you". ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ — He shows mercy to His servants with a mercy by which they do not show mercy to one another, so He rewards their good-doers and forgives their wrong-doers.

His words, ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It was said this shirt is the one Allah clothed Abraham with when he was cast into the fire; Abraham clothed Isaac with it, and Isaac clothed Jacob with it.

Jacob had placed this shirt in a case and hung it on Joseph's neck, since he feared the evil eye for him. Gabriel informed Joseph to send it to Jacob so that his sight would return to him, for in it was the scent of Paradise, and the scent of Paradise does not fall upon a sick person without his being healed, nor upon one afflicted without his being relieved. ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, i.e. he will become seeing, on the reading that "ya'ti" is one of the sister verbs of "kāna". al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. as-Suddi said: he will return seeing. It was said: its meaning is: "he will come to me in Egypt, and he will be seeing, the blindness having gone from him," and this is supported by His words ﴿and bring me all your family together﴾, i.e. all who are included in the word "family", of women and descendants. It was said they were about seventy, and it was said ninety-three.

(p-713) ﴿When the caravan departed﴾, i.e. it set out, departing from Egypt towards Syria. One says *fasala fusulan*, and *fasaltuhu faslan*, intransitive and transitive; and one says *fasala min al-balad fusulan* when he has separated from it and passed its walls. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e. Jacob, to those with him among his family in the land of Canaan: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾. It was said: a wind arose and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob across the great distance, and so he informed them of what he found. Then he said ﴿"Unless you think me senile"﴾, i.e. unless you attribute me to *fand*, which is the loss of reason from old age; one says *afnada al-rajul* when he becomes senile and his mind changes.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lawla an tusaffihuni* — unless you call me foolish — so he made *fand* into *safah*. az-Zajjaj said: *lawla an tujahhiluni* — unless you call me ignorant — so he made *fand* into ignorance. What supports the view of those who said it means foolishness is the words of an-Nabigha:

*Except Solomon, when the Sovereign said to him: "Stand in the wilderness and restrain it from fand."*

That is, restrain it from foolishness.

Abu ʿUmar ash-Shaybani said: *at-tafnid* is disparagement, and from it is the poet's words:

*O my two companions, leave off reproach and disparagement; what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

It was said: it is lying, and from it is the poet's words:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the saying of the true-speaking one any falsehood?*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ﴿unless you think me senile﴾ — unless you weaken my opinion.

The like of this is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda.

al-Akhfash said: *at-tafnid* is blame and weakness of opinion.

All these meanings return to incapacitating and weakening opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, and *afnada* when he spoke with error, and *al-fanad* is error in speech. Among what indicates its use for blame is the poet's words:

*O my two blamers, leave off blaming and reproach; love has lasted long, and you two have prolonged the disparagement.*

Jacob informed them that the breeze had carried to him the scent of his beloved, and that were it not for what he feared of their disparagement, he would not have doubted it:

*For the breeze, when it breathes upon the soul of one grieving, its griefs are dispelled.*

*When I say this, as I try to forget, the breeze of the morning stirs me, from wherever the dawn rises.*

*And indeed the breeze blows to me from its land, so the touch of your breeze delights and sweetens.*

﴿They said: "By Allah, you are certainly in your old error"﴾, i.e. those present with him from his family said: "Indeed you, O Jacob, are in your going astray from the path of rectitude that you were upon of old, through excess of your love for Joseph, not forgetting him nor slackening from him." The tongue of Jacob's state says to them:

*None knows longing except one who suffers it, nor passion except one who endures it.*

*Do not blame the yearning one in his longings until your inner parts are in his inner parts.*

It was said: the meaning is: "you are in your ancient madness"; and it was said: "in your ancient love."

They said this to him because the arrival of the bearer of good news had not yet reached them. ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾. The commentators said: the bearer was Judah son of Jacob. He said to his brothers: "I brought him the shirt stained with blood; so give me your shirt today, that I may inform him you are alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." ﴿He threw it over his face﴾, i.e. the bearer threw Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, or Jacob threw it over his own face. ﴿He regained his sight﴾. *Irtidad* is the reverting of a thing to a condition it was previously in; the meaning: he returned and came back to his former state of sound sight. ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you?"﴾, i.e. Jacob said to those with him among his family, to whom he had said: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾: "Did I not tell you this statement, and you said what you said?" His words ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be a fresh independent statement not connected with the saying, or the clause ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be the content of the saying, and he intends by it to inform them of what he had said earlier: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ They asked him to seek forgiveness for them and acknowledged their sin. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the sense being: when they returned from Egypt and reached their father, they said this statement, and he promised them what they had asked of him.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. It was also said that he postponed it until he had obtained their pardon from Yusuf, and he did not know that Yusuf had already forgiven them. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ gives the reason for what came before it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His words ﴿no reproach﴾ that he said: "No reproach" means no rebuke.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he turned to the people and said, 'What do you say, and what do you think?' They said, 'A noble cousin.' So he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today; may Allah forgive you.﴾" Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Asking needs of the young is easier than asking them of the elders. Have you not seen the words of Yusuf, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾? And Ya'qub said, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾"

I say: In this statement there is room for examination. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

(p-712) The interrogative in His words, ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ (hal ʿalimtum), is for rebuke and reproach. They were certainly aware of it, but he intended what we have mentioned. It is also understood from it the magnification of the event, since it carries the force of: "How great is the matter you committed against Joseph and his brother, and how ugly is what you undertook!" It is like saying to a wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" As for what they did to Joseph, it is what preceded, which Allah, glorified is He, related to us in this surah. As for what they did to his brother, a group of exegetes said: it is what they inflicted upon him of grief at being separated from his brother Joseph, and the humiliation and abuse he suffered from them. He did not ask them about what they did to their father Jacob, although he had suffered from them what Allah related earlier of various kinds of harm.

al-Wahidi said: He did not mention his father Jacob, despite the great grief that befell him through separation from him, out of honour for him, elevating his rank, and knowledge that this was a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, to increase his degree with Him. ﴿while you were ignorant﴾ — he negated knowledge from them and affirmed the attribute of ignorance, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires. It was said: he attributed ignorance to them with the intent of excusing them and lightening the matter for them, as if he said: you undertook that evil and reprehensible act at a time when you did not know its sin and your understanding fell short of its consequence and what follows from it; or he meant that they were then in the time of youth and the age of childhood, as an excuse for them and a repelling of the shame and bewilderment that overtook them, while he and they knew that at that time they were grown men.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a statement without interrogation. The rest read it as a confirmatory interrogative, and this was from them in the manner of amazement and astonishment. It was said: the reason they recognised him merely by his words to them, ﴿what you did to Joseph and his brother﴾, is that when he said that to them they became alert and understood that none would address them with such a thing except him. It was said: when he said this to them he removed the crown from his head, and so they recognised him. It was said: he smiled, and they recognised his front teeth. ﴿He said: "I am Joseph, and this is my brother."﴾ He answered them by acknowledging what they had asked him about.

Ibn al-Anbari said: he stated the name, saying "I am Joseph", and did not say "I am he", to magnify what had befallen him from the injustice of his brothers, as if he said: "I am the one wronged, whose sanctity was violated, the one they intended to kill." He was content with stating the name instead of these meanings. He said "and this is my brother", although they knew him and did not deny it, because his purpose was: "and this is my brother, the wronged one, like my own wronging." ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾ by delivering us from what we were tried with. It was said: Allah has been gracious to us with every good in this world and the next. It was said: by bringing us together after separation. There is no barrier to intending all of that. ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ — the majority read "yattaqi" with a jussive, taking "man" as a conditional. Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' retained in "yattaqī", as in the words of the poet:

*Did it not reach you, while the news spreads, of what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?*

It was said that he made "man" a relative pronoun, not a conditional, but this is far-fetched. The meaning: whoever performs righteousness, or does what protects him from sins and is patient through calamities, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ in general terms, so that what the context indicates enters it first and foremost. He used the apparent noun where the place called for a pronoun, i.e. "their reward", to show that those described with piety are described with the quality of excellence.

﴿They said: "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, i.e. He has chosen and favoured you over us by what He has singled you out with of the attributes of perfection. This is an acknowledgment from them of his virtue and great station.

That does not necessarily mean they were not prophets, since the ranks of the prophets differ. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾, i.e. indeed the matter was so.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *khati'a* and *akhta'a* have one meaning. al-Azhari said: the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is one who intends what is right but arrives at something else; from it is their saying: "The mujtahid errs and is right." The sinner (*khati'*) is one who deliberately does what is not fitting.

They spoke this statement, which includes acknowledgment of error and sin, seeking to win his pardon and to draw out his forgiveness.

﴿He said: "No reproach upon you today"﴾. *Tathrib* means censure and rebuke, i.e. no censure, no rebuke, and no blame upon you.

al-Asmaʿi said: *tharrabtu ʿalayhi* — I made his deed ugly to him.

az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: no corruption of what is between me and you of sacred kinship and the right of brotherhood; and for you with me there is reconciliation and pardon. The original sense of *tathrib* is corruption, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: my reproach of you has ceased upon your acknowledgment of the sin.

Thaʿlab said: "Tharraba fulan ʿala fulan" means he enumerated his sins against him. The original sense of *tathrib* derives from *ath-thurb*, the fat that covers the paunch, and its meaning is removing the *tathrib*, just as *tajlid* and *taqri'* are removing the skin and the scraping. The accusative of "today" is governed by *tathrib*, i.e. "I do not reproach you," or it is governed by an implied verb in "upon you," which is stable or fixed or the like, i.e. "no reproach is stable or fixed upon you."

Al-Akhfash permitted pausing at "upon you," so that "today" is connected with the verb that follows it. Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned something like this.

Then he prayed for them with his words ﴿May Allah forgive you﴾, on the reading of pausing at "today", or he informed them that Allah had forgiven them that day, on the reading of pausing at "upon you". ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ — He shows mercy to His servants with a mercy by which they do not show mercy to one another, so He rewards their good-doers and forgives their wrong-doers.

His words, ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It was said this shirt is the one Allah clothed Abraham with when he was cast into the fire; Abraham clothed Isaac with it, and Isaac clothed Jacob with it.

Jacob had placed this shirt in a case and hung it on Joseph's neck, since he feared the evil eye for him. Gabriel informed Joseph to send it to Jacob so that his sight would return to him, for in it was the scent of Paradise, and the scent of Paradise does not fall upon a sick person without his being healed, nor upon one afflicted without his being relieved. ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, i.e. he will become seeing, on the reading that "ya'ti" is one of the sister verbs of "kāna". al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. as-Suddi said: he will return seeing. It was said: its meaning is: "he will come to me in Egypt, and he will be seeing, the blindness having gone from him," and this is supported by His words ﴿and bring me all your family together﴾, i.e. all who are included in the word "family", of women and descendants. It was said they were about seventy, and it was said ninety-three.

(p-713) ﴿When the caravan departed﴾, i.e. it set out, departing from Egypt towards Syria. One says *fasala fusulan*, and *fasaltuhu faslan*, intransitive and transitive; and one says *fasala min al-balad fusulan* when he has separated from it and passed its walls. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e. Jacob, to those with him among his family in the land of Canaan: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾. It was said: a wind arose and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob across the great distance, and so he informed them of what he found. Then he said ﴿"Unless you think me senile"﴾, i.e. unless you attribute me to *fand*, which is the loss of reason from old age; one says *afnada al-rajul* when he becomes senile and his mind changes.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lawla an tusaffihuni* — unless you call me foolish — so he made *fand* into *safah*. az-Zajjaj said: *lawla an tujahhiluni* — unless you call me ignorant — so he made *fand* into ignorance. What supports the view of those who said it means foolishness is the words of an-Nabigha:

*Except Solomon, when the Sovereign said to him: "Stand in the wilderness and restrain it from fand."*

That is, restrain it from foolishness.

Abu ʿUmar ash-Shaybani said: *at-tafnid* is disparagement, and from it is the poet's words:

*O my two companions, leave off reproach and disparagement; what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

It was said: it is lying, and from it is the poet's words:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the saying of the true-speaking one any falsehood?*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ﴿unless you think me senile﴾ — unless you weaken my opinion.

The like of this is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda.

al-Akhfash said: *at-tafnid* is blame and weakness of opinion.

All these meanings return to incapacitating and weakening opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, and *afnada* when he spoke with error, and *al-fanad* is error in speech. Among what indicates its use for blame is the poet's words:

*O my two blamers, leave off blaming and reproach; love has lasted long, and you two have prolonged the disparagement.*

Jacob informed them that the breeze had carried to him the scent of his beloved, and that were it not for what he feared of their disparagement, he would not have doubted it:

*For the breeze, when it breathes upon the soul of one grieving, its griefs are dispelled.*

*When I say this, as I try to forget, the breeze of the morning stirs me, from wherever the dawn rises.*

*And indeed the breeze blows to me from its land, so the touch of your breeze delights and sweetens.*

﴿They said: "By Allah, you are certainly in your old error"﴾, i.e. those present with him from his family said: "Indeed you, O Jacob, are in your going astray from the path of rectitude that you were upon of old, through excess of your love for Joseph, not forgetting him nor slackening from him." The tongue of Jacob's state says to them:

*None knows longing except one who suffers it, nor passion except one who endures it.*

*Do not blame the yearning one in his longings until your inner parts are in his inner parts.*

It was said: the meaning is: "you are in your ancient madness"; and it was said: "in your ancient love."

They said this to him because the arrival of the bearer of good news had not yet reached them. ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾. The commentators said: the bearer was Judah son of Jacob. He said to his brothers: "I brought him the shirt stained with blood; so give me your shirt today, that I may inform him you are alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." ﴿He threw it over his face﴾, i.e. the bearer threw Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, or Jacob threw it over his own face. ﴿He regained his sight﴾. *Irtidad* is the reverting of a thing to a condition it was previously in; the meaning: he returned and came back to his former state of sound sight. ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you?"﴾, i.e. Jacob said to those with him among his family, to whom he had said: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾: "Did I not tell you this statement, and you said what you said?" His words ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be a fresh independent statement not connected with the saying, or the clause ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be the content of the saying, and he intends by it to inform them of what he had said earlier: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ They asked him to seek forgiveness for them and acknowledged their sin. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the sense being: when they returned from Egypt and reached their father, they said this statement, and he promised them what they had asked of him.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. It was also said that he postponed it until he had obtained their pardon from Yusuf, and he did not know that Yusuf had already forgiven them. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ gives the reason for what came before it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His words ﴿no reproach﴾ that he said: "No reproach" means no rebuke.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he turned to the people and said, 'What do you say, and what do you think?' They said, 'A noble cousin.' So he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today; may Allah forgive you.﴾" Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Asking needs of the young is easier than asking them of the elders. Have you not seen the words of Yusuf, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾? And Ya'qub said, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾"

I say: In this statement there is room for examination. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

(p-712) The interrogative in His words, ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ (hal ʿalimtum), is for rebuke and reproach. They were certainly aware of it, but he intended what we have mentioned. It is also understood from it the magnification of the event, since it carries the force of: "How great is the matter you committed against Joseph and his brother, and how ugly is what you undertook!" It is like saying to a wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" As for what they did to Joseph, it is what preceded, which Allah, glorified is He, related to us in this surah. As for what they did to his brother, a group of exegetes said: it is what they inflicted upon him of grief at being separated from his brother Joseph, and the humiliation and abuse he suffered from them. He did not ask them about what they did to their father Jacob, although he had suffered from them what Allah related earlier of various kinds of harm.

al-Wahidi said: He did not mention his father Jacob, despite the great grief that befell him through separation from him, out of honour for him, elevating his rank, and knowledge that this was a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, to increase his degree with Him. ﴿while you were ignorant﴾ — he negated knowledge from them and affirmed the attribute of ignorance, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires. It was said: he attributed ignorance to them with the intent of excusing them and lightening the matter for them, as if he said: you undertook that evil and reprehensible act at a time when you did not know its sin and your understanding fell short of its consequence and what follows from it; or he meant that they were then in the time of youth and the age of childhood, as an excuse for them and a repelling of the shame and bewilderment that overtook them, while he and they knew that at that time they were grown men.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a statement without interrogation. The rest read it as a confirmatory interrogative, and this was from them in the manner of amazement and astonishment. It was said: the reason they recognised him merely by his words to them, ﴿what you did to Joseph and his brother﴾, is that when he said that to them they became alert and understood that none would address them with such a thing except him. al-Asmaʿi said: *tharrabtu ʿalayhi* — I made his deed ugly to him.
