That is, restrain it from foolishness.

Abu ʿUmar ash-Shaybani said: *at-tafnid* is disparagement, and from it is the poet's words:

*O my two companions, leave off reproach and disparagement; what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

It was said: it is lying, and from it is the poet's words:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the saying of the true-speaking one any falsehood?*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ﴿unless you think me senile﴾ — unless you weaken my opinion.

The like of this is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda.

al-Akhfash said: *at-tafnid* is blame and weakness of opinion.

All these meanings return to incapacitating and weakening opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, and *afnada* when he spoke with error, and *al-fanad* is error in speech. Among what indicates its use for blame is the poet's words:

*O my two blamers, leave off blaming and reproach; love has lasted long, and you two have prolonged the disparagement.*

Jacob informed them that the breeze had carried to him the scent of his beloved, and that were it not for what he feared of their disparagement, he would not have doubted it:

*For the breeze, when it breathes upon the soul of one grieving, its griefs are dispelled.*

*When I say this, as I try to forget, the breeze of the morning stirs me, from wherever the dawn rises.*

*And indeed the breeze blows to me from its land, so the touch of your breeze delights and sweetens.*

﴿They said: "By Allah, you are certainly in your old error"﴾, i.e. those present with him from his family said: "Indeed you, O Jacob, are in your going astray from the path of rectitude that you were upon of old, through excess of your love for Joseph, not forgetting him nor slackening from him." The tongue of Jacob's state says to them:

*None knows longing except one who suffers it, nor passion except one who endures it.*

*Do not blame the yearning one in his longings until your inner parts are in his inner parts.*

It was said: the meaning is: "you are in your ancient madness"; and it was said: "in your ancient love."

They said this to him because the arrival of the bearer of good news had not yet reached them. ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾. The commentators said: the bearer was Judah son of Jacob. He said to his brothers: "I brought him the shirt stained with blood; so give me your shirt today, that I may inform him you are alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." ﴿He threw it over his face﴾, i.e. the bearer threw Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, or Jacob threw it over his own face. ﴿He regained his sight﴾. *Irtidad* is the reverting of a thing to a condition it was previously in; the meaning: he returned and came back to his former state of sound sight. ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you?"﴾, i.e. Jacob said to those with him among his family, to whom he had said: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾: "Did I not tell you this statement, and you said what you said?" His words ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be a fresh independent statement not connected with the saying, or the clause ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be the content of the saying, and he intends by it to inform them of what he had said earlier: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ They asked him to seek forgiveness for them and acknowledged their sin. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the sense being: when they returned from Egypt and reached their father, they said this statement, and he promised them what they had asked of him.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. It was also said that he postponed it until he had obtained their pardon from Yusuf, and he did not know that Yusuf had already forgiven them. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ gives the reason for what came before it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His words ﴿no reproach﴾ that he said: "No reproach" means no rebuke.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he turned to the people and said, 'What do you say, and what do you think?' They said, 'A noble cousin.' So he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today; may Allah forgive you.﴾" Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Asking needs of the young is easier than asking them of the elders. Have you not seen the words of Yusuf, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾? And Ya'qub said, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾"

I say: In this statement there is room for examination. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

(p-712) The interrogative in His words, ﴿Do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother?﴾ (hal ʿalimtum), is for rebuke and reproach. They were certainly aware of it, but he intended what we have mentioned. It is also understood from it the magnification of the event, since it carries the force of: "How great is the matter you committed against Joseph and his brother, and how ugly is what you undertook!" It is like saying to a wrongdoer: "Do you know whom you disobeyed?" As for what they did to Joseph, it is what preceded, which Allah, glorified is He, related to us in this surah. As for what they did to his brother, a group of exegetes said: it is what they inflicted upon him of grief at being separated from his brother Joseph, and the humiliation and abuse he suffered from them. He did not ask them about what they did to their father Jacob, although he had suffered from them what Allah related earlier of various kinds of harm.

al-Wahidi said: He did not mention his father Jacob, despite the great grief that befell him through separation from him, out of honour for him, elevating his rank, and knowledge that this was a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, to increase his degree with Him. ﴿while you were ignorant﴾ — he negated knowledge from them and affirmed the attribute of ignorance, because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires. It was said: he attributed ignorance to them with the intent of excusing them and lightening the matter for them, as if he said: you undertook that evil and reprehensible act at a time when you did not know its sin and your understanding fell short of its consequence and what follows from it; or he meant that they were then in the time of youth and the age of childhood, as an excuse for them and a repelling of the shame and bewilderment that overtook them, while he and they knew that at that time they were grown men.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Joseph?"﴾ Ibn Kathir read "innaka" as a statement without interrogation. The rest read it as a confirmatory interrogative, and this was from them in the manner of amazement and astonishment. It was said: the reason they recognised him merely by his words to them, ﴿what you did to Joseph and his brother﴾, is that when he said that to them they became alert and understood that none would address them with such a thing except him. It was said: when he said this to them he removed the crown from his head, and so they recognised him. It was said: he smiled, and they recognised his front teeth. ﴿He said: "I am Joseph, and this is my brother."﴾ He answered them by acknowledging what they had asked him about.

Ibn al-Anbari said: he stated the name, saying "I am Joseph", and did not say "I am he", to magnify what had befallen him from the injustice of his brothers, as if he said: "I am the one wronged, whose sanctity was violated, the one they intended to kill." He was content with stating the name instead of these meanings. He said "and this is my brother", although they knew him and did not deny it, because his purpose was: "and this is my brother, the wronged one, like my own wronging." ﴿Allah has been gracious to us﴾ by delivering us from what we were tried with. It was said: Allah has been gracious to us with every good in this world and the next. It was said: by bringing us together after separation. There is no barrier to intending all of that. ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient﴾ — the majority read "yattaqi" with a jussive, taking "man" as a conditional. Ibn Kathir read it with the yā' retained in "yattaqī", as in the words of the poet:

*Did it not reach you, while the news spreads, of what the she-camel of the sons of Ziyad suffered?*

It was said that he made "man" a relative pronoun, not a conditional, but this is far-fetched. The meaning: whoever performs righteousness, or does what protects him from sins and is patient through calamities, ﴿then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ in general terms, so that what the context indicates enters it first and foremost. He used the apparent noun where the place called for a pronoun, i.e. "their reward", to show that those described with piety are described with the quality of excellence.

﴿They said: "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us"﴾, i.e. He has chosen and favoured you over us by what He has singled you out with of the attributes of perfection. This is an acknowledgment from them of his virtue and great station.

That does not necessarily mean they were not prophets, since the ranks of the prophets differ. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. ﴿And indeed we were sinners﴾, i.e. indeed the matter was so.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *khati'a* and *akhta'a* have one meaning. al-Azhari said: the one who errs (*mukhti'*) is one who intends what is right but arrives at something else; from it is their saying: "The mujtahid errs and is right." The sinner (*khati'*) is one who deliberately does what is not fitting.

They spoke this statement, which includes acknowledgment of error and sin, seeking to win his pardon and to draw out his forgiveness.

﴿He said: "No reproach upon you today"﴾. *Tathrib* means censure and rebuke, i.e. no censure, no rebuke, and no blame upon you.

al-Asmaʿi said: *tharrabtu ʿalayhi* — I made his deed ugly to him.

az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: no corruption of what is between me and you of sacred kinship and the right of brotherhood; and for you with me there is reconciliation and pardon. The original sense of *tathrib* is corruption, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: my reproach of you has ceased upon your acknowledgment of the sin.

Thaʿlab said: "Tharraba fulan ʿala fulan" means he enumerated his sins against him. The original sense of *tathrib* derives from *ath-thurb*, the fat that covers the paunch, and its meaning is removing the *tathrib*, just as *tajlid* and *taqri'* are removing the skin and the scraping. The accusative of "today" is governed by *tathrib*, i.e. "I do not reproach you," or it is governed by an implied verb in "upon you," which is stable or fixed or the like, i.e. "no reproach is stable or fixed upon you."

Al-Akhfash permitted pausing at "upon you," so that "today" is connected with the verb that follows it. Ibn al-Anbari also mentioned something like this.

Then he prayed for them with his words ﴿May Allah forgive you﴾, on the reading of pausing at "today", or he informed them that Allah had forgiven them that day, on the reading of pausing at "upon you". ﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ — He shows mercy to His servants with a mercy by which they do not show mercy to one another, so He rewards their good-doers and forgives their wrong-doers.

His words, ﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾. It was said this shirt is the one Allah clothed Abraham with when he was cast into the fire; Abraham clothed Isaac with it, and Isaac clothed Jacob with it.

Jacob had placed this shirt in a case and hung it on Joseph's neck, since he feared the evil eye for him. Gabriel informed Joseph to send it to Jacob so that his sight would return to him, for in it was the scent of Paradise, and the scent of Paradise does not fall upon a sick person without his being healed, nor upon one afflicted without his being relieved. ﴿Throw it over my father's face; he will regain his sight﴾, i.e. he will become seeing, on the reading that "ya'ti" is one of the sister verbs of "kāna". al-Farra' said: he will return seeing. as-Suddi said: he will return seeing. It was said: its meaning is: "he will come to me in Egypt, and he will be seeing, the blindness having gone from him," and this is supported by His words ﴿and bring me all your family together﴾, i.e. all who are included in the word "family", of women and descendants. It was said they were about seventy, and it was said ninety-three.

(p-713) ﴿When the caravan departed﴾, i.e. it set out, departing from Egypt towards Syria. One says *fasala fusulan*, and *fasaltuhu faslan*, intransitive and transitive; and one says *fasala min al-balad fusulan* when he has separated from it and passed its walls. ﴿Their father said﴾, i.e. Jacob, to those with him among his family in the land of Canaan: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾. It was said: a wind arose and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob across the great distance, and so he informed them of what he found. Then he said ﴿"Unless you think me senile"﴾, i.e. unless you attribute me to *fand*, which is the loss of reason from old age; one says *afnada al-rajul* when he becomes senile and his mind changes.

Abu ʿUbayda said: *lawla an tusaffihuni* — unless you call me foolish — so he made *fand* into *safah*. az-Zajjaj said: *lawla an tujahhiluni* — unless you call me ignorant — so he made *fand* into ignorance. What supports the view of those who said it means foolishness is the words of an-Nabigha:

*Except Solomon, when the Sovereign said to him: "Stand in the wilderness and restrain it from fand."*

That is, restrain it from foolishness.

Abu ʿUmar ash-Shaybani said: *at-tafnid* is disparagement, and from it is the poet's words:

*O my two companions, leave off reproach and disparagement; what has passed of my affair cannot be returned.*

It was said: it is lying, and from it is the poet's words:

*Is there in the boasting of the noble any crookedness, or in the saying of the true-speaking one any falsehood?*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ﴿unless you think me senile﴾ — unless you weaken my opinion.

The like of this is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda.

al-Akhfash said: *at-tafnid* is blame and weakness of opinion.

All these meanings return to incapacitating and weakening opinion. One says *fannadahu tafnidan* when he made him incapable, and *afnada* when he spoke with error, and *al-fanad* is error in speech. Among what indicates its use for blame is the poet's words:

*O my two blamers, leave off blaming and reproach; love has lasted long, and you two have prolonged the disparagement.*

Jacob informed them that the breeze had carried to him the scent of his beloved, and that were it not for what he feared of their disparagement, he would not have doubted it:

*For the breeze, when it breathes upon the soul of one grieving, its griefs are dispelled.*

*When I say this, as I try to forget, the breeze of the morning stirs me, from wherever the dawn rises.*

*And indeed the breeze blows to me from its land, so the touch of your breeze delights and sweetens.*

﴿They said: "By Allah, you are certainly in your old error"﴾, i.e. those present with him from his family said: "Indeed you, O Jacob, are in your going astray from the path of rectitude that you were upon of old, through excess of your love for Joseph, not forgetting him nor slackening from him." The tongue of Jacob's state says to them:

*None knows longing except one who suffers it, nor passion except one who endures it.*

*Do not blame the yearning one in his longings until your inner parts are in his inner parts.*

It was said: the meaning is: "you are in your ancient madness"; and it was said: "in your ancient love."

They said this to him because the arrival of the bearer of good news had not yet reached them. ﴿When the bearer of good news came﴾. The commentators said: the bearer was Judah son of Jacob. He said to his brothers: "I brought him the shirt stained with blood; so give me your shirt today, that I may inform him you are alive, and gladden him as I grieved him." ﴿He threw it over his face﴾, i.e. the bearer threw Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, or Jacob threw it over his own face. ﴿He regained his sight﴾. *Irtidad* is the reverting of a thing to a condition it was previously in; the meaning: he returned and came back to his former state of sound sight. ﴿He said: "Did I not tell you?"﴾, i.e. Jacob said to those with him among his family, to whom he had said: ﴿"Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph"﴾: "Did I not tell you this statement, and you said what you said?" His words ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be a fresh independent statement not connected with the saying, or the clause ﴿"I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ may be the content of the saying, and he intends by it to inform them of what he had said earlier: ﴿"I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾ [Yusuf: 86].

﴿They said: "O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners."﴾ They asked him to seek forgiveness for them and acknowledged their sin. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the sense being: when they returned from Egypt and reached their father, they said this statement, and he promised them what they had asked of him.

﴿He said: "I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾

﴿He said, "I will ask my Lord to forgive you."﴾ Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: Ya'qub intended to ask forgiveness for them at the time of *al-sahar* (the last part of the night), because that is more fitting for the answering of supplication, and not because he withheld forgiveness from them. It was also said that he postponed it until Friday night. It was also said that he postponed it until he had obtained their pardon from Yusuf, and he did not know that Yusuf had already forgiven them. The clause ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ gives the reason for what came before it.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah concerning His words ﴿no reproach﴾ that he said: "No reproach" means no rebuke.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he turned to the people and said, 'What do you say, and what do you think?' They said, 'A noble cousin.' So he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today; may Allah forgive you.﴾" Ibn Mardawayh reported a similar hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* reported a similar hadith from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Asking needs of the young is easier than asking them of the elders. Have you not seen the words of Yusuf, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾? And Ya'qub said, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you.﴾"

I say: In this statement there is room for examination. They asked Yusuf to pardon them when they said, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, and he said, ﴿No reproach be upon you today﴾, because what they intended was that he would issue a pardon for them. They asked their father Ya'qub to ask Allah to forgive them, and that can only happen by his asking Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for it. There is a difference between the two situations. Therefore Ya'qub's promise to them was not a withholding of his asking Allah on their behalf, especially if what was mentioned earlier is correct, that he delayed it until the time of answering, for if he had asked for it for them immediately, he would not have gained knowledge of its acceptance.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: "When the matter of Yusuf's brothers happened as it did, Ya'qub wrote to Yusuf, while he did not know that he was Yusuf: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim to the Chief of the family of Pharaoh. Peace be upon you. I praise Allah to you, there is no god but Him. To proceed: we are a household upon whom the causes of trials are constant. My grandfather Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was thrown into the fire in obedience to his Lord, so Allah made it cool and safe for him. Allah commanded my grandfather to sacrifice my father, and Allah ransomed him with what He ransomed him with. I had a son, who was among the dearest of people to me, and I lost him, and his loss took away the light of my sight. He had a full brother whom, when I remembered him, I would embrace to my chest, and he would take away some of my grief. He is the one detained with you on (p-714) accusation of theft. I inform you that I did not steal, and I did not bear a thief.'" When Yusuf read the letter he wept and cried out, and said, ﴿Take this shirt of mine and cast it over the face of my father; he will regain his sight.﴾

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Take this shirt of mine﴾: that when Nimrod threw Ibrahim into the fire, Jibril descended to him with a shirt from Paradise and a rug from Paradise. He dressed him in the shirt and seated him on the rug, and sat with him conversing. Then Allah revealed to the fire, ﴿O fire, be cool and safe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69]. And had He not said "and safe," the cold would have harmed him.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that "Allah clothed Ibrahim in a garment from Paradise, and Ibrahim clothed Ishaq with it, and Ishaq clothed Ya'qub with it. Ya'qub then took it and placed it in a tube of iron and hung it on the neck of Yusuf. Had his brothers known it when they threw him into the well, they would have taken it. When Allah willed to return Yusuf to Ya'qub, there were forty years between his dream and its interpretation. He commanded the bearer of good news to give him the glad tidings from eight stages away. Ya'qub then smelled his scent and said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾. When he cast it over his face, he returned seeing. Nothing from Paradise falls upon an affliction of the afflictions of this world without curing it, by the permission of Allah."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿When the caravan departed﴾ that he said: "When the caravan set out, the wind blew and brought Ya'qub the scent of Yusuf's shirt, and he said, ﴿Indeed, I detect the smell of Yusuf, were it not that you think me senile﴾," meaning, "you think me foolish."

He smelled his scent from a distance of eight days.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of ten days.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from another route from him that he said: He smelled it from a distance of eighty farsakhs.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also, concerning ﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾, that he said: "You think me ignorant."

Ibn Jarir reported from him also that he said: "You think me a liar."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid that he said: "You think me senile"; they say, "your mind has gone."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Rabi' that he said: "Were it not that you think me foolish."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Indeed, you are in your old error﴾ that he said: "Your old mistake."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "Your old madness."

Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid that he said: "Your old love."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The bearer of good news is the messenger (al-bareed)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from al-Dahhak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan that he said: "The bearer of good news is Yahudha ibn Ya'qub."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan that he said: "When the bearer of good news came to Ya'qub and cast the shirt upon him, he said, 'On what religion did you leave Yusuf?' He said, 'On Islam.' He said, 'Now the blessing is complete.'"

Abu 'Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ that he said: "Ya'qub postponed it for his sons until al-sahar." Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, and he used to pray at al-sahar."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "He postponed it for them until al-sahar, because the supplication at al-sahar is answered."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him also that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ), in his narration, said, 'It is the saying of my brother Ya'qub to his sons, ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, meaning, until the night of Friday comes.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 99–101:

His saying: ﴿When they entered upon Yusuf﴾. There is probably an omitted, implied element in the speech, which is: Ya'qub, his sons and his household set out for Egypt. So when they entered upon Yusuf, he took his two parents to himself, that is, he embraced them and lodged them with him.

The exegetes said: What is meant by "the two parents" here is Ya'qub and his wife, Yusuf's maternal aunt, because his mother had died in giving birth to his brother Binyamin, as has been mentioned earlier. It was also said: Allah restored his mother to life, in fulfilment of the dream, so that she prostrated to him. ﴿And he said: Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security﴾ from what you dislike, for in the past they had feared the kings of Egypt, and would not enter it except with a pass from them.

It was said: the restriction by the will (of Allah) refers to the security, and there is no obstacle to its referring to everything, because their entry does not happen except by the will of Allah the Glorified, just as they will not be secure except by His will. It was also said: the restriction by the will refers to his saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ [Yusuf: 98], and this is far-fetched.

The apparent sense of the Qur'anic wording is that Yusuf said this to them, namely: "Enter Egypt" before their entering. It has been said in explanation of this that he met them outside Egypt, and stood waiting for them in a place or a tent; they entered upon him, so ﴿he took his two parents to himself and said: Enter Egypt﴾, and when they entered Egypt and entered upon him a second time in his place in Egypt.

﴿And he raised his two parents upon the throne﴾, that is, he seated them with him on the couch on which he sat, as is the custom of kings. ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, that is, the two parents and the brothers; the meaning is that they fell down before Yusuf in prostration. That was permissible in their law, being treated as a greeting. It was also said: it was not a prostration, but merely a bowing, and that was their greeting. This contradicts the meaning of ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾, for falling down (khurur) in the language, when qualified by prostration, cannot occur except by placing the face on the ground. It was also said: the pronoun in His saying "before him" refers to Allah the Glorified, that is, they fell down in prostration to Allah, and this is very far-fetched. It was also said: the pronoun refers to Yusuf, and the lam is for causation, that is, they fell down on his account; this too is far-fetched.

And Yusuf said: ﴿O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream﴾, meaning the one mentioned earlier, that is, from before this time. ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾ by the fulfilment of its interpretation in the way it indicated. (p-715) ﴿And He was good to me when He took me out of the prison﴾. The original usage is that the verb of goodness (ahsana) takes "ila" (to), and it may take "bi" (with), as in His saying: ﴿and to parents, goodness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83] [al-Isra': 23]. It was said: he included in "ahsana" the meaning of "lataf" (to be gentle), that is, He was gentle to me while being good. He did not mention bringing him out of the well, because mentioning it contains some reproach to the brothers, and he had said: ﴿No reproach upon you﴾. The cause of his imprisonment and the length of his stay in it have already been mentioned. It was also said: the reason for not mentioning his removal from the well is that the favour in bringing him out of prison was greater than the favour in bringing him out of the well; but this is open to question. ﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾, that is, the badiyah (desert), and it is the land of Canaan in Syria, and they were people of livestock and the open country. It was said: Allah did not send a prophet from the desert, and that the place in which Ya'qub lived is called Bada, and Jamil meant it when he said:

"You are the one who made the people of Bada beloved to me, while my homelands are other lands than those two."

And this is open to question. ﴿After Satan had incited discord between me and my brothers﴾, that is, he spoiled matters between us and set some of us against others. It is said "nazaghahu" when one pricks him, so its origin is from pricking a beast to make it walk faster. Yusuf attributed his brothers' wrongdoing to Satan, out of nobility and courtesy. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾. Al-Latif is the gentle, the kind. Al-Azhari said: al-Latif is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, its meaning being the gentle toward His servants; it is said: "latufa fulan bi-fulan, yalutfu" when he was gentle with him. 'Amr ibn Abi 'Amr said: al-Latif is the One who brings your desire to you gently.

Al-Khattabi said: al-Latif is the Benevolent toward His servants, who is gentle with them from where they do not know, and brings about their interests from where they do not expect. It was also said: al-Latif is the One who knows the subtleties of affairs. The meaning of ﴿in what He wills﴾ is: for the sake of what He wills, until it comes in the right way. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾, that is, the Knower of affairs, the Wise in His acts.

When Allah had completed His blessing upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, by delivering him from great trials and by granting him kingship and teaching him knowledge, his soul yearned for the lasting otherworldly good that does not end.

So he said: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom﴾. The "min" is partitive, that is, some of the kingdom, for he was not given the whole kingdom; he was given a particular kingdom, namely the rule of Egypt in a particular time. ﴿And taught me of the interpretation of narrations﴾, that is, some of it, for he was not given all the knowledge of interpretation, whether it is meant as general knowledge and understanding, or merely the interpretation of dreams. It was said: the "min" is for kind, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. It was also said: it is superfluous, that is: You gave me the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of narrations. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in the accusative as an attribute of "Lord", since it is an addressed noun with a suffix; it may also be in the accusative as a vocative with an implied particle, that is: O Originator. The fatir is the Creator, the Producer, the Inventor, the Originator. ﴿You are my Guardian﴾, that is, my Helper and the one who manages my affairs ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾; You are my guardian in both. ﴿Cause me to die in submission and join me with the righteous﴾, that is, cause me to die upon Islam, not leaving me until I die, and join me with the righteous among the prophets, from my forefathers and others, so that I may attain their reward from You and their ranks with You.

It was said: when he made this supplication, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, caused him to die. It was said: his age when he was thrown into the well was seventeen years, and during slavery, imprisonment and kingship, he spent eighty years until his father Ya'qub came, upon him be peace. Then he lived after their reunion until his life was completed to the measure that will be mentioned later, and Allah caused him to die.

It was said: no one wished for death except Yusuf, neither a prophet nor anyone else.

The majority held that he did not wish for death by this supplication, but rather he asked his Lord to cause him to die upon Islam and join him with the righteous among His servants when his appointed time arrived.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Ya'qub entered Egypt in the reign of Yusuf when he was one hundred and thirty years old, and he lived in his reign thirty years, and Yusuf died when he was one hundred and twenty.

Abu Hurayrah said: And it has reached me that the age of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was one hundred and ninety-five years.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿He took his two parents to himself﴾, he said: his father and his mother; he embraced them.

They both narrated from Wahb, who said: and his maternal aunt, for Yusuf's mother had died in the childbirth of his brother Binyamin. Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And He raised his two parents upon the throne﴾, he said: the couch. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Adi ibn Hatim concerning His saying: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, he said: it was the greeting of those before you, and Allah gave you the salam in its place.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd who said: That was a prostration of honour, just as the angels prostrated in honour to Adam, and it was not a prostration of worship.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, he said: He was gentle to Yusuf, and arranged for him when He brought him out of the prison, and brought his family from the desert, and removed from his heart the prick of Satan and his incitement against his brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: No prophet asked for death except Yusuf.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, who said: He longed to meet Allah and loved to join Him and his forefathers.

So he asked Allah to cause him to die and to join him with them. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾, he said: meaning Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah who said: meaning the people of Paradise.

Al-Khattabi said: al-Latif is the Benevolent toward His servants, who is gentle with them from where they do not know, and brings about their interests from where they do not expect. It was also said: al-Latif is the One who knows the subtleties of affairs. The meaning of ﴿in what He wills﴾ is: for the sake of what He wills, until it comes in the right way. ﴿Indeed He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾, that is, the Knower of affairs, the Wise in His acts.

When Allah had completed His blessing upon Yusuf, peace be upon him, by delivering him from great trials and by granting him kingship and teaching him knowledge, his soul yearned for the lasting otherworldly good that does not end.

So he said: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom﴾. The "min" is partitive, that is, some of the kingdom, for he was not given the whole kingdom; he was given a particular kingdom, namely the rule of Egypt in a particular time. ﴿And taught me of the interpretation of narrations﴾, that is, some of it, for he was not given all the knowledge of interpretation, whether it is meant as general knowledge and understanding, or merely the interpretation of dreams. It was said: the "min" is for kind, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. It was also said: it is superfluous, that is: You gave me the kingdom and taught me the interpretation of narrations. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ is in the accusative as an attribute of "Lord", since it is an addressed noun with a suffix; it may also be in the accusative as a vocative with an implied particle, that is: O Originator. The fatir is the Creator, the Producer, the Inventor, the Originator. ﴿You are my Guardian﴾, that is, my Helper and the one who manages my affairs ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾; You are my guardian in both. ﴿Cause me to die in submission and join me with the righteous﴾, that is, cause me to die upon Islam, not leaving me until I die, and join me with the righteous among the prophets, from my forefathers and others, so that I may attain their reward from You and their ranks with You.

It was said: when he made this supplication, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, caused him to die. It was said: his age when he was thrown into the well was seventeen years, and during slavery, imprisonment and kingship, he spent eighty years until his father Ya'qub came, upon him be peace. Then he lived after their reunion until his life was completed to the measure that will be mentioned later, and Allah caused him to die.

It was said: no one wished for death except Yusuf, neither a prophet nor anyone else.

The majority held that he did not wish for death by this supplication, but rather he asked his Lord to cause him to die upon Islam and join him with the righteous among His servants when his appointed time arrived.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Ya'qub entered Egypt in the reign of Yusuf when he was one hundred and thirty years old, and he lived in his reign thirty years, and Yusuf died when he was one hundred and twenty.

Abu Hurayrah said: And it has reached me that the age of Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah, was one hundred and ninety-five years.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿He took his two parents to himself﴾, he said: his father and his mother; he embraced them.

They both narrated from Wahb, who said: and his maternal aunt, for Yusuf's mother had died in the childbirth of his brother Binyamin. Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And He raised his two parents upon the throne﴾, he said: the couch. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Adi ibn Hatim concerning His saying: ﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾, he said: it was the greeting of those before you, and Allah gave you the salam in its place.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Zayd who said: That was a prostration of honour, just as the angels prostrated in honour to Adam, and it was not a prostration of worship.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾, he said: He was gentle to Yusuf, and arranged for him when He brought him out of the prison, and brought his family from the desert, and removed from his heart the prick of Satan and his incitement against his brothers.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: No prophet asked for death except Yusuf.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, who said: He longed to meet Allah and loved to join Him and his forefathers.

So he asked Allah to cause him to die and to join him with them. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾, he said: meaning Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah who said: meaning the people of Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 12, verses 102–108:**

.

The address in His words ﴿That﴾ is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). *Dhalika* ("that") is the subject (*mubtada'*, grammatical subject), and its predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿of the news of the unseen﴾. ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ is a second predicate.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is also possible that *dhalika* means *alladhi* ("which"), and ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ is its predicate, meaning: "That which is of the news of the unseen, We reveal it to you."

The meaning is: God informs His Messenger (ﷺ) that this account He has related to him about the affair of Joseph and his brothers is among the reports that were hidden from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So God revealed it to him and informed him of it, and he had nothing of that knowledge before the revelation. This also contains an allusion to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they were denying what he (ﷺ) brought, out of obstinacy, envy and hostility, even though they knew the reality of the matter. ﴿And you were not with them﴾, that is, with the brothers of Joseph, ﴿when they resolved on their plan﴾. *Ijma' al-amr* means determining upon it, that is: you were not with the brothers of Joseph when they all resolved to throw him into the well, while they were scheming against him, that is, against Joseph, in this act that they did to him, and plotting harm against him. It was also said that the pronoun refers to Jacob, meaning: they were scheming against Jacob when they came with Joseph's shirt smeared with blood and said, "A wolf has eaten him."

If the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not present with them when they did that, then his knowledge of it through direct witnessing is negated. Nor was he among a people who had knowledge of the circumstances of past nations, nor did he mix with them or they with him. Thus his knowledge of it through transmission from others is also negated. Therefore, there remained for his knowledge of it no way except the bare revelation from God, glorified is He. This necessitates belief in what he brought. However, those disbelievers who were contemporaries of his did not believe in it.

God, glorified is He, said, mentioning this: ﴿And most people, however eager you are, will not be believers﴾. That is: most of the people contemporary with you, O Muhammad, or most people in general, will not be believers in God, even if you were eager for their guidance and exerted yourself in that, because of their insistence on disbelief, which is the religion of their fathers. One says *haraşa yahrişu*, like *daraba yadribu*. In a weak dialect one says *hariša yahraşu*, like *hamida yahmadu*. *Al-hirş* is seeking a thing with striving.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: most people will not be believers, even if you were eager to guide them, because you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Quraysh and the Jews asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the story of Joseph and his brothers, and he explained the two of them with a thorough explanation, hoping that this would be a cause of their Islam. But they contradicted his expectation, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) grieved over that, so God consoled him with His words: ﴿And most people...﴾, the verse.

﴿And you ask them no wage for it﴾, that is, for the Qur'an and what you recite to them of it, or for faith and your eagerness for its occurrence among them, or for what you tell them of this account, as a wage of wealth that they give you and set aside for you, as their rabbis do. ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for all the worlds﴾, that is: it is nothing but a reminder for all the worlds entirely, not restricted to them alone.

﴿And how many a sign there is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said, and most of them hold, that *ka'ayyin* originally was *ay* (*ayyun*), to which the particle of comparison *ka* was added. But the individual meaning of the two particles disappeared, and the combination became like a single noun with the meaning of the interrogative-informative *kam* ("how many"). The more common usage is to put *min* before its specifier (*tamyiz*, specification), and this specification is of the *ka* and not of *ayyun*, as in: *mithluka rajulan* ("someone like you, a man").

This matter has already been discussed fully in Al 'Imran.

The meaning is: how many a sign there is that points them to the oneness of God, existing in the heavens, in that they are raised without pillars, adorned with shining, moving stars and fixed ones; and on the earth, in its mountains, deserts, seas, plants and animals, which point them to the oneness of God, glorified is He, and that He is the Creator of all that, the Provider of it, the Giver of life and Causer of death. But most people pass by these signs without reflecting upon them, without thinking about them, and without attending to what they indicate of the existence of their Creator, and that He alone deserves divinity, even though they are witnessing them. ﴿They pass by them while turning away from them﴾. Even if they look at them with their eyes, they have turned away from what is the fruit of looking with the eye, which is reflection, consideration and inference.

Ikrima and Amr ibn Fa'id read *al-ard* in the nominative, as the subject, with its predicate being ﴿they pass by them﴾. Al-Suddi read it in the accusative, by supposing a verb.

Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿they walk upon them﴾ (*yamshuna 'alayha*).

﴿And most of them do not believe in God﴾, that is: most people do not affirm and acknowledge God as the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and Causer of death, ﴿without associating others with Him﴾, that is, with God, worshipping others along with Him, as the Jahiliyyah used to do. They acknowledge God, glorified is He, and that He is their Creator: ﴿If you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]; ﴿If you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. But they used to attribute partners to Him and worship them so that they would bring them closer to God: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to God﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. Similar to these are those who took their rabbis and monks as lords besides God, and those who believe that the dead can do what only God, glorified is He, can do, as many worshippers of graves do. This is not contradicted by what has been said, that the verse was revealed about specific people, because the consideration is with what the wording indicates, not with what the cause of revelation restricts it to, regarding the ruling's applicability to whoever is the cause of its revelation.

﴿Are they then secure from an overwhelming punishment from God coming upon them﴾. The interrogative is for denunciation. *Al-ghashiyah* is what covers and overwhelms them of punishment, like His saying: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. It was also said: it is the Hour; it was also said: the thunderbolts and calamities. There is no barrier to taking it in general. ﴿Or the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly. *Baghtatan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*, state) element.

Al-Mubarrad said: From the Arabs there came a circumstantial element after an indefinite noun, which is their saying: *waqa'a amrun baghtatan* ("a matter occurred suddenly"). One says *baghatahumu al-amru baghtan wa baghtatan* when it came upon them unexpectedly. ﴿while they are unaware﴾ of its coming. It is also permissible for *baghtatan* to be in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun.

﴿Say: This is my way﴾, that is: say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists: this call to which I call, and the path upon which I am, is my way, that is, my method and my sunnah. So the demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is *sabili* ("my way"). This is explained by His saying: ﴿I call to God with insight﴾, that is, with clear proof. *Al-basirah* is the knowledge by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. The clause is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial element. ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾, that is, and whoever follows me and is guided by my guidance also calls to it.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: whoever follows me calls to God just as I call.

In this is evidence that every follower of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has the duty to take him as a model in calling to God, that is, to faith in Him, His oneness, and acting upon what He legislated for His servants. (p-717) ﴿Glory be to God; I am not of those who associate others with Him﴾, that is: and say, O Muhammad, to them: Glory be to God, and I am not of those who associate others with God, who take rivals besides Him.

Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also permissible that the speech be complete at His saying: ﴿I call to God﴾, then one begins: ﴿with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And you were not with them when they resolved on their plan while they were scheming﴾ that he said: they are the sons of Jacob, when they schemed against Joseph.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada regarding the verse that he said: ﴿And you were not with them﴾ while they were throwing him ﴿into the depths of the well﴾, while they were scheming against Joseph.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿And how many a sign﴾ that he said: how many a sign there is in the sky, meaning its sun, its moon, its stars and its clouds; and on the earth, what is in it of creatures, rivers, mountains, cities and palaces.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him﴾ that he said: Ask them who created them, and who created the heavens and the earth, and they will say, "God." That is their faith, while they worship other than Him.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from 'Ata' regarding His saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him﴾ that he said: They used to know that God is their Lord, that He is their Creator, and that He is their Provider, and yet with that they used to associate others with Him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak regarding the verse that he said: They used to associate others with Him in their talbiyah (invocation during pilgrimage). They would say: "Here I am, O God, here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You; You own him and what he owns."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan regarding the verse that he said: That is the hypocrite who acts for show, and he is a polytheist by his deed.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿an overwhelming punishment from God﴾ that he said: A calamity that covers them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿This is my way﴾ that he said: Say, "This is my call."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ that he said: My prayer.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding the verse that he said: My command, my will and my path. And both narrated from Qatada regarding His saying: ﴿with insight﴾, that is, upon guidance, ﴿I and whoever follows me﴾.

Nor was he among a people who had knowledge of the circumstances of past nations, nor did he mix with them or they with him. Thus his knowledge of it through transmission from others is also negated. This refutes those who claim that there were four prophetesses among women: Hawwa' (Eve), Asiya, the mother of Musa (Moses), and Maryam (Mary). The sending of prophets from among men and not women was a well-known matter among the Arabs, to the point that Qays ibn Asim said about Sajah, the false prophetess:

"Our prophet has become a female, around whom we circle,
and the prophets of Allah have become males."

"So the curse of Allah and of all the people
be upon Sajah and whoever has made us blame ourselves."

﴿We reveal to them﴾ as We reveal to you, ﴿from among the people of the towns﴾, that is, the cities, not the people of the desert, because of the prevalence of harshness and cruelty among the Bedouins, and because the people of the cities are more complete in intellect, more perfect in forbearance, and more exalted in merit. ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ This refers to the polytheists who denied the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. That is: have these polytheists not traveled and looked upon the places of destruction of the past nations, so that they might take warning from them and cease from the denial they are engaged in? ﴿And the Home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah﴾, that is, the Home of the Last Hour, or the state of the Hereafter, with the qualified noun omitted.

Al-Farra' said: the "Home" is the Hereafter itself, and a thing is attributed to itself because the wording differs, as in "the day of Friday," "the prayer of the first (Dhuhr)," and "the mosque of the congregation." The discussion of this is explained in the books of i'rab (grammatical analysis of the Qur'an).

By "this Home" is meant Paradise, that is: it is better for the God-fearing than the home of this world.

It was read as ﴿wa-la-dar al-Akhirah﴾ (with the lam of emphasis). Nafi', 'Asim and Ya'qub read ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ with the ta' (second person, addressing them directly). The rest read it with the ya' (third person).

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired﴾: this clause of limit (ghayah) refers to an omitted element indicated by the context. Its estimated meaning is: "We did not send before you, O Muhammad, any but men, and We did not hasten punishment upon their nations who did not believe in what they brought, until, when the messengers despaired of victory through the punishment of their people." Or: "until, when the messengers despaired of the faith of their people because of their immersion in disbelief." ﴿And they thought that they had been denied﴾.

The meaning is: the people thought that the messengers had lied to them about what they reported of the punishment, and that they had not been truthful. It was also said the meaning is: the people thought that the messengers had lied about their claim of victory over them. It was also said the meaning is: the messengers thought that their own selves had lied to them when they told them that they would be given victory over them, or that their hope of victory had deceived them.

The rest read ﴿kuddhibū﴾ with the doubled (stressed) form. The meaning in this reading is clear: the messengers thought that their people had denied them regarding what they had promised them of punishment. It is also permissible that the subject of "thought" is the people to whom the messengers were sent, in the sense that they thought the messengers had lied about what they brought of promise and threat.

Mujahid and Humayd read ﴿qad kadhabū﴾ with fatha on the kaf and dhal, lightly (unstressed), in the sense: "the people of the messengers thought that the messengers had lied." It has been said that thinking (zann) in this verse means certainty (yaqin), because the messengers were certain that their people had denied them, and this was not merely a supposition on their part. What should be said about interpreting "thinking" as "certainty" in a case like this is that it is interpreted by its original meaning in situations where there is merely supposition, as in the preceding examples.

﴿Our victory came to them﴾, that is, [p. 718] the victory of Allah, glory be to Him, came to the messengers suddenly, or the victory of Allah for His messengers came to the people of the messengers who denied them, by the sending of punishment upon the deniers.

﴿So whom We willed was saved﴾. 'Asim read ﴿fa-nujjiya﴾ with a single nun.

The rest read ﴿fa-nunjiya﴾ with two nuns. Abu Ubayd preferred the first reading, because it is written so in the Mushaf of 'Uthman.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿fa-naja﴾ in the active form. In the first reading, "man" (whom) is in the nominative position as the deputy subject; in the second reading it is in the accusative position as the object; and in the third reading it is in the nominative position as the subject. Those whom Allah saved are the messengers and those who believed with them, while the deniers were destroyed.

﴿And Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people﴾ when it descends upon them. In this is a statement that the one whom Allah wills to save from punishment is anyone other than these criminals.

﴿Certainly in their stories﴾, that is, the stories of the messengers and of the nations to whom they were sent, or in the story of Yusuf, his brothers and his father, ﴿is a lesson for those of understanding﴾. "Ibrah" (lesson) is reflection and insight that frees one from ignorance and bewilderment.

It has been said: it is a type of consideration (i'tibar), namely crossing from a known side to an unknown side. "Ulu al-albab" (those of understanding) are those of sound intellects who take lessons by their intellects and thus grasp what contains the interests of their religion. This story is a lesson because of what it includes of reports that correspond to reality, despite the long span of time between the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and the messengers whose stories are related, among whom are Yusuf, his brothers and his father, even though he (the Prophet) did not know their news and did not associate with their scholars.

It has also been said: the elaboration of every thing from the story of Yusuf with his brothers and father.

It has been said: the intended meaning is not its general implication, but rather the principles and rules and what they lead to. ﴿And guidance﴾ in this world, by which everyone whom Allah wills to guide is guided, ﴿and mercy﴾ in the Hereafter, by which Allah shows mercy to His servants who act upon what it contains, meeting the condition of true faith. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿We sent not before you any but men﴾: he said, that is, they were not from the people of heaven as you claimed.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾: he said, "How Allah punished the people of Nuh, the people of Lut, the people of Salih and the nations whom Allah punished."

Al-Bukhari and others narrated through the chain of 'Urwah that he asked Aisha about the words of Allah, glory be to Him, ﴿until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied﴾. I said: "Perhaps it is 'and they thought that they had been denied' with the lightened form?" She said: "God forbid! The messengers would never think that about their Lord." I said: "Then what is this verse?" Abu Ubayd, Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he used to read "qad kudhibū" in the lightened form, and he said: "The messengers despaired of their people that they would respond to them, and their people thought that the messengers had lied to them about what they brought." ﴿Our victory came to them﴾: he said, "Our victory came to the messengers."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, who said: ﴿Their victory came to them﴾ is the punishment.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi: ﴿And Our punishment is not averted﴾, he said: "His punishment."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿Certainly in their stories﴾ [p. 719]: he said, "Yusuf and his brothers."
